Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 4, verse 1 (part 1 of 2):

Lesson 03: An Overview

This first passage of the surah, together with its opening verse, begins with a call to people to turn exclusively to the one Lord and the one Creator. It explains that all people were created from one single pair of parents, and that they have spread out from one single family. The human self (nafs) is in reality the essence of humanity, and the human family is in reality the unit of human society. Therefore, within the human soul the feelings of God-fearing awareness are stirred, and the family system is strengthened by the feeling of maintaining kinship ties (silat al-rahm), so that upon this firm foundation the duties of mutual takaful (Social Security) and mutual love may flourish within a family. After that, the principles of mutual love and mutual support may be established throughout all of humanity. In short, all the legislation carried out in this surah and all the consolidation of humanity are based on this principle.

The portion of the verses, alongside the principles and laws mentioned above, also gives guidance regarding the social and collective responsibilities toward orphans found within any society or family. Instructions are given on how to supervise orphans and how to safeguard their property. Likewise, principles have been laid down for the distribution of inheritance among family members, in which the shares of relatives from various lines have also been determined. The differences in shares under different circumstances have also been stated. All of this has been done in the light of the all-encompassing human principle mentioned in the opening verse. This all-encompassing human principle has been repeatedly restated in this lesson: at the beginning of some verses, in the middle of others, and at the conclusion of some verses. It also affirms the truth that all of this guidance and legislation is the exclusive right of divine lordship (rububiyyah). In the Islamic system, every kind of legislation is a manifestation of this attribute of Lordship of Allah, may His majesty be exalted.

Commentary on the Verse Itself

Translation: "O people! Fear your Lord, who created you from a single soul, and from it created its mate, and from the two of them spread forth many men and women. And fear Allah, by whom you ask one another [for your rights], and be mindful of the ties of kinship. Indeed, Allah is ever watchful over you."

This address is directed entirely to humanity. It is addressed to them as human beings, so that they all may return to the one Lord. It is He who created them, and He who created all these human beings from a single soul. Then from that soul He created its mate, and then from the two of them He propagated lineage and spread many men and women throughout the earth.

Apparently these matters seem very simple and elementary, but in reality they are great truths. They are very weighty matters, and they have profound effects on human life, if these "people" pay heed to these matters and endeavor to understand them. Through these matters, a great transformation would take place in human life on this earth, and people would easily move from jahiliyyah, or various forms of jahiliyyah, to a life of faith, a life of guidance, and a civilized life worthy of humanity. This civilized life would suit the human self and would also accord with the pleasure of its Creator and Lord.

This verse sets out the foundational truths which provide the following fields for the heart and vision:

(1): It informs all of humanity of what its origin is, and advises it to return to its Creator who, having created it, settled it upon this earth. These verses show that "humanity," having forgotten this its origin, has forgotten everything, and none of its affairs has remained correct.

The reality is that people came into this earth when previously they were not on it. The question is: who brought them into this world? Their own will had no part in their arrival here, because before coming here they were non-existent, and for the non-existent no concept of will is possible. For the non-existent cannot make any decision about coming into this world or not coming. Therefore, necessarily, some being other than human brought humans here and settled them. That will was separate from the human self. It was a higher will which decided the creation of humanity. And this "creating will" was not a human will. This higher will laid down the courses for humanity to live and to pass its life here. It is this other will that brought the human being into existence, granted the human being human attributes, and gave the human being its qualities and capacities. It gave the human being the laws by which it could act and harmonize with this universe, because it was a newcomer to this universe, and it had no knowledge even of the place from which it had come. Nor did the human being possess any capacities other than those which this higher will bestowed upon it.

This is the truth which, if present-day humanity were to take it to heart, it would be guided onto the right path from the very first day. Although this truth is entirely clear, it is regrettable that humanity is completely heedless of this self-evident supreme truth.

The reality is that the exalted and great divine will which brought humanity here, here gave it courses for living and granted it the power and capacity to live in this universe. This same great will is the owner of the entire universe of humanity. It is this will which exercises every kind of disposition over human affairs. And it is this will which makes every kind of arrangement for humanity here. Therefore, this divine will alone deserves to set out the courses of the system of life for humanity, to lay down codes and laws for it, and to establish values of life and principles of good and evil for it. It is this will to which humanity should turn, and it is the standards of good and evil of this will and its laws to which it is obligatory to turn at the time when disputes arise among them regarding any matter. For that will is the Lord of the worlds, who is One without partner.

(2): The truths stated in this verse demonstrate that this human race has come into existence as the result of one single will. All humans have been born from one single womb. They have one common bond between them. They have spread from one single root, and their lineage is also one.

If people were to firmly grasp this one truth alone, most of the sectarian divisions that have overtaken their thinking, and which have come into being in the practical lives of humans in later periods, would be eliminated. These divisions have created sects among the common people who were born from one single soul, and have torn into pieces those born of one single mother. Yet these conditions came upon humanity later, and it was not appropriate that these conditions should extinguish the true feelings of mercy and love among humans, whereas the observance of that mercy and love was essential. Being the offspring of one soul, mutual human love was necessary, and alongside that, connection with their Lord and Creator, regard for His rights, and fear and God-consciousness (taqwa) in the heart were also necessary.

If this truth alone were firmly established, all sectarian tensions would end. At present, all of humanity has tasted well the ravages of sectarian tension. Sectarian tensions persist on this earth, nations are founded on the basis of race and color, people have completely forgotten their human genealogy, and then they have also cast behind their backs their relationship of lordship with their Lord.

If humans were to accept this truth and firmly establish it in their convictions, then the system of class slavery prevalent in India would immediately vanish from this world. Likewise, the blood that flows like water in the class wars within the socialist countries of the East would come to an end, and the fitnah of nationalism, which is the foundational benefit of the intellectual concepts and philosophies of modern jahiliyyah, would also end. And this would become the starting point for the ending of class conflict in the world, in which there is always an effort for one class to attain leadership and dominion over the other classes, and in which the truth is forgotten that all humans are in reality born from one single soul, and that their Creator, the Lord of majesty, is also one.

(3): The third truth to which this verse points is that humanity was created from a single self (nafs wahidah), and from that self its mate was created. If humanity were to reflect upon this and grasp its reality, it would resolutely make amends for the errors and painful notions into which it has fallen at various times regarding the female sex. Humanity has attached strange and wondrous notions to woman. She has been regarded as the source of filth and sin. She has been considered the cause of every calamity and every evil. Yet by her nature and her temperament she is a part of the first self, that is, Adam. And Allah, the Exalted, created her precisely so that she would be his companion and partner, and through her the human race would be propagated. Therefore, there is no difference in the nature of men and women; rather, there is a difference in their capacities and in their sexual duties.

In this matter, humanity wandered in the wilderness for a long period and went astray. It deprived woman of all human rights and denied her human dignity. For a long time, the woman suffered oppression, and this was solely due to those false ideas and notions which had no reality. But when those false ideas were corrected, the other pan of the scale was made far too heavy. Woman was turned into an unbridled creature. She forgot her status: that, though she is certainly a human being, she was created for other human beings. She is one soul, but she was created for another soul. She is a part of humanity, but she is complementary to the other part. Man and woman are not two separate complete personalities, rather they are a pair and hold a complementary status for one another.

After this great and long-standing error, the Islamic system of life brought humanity back and placed it upon the true path, and gave it correct concepts.

(4): In this verse there is also an indication of the truth that the family is the basic cell of life. It is the divine purpose in the world that this human plant should flourish within a family. Therefore, first a single soul was created, and after that its mate was created from that very soul. Thus this initial family consisted of two individuals. And after that, "from the two of them many men and women were created." Had God so willed, He could have created many men and many women at once from the start, and then given them the form of many pairs. And many families would have come into existence right from the beginning. And from the very beginning there would not have been the bond of the womb among them, and their only connection would have been the shared relationship of being the first batch of creation of one Creator, and nothing more. This alone would have been their first connection and link. But Allah, the All-Knowing, the All-Aware, had a wisdom in view. Allah the Exalted desired to establish firm bonds among people. The first bond was that their Lord is one, and this has been and remains the source of all human bonds. After that comes the bond of mutual kinship (silat al-rahm), by which a family comes into being, beginning with one man and one woman. These two came from one self, their nature is also one, and their innate disposition is also one; the initial family too is one, from which many men and women then spread. The first link among all these individuals is the oneness of Lordship (wahdaniyyat al-rububiyyah), and after that is the link of the unity of the family. And the family is the basic cell upon which the foundation of human society is laid. Yet belief and doctrine come first in order, even before this family bond.

This is the wisdom behind the importance given in the Islamic system of life to the family system, and why all measures are adopted for the consolidation and strengthening of the family. Its foundation is made firm, and it is protected from all factors and influences which could in any way cause its weakness. The first influence in the destruction of the family system is that people adopt a method of conduct contrary to the natural way, and do not properly recognize the capacities of man and the capacities of woman, and do not create a balance between the capacities of both man and woman, nor are these forces employed in the formation and building of a family consisting of a man and a woman.

In this surah and in other surahs as well, countless measures have been adopted in the Islamic system for the formation and strengthening of the family. But the family system could not have been firmly established on sound foundations so long as the cruel treatment of the age of jahiliyyah toward women was maintained, whether that jahiliyyah was ancient or modern, and so long as those demeaning ideas and notions associated with women from the age of jahiliyyah had not been eradicated. This is why Islam first ended the oppression upon women, and afterward the Qur'an, by giving her an honored station in human society, dispelled the outdated notions about her. (5): Finally, it is worth noting that after creating all of mankind from a single soul and a single family, the great variation in forms and capacities among the human race is such that no two individuals, throughout the whole course of human history, have ever been entirely identical. Moreover, the number of people who came and went in past historical periods is not known. This difference of shapes, the diversity of features, the difference of temperament and disposition, the difference of consciousness and morals, the difference of aptitudes and abilities, and the difference of inclinations and interests, in short, this all-encompassing and many-sided variety, shows that Allah is the incomparable Creator and Originator. He is All-Wise and All-Knowing, and in this human garden of His, among its many-colored flowers, there is an inexhaustible provision for the heart and the eye. Every child who is born possesses a new personality, and is unique in its own right. This work belongs to the Absolute Powerful alone, and this craftsmanship lies within no one's power except that of the Divine Being. He is the One whose will is unrestricted, and whatever He wills comes to pass. He is "Kun fa-yakun" (Be, and it is), He is Great, and only He can establish such complete distinction and variation among countless human personalities, since all human beings have spread from one father alone, Adam.

Contemplation on human personalities and individuals in this manner is a guarantor that it will grant the believing heart further provision of intimacy and love upon the foundational provision of taqwa (God-consciousness) and faith. Such contemplation is profit upon profit, and elevation upon the height of thought.

After this multitude of thoughts and ideas, at the conclusion of this opening verse, people are called to fear God. They are summoned to the fear of that God in whose name they ask one another and invoke Him. Attention is also drawn to the need that they maintain the bond of kinship in their mutual relations, because all of you, in the final analysis, have one origin.

"Fear Allah, by whom you demand your rights from one another."

Fear that God in whose name you make covenants with one another, contract marriages with one another, and some of you demand your rights and loyalty from others invoking His name; you swear by His name. In short, in your mutual dealings, relationships, kinship ties, and business affairs, adopt a manner of God-fearing conduct.

In the Qur'an, the meaning of taqwa and fear of God is clear, since it is mentioned again and again in the Qur'an. As for the statement "fear the ties of kinship," this is a peculiar style of speech whose conscious shadow falls upon the self, and the human self, upon this conscious awareness, automatically derives the meaning: fear the ties of kinship, sharpen your sense regarding those relationships, be conscious of their rights, avoid oppression and violation of those rights, avoid touching and scratching them, do not cause pain within the relationship, do not wound the feelings of relatives, and do not usurp their rights. In short, keep your sense sharp in matters of kinship, show respect, give love to the relationship, and live in the shade of love.

The conclusion lies under Allah's watch.

"Know well that Allah is watching over you."

And how terrible is His watch when the Divine Being Himself is the watcher! He is the Lord, the Creator, and is well informed about all His creation. He is such an All-Knowing, All-Aware One that no matter remains hidden from Him. Neither outward actions are concealed from Him, nor hidden thoughts.

After this majestic and impactful opening, and the simple natural truths stated within it, and the great foundational principle for all humanity, there begins a discussion of the fundamental matters upon which the collective system and collective life of a society are established. For example: mutual economic cooperation and mutual support of the family and the community; protection of the rights of the weak in society; protection of the rights of women in society and the determination of their station of dignity; protection of the general wealth of society; and a distribution of inheritance and estate that ensures justice and in which all members benefit the society's welfare.

First, those who have been appointed as guardians over the property of orphans are commanded that when those orphans reach maturity, their full wealth be returned to them; and that these guardians should not marry orphan girls merely so that their wealth comes into their control. However, among orphans, those about whom there is fear that if their wealth is handed over to them they will squander it, it is permissible not to give them their wealth, because the wealth of every person is in reality the collective wealth of society. It contains the collective interest of society. Therefore, this wealth cannot be handed over to a person who would ruin it, even though he is its owner. And that dealings with women should be conducted in kindness, according to the principles of justice.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 4, verse 2:

And if you fear that you will not deal justly with orphans, then marry those women who seem good to you, two, three, or four. But if you fear that you will not be able to act justly, then [marry] only one, or [keep to] those whom your right hands possess. That is nearer to preventing injustice.

And give the women their dowries graciously. But if they give you a portion of it willingly, then you may consume it with enjoyment and satisfaction.

And do not give the foolish your property, which Allah has made a means of support for you, but provide for them from it and clothe them, and speak to them words of good counsel.

And test the orphans until they reach marriageable age. Then if you find in them sound judgment, hand over to them their property. And do not consume it excessively and hastily, fearing that they will grow up and claim it. Whoever among the guardians is wealthy should abstain, and whoever is poor should eat according to what is reasonable. Then when you hand over their property to them, call witnesses against them, and Allah is sufficient as Reckoner.

As we mentioned above, these emphatic instructions show that in the jahili (pre-Islamic) society of the Arabs, women, children and the weak were brutally oppressed. The traces of this Days of Ignorance (jahiliyyah) were still present in the Islamic society of Madinah, because the Islamic society of Madinah had come into being by breaking away from the jahili society of Arabia, and the Qur'an was refining and training it, adorning the Islamic community with new values and new concepts, giving the Muslims a new consciousness, forming new characteristics in them and establishing new customs.

(Verse) "Wa atu al-yatama amwalahum wa la tatabaddalu al-khabitha bil-tayyib, wa la ta'kulu amwalahum ila amwalikum, innahu kana hubban kabira." (2)

Translation: "Give the orphans their property, do not exchange the bad for the good, and do not consume their property along with your own property; this is a great sin."

Give orphans the property that is under your control, and do not do this: when giving property to orphans, give them worthless goods and keep the valuable for yourselves. For example, take their good land for yourselves and give them your inferior land; likewise take the good livestock for yourselves and give them useless livestock; or, when dividing, give them the poorer share; or, in cash, give them counterfeit coins, since cash includes both valuable and counterfeit coins. Also, do not mix their wealth with your wealth and consume it, whether all of it or any part of it. In the sight of Allah this is a major sin, and Allah warns you against this great sin.

All these incidents were commonly occurring in society at the time Islam came and these instructions were addressed to people. This address itself shows that among those being addressed there were people who committed such mistakes, and these matters were among the surviving traces of jahiliyyah. Such matters are generally found in every jahili system. Today we see these very things daily with our own eyes in villages and cities, in the systems of modern jahiliyyah. Even today orphans' wealth is consumed through various methods, and various pretexts and excuses are fabricated for this. Even today, despite elaborate legal measures and the strict supervision of government officials over orphans' property, guardians embezzle the wealth and property of those in their care. The truth is that the difficulties in this matter cannot be resolved through legislation and government supervision alone; these will never succeed in this matter. Therefore, if there is a solution to it, it lies only in taqwa (God-consciousness) and fear of Allah. It is taqwa which places a guard within the heart and conscience. Only after that can legislation and the supervision of government officials become effective. It was precisely this taqwa that brought about astonishing events after the revelation of this verse. The guardians of orphans began such caution that the property of orphans was separated from their own property, and their food and drink were separated, so that the Companions might completely escape falling into this great sin, concerning which Allah warned, saying, "This is a great sin."

On this earth, no reformative scheme can succeed through legislation and collective organization alone. Before legislation and organization, it is necessary to place a guard of fear of Allah and taqwa within hearts, so that the heart is possessed and the conscience is willing to establish order and act upon the law. This taqwa cannot become zealous about any order or law until that law proceeds from a source which is not unaware of all the secret matters of humans, and which does not hold dominion over the conscience. Only in such circumstances does an intense sense arise within an individual's heart that he must respect the law, that he should not betray Allah, Glorified is He, and that he should not adopt an attitude of conflict with His command and His will. This is because Allah, the Exalted, is well aware of both the intention of the individual and his deeds. Under the pressure of this sense, his steps wobble in the matter of committing sin; he begins to tremble from fear, and his zeal of fear of Allah is stirred.

Allah knows His servants well and is thoroughly acquainted with their nature. He Himself is the Creator of the human soul and its nerves, and in accordance with their creation He has made His law a law for them, made His Shari'ah their Shari'ah, made His system of life a system for them, and given His own method and procedure for its implementation, so that the weight of these things may be felt in people's hearts, and they may not dare to violate this law and method, and so that they may fear Allah. Allah, the Exalted, well knew that no legal system in the world can succeed unless it is attributed to the Divine Being, because people's hearts hold fear of the Divine Being and hope for His mercy. Moreover, they have complete certainty that Allah knows the secrets of the heart and is the Knower of the hidden intentions of the heart. Furthermore, a law made by man functions and is implemented only so long as the fear of apprehension remains and the strictest outward supervision is doing its work, which has no entry or effect on people's hearts; but as soon as this outward supervision weakens, people begin to violate the law, or whenever they find an opportunity for a pretext or excuse, even though they may know that if they are caught they will be severely reprimanded and will suffer loss of life and property.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 4, verse 3 (part 1 of 4):

(Verse) "And if you fear that you will not act justly with the orphans, then marry those women that please you, two or three or four. But if you fear that you will not be just, then only one, or those whom your right hands possess. That is more suitable, that you may not incline toward injustice."

Urwah ibn al-Zubayr (raḍiyallāhu ʿanhu) narrated that he asked Ḥaḍrat ʿĀʾishah (raḍiyallāhu ʿanhā) about the meaning of the verse, "If you fear that you will not act justly with the orphans." She said: "Nephew, this refers to the orphan girl who was under the guardianship of her guardian (walī). She shared in his property, and he was interested in her wealth and her beauty. So her guardian wished to marry her without paying her a dower (mahr), and without giving her the rights that other interested suitors were ready to give her. Therefore, in this verse Allah commanded these guardians that they may marry orphans in their care only if they can act justly with them and pay them a dower according to their standard. If they cannot do this, they should marry other women."

Urwah said that ʿĀʾishah (raḍiyallāhu ʿanhā) said: "After the revelation of this verse, people asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) for a ruling, and then this verse was revealed: 'They ask you concerning women. Say: Allah gives you a ruling concerning them, and [He reminds you of] what is recited to you in the Book concerning the orphan women, to whom you do not give what is prescribed for them, and whom you desire to marry.'" (4:127) ʿĀʾishah (raḍiyallāhu ʿanhā) said that Allah's statement, "and whom you desire to marry," refers to the case where the guardian has neither wealth nor beauty in her, so they were forbidden to marry an orphan who has wealth and beauty unless they act justly with her, because when she had neither wealth nor beauty they would not marry such orphans. (Bukhari)

The above ḥadīth of ʿĀʾishah (raḍiyallāhu ʿanhā) depicts some of the customs of the days of ignorance (jāhiliyyah), which had continued in the Islamic society from the pre-Islamic period. Therefore these verses of the Holy Qur'an were revealed, and by prohibiting them their root was cut off. In short, after giving these lofty guidelines, the matter is again left to the conscience of the human being and his inner God-consciousness (taqwā). It is said: "And if you fear that you will not act justly with the orphans."

This matter is connected solely with the human heart and conscience and with the awareness of fear of God. If a guardian fears that he will not be able to act justly, then he should abstain from this kind of marriage. But the wording of the verse is general; the command and guidance is that justice be practised in every situation of justice, whether it relates to the dower or to other ups and downs of life. For example, he may contract this marriage only for wealth, with no interest in the woman herself; or he may have no inclination toward good companionship with her; or there may be a great difference in the ages of the man and the woman, making harmony impossible; or the man may not be serious about the marriage. Sometimes the situation is such that the girl, out of shame and modesty, cannot say anything, or she fears that if she marries outside, her wealth will be lost, and so on. In circumstances where justice is not possible, this is the method of the Holy Qur'an: it places a watchman within the conscience and establishes the supervision of taqwā. The first verse concluded with these words: "Indeed Allah is ever a Watcher over you." (4:1) (Allah is watching over you.)

If guardians do not find within themselves the ability to act justly with these orphan women, there are many other women besides them, so in order to protect oneself from suspicion and doubts, the most appropriate course is that they marry other women.

(Verse) "And if you fear that you will not act justly with the orphans, then marry those women that please you, two or three or four. But if you fear that you will not be just, then only one, or those whom your right hands possess. That is more suitable, that you may not incline toward injustice."

Translation: "If you fear that you will not act justly with the orphans, then marry from among the women who please you, two, three, or four. But if you fear that you will not be able to act justly with them, then have only one wife, or take those women who have come into your possession. This is closer to avoiding injustice."

The permission of plurality of wives is conditional. If you fear injustice, then confine yourselves to one, or take a woman from among those whom your right hands possess.

It is appropriate here, given these safeguards, to say something about the wisdom and benefit of the permission of plural marriage, especially in our present age, in which people consider themselves more knowledgeable than their Lord, the Lord who created them, and they think that they have greater insight than the Creator, exalted is He, into human life, human nature and human interests. They speak on these matters merely on the basis of their personal opinions and carnal desires, and they grope in ignorance and darkness. It is as though they themselves have created the modern circumstances and needs, they understand them well, and they can deal with these circumstances by themselves; and as though these circumstances were not before Allah, nor did Allah make any decision about them at the time when He was legislating for humankind.

The claims of such people and their decisions in this matter are based on ignorance and blindness of vision, while in one respect this is an extreme of arrogance and a clear insolence before the Divine Court. In its inner meaning, this is misguidance and straying, and a kind of disbelief (kufr). Yet despite this, people go on saying such things, and there is no one who challenges these ignorant, blind-sighted, arrogant, astray and disbelieving people, although they are making such an audacious move against Allah and His Shariah that it is intolerable. They are laying hands upon Allah and upon His majesty, and they are committing this abominable act against the Divine Being and the system of life He has prescribed. And they are carrying on their work with great ease, success and security, and they are receiving open support from those quarters that are interested in this work continuing against Muslims and their religion.

This issue, namely the question of plural marriage, which Islam has permitted with these safeguards and conditions, should be addressed with great simplicity, clarity and a decisive approach, keeping in view the circumstances and realities that actually exist in any society and existed at that time as well.

Imam al-Bukhari (raḥmatullāhi ʿalayh) narrated with his chain in his Musnad that Ghaylan ibn Salamah al-Thaqafi embraced Islam, and at that time he had ten wives. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) instructed him: "Choose four of them."

Imam Abu Dawud narrated that ʿUmayr al-Asadi said: "When I accepted Islam I had eight wives. I mentioned this to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and he said: 'Choose four of them.'"

Imam al-Shafiʿi (raḥmatullāhi ʿalayh) said in his Musnad: A man informed me, who had heard this from Abu al-Zinad, who was told by ʿAbd al-Majid, who was told by Suhayl ibn ʿAbd al-Rahman, who narrated from ʿAwf ibn al-Harith, who narrated from Nawfal ibn Muʿawiyah al-Dayli, who said: "When I embraced Islam I had five wives. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) instructed me: 'Choose four of them, whichever you wish, and separate from the one you want.'"

When Islam came, people had ten or even more than ten wives, and there was no restriction on the number of wives. In these circumstances Islam imposed a restriction on the number and commanded that no Muslim may exceed this limit; that is, he may go only up to four. Along with this, Islam imposed one more condition: if the number is more than one, then establishing complete justice and equity among them is also obligatory. If someone thinks that he will not be able to act justly, then it is incumbent upon him to be content with one wife, or with those women who are owned by someone.

From this background it becomes clear that Islam did not permit plural marriage absolutely. Islam set a limit on the number of wives: if the number is more than one, then establishing complete justice and equity among them is obligatory. If someone thinks he will not be able to act justly, then it is incumbent upon him to be content with one wife, or with those women who are owned by someone.

From this background it becomes clear that Islam did not permit plural marriage absolutely. Islam set a limit on the number of wives, and Islam did not leave this matter merely to the desire of man, but made it conditional upon the requirement of justice and equity. If there is no justice, then plural marriage is not permitted.

Now the question is: why did Islam permit plural marriage at all? The Islamic system of life has been designed for human beings. It is a positive and practical system. It is in harmony with human nature and human existence. It has been devised according to human circumstances and human needs. It has been designed keeping in view the changing days and nights of humanity in different circumstances, different regions and different times. It is in fact a positive and realistic system. It takes human beings as they actually are in any age. It begins its journey from the very point where a person stands, and from there it raises him to the lofty stages of progress, until it brings him to the zenith. It neither denies nor looks upon the true nature of humanity with aversion. It does not ignore or act carelessly toward the real facts of human life. In its process of human reform and progress, it neither applies violence nor acts with imbalance.

The Islamic system of life is not empty boasting, nor is it idle chatter, nor an empty and unreal ideal. It is not based merely on imagination and hopes, such that it conflicts with human nature, has no connection with human realities and circumstances, and vanishes like vapour in the air. Rather, it is a system that takes into account the creation of human beings. It calls for purity in human society, and therefore it does not merely promote materialism in human society, that kind of materialism which corrupts the face and features of a person and pollutes human society, and all of this in the form of the so-called necessity-snares which contradict realities. Rather, Islam guides that a situation be created in which the creation of humanity is protected, in which society is pure, and all this is attained with ease and with very little struggle, such that individuals and society are required to exert the least effort.

When we keep these fundamental concepts of the Islamic system of life in view and then reflect on the question of plural marriage, the conclusions that come before us are these:

(1) First, the reality clearly emerges that in most societies there are circumstances in which the number of women of marriageable age exceeds the number of men of marriageable age. These situations have occurred in past societies as well as exist in present-day societies. Moreover, the excess of women has never exceeded a ratio of 1:4. This variation has always remained between one and four.

Now the question is: what solution shall we adopt for such a situation, since such circumstances keep arising repeatedly, although the ratio between men and women fluctuates? Is there a remedy for such a situation?

Can this situation be remedied merely by shrugging the shoulders? Is it possible for us to remain indifferent to such a situation and leave it as it is, letting circumstances determine their own course and accepting whatever situation arises?

Problems are not solved merely by shrugging the shoulders, and for any reasonable person, the solution of letting things take whatever course they choose and accepting it is not acceptable. For any self-respecting person and any serious individual, this position will not be acceptable, if he regards the human race with respect.

Therefore there is a need for some order and system to exist, and for a practical step to be taken to resolve this problem. After deliberation we have reached the conclusion that there are only three possible solutions to this problem:

(1) That every person who is of marriageable age marries one woman of marriageable age. And as for the others, one or two women remain (without husbands), and they are left thus without a husband and never find a husband for the rest of their lives.

(2) That every person who is of marriageable age performs a legal marriage with one woman of marriageable age, and with her he maintains lawful relations, but with other women he forms friendships and forbidden, unlawful relations, that is, with women who have no husbands. Thus their relations are unlawful, and they live their lives in darkness.

(3) The third option is that those of marriageable age marry more than one woman of marriageable age, and likewise a man maintains lawful relations with more than one woman; he has a wife, and he lives openly with her within the light and the framework of the law, and no theft or illicit immorality is committed.

Consider carefully: the first option is contrary to human nature, and it is not possible for a woman to spend her entire life in solitude and not form a bond with any man. This reality cannot be refuted by the claims of those loose-tongued people who assert that a woman can become independent of men through labour and employment. For this issue is far too lofty for the understanding of such superficial, unserious and ignorant chatterers, because they are unaware of human nature. A woman's thousand labours and her thousand jobs cannot make her independent of her natural need and natural demands, whether these demands are physical or demands of her intellect and soul. They are that a woman should remain within her family in peace and tranquillity while the man struggles to earn a livelihood; likewise, after his economic struggle and economic activities, a man too feels the need to return to a family. In this matter, man and woman are equal, for they were created from one soul and have one nature.

The second option is entirely contrary to the pure inclinations of Islam, and it also does not sit well with the pure social system of Islam. Moreover, this situation is against the Islamic nobility of woman. Those who are not opposed to the spread of nudity and immorality in society are the very people who consider themselves more knowledgeable than Allah, and these people lay hands on the Shari'ah of Allah. They commit this act merely because there is no one to stop their hand from this vile deed. Rather, people of this kind receive every kind of encouragement from the enemies of the Islamic Shari'ah.

Now only the third situation remains, and Islam has adopted it. Islam has permitted only polygyny (ta'addud al-zawjat), and has imposed many limits and conditions upon it. This permission has been given by Islam to resolve a real situation in which merely shrugging the shoulders yields no benefit, nor can such real circumstances and difficulties be solved by mere philosophical claims. Islam has adopted this third situation because it is the constructive solution to this actual situation, and a positive course of action: namely, dealing with the human being as he is, with his present nature and his present circumstances, while keeping in view the aims of pure morality and a clean and wholesome society, and in accordance with the method Islam has prescribed for lifting human beings out of the quagmire of immorality and filth, that is, taking a person by the hand with great gentleness and affection and bringing him to the zenith.

That was one aspect. Next, we see that in human societies, whether ancient or modern, of today or of yesterday, there is another reality which can be neither denied nor ignored: that a man's capacity and ability to father children extends to the age of seventy or even beyond, whereas in a woman this ability ends at around the age of fifty. Thus there come about twenty years in which a man still has the capacity to father children while a woman does not have that capacity. It is also clear that Allah created man and woman separately and made their union the means of continuing the life of the species and of the human race. The population of this earth is organised through the multiplication and spread of the human population. Therefore it would be contrary to human nature for us to introduce a custom by which a man would be unable to perform his natural functions for twenty years, whereas the law Islam has enacted is suitable for the circumstances of every age and every kind of society, and is also in harmony with natural demands. Moreover, this law is only in the form of permission: it has not been made obligatory that every person must necessarily marry four times. Rather, a general permission has been granted and a kind of latitude has been created for people, so that if they are in need they may benefit from it in a state of necessity. This is the harmony that is always found between divine law and human nature. The consideration of this balance and harmony is generally not observed in laws made by humans, because human affairs are always limited, and a person is often unable to study far-reaching individual circumstances and details. Many aspects remain hidden from him, and many conditions and contingencies of life lie outside his scope.

In relation to the above-mentioned reality, it sometimes happens that a man desires to have more children while the woman has no interest in bearing further children. This lack of interest is sometimes due to advanced age and sometimes due to illness, and in such circumstances both parties also sincerely wish to remain bound in the marital relationship and not to separate from one another. Now, in such circumstances, what solution will we propose?

Will these problems be solved by merely shrugging the shoulders? Or will the matter be resolved by one of the spouses dashing their head against the wall, or shall we dismiss these resources and genuine questions with idle talk and, with witty banter, move on?

The truth is that real problems have never been solved by witticisms and by mere shrugging of the shoulders. Life and its natural realities are serious matters. The difficulties of life are real, and their solution is possible only through realism.

The solution to this question is also possible only through three ways:

(1) That we impose a restriction upon the man that he must cease the performance of his natural functions after the age of fifty, and we tell him: "O man, this matter no longer concerns you; moreover, it is contrary to the dignity, nobility, honour and rights of the woman who is in your nikah."

(2) The second option is that we leave such a person free, and he may go about forming relationships with whatever woman he wishes.

(3) The third option is that we permit him to keep more than one wife, in accordance with his circumstances and his needs, and thereby we also avoid compelling the first wife to be divorced.

As for the first option, it is contrary to human nature. The human soul cannot bear such celibacy; human nerves and the human self cannot tolerate such a restriction. And if we impose this restriction by law and force, then in that case family life would become a torment of hell for society, and every person would dislike family life because of these difficulties and afflictions, and dreadful consequences would follow; and all these matters are those which Islam does not wish for any society, because Islam's policy is that it makes a home peaceful, and makes a man's wife for him a beloved and a garment.

The second option is contrary to the moral inclinations of Islam, and it is also contrary to the course on which Islam wishes the development of human life to proceed. Moreover, it is contrary to the method Islam has adopted for the purification and cleansing of human society. For Islam makes human society fit to raise it from the level of an animal to the most noble station of the human being.

Now only the third option remains, which also fulfils the genuine natural needs of a human being. It is in harmony with Islam's moral outlook, and it also keeps in view the marital rights of the first wife; in this form too it is possible for the spouses to continue their married life according to their wishes, and the memories they share with one another remain intact in their place; and it becomes possible and easy for a person to keep his life advancing towards progress with gentleness, ease and realism.

And this same situation confronts a person when his wife is barren, and the man has the natural desire to have children. Even in such circumstances there are only two options, and there is no third:

(1) That the husband divorces her and, by bringing another wife, fulfils through her his natural desire to have offspring.

(2) That he takes a second wife but keeps the first in his marital bond as well, and fulfils her rights.

In our age, some men and women, presenting themselves as intellectuals, talk such nonsense that the first option is better than polygyny. But at least ninety-nine out of a hundred women will prefer polygyny to divorce in such circumstances. And if anyone were to advise them to take a divorce, they would spit in his face and curse those counsellors who advise them that homes should be ruined, and that nothing at all should be gained in exchange for that ruin. For if a woman's barrenness has become evident and she takes a divorce, who is there who would be ready to take her into marriage? By contrast, it often happens that when a husband takes a second wife upon a barren woman, the former wife feels great affection and love for the children born to the second wife. For children in a home are like flowers, and when they come into a house after such long waiting, the feeling of deprivation is removed and liveliness and cheer enter the home.

In short, wherever we go and carry out a realistic, practical study of human life, these circumstances do not support any nonsense opposed to plurality of wives, nor is the opinion of these so-called intellectuals supported from anywhere. The facts and realities of life do not support the superficial chatter, the waywardness, and the freedom of thought and action of these intellectuals, because this subject is extremely serious, and in it a definite and decisive stance is needed rather than chatter. In short, it is only through deep reflection on the realities of life that the profound wisdom of the Creator becomes clear, by which He has made plurality of wives lawful subject to the conditions and limits laid down in the Qur'an. He says:

(Verse) "Marry such women as seem good to you, two, three or four; but if you fear that you will not be able to act justly, then [marry] only one."

The permission and concession of plurality of wives has been granted in view of the practical realities of life and the demands of human nature. By this means the Shari'ah has saved human society, under the pressure of natural demands and the realities of life, from falling into waywardness and psychological conflict; and by the condition to which this permission has been tied, it has saved married life from anarchy and disorder. It has also protected the wife from domestic oppression and tyranny, and protected her honour as well, and safeguarded her from unnecessarily humiliating treatment. With complete caution, the woman has been shielded from circumstances in which she might be subjected to humiliating treatment. And, in view of necessary conditions and the bitter realities of life, along with the permission for plurality of wives, complete justice and fairness towards the woman has been guaranteed.

Whoever understands the spirit of Islam and its policy could never say that plurality of wives is in Islam desirable in itself, and permissible without natural and collective social necessities, and that mere sensual pleasure and abandoning one wife in favour of another is a ground for its legitimacy, just as a person abandons one friend for another. Rather, it has been permitted in a real situation: it has been permitted to overcome certain social difficulties, and such difficulties are an inevitable part of life in every society.

Now, if at some point in human history some people took improper advantage of this Islamic permission and concession, and by using it turned married life into a stage for animal pleasure, changing their wives the way friendships change, then Islam is not responsible for that situation. Nor can such debauched people be representatives of Islam. Such people have fallen into so deep a pit of degradation merely because they had drifted away from Islam and were unable to grasp the pure, clean and noble spirit of Islam. Moreover, they were living in societies over which Islam did not rule, in which the Islamic system of law and the Shari'ah were not enforced, and over which Islamic laws did not prevail, so that they might have been obedient to the Islamic policy and the Islamic Shari'ah, that people might have acted upon the teachings of Islam and the Shari'ah of Islam, and that Islam's etiquette and Islamic traditions might have been observed.

The Islamic family life of past centuries developed certain defects, and the responsibility for them lies with the societies that were hostile to Islam and had freed themselves from the Islamic Shari'ah and Islamic law. It was these societies that were responsible for those "palaces" and those "harems," which came into being in the most base manner, and it was these same societies that turned family life into a stage drama of animal pleasure-seeking. Therefore, those who wish to remove these faults from family life and to establish it on sound principles should call people back to the Islamic system of life and the rule of the Islamic Shari'ah. They should strive to rebuild society on the foundations of purity, chastity, steadfastness and moderation. Whoever is a reformer and desires reform should call people back only to the Islamic system of life. If someone seeks reform in this single family aspect alone, it is not possible. A revolution in the entire system of life is necessary, because Islam is a complete system of life and it can be established only when it is established fully and in every respect.

The justice mentioned here, and that which is required, is all-encompassing justice: justice in dealings, justice in expenditure, justice in good conduct between the wives, justice among all of them in intimacy. As for justice in inward feelings and in the deep inclinations of the human soul, Islam does not demand it from any person, because deep psychological inclinations lie outside the sphere of a person's control and will. The justice meant here is the justice that Allah Himself has explained elsewhere in this same surah: ﴿And you will never be able to be equitable between wives, even if you strive to do so; so do not incline entirely to one and leave the other as if suspended﴾ [4:129]. Some modernists have drawn from this verse the meaning that since complete justice is impossible, polygamy has consequently become forbidden. But this is not the meaning. Islamic Shari'ah is a most serious law, and it does not indulge in such levity that in one verse it permits a matter and in another verse indirectly withdraws that permission, like someone who gives with the right hand and snatches back with the left. Therefore, the justice mentioned in the first verse, and the instruction that if you cannot maintain such justice then be content with one wife only, refers to justice in the affairs of life, in the maintenance of wives, in social treatment, and in intimacy. Beyond these matters, there is also justice and equality in all other manifestations of life, so that apparently no wife should seem to be of lesser status than another, and no one should be given preference over the other wives. This is as the Seerah of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) shows: although he was the best of mankind, and although all his companions and neighbours knew that he had greater love for ʿĀ'ishah (may Allah be pleased with her) and that her place in his heart was greater, and in this regard none of his other noble wives shared with her. This is because no person has control over his heart. The hearts are between two of the fingers of the All-Merciful, and it is Allah's will to turn hearts as He wishes. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was well aware of his religion and well acquainted with his own inward feelings. He used to say: "O Allah, this is the division that is within my control, and I have made it; so do not blame me for that over which I have no control, but which is in Your hand." (1) (Abu Dawud, Tirmidhi and Nasa'i)

Before concluding this topic, it is necessary to clarify once more this point. The Islamic system of life did not introduce the principle of plural marriage in this world. Rather, the existing system had unlimited plural marriages, and Islam fixed the limit at four. Moreover, Islam did not command that you must have more than one wife for no reason; rather, Islam permitted it and restricted this permission with conditions and limits. And it permitted it so that the real problems and difficulties of human life might be resolved, and in some circumstances the needs of human nature might be fulfilled. These natural demands and real necessities of life, of which we have spoken above, some of which have not yet been even slightly perceived, will also include circumstances that will arise in the future, in which this concession will prove useful, just as the guidance of the Islamic system of life and the wisdoms of the Islamic Shari'ah continually become manifest day after day. This is because it is a divine system of life, and human understanding in its past history has been unable to encompass all its wisdoms and benefits. Every Islamic legislation contains within it benefit and wisdom, whether human understanding can perceive it or not, and whether human history attains this understanding earlier or later, because this understanding is extremely limited.

Now we discuss the arrangement that Islam made for the need arising from the inability to maintain complete justice and equity.

﴿But if you fear that you will not be able to be just, then [marry] one, or those your right hands possess﴾ [4:3].

Meaning: if there is a fear of not being able to maintain justice, then the only course determined is to be content with one wife. In that case, the permission for more than one is cancelled, or [you may take] those women who are in your possession, using them as slave-girls or taking them as wives, since the words of the verse have not restricted any particular form.

In the commentary of the second part of Fi Zilal al-Quran, we presented a brief discussion on the issue of slavery. It is appropriate here to discuss somewhat the matter of having intimacy with female slaves.

By marrying female slaves, their trust, their nobility and their human dignity are restored. Through this marriage they gain freedom, and along with this the child of such a woman also becomes free. Even if the husband does not grant her freedom at the time of marriage, once she bears a child she is called umm walad (a slave woman who has borne her master's child). Her owner can no longer sell her, and upon the owner's death she becomes free. Before that, the children born to her are free. And if an owner has intimacy with his female slave without marriage, once she bears a child she becomes an umm walad. Her sale becomes prohibited, and upon the death of the owner she becomes free. Furthermore, if an owner acknowledges the paternity of his slave-girl's child, that child too is considered free, and generally people do make such an acknowledgment.

Therefore, among the various measures (devices) that Islam established for the freedom of enslaved women, marriage to one's own slave-girl and intimacy with her is also a means of their freedom. Nevertheless, at times intimacy with a female slave without marriage may seem distasteful to the heart. But we must keep in mind that the issue of slavery was, and still is, a collective necessity. As we stated earlier, when the head of an Islamic state, who implements the Shari'ah, declares war, the enslavement of women taken as captives is a collective and international necessity, and likewise having intimacy with those women is also a collective necessity. This is because free women from the Islamic camp who fell into the enemy's captivity met a fate worse than that of the women captured from the camp of the unbelievers and brought into the Islamic camp.

Furthermore, it should also remain in our view that these captured women too have natural demands and desires, and these desires and inclinations must also be taken into account. Islam, being a system of life that is so natural, can by no means ignore these true natural emotions, since this system itself is founded upon natural principles. Now, the ways to fulfil the natural desires of enslaved women are either that they be given in marriage to a master or to a non-master, or that the owner, if he has need, have intimacy with his slave-girl; for as long as the institution of slavery exists, or else they are given complete permission to satisfy their sexual desire wherever they wish. In this last case, there would certainly be a danger of sexual anarchy and sexual licentiousness spreading and becoming general throughout the entire Islamic society, and in that case no regulation could be enforced upon sexual relations, because in this way they would enjoy complete freedom for prostitution and sexual friendship.

And this situation actually existed in the age of ignorance (jahiliyyah) before Islam.

After the first century, in some periods of Islamic history there was a great abundance of slave-girls. This army of slave-girls was produced through purchase, slave-trading and kidnapping; they were gathered into great palaces and made a means of animal sexual gratification. And in the herds of these slave-girls, nights of revelry were spent, dance, music, eating and drinking bazaars remained hot. Some people in Islamic history portrayed this realistically, and some exaggerated in this field. All of this was not Islam, nor was it any achievement of Islam, nor did Islam give anyone any such instructions. It would not be right to attribute such events to Islam, nor can it be permitted to regard these events as part of the true history of Islam.

The part of Islamic history will consist of those events that were brought about in accordance with the Islamic ideology, the Islamic conception of life, and the Islamic values and standards. As for those events that took place in those societies which ascribed themselves to Islam but were not in accordance with Islamic principles and foundations, it would be wholly unjust to attribute those events to Islam, because those events occurred only because people deviated from the Islamic system of life.

The truth is that Islam has its own framework apart from the lives of Muslims, and in every age Islam has had its own framework. This is because Muslims did not devise the Islamic blueprint or framework; rather, it is the blueprint of the Islamic system of life that produced Muslims in the world, and a society of Muslims came into existence. Islam is the origin, and Muslims hold the position of a branch in relation to it. Muslims came into being through the creation of Islam. Therefore, Islam is not what people suppose Islam to be, nor are Islam those deeds and actions that the people of Islam commit; rather, the actions and conduct of people will be Islam only if they are in accordance with the Islamic principles of life and the Islamic conception of life. The fundamental framework is the principled Islam, by which we shall weigh the lives of people, to see how far they are in accordance with Islam and how far they are against Islam.

But the two systems of life operating in the world, which are built upon the theories of human beings, or whose foundation is religions made by human beings, are different in this respect. This is because when such people abandon Islam and once again enter into jahiliyyah, they are in effect denying Allah, even though they claim to believe in Allah. This is because the first manifestation of faith in Allah is that a believer derives his system from the Islamic methodology and establishes it upon the Islamic Shari'ah. Without this great fundamental principle, faith has no value. This is because in such a case, for people, concepts subject to change and lives that change are implemented.

As for the situation of the Islamic system of life, the Islamic system has not been devised by people for themselves; its formulation and explanation have been made by the Lord of mankind, who is also their Creator, their Owner and their Provider. Within this system, people will either obey it and align their conduct and customs with it, and then the days and nights of such people will be the days and nights of Islamic history; or else the situation will be that they deviate from it, or abandon it entirely, and in that case their days and nights will not be considered part of Islamic history. That will be regarded as a deviation from Islamic history.

While studying Islamic history, it is absolutely necessary to keep this perspective in view. Only from this standpoint can the Islamic concept of history be understood. The Islamic concept of history is different from all other concepts of history, because in the ideas of other societies, the practical condition of those societies is also kept in view, and it is regarded as a practical expression of some ideology or religion. In accordance with this practical manifestation, discussion then takes place regarding softness and change within that religion or ideology. That is, the discussion of the ideology is conducted with the society in view which claims to hold that ideology. And then the intellectual changes that occur within that society regarding that ideology are discussed. After this, these people apply the same methodology of discussion to the study of the Islamic system as well, although because of the unique nature of Islam, this methodology does not fit it. Therefore, those who study Islam by this methodology make dangerous errors in determining the true meaning of Islam.

At the end of this verse, the wisdom behind all these arrangements is made clear: all of them are being put in place so that you may be protected from committing injustice and oppression. (Ayah) "Dhalika adna alla ta'ulu" – "This is closer to avoiding injustice." That is, if you cannot act justly, then refrain from taking these orphan girls into your marriage, and instead marry other women: two, three, or four each. And if justice is not possible, then be content with only one, or with those women whom you own (your female slaves). This is the course nearest to ensuring that you avoid injustice and do not commit oppression.

From this it is known that the pursuit of justice and fairness in every matter is the goal of the Islamic system of life, and that justice is required in every part of Islam's particulars. A family, in which all its members reside, has a greater need for the establishment of justice and fairness than other places, because in the building of a society and the formation of any collective system, the family holds the status of the first foundation. The family is the starting point of collective life. Nations are trained within the mould of the family. Here the personalities of human beings are formed, and colour is given to them. If the foundation of the family system is not based on justice, fairness, brotherhood and love, then justice will not be established in the whole of society. (1) (See my book "As-Salam al-Alami wal-Islam", the chapter "Salam al-Bayt" [Peace of the Home].)

In this same connection, some other rights of women are explained here, because at the beginning of this surah their mention was made with particular emphasis, and the surah was also named "An-Nisa'" (The Women). Therefore, before concluding the discussion about orphan women, it was appropriate to explain some of their rights.

(Ayah 4) "And give the women their bridal gifts (mahr) graciously. But if they, of their own accord, give you a part of it, then consume it with pleasure and without harm."

This verse lays down a clear right for the woman, which is her personal right: her mahr. It also hints that in the Age of Ignorance (Jahiliyyah) this right of women was usurped through various pretexts. One form was that the woman's guardian (wali) would take this mahr and then use it himself, just as a person takes the price of something he has sold. Another form of usurping this right was through the practice of shighar (nikah shighar), in which one guardian would give the girl in his guardianship in marriage to another man on the condition that the second guardian would give a girl under his own guardianship in marriage to the first guardian or one of his relatives. Thus one girl would be exchanged for another girl. This bargain took place between two guardians, and the two girls received nothing from it, just as two animals are exchanged with each other. Islam completely forbade nikah shighar and ordered that marriage should take place only in the manner in which both parties are directly agreed and act by their own choice. It also established that mahr is the right of the woman alone: she herself shall receive it, and her guardian has no right to take it. Islam made the fixing of mahr obligatory so that the woman may take it into her possession, because it is a duty for her. It is an obligatory and due right which can in no way be abrogated or suspended. It was made obligatory that the man pay this right willingly, and pay it with a contented heart, in the way a person gives a gift only out of his own willing pleasure. Although it is an obligation, it should be paid with such good will and happiness as though it were not an obligation at all. Yes, after payment, if the woman, with her full consent and goodwill, returns this entire mahr or some part of it to her husband, then she is fully free in this matter. What she returns must also be given with complete freedom and good will, without any compulsion. In that case, it is lawful for the man to consume this mahr; indeed, he may enjoy it without any inner unease. In short, relations between spouses must be based on full consent. Both parties should be entirely free, and whatever dealings they have with one another should be carried out with joy and freedom, and love is such a thing that there should be no bitterness in it from any direction.

In this way the Islamic system of life eliminated yet another remnant of the Age of Ignorance, which was prevalent in Arab society regarding women's mahr. The complete rights of women over their persons and their mahr and property were restored. Thus her honour and dignity were restored. However, along with the restoration of these legal rights, the mutual relations between husband and wife were not handed over to dry legal standards; rather, the avenues of consent, love and mutual generosity were kept open in this regard, because husband and wife have to live together jointly, and it is necessary to remove these relations from a dry legal atmosphere and keep them fresh with the dew of mutual love and kindness.

When this subject concludes here, one matter leads to another. Since it was felt necessary that the discussion of orphan women be joined with a discussion of ordinary women, it was also appropriate here to mention the financial rights of orphans. It is explicitly commanded that their wealth be returned to them in full, whereas earlier, in verse 2, it was stated that their wealth be handed over to them.

Whether wealth belongs to orphans or to adult men and women, before it is the individual ownership of those people, it is the wealth of the entire society. The wealth given to a society is that on which the whole society is established, and from the wealth circulating in that society the whole society benefits, and this benefit comes through its good management. Thus the original owner of all wealth is the general society, and orphans and other heirs are made its owners only so that they may further develop this wealth, and this development should be with the permission of the collective system; they themselves should benefit from it and society too should benefit. It will remain in these private hands only as long as they have the capacity to grow it and increase it, and they adopt correct conduct in disposing of and managing this same wealth. Within this collective sphere, individual property rights remain (1) (for details see my book Al-Adala al-Ijtima'iyyah, the chapter "Financial Policy"). As for those immature orphans who are wealthy but are incapable of managing their financial affairs and cannot develop it, their wealth will not be placed under their control; they will be deprived of the right to dispose of their property and to run it by their own hands and under their own supervision. Although the right of their individual ownership over these properties remains with them, it is not permissible to snatch this wealth from them. Only that wealth shall be placed in the custody of those individuals of society who are able to manage it well. Yes, in this matter, preference will be given to those who have kinship and blood relation with the orphan, so that the system of family support also continues alongside. This is because the collective support system of the great society is established through the support system of the family. Yes, for the foolish people, provision will be made for their expenses and for their proper maintenance.

(Verse 5) "And do not give the foolish your wealth, which Allah has made a means of support for you, but provide for them from it and clothe them, and speak to them with kindly words."

Discernment between folly and wisdom becomes evident after maturity. Generally, the difference between the foolish and the wise becomes clear. Therefore there is no need for the law to set down a formula for this; every family distinguishes well who among them is foolish and who is wise. They experience clearly that this one is mature (rashid) and that one is foolish (safih), and moreover, a person's dealings and transactions are not hidden from society either. Accordingly, the examination will be whether the orphan has reached maturity or not. Here the verse expresses this maturity by the word nikah (marriage), because among the important effects of maturity is marriage.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 4, verse 6:

(Verse) "And test the orphans until they reach the age of marriage; then if you find in them sound judgment, hand over to them their property, and do not consume it extravagantly and hastily, fearing that they will grow up. Whoever is wealthy should abstain (from taking anything), and whoever is poor may eat according to what is reasonable. Then when you hand over their property to them, have witnesses over them; and Allah suffices as Reckoner."(6)

On reflecting on this verse, it becomes clear how strictly the Shariah has acted regarding the handing over of orphans' wealth to them when they reach maturity. It becomes evident that the Shariah emphasizes taking action to return their wealth to them as quickly as possible after they reach puberty and come of age. That is, as soon as they mature, their wealth should be handed over to them. And this wealth should be handed over completely and intact. Moreover, as long as it is in the custody of the guardian, it should be protected with honesty, and it should not be spent recklessly, under the fear that the orphans are about to reach maturity and the wealth will have to be returned to them. Furthermore, it is the policy of the Shariah that if the guardian is wealthy, he should take no compensation for this supervision and protection; and if he is needy, he should eat according to what is reasonable, to the minimum extent necessary. The Shariah also makes it obligatory that when an orphan's property is being handed over to him, witnesses must definitely be established over it. And, above all, Allah's witnessing is established over every event, and the reckoning before Allah will be the final reckoning.

(Verse) "And Allah suffices as Reckoner." (6)

All this emphasis and stress, all these details and explanations, and all these admonitions and reminders, are evidence of the fact that in the society where the Islamic system was enforced, the rights of orphans were being violated everywhere. Besides orphans, the wealth of other weak people was also being consumed. It was because of the need to abolish this custom that such strong emphasis and insistence became necessary, and the need arose to record the detailed particulars within the Holy Quran, so that in future people could not evade the law through legal tricks and pretexts, and no path of escape from the law would remain open.

In this way, the system of life kept erasing every trace of jahiliyyah (ignorance) from the intellectual and practical world of Muslims, and kept planting the banners of Islam in its place. The remnants of jahiliyyah were being effaced, and the face of society was being cleansed of those ugly stains. In their place, the beautiful features of Islam kept appearing. Thus a modern society kept taking shape. The customs and traditions of the modern society kept being established. Its principles, regulations, laws and orders kept being revealed. And all of this took place in an atmosphere of fear of God and under Allah's supervision. The final guarantee of Islamic law and Islamic commands was regarded as the fear of and the pleasure of the Divine Being. The truth is that, apart from the fear of God, the pleasure of God and the concept of Allah's supervision, there is no guarantee for the establishment and functioning of any legal system in this world. The real basis lies in this: "And Allah suffices as Reckoner."

The custom of the jahiliyyah was that they did not give inheritance to girls and children. This was the general practice. However, in some places the opposite was also the case, but rarely. Their reason for this was that these people did not ride horses and did not take part in fighting against the enemy. As it were, the real basis was war. The Islamic legal system founded inheritance on the principle of kinship, which was the true cause of the distribution of inheritance. Yes, just as degrees of kinship differ, so too the shares and obligations of relatives differ, as the details that follow later will show. The Islamic system founded the inheritance system on the system of kinship because Islam regards the family as the unit of the system of collective mutual support. It first establishes a system of mutual maintenance among the members of one family. And this family system too exists within the framework of the collective system of support. Moreover, under the principle that rights are determined in proportion to responsibilities, responsibilities are imposed on close relatives regarding any poor member of the family according to their kinship. For example, in homicide, the payment of blood money is also made on the principle of kinship and blood relationship. Likewise, the payment for the dressing of wounds was also made on the principle of kinship. Therefore, justice demands that if a relative dies and leaves an estate, it should be distributed on the principle of kinship, because the Islamic system of life is a complete and mutually coherent system. And this comprehensiveness and harmony become well evident when rights and duties are defined within it.

In short, in the distribution of inheritance, the Shariah has generally kept these close responsibilities in view. Some people find fault with the principles of distribution of this law; they do so because they are in fact prepared to be disrespectful toward the dignity of the Divine Being. Yet their own condition is that they do not even know human nature well, nor do they understand well the various conditions of human life. But the truth is that if these people properly comprehended the principles on which the foundation of Islam's inheritance system has been laid, they would never dare to do so.

The fundamental principle of the Islamic inheritance system is social security. The Shariah has founded this system of mutual support on principles that are extremely firm, and in establishing these principles Islam has also kept in view the natural inclinations of the human soul. These are inclinations whose Creator is Allah, and Allah has not created these inclinations within human nature in vain. These natural tendencies play an important role in the growth and survival of human life.

The ties of close or distant kinship within a family are natural ties and extremely real ties, and they are ties that were not created by any single generation or society, nor does the agreement of whole human generations have any part in their creation. Therefore, no one can deny the realism and depth of these ties, or their importance in the preservation, progress and exaltation of human life; and if anyone denies the importance of these real ties, he deserves to be entirely disregarded. For this reason Islam has made the family's system of mutual support the unit of its system of support. And it has then made that family support unit the milestone of its collective and national system of support. Islam has made the inheritance system a manifestation and symbol of this family system of support, while its other beneficial effects on the economic, social, economic and political order are also well established.

If this first step in mutual support fails for a person, and families fail to support an individual, then the local Muslim society comes forward and supports that person.
