And if the neighbourhood and the local society also fail, then after that the Islamic state is responsible for the support of all those who cannot manage their own affairs. The benefit of this arrangement is that the task of providing for all needy people does not fall suddenly on the shoulders of the governmental administration alone. This arrangement has been made so that, as a result of mutual support within a family and a limited society, feelings of mutual love, kindness, compassion and sympathy arise in the hearts of the members of society, and because of these feelings, the natural virtues of mutual cooperation and sympathy flourish among people, and these are entirely real, with no pretence in them. Apart from this family support, having feelings of help and sympathy toward relatives is a human act which only a corrupt-natured and base-minded wicked person could disregard. Supporting within a family is an act which has very beneficial effects on human nature and temperament, which are entirely in accordance with human nature. A person's awareness that his personal struggle is a beneficial act for all his relatives, especially for his own children, doubles his power of action because of this awareness; and similarly a person's struggle proves indirectly beneficial to the whole society, because in the Islamic system of life there are no gaps kept between the individual and the community. (1) (For details see the chapter "The Individual and Society" in the book Al-Insan Bayna al-Maddiyyah wal-Islam by Muhammad Qutb, and the author's book Al-Adalah al-Ijtima'iyyah fi al-Islam, the chapter on collective mutual support and financial policy, and my book Dirasat Islamiyyah.)

Because the entire ownership of an individual is in fact also the ownership of the whole society, should society need it. (2) (For details see the chapter "The Individual and Society" in the book Al-Insan Bayna al-Maddiyyah wal-Islam by Muhammad Qutb, and the author's book Al-Adalah al-Ijtima'iyyah fi al-Islam, the chapter on collective mutual support and financial policy, and my book Dirasat Islamiyyah.)

In the light of this final principle, all those objections raised against the Islamic inheritance system are dispelled, in which it is said that this system transfers inheritance even to those who have made no struggle for it. This is because the heir is in reality a continuation of the deceased, and if this deceased person had been in need and the heir wealthy, then the heir, under his Islamic and social obligations, would have supported him. And after these matters, this principle is firmly established: that this wealth, whoever holds it and however it is distributed, is the collective wealth of the whole society, and it may be used for collective needs. (3) (For details see the chapter "The Individual and Society" in the book Al-Insan Bayna al-Maddiyyah wal-Islam by Muhammad Qutb, and the author's book Al-Adalah al-Ijtima'iyyah fi al-Islam, the chapter on collective mutual support and financial policy, and my book Dirasat Islamiyyah.)

Apart from these matters, the bond between heir and deceased, especially between the deceased and his offspring, is not merely a financial bond. Even if we cut financial interests between heir and deceased by law, the blood ties and other ties that exist between them are not severed by cutting.

Forefathers and other relatives transmit to their children, grandchildren and relatives not only material inheritance, but also their good abilities, good habits, bad habits and weaknesses. Thus they also transmit certain hereditary diseases to their children and grandchildren, and if they are healthy, they also pass on their health as an inheritance. Likewise, a person's good or bad character, his virtues and vices, and his intelligence or dullness are also transmitted by heredity. All these qualities, transferred to heirs, affect their lives permanently, and the heirs must bear their consequences. Therefore, justice demands that if the deceased has any property, it too be transferred to the heirs. For if we do not give a person's property to his heirs, it is our duty to free the heirs from hereditary diseases, moral weaknesses, bad conduct and mental and physical weaknesses as well, and this is not possible even if we devote all our resources to this task.

Because of these natural and factual realities of human life, and because of the other wisdoms hidden within the divine Shariah, Allah has ordained this present system of distribution of inheritance. (4) (For details see the chapter "The Individual and Society" in the book Al-Insan Bayna al-Maddiyyah wal-Islam by Muhammad Qutb, and the author's book Al-Adalah al-Ijtima'iyyah fi al-Islam, the chapter on collective mutual support and financial policy, and my book Dirasat Islamiyyah.) He says.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 4, verse 7:

(Verse) "For men there is a share of what the parents and the near relatives leave, and for women there is a share of what the parents and the near relatives leave, whether it be little or much, a share ordained."(7)

This is the general principle by which Islam, a full fourteen hundred years ago, gave women the rights that men at that time already possessed. This was a principled decision, just as the protection of the rights of orphans was established, whereas in the society of that time the rights of the young and of orphans were commonly trampled. And these rights were trampled because in the Age of Ignorance (Jahiliyyah) the worth and value of human beings was not determined by their human standing, but by how much they were useful in the productive process and then how much they were useful in war. In these circumstances Islam presented a divine system, which first of all looked at the human being as a human being. This is because the human standing of a person can never be separated from him in any circumstance. Human standing is the fundamental standing, and after it the consideration of all other standings within a family or within a society comes.

As the details will come before the readers later, in the law of inheritance (mirath) in Islam, the presence of certain relatives causes certain other heirs to be excluded (mahjub). Those relatives do exist, but they receive nothing from the inheritance, because closer relatives take their right before them. Such persons are called mahjub (excluded heirs). Therefore, here, at the time of the division of inheritance, an unspecified right is kept for such people, when they are present at the time of the division of the inheritance and are also deserving. This right has been kept to console such people. It is obvious that they will see the property being divided while they are deprived. Therefore, consoling them is desired. Moreover, through this the family relatives and bonds will also be strengthened and heartfelt affection will increase. Similarly, regarding other orphans and the needy, advice is given here that the dividers should certainly give them something as well.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 4, verse 8:

(Verse) "And when the distribution is attended by relatives, orphans and the needy, then provide for them from it and speak to them words of kindness." (8)

Scholars have related many opinions about this verse. Some have said that this verse is abrogated (mansukh), and that it has been abrogated by the verse of inheritance, in which the shares of all people have been fixed. Some have said that it is abrogated and yet still in effect (qa'im). Some have said that acting upon its meaning and implication is obligatory and compulsory. Others have said that acting upon it is recommended (mustahabb), and that it is up to the heirs whether they act upon it or not. In my view there is no reason for its abrogation. Rather, these verses are among the muhkamat (clear, definitive verses), and acting upon it is obligatory. This is because, firstly, on its apparent reading it is unrestricted (mutlaq). Secondly, in the Islamic system of life, general support and benevolence are greatly loved. In any case, this is a separate category, and it is in addition to the shares that are specified in the verses that follow.

Before the explanation of the heirs' shares begins, emphasis is once again placed on the fact that consuming the property of orphans is a very dangerous crime. This repeated emphasis is made so that it strikes the hearts of the believers with two severe pinches. The first pinch is intended to awaken the paternal compassion hidden within their hearts. Every father has a natural love for children, especially when they are in a state of great weakness and helplessness, and that the feeling of fear of God is the best examiner and overseer. The second pinch is intended to awaken within their hearts the emotions of fear and the dread of an evil end: the fear of the fire of Hell, which is presented here in a tangible, visible and frightening manner.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 4, verses 9–10:

(Verse) "And let those fear [Allah] who, if they left behind them weak offspring, would be anxious for them. So let them fear Allah and speak words of appropriate justice. Indeed, those who consume the properties of orphans unjustly are only consuming fire into their bellies, and they will [soon] burn in a Blaze." (01)

This first touch reaches the heart's inner covering. A father, filled with tender love, is given an image concerning his small and weak children: just think, if you had small children, who were feeble, and upon whom no one had mercy, and no one was their guardian or protector who would place a hand of compassion on their heads. This is the very condition of those orphans whose destiny is entrusted to you. The shade of their fathers has been lifted from their heads. They do not know that tomorrow, when you are no longer present, your own children may be under the guardianship of other living guardians, just as these present children are under your guardianship. After this touch, they are advised that alongside this image, they should keep the fear of Allah constantly in their hearts regarding these children, and its reward will be that tomorrow Allah will arrange the management of your children through such God-fearing guardians, who will carry out this duty with fear of God, caution and love. Then they are also advised to speak plain and straightforward words concerning these orphans, that is, during their upbringing, supervision, and the care of their wealth and property.

And what is this second touch? Terrifying are those who devour blazing embers in the same way one swallows a morsel of food. What a frightening picture this is: at last they enter Hell, and within their bellies is also Hell. This wealth which they consume, the property of orphans, is as though they were consuming burning coals of fire. In the end they will enter Hell, and it will reduce their stomachs and their skins to ashes. Outwardly there is fire, and inwardly there is fire, a embodiment of fire which both the belly and the skin feel. The eyes see this picture, and in it the belly, the body and the skin all burn.

This impactful mode of expression of the Holy Qur'an had a profound effect upon the Companions and the Muslims. These powerful indications of the texts washed away the filth of ignorance from the minds and hearts of the people of faith, and shook their hearts so much that they shook off every kind of dust of ignorance. In that place, they created within these believing hearts the sentiments of God-fearing, fear of Allah, caution and accountability. Their condition became such that they regarded the property of orphans as untouchable. They saw that there was fire within that wealth, and this conviction had been created in their hearts by the impact of these verses. Their state became such that they did not even bear to touch the properties of orphans, and they fled from those properties as a fox flees in fear.

Through Ata ibn al-Sa'ib, Sa'id ibn Jubayr (may Allah be pleased with him) narrated from Ibn Abbas (may Allah be pleased with him) that when this verse was revealed, "Indeed, those who consume the properties of orphans unjustly," those who had orphans in their care separated the cooking of the orphans' food from their own. Their eating and drinking was separated, and sometimes some of the food left over from theirs was set aside for them, so that they might eat it at another time or it would spoil. This matter became a source of hardship for them, and the complaint was made before the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), whereupon this verse was revealed:

(Verse) "They ask you concerning orphans. Say, 'Reforming them is best. And if you mix your affairs with theirs, then they are your brothers. And Allah knows the corrupter from the reformer. And if Allah had willed, He could have put you in difficulty.'"

Translation: "They ask you about how to deal with orphans. Say: the course of action in which there is good for them is best to adopt. If you keep your expenses and living arrangements shared with them, there is no harm in it. After all, they are your brothers. Allah knows well both the one who does wrong and the one who does good. Had Allah willed, He would have been strict with you in this matter."

After this, the Companions (may Allah be pleased with them all) combined the orphans' food with their own food, and their drink with their own drink.

Thus the Qur'anic method of education elevated the faith and conscience of those people, and they became a shining star on the horizon of humanity. It purified their hearts and minds from all the pollutions of ignorance, and this purity and refinement was astonishing in that society.

Now the discussion reaches the system of inheritance. The opening of the discourse goes thus: Allah enjoins you concerning your children. From this injunction it becomes evident that Allah is most merciful, most beneficent and most just, and that He is more merciful and compassionate than parents. Through this mode of address it is also indicated that the ultimate reference and end of this whole system is the blessed Person of Allah. It is Allah alone who decides between a father and his children, and He determines rights even among relatives. The task of people is only to learn and take guidance from Allah, and to implement His commands and injunctions. This is the very meaning of religion. As we stated at the beginning of the surah, one of the major themes and central axes of this surah is the clarification of the concept of religion. Accordingly, the discussion of the system of inheritance begins thus.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 4, verse 11 (part 1 of 2):

(Verse) "Allah instructs you concerning your children: a male's share is equal to that of two females." After this sentence, the shares of all the heirs are then mentioned. This distribution and appointment is under the general principle that it is guidance and an injunction from Allah. Its details are given in two long verses. In the first verse, the distribution of inheritance is between the roots (usul) and the branches (furu'), that is, between parents and children, and in the second verse, the shares of inheritance of the marital relationship and of kalalah are mentioned. Then some supplementary rulings come at the end of this surah concerning kalalah (the details are forthcoming).

(Verse) "Allah instructs you concerning your children: a male's share is equal to that of two females. If there are only daughters, more than two, for them is two-thirds of what he leaves; and if there is only one, for her is half. And for each of his parents is a sixth of what he leaves, if he had children. But if he had no children and his parents inherit from him, then for his mother is a third. And if he has brothers, then for his mother is a sixth, after any bequest he [may have] made or debt. Your fathers and your sons—you do not know which of them are nearer to you in benefit. [This is] an obligation [imposed] by Allah. Indeed, Allah is ever Knowing and Wise." (11) "And for you is half of what your wives leave if they have no child. But if they have a child, for you is one-fourth of what they leave, after any bequest they [may have] made or debt. And for the wives is one-fourth of what you leave if you have no child; but if you have a child, for them is one-eighth of what you leave, after any bequest you [may have] made or debt. And if a man or woman leaves neither ascendants nor descendants as heirs but has a brother or a sister, then for each one of them is a sixth. But if they are more than that, they share a third, after any bequest that has been made or debt, without being harmful. [This is] an ordinance from Allah, and Allah is Knowing and Forbearing." (21)

Translation: "Allah instructs you concerning your children, and Allah is All-Knowing and Gentle."

These two verses and the third verse of this surah set out the basic rules of the science of inheritance ('ilm al-mirath). The third verse of this surah is: (Verse) "They ask you concerning kalalah. Say: Allah gives you a ruling concerning kalalah. If a man dies leaving no child and he has a sister, she will have half of what he leaves, and he inherits from her if she has no child. If there are two sisters, they will have two-thirds of what he leaves. And if there are brothers and sisters, men and women, the male will have the equal of the share of two females. Allah makes clear to you, lest you go astray, and Allah is Knowing of all things." (176)

Translation: "They ask you for a legal ruling concerning kalalah. Say: Allah gives you a ruling concerning kalalah: if a man dies without child, and he has a sister, she takes half of what he leaves, and he inherits from her if she has no child. If there are two sisters, they take two-thirds of what he leaves. And if there are brothers and sisters, men and women, the male has the share of two females. Allah explains to you so that you do not go astray, and Allah has knowledge of everything."

In these three verses, the principles of the science of inheritance have been codified. Further subsidiary matters of these principles have been explained in the Sunnah of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and in the statements of the Companions. After that, the jurists (fuqaha') have exercised ijtihad on these principles and roots and stated detailed rulings. There is no room here to mention the details of these subsidiary matters; the details can be studied in books of fiqh. Here, in Fi Zilal al-Quran, we will only explain these verses, as well as the concluding remarks at the end of these verses and the fundamental principles of the Islamic system of life stated in them.

(Verse) "Allah instructs you concerning your children: a male's share is equal to that of two females." Translation: "Allah enjoins upon you regarding your children that a male's share shall be equal to two females."

From this opening verse it is known, as we have said before, that this is the fundamental principle (asl al-usul) of the science of inheritance, and what the source of this science is, and from which origin this science has emerged. It also contains an indication that Allah is more merciful and compassionate to people than parents are, and that the shares He has prescribed for them are for their benefit. Such a distribution cannot even be made by parents themselves. These two meanings are interconnected and complete each other.

It is Allah who enjoins, Who prescribes the shares, and Who distributes inheritance among people. Likewise, He enjoins in every matter, prescribes obligations and duties, and in the same way He distributes sustenance to creatures in this universe. All these regulations, laws and statutes also come from Him. It is Allah from Whom people derive principles in all the circumstances of their lives, and one of these circumstances is the distribution of estates among people, including among their own children. This is the religion of Islam. If people do not accept the injunctions and regulations of Allah in all the circumstances of their lives, this would not be religion, and it would not be an Islamic condition for them to derive principles for their affairs of life, whether major or minor, from some other source. Such a situation would be either shirk or open disbelief (kufr sarih), and it would again be the same jahiliyyah for whose roots, to uproot them from people's lives, Islam came into this world.

Here, what Allah enjoins, makes obligatory and commands, so that rulings in people's lives are applied accordingly, all these rulings are extremely beneficial and useful for people, especially those that relate to their particular personal matters, such as the distribution of their wealth and the shares of their children within it. And this distribution is more beneficial than the divisions that they make among themselves, and than what they prefer for their children. This is because people do not have the right to say that they will choose for themselves whatever they wish, and that they know well what is beneficial for them and what is not. This is because such a claim, apart from being false in itself, is a baseless audacity, willfulness, and a claim of greater knowledge in the face of Allah, Glorified is His majesty. It is an assertion that only a most audacious and ignorant person could make.

Awfi reported from Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with him), concerning the verse "Allah instructs you concerning your children: a male's share is equal to that of two females," his statement that when the laws of inheritance were revealed and Allah prescribed the shares in them—the share of the son, the share of the daughter and the share of the parents—people found it very objectionable, or some people disliked it. Their objection was that a woman is given a quarter and an eighth, a daughter is given a half, and a young child's share was also fixed, even though none of these people participates in fighting at the time of battle, and none of them can seize spoils of war after the battle. "Remain silent about these rulings, perhaps the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) will forget them, or we may request him regarding them and he may change them." So they said: "O Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), you give a girl half of her father's estate, although she does not ride a horse and does not take part in war. Then a minor child is given inheritance, and he cannot do anything for us. In the days of jahiliyyah they used to give inheritance only to those who took part in battle, and they used to give it to the eldest in the distribution, and then to whoever came next in order." (Narrated by Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Jarir.)

In short, this was the logic of Arab jahiliyyah, and therefore the rulings of the law of inheritance were disturbing to some of them. These people confronted the obligations of Allah and His just distribution, although this distribution was extremely wise. And this is also the logic of modern jahiliyyah, which creates unease in the hearts of some people. Therefore this logic too comes forward in opposition to the obligations and distribution of Allah. Although modern jahiliyyah differs in nature from Arab jahiliyyah in some respects. The logic of today's jahiliyyah is: why should we distribute an estate to those who did not labour or toil in earning that estate, nor bore any hardship in it? This mentality too has not grasped Divine wisdom. Moreover, this logic in reality contains severe impudence, and in impudence and audacity both ancient and modern jahiliyyah are equal.

(Verse) "For the male is the equal of the share of two females." That is, if the only heirs of a male are his children, sons and daughters, then the whole estate will go to them, and the male's share will be double the female's share, that is, one share for a daughter and two shares for a son.

It should be kept in view here that this difference and distinction in their shares is not made because one sex has superiority over the other; rather, this difference in shares is maintained because the duties the Islamic system has placed upon men and women in family life, this difference of shares is extremely balanced and just in accordance with them.

Beyond family life, in the collective affairs of the Islamic society too, more obligations are placed upon men than upon women. A man marries a woman and he also provides for her maintenance. He also provides for the maintenance of his children. And these responsibilities remain attached to him even when he divorces that woman. As for the woman, either she herself is responsible for her needs, or the situation is that before marriage and after marriage too, the man is responsible for her maintenance, and she is in no way responsible for the maintenance of her husband and her children. Now the position is that the man bears two-thirds of the family's needs compared with the woman. Likewise, in collective matters too, the man's responsibilities are double those of the woman. Therefore these shares prescribed by Allah are, on one hand, just, and on the other hand, in accordance with the saying "a share according to the burden," this distribution becomes equitable. And every objection to this distribution is either based on ignorance, or it is raised due to baseless audacity and impudence in the presence of Allah, Exalted is He. Moreover, its aim is to uproot the foundations of the Islamic social and family system and to create chaos within a peaceful life.

The distribution begins thus: how the inheritance of the father and grandfather will be distributed among the children, He says:

(Verse) "And if there are only daughters, more than two, then for them is two-thirds of what he leaves; and if there is only one, then for her is half." Translation: "If the heirs are daughters more than two, they shall be given two-thirds of the estate, and if there is only one daughter as heir, half of the estate is hers."

That is, if there are only two or more daughters and no sons, they will be given two-thirds. And if there is only one daughter and no son, then half will be hers, and the remainder goes to the 'asabat, to the nearest 'asabah. The 'asabat are these persons: father, grandfather, full brothers, consanguine brothers (half-brothers through the father), uncles, and then the children of the paternal grandfather. The wording of this verse is: "If the heirs are more than two daughters, then for them is two-thirds." The question arises: if there are two, what is the ruling for them? Their share is also two-thirds, which is established from a hadith. Moreover, it would also be established by analogy to the share of the two sisters, which was mentioned in the concluding verse of this surah concerning the issue of kalalah.

Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi and Ibn Majah narrated from 'Abdullah ibn Muhammad ibn 'Aqil, from Jabir, who said: The wife of Sa'd ibn al-Rabi' came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: "O Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), these are the two daughters of Sa'd ibn al-Rabi'. He was martyred with you at Uhud. Their paternal uncle has taken all the property, and if they have no property, who will marry them?" He (ﷺ) said: "Allah will certainly decide about this." At that occasion the verse of inheritance was revealed. The Prophet (ﷺ) sent for their uncle and commanded: "Give the two daughters of Sa'd two-thirds, give the wife one-eighth, and the rest is yours." This was the distribution of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) himself. He (ﷺ) gave two-thirds to the two daughters. Therefore, if there are two or more daughters, they will receive two-thirds.

As for the analogy to the final verse of the surah, it concerns sisters: (Verse) "And if they are two sisters, then for them is two-thirds of what he leaves." Translation: "And if they are two sisters, they shall receive two-thirds of what he leaves."

Therefore, if a father has two daughters, they will receive two-thirds by way of priority, by analogy to two sisters, because if there is one daughter there is also a half share, and if there is one sister (in kalalah) there is also a half share, and the share of two daughters will be the same as that of two sisters.

After describing the shares of the children, now the mention of the shares of the parents begins, provided they are alive. These shares differ according to the presence or absence of the deceased's children.

"If the deceased has children, then each of his parents should receive a sixth of his estate; and if he has no children and his parents alone are his heirs, then the mother is given a third of the property."

The circumstances of parents in inheritance are many. The first circumstance is that both parents are present and the deceased also has children. In this case, each of them will receive a sixth. The remainder is distributed among the deceased's sons or sons and daughters according to their shares; the male's share is double the female's. Now, if the deceased's children include only one daughter, she will receive half of the remainder, and each of the parents will receive a sixth. Now the remainder (61) goes to the father as 'asabah. In this case the children inherit both as sharers (dhawu al-furud) and as 'asabah. But if the deceased has two or more daughters, then they receive two-thirds, and each of the parents receives a sixth.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 4, verse 11 (part 2 of 2):

The second case is when the deceased leaves no children, no brothers or sisters, and no husband or wife. In this case the mother, as a sharer (dhu al-furud), receives one-third, and the whole remainder goes to the father as an agnatic heir ('asabah). In this case the father's share becomes double that of the mother. Now, if there is a husband or a wife besides the parents, then the husband receives one-half, and if it is a wife, she receives one-quarter, and the mother receives one-third. (Either the mother receives one-third of the entire estate, or one-third of the remainder after deducting the share of the husband or wife, as there are two opinions among the jurists.) And whatever remains after the mother's share goes to the father as 'asabah, provided that the father's share is not less than the mother's.

The third case is when the parents are present along with the deceased's brothers and sisters. These brothers may be full siblings (from both parents), or paternal siblings only, or maternal siblings only. In this case, in the presence of the father, these siblings receive nothing and are excluded (mahrum), because the father is the nearest 'asabah for the deceased after the son, and when a nearer heir is present, a more distant one does not inherit. However, although they are excluded, these brothers do affect the mother's share, which is reduced from one-third to one-sixth. In this case the mother receives one-sixth, and everything else goes to the father, provided that there is no husband or wife of the deceased. However, if there is only one brother, the mother's share remains one-third, just as it was in the case where the deceased has no children and no brothers.

But these shares of the parents are to be given after the payment of debts and the execution of bequests.

(Verse) "min ba'di wasiyyatin yusi biha aw dayn" (after any bequest he may have made or debt).

Translation: "These shares are to be taken out only after the bequest which the deceased made has been carried out and the debt that is upon him has been paid."

Ibn Kathir has written: "The scholars, both past and present, have agreed that debt takes precedence over bequest." The wisdom in giving debt precedence over bequest is clear. This is because debt involves the rights of a third person, and its payment from the deceased's property is obligatory, since he himself took the loan, provided that the deceased's property exists. This is because the Shariah has greatly stressed freeing the deceased from the responsibilities of debt, so that mutual trust in the collective life of society may be maintained and the atmosphere of mutual confidence within society may remain. This is why, even after a person's death, the Shariah does not suspend the debts owed by him.

It is narrated from Abu Qatadah (may Allah be pleased with him) that he said: a man said, "O Messenger of Allah, tell me, if I am killed, will all my sins be forgiven?" The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Yes, if you are killed while you are patient in the face of hardship, sincere in intention, and advancing, not fleeing." After this, the man asked (the question) twice more. What did the Prophet (ﷺ) say? He repeated the same thing and added: "Except debt, for Jibril (peace be upon him) has informed me of that." (Narrated by Muslim, Malik, Tirmidhi and Nasa'i.)

It is also narrated from Abu Qatadah: a man was brought before the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and he said: "Perform the funeral prayer for him yourselves, for he is under debt." I then said, "O Messenger of Allah, the debt is upon me." The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Will you fulfil it?" I said, "I will fulfil it."

The fulfilment of a bequest is necessary because the deceased's intention has become attached to it. The Shariah has allowed for bequests because in some circumstances certain relatives are excluded from inheritance, and this exclusion occurs due to the presence of other relatives. Sometimes these excluded people are disabled and needy, or it is in the interest of the whole family to give them something, and sometimes, because of it, jealousy, rancour and disputes within the family are prevented. However, it is an established principle that a bequest in favour of an heir is not valid. And a bequest is also limited to one-third of the estate. Because of these two matters, the deceased also cannot exclude any heir.

(Verse) "Abaukum wa abnaukum la tadrūna ayyuhum aqrabu lakum nafʿan, fariḍatan min Allah, inna Allah kana ʿalīman ḥakīman."

Translation: "You do not know which of your parents and your children is nearer to you in benefit. This is an obligation from Allah; indeed Allah is All-Knowing, All-Wise."

At the end of this verse, various purposes are touched upon. The first touch is for the purpose that, by perceiving it, people should be pleased with this allocation of shares from the Qur'an and accept it willingly. It may be that some people, overwhelmed by the emotion of love, prefer children over the father, since every human being's natural inclination is greater towards his children. And some people are such that their awareness of morality and manners is more mature than towards their parents, and they prefer parents over children. Some cannot decide between respect for parents and their natural inclination towards children. Sometimes a family adopts a fixed line due to the mentality of customs and traditions, just as at the time of the revelation of the Qur'an, in the prevailing law of inheritance, only the family mentality was operating under the customs of that time. We have already mentioned some of the customs of the Arabs earlier. In these circumstances, Allah the Exalted deemed it fitting to fill the hearts of the believers with submission, contentment, peace and tranquillity, so that they would accept Allah's commands gladly and willingly. Allah gives them the awareness that complete knowledge of everything rests with Allah alone, and that they do not have full knowledge of which of their relatives is more beneficial to them and which less, nor do they know which distribution is more beneficial.

(Verse) "Abaukum wa abnaukum la tadrūna ayyuhum aqrabu lakum nafʿan"

Translation: "You do not know which of your parents and your children is nearer to you in benefit."

The second touch given to this theme is that the real issue is not which is beneficial to you and which is more beneficial. The real issue is religion, the legal system and the Shariah, and these shares being fixed are (verse) "fariḍatan min Allah" – "an obligation from Allah." These shares have been fixed by Allah. Allah is the One who created both parents and children. He is the One who grants wealth and property. He is the One who imposes obligations and shares, and He is the Distributor. And He is the One who has the right to legislate; human beings do not have the authority to make laws for themselves, nor are they free to devise a system of government according to their desires, because they do not know where their interest lies. That belongs to Him alone.

(Verse) "Inna Allah kana ʿalīman ḥakīman"

Translation: "Indeed Allah is All-Knowing, All-Wise."

This is the third touch given in this commentary: that despite this law being a divine decree and obligatory for them in every circumstance, it is also based on profound wisdom and broader interest. Allah has given this command on the basis of His vast knowledge, whereas the knowledge of human beings is limited. Within it operates His profound wisdom, whereas human beings are merely followers of their own desires.

In this legislation there is repeated emphasis that matters should be returned to their true foundation, and its true foundation is ideological. This ideological basis rests on the understanding of religion that all one's decisions should be referred to Allah, and that obligations should be taken from Him, being content with His wisdom. "These shares have been fixed by Allah, and Allah is indeed All-Knowing, and knows all interests."

Next, the remaining shares are determined as follows.

(Verse) "And for you is half of what your wives leave, if they have no child. But if they have a child, for you is one-fourth of what they leave, after any bequest they make or debt. And for the wives is one-fourth of what you leave, if you have no child. But if you have a child, for them is one-eighth of what you leave, after any bequest you make or debt."

Translation: "If a husband dies without children, the wife's share is one-fourth. If there are children, whether sons or daughters, one or many, from this wife or from another wife, or if there are grandsons from a son, then in these cases the wife's share is reduced from one-fourth to one-eighth. The payment of debts and the fulfilment of bequests come first in every case."

Likewise, two wives, three wives and four wives are counted as one wife. All of them share in the one-fourth or the one-eighth. And now comes the final ruling on inheritance, which is known by the name of the issue of kalalah.

(Verse) "And if a man leaves an inheritance as kalalah (one with neither ascendants nor descendants), or a woman, and he has a brother or a sister, then each of the two gets one-sixth. But if they are more than that, they share in one-third, after any bequest that is made or debt, without causing harm."

The meaning of kalalah is that a person is an heir from his collateral relatives, and the reason for his inheritance is not that he is from the ascendants or the descendants. That is, the relationship is weak, not as strong as the relationship of ascendants and descendants. Someone asked Abu Bakr al-Siddiq (ra) about kalalah, and he said: "I will speak on this matter according to my own opinion. If it is correct, it is from Allah; and if it is wrong, it is from Satan, and Allah and His Messenger (ﷺ) are free of it. Kalalah is one who has neither children nor parents." When Umar (ra) became caliph after Abu Bakr (ra), he said: "I am ashamed to oppose the opinion of Abu Bakr." (This narration has been transmitted by Ibn Jarir from al-Shabi.)

Ibn Kathir says: "It is reported from Ali, Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn Abbas, and Zayd ibn Thabit (may Allah be pleased with them). Al-Shabi, al-Nakha'i, al-Hasan, Qatadah, Jabir, Ibn Zayd and al-Hakam also held this view. The people of Madinah, the people of Kufa and the people of Basra also hold this view. The opinion of the seven jurists is also this. The opinion of the four imams is also this. Scholars of earlier and later times agree on it, and many have transmitted that consensus has been established on it."

(Verse) "And if a man leaves an inheritance as kalalah, or a woman, and he has a brother or a sister, then each of the two gets one-sixth. But if they are more than that, they share in one-third."

Translation: "And if the man or woman whose estate is to be divided is kalalah (has no children and whose parents are also not alive), but has a brother or sister, then each brother and sister will get one-sixth. And if there are more brothers and sisters than one, they will share in one-third of the entire estate."

Here, "a brother and a sister" means the brother and sister who are related to the deceased only through the mother, that is, uterine siblings. If they are full siblings, or if the siblings are only from the father's side, then their inheritance follows the last verse of this surah, and in that case a brother's share is double a sister's. It is not like this verse, where each gets one-sixth whether male or female. So this ruling is, in effect, for uterine siblings, because uterine siblings inherit only as sharers (dhu al-furud), each receiving one-sixth, and they have no share as residuaries (asabah). Residuaries are those who take the entire estate, or what is left after the sharers (dhu al-furud) receive their portions, as residuary heirs (Rosiduc).

(Verse) "But if they are more than that, they share in one-third of the entire estate."

Translation: "And if there are more brothers and sisters than one, they share in one-third of the entire estate, regardless of how many they are. The commonly accepted opinion is that they receive equal shares as sharers. Although some jurists also hold that in this case they do not divide equally, but divide according to the general principle that a male receives the equivalent of two females. However, the first commonly accepted opinion appears more correct, because the other opinion does not agree with the one-sixth that this verse fixes for each in the case of one brother and one sister.

Uterine siblings, who share only the mother's relationship with the deceased, have a distinct status compared to the other heirs.

(1) The first distinguishing feature is that in inheritance, the share of males and females is equal.

(2) They receive inheritance only when the deceased is kalalah. Therefore, if the deceased has a father, grandfather, son or grandson, they receive nothing from the inheritance.

(3) Their rights do not exceed one-third, even if their number greatly increases.

(Verse) "After any bequest that is made or debt, without causing harm." Translation: "After the bequest that has been made is carried out, and the debt the deceased left is paid, provided it is not harmful." This verse warns that a bequest should not be made in order to harm the heirs. Rather, a bequest should be according to justice and benefit. And the debt should be paid even before the bequest, and both must be settled before the distribution of inheritance, that is, the bequest and the debt.

Now, at the end of the second verse there also comes the same concluding statement that came at the end of the first verse.

(Verse) "An injunction from Allah, and Allah is All-Knowing, Forbearing."

The repetition of this concluding theme is because emphasis is desired regarding the system of inheritance. For the rulings of inheritance the word "wasiyyah" (injunction) has been used. This injunction is from Allah, and its accounting will also be before Him. This injunction is neither according to any desire of the self, nor following the carnal desires of anyone. It is based on true knowledge and awareness. Therefore obedience to this law of inheritance is obligatory, because its source is the Being who has the right to legislate and regulate for humans. And its system and regulations must also be accepted by humans, because it comes from the All-Knowing and the Forbearing; it is wise and compassionate.

The fundamental principle of the Islamic worldview is that the source of all laws is the Divine Being. Therefore, throughout this entire process of legislation, this truth is repeatedly emphasized. If this foundational principle is not accepted, it would amount to disbelief, disobedience and exit from the religion. The two verses that follow decide this matter, and these two verses are a forceful conclusion to the entire system of inheritance given in this surah. They explain that the system of inheritance is in reality among the limits set by Allah.

This system of inheritance and this legal Shariah, which has been established for the distribution of inheritance, and which Allah has laid down in accordance with His knowledge and wisdom. Its purpose is to organise the family system within a family, and to make the collective and economic relations of society stable. "These are the limits set by Allah." And these limits have been established so that they may be milestones in these familial and economic relations, and decisive in the distribution of estates.

Those who obey Allah in this matter will remain forever in success, and this is their great triumph. And those who transgress these limits and disobey Allah and His Messenger in this matter will enter the Hellfire, remaining in it forever. And this will be a painful and humiliating punishment for them.

Why will this be so? Why should obedience to Allah or disobedience to Him in this matter produce such great consequences, when the law of inheritance is, after all, only a small part of the system of Shariah? Only one part, and such severe punishment for one part?

Apparently, this dreadful punishment seems far too great for the offence. But it seems so only to the one who has not reached the reality and depth of this matter.

Many verses of this surah speak continuously to express this reality, and their explanation and commentary come later, and we indicated this when presenting the introduction to this surah. These are the verses in which the meaning of the word din (religion) is explained, the conditions of faith are stated, and in which the definition of Islam is given. Nevertheless, it is appropriate that we give here a brief note on this matter, to the extent necessary for the explanation and understanding of these two verses, which are the conclusion and commentary of the verses of inheritance.

The fundamental question of this din, the religion of Islam, and indeed of all the divine heavenly religions sent by Allah through His messengers throughout the whole history of humanity, has always been this: who holds the right of sovereignty over this earth? Who is the Lord of these people? The answer to these two questions is given in these verses, and all the matters of this religion are settled in the light of these answers, and all the affairs of people are settled in the light of these same answers.

Now, what is the answer to this question? Who holds the right of sovereignty and lordship over this earth? Only Allah, alone; no one of His creation shares this right with Him. This is the very essence of faith, this is the very essence of Islam, and this is the religion of Islam. And if this right of sovereignty and lordship is given to any creature, and they are made partners with Allah, or this right is given to anyone independently apart from Allah, then this is clear shirk and manifest kufr.

Either sovereignty and lordship belong to Allah alone, without partner, and in that case people enter only the religion of Allah alone and enter only into the obedience of Allah alone, and its practical form will be that people follow the Islamic system of life. For in this case the right to prescribe a system of life for people belongs to Allah alone; it is Allah alone who lays down for people the ways, laws and regulations; then it is Allah alone who determines for people the standards of good and bad, and who organises the detailed ways and order of their life. And for no individual or society other than Allah will there be any such rights, and their only course will be to obey the Divine Shariah, because this obedience is the logical requirement of Allah's divinity, sovereignty and lordship, and the sole manifestation and particular form of this requirement is the system of Shariah.

And if this is not the case, then the other alternative is that the right of sovereignty and lordship is not held by any of Allah's creation. This right is either held in partnership with Allah, or it is held by these people independently. In this case, those who accept this right will be considered to have entered the religion of these non-Allah powers; thus they will be worshipping others than Allah. Then this will be obedience to others than Allah on the part of man, and its practical form will be that these people become followers of the ways of life, the regulations, the laws and the standards of good and bad prescribed by others than Allah, and all these things have been formulated by some humans. In this legislation and codification they will not be referring to the sovereignty of Allah or to His Book, but all these things will be shaped by some other references, and some other sources will be their sources of authority. Therefore this condition will be devoid of religion, faith will be absent, and there will be no Islam, while this condition is a condition of shirk, kufr, fisq and disobedience.

This is the real truth of the matter. Therefore, in this regard, if anyone breaks just one of the limits of Allah, or entirely rejects the whole Shariah, there is no difference in the actual reality. For one limit is also din, and the whole Shariah is also din. Hence the real target in this is this principle: whether people are affirming Allah as one without partner in sovereignty and lordship, or whether they are associating someone with Him in it, or setting aside the Being of Allah and accepting the sovereignty and lordship of some other people. As for the question of what people verbally claim, that they have entered the religion of Islam and are Muslims, if this claim is not reflected in their conduct, then there is no Islam.

This is that great reality to which the conclusion of these verses of inheritance points. It explains that the assignment of the shares of heirs in the system of inheritance is directly connected with obedience to Allah and to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). Otherwise, in this matter, there will be disobedience to Allah and His Messenger. Or its outcome will be gardens beneath which rivers flow, or its end will be in the form of a humiliating punishment which will be given eternally in the fire of Hell.

And this is the great reality whose expression has been repeated in several verses of this surah, and it has been stated in such a clear and decisive manner that no room has been left in it for any interpretation or hypocrisy.

To those who still introduce themselves in terms of Islam, I would give this invitation: let them clear their minds about this, and see how far they have moved away from the Islamic system of life and the religion of Islam.

After this discussion, it is now necessary to say a few words about the inheritance system of Islam, before which, in connection with (Qur'an 4:7) "For men is a share of what they earn, and for women is a share of what they earn," we stated this general principle, and likewise in connection with (Qur'an 4:11) "For the male is the equivalent of the share of two females," we also discussed it.

The inheritance system of Islam is an extremely just system, and one most harmonious with human nature. It is also most suitable to the practical realities of family life. This becomes clear when we make a comparative study of this system with all the systems that have prevailed in human history or prevail now, whether in ancient ignorance or modern ignorance. In no region of the world and in no nation or community has the system taken into account all the aims of the collective maintenance of the family in such a way. Each person's share and their responsibilities within the family have been determined with regard to one another. For example, the mother and father, who are among the sharers with fixed portions (dhawu al-furud), come first. After them, in this system, importance is given to the agnatic heirs ('asabat). This is because in the absence of parents, the maintenance of an orphan falls upon the agnatic heirs. It is these agnates who bear shares in paying blood money (diyah) and other collective liabilities. Therefore the Islamic system of inheritance is extremely fitting and suitable.

The foundation of this system rests on the principle that this family system has come into being from a single human soul. Therefore, neither children nor women will be deprived, merely because they are women or minors. Thus, if this system makes distinctions of rank in practical responsibilities, it makes no distinction on the basis of the essential nature of humanity. Therefore, in granting rights, no distinction is made in it between the sexes, male and female. Whatever difference there is has been made with regard to collective responsibilities, which arise from the collective maintenance of the family.

This system is in full accord with the nature of all living things and especially with human nature, and with the natural human inclination by which he wishes to maintain a deep connection with his offspring, and that through this progeny his existence is, as it were, given continuity. Therefore, because of this system of inheritance, a person remains content that what he stores up, in the form of wealth, through his effort and struggle, and what is his natural desire, is that the fruit of his labour should reach his children, and that his future generation should not be deprived of it. And the conviction that the fruit of his struggle will reach his children serves as a spur to his striving. He will increase his effort and endeavour further, and this will also be economically beneficial for the whole society. And because of this continuous striving, there will be no decline in the collective system of mutual support of society; rather, in this system it has been fully taken into account.

And the final point is that the inheritance system of Islam shatters the accumulated wealth of an individual when it reaches extremes, and redistributes it afresh. Therefore this system does not allow wealth to gather in one place, nor does it leave it frozen in a few hands. For example, in contrast to a system in which the entire inheritance goes to the eldest son, or is confined within a limited circle of close relatives. In this respect, this system is a means that renews the functioning of economic activity in society and keeps it balanced. And in it there is no visible intervention by any administration or any collective system, which no individual accepts willingly, since love of wealth and greed have been deposited in human nature. As for this continuous breaking of concentrations and repeated redistribution in the Islamic system of inheritance, it continues ongoing, and the human soul also accepts it gladly, because this system is in accordance with human nature and its natural love of property and its greed. And this is the real difference and distinction between this divine system of life and those other systems which man has devised for man. Lesson 13 at a glance:

In the first lesson of this surah, attention was given to the organisation of collective life within the Islamic society, and it was purified of all the impurities of jahiliyyah. In it, the rights of the helpless people of society, of orphans, and the protection of their property were guaranteed, and this protection and safeguarding was provided to them within the natural framework of a family, under collective supervision. After this, the principles of inheritance within a family were stated, and then all these rights and safeguards were linked to the worldview that Allah is the sovereign and Lord of all people. And it is He who, by His command and will, created this creation from a single soul, and that Allah began the collective order of humanity with the unit of a family. Then collective responsibilities of maintenance were imposed within that family. And this regulation of all the circumstances of life was linked to the knowledge and wisdom of Allah and to the limits and bounds He has prescribed, and it was decided that if they obey Allah they will deserve the reward of Paradise, and if they commit disobedience they will deserve the punishment of Hell.

The second lesson now organizes the collective life of the Islamic society from another angle, and cleanses it from the pollutions of jahiliyyah (the pre-Islamic age of ignorance) from another side. That is, it is purified from the licentiousness and immorality of jahiliyyah. For such people, it has been prescribed that they be separated from society and that restrictions be placed on their movement, unless they give up their conduct and sincerely repent, are ready to lead a pure life, and are prepared to return to the Islamic society anew with pure morals and character.

Then, in this second part, woman has been freed from the oppressions under whose millstone she was crushed in the days of jahiliyyah. She used to be buried alive, was treated with contempt, and various kinds of cruelties were inflicted upon her, so that the Islamic society might be built on healthy and firm foundations, with a general atmosphere that is pure and clean, and with a structure resting on a most solid base, with the family as its first brick.

At the end of this part, a further aspect of the family is regulated, namely the circle of prohibited relations (muharramat). Legislation has been made for this under the Shariah, and its method adopted is that the prohibited relations have been mentioned, and all other daughters of Adam have been declared lawful for man.

With these subjects this lesson also concludes, and this juz' of the Qur'an also reaches its end.

This system of inheritance and this legal Shariah, which has been established for the distribution of inheritance, and which Allah has laid down in accordance with His knowledge and wisdom. Its purpose is to organise the family system within a family, and to make the collective and economic relations of society stable. "These are the limits set by Allah." And these limits have been established so that they may be milestones in these familial and economic relations, and decisive in the distribution of estates.

Those who obey Allah in this matter will remain forever in success, and this is their great triumph. And those who transgress these limits and disobey Allah and His Messenger in this matter will enter the Hellfire, remaining in it forever. And this will be a painful and humiliating punishment for them.

Why will this be so? Why should obedience to Allah or disobedience to Him in this matter produce such great consequences, when the law of inheritance is, after all, only a small part of the system of Shariah? Only one part, and such severe punishment for one part?

Apparently, this dreadful punishment seems far too great for the offence. But it seems so only to the one who has not reached the reality and depth of this matter.

Many verses of this surah speak continuously to express this reality, and their explanation and commentary come later, and we indicated this when presenting the introduction to this surah. These are the verses in which the meaning of the word din (religion) is explained, the conditions of faith are stated, and in which the definition of Islam is given. Nevertheless, it is appropriate that we give here a brief note on this matter, to the extent necessary for the explanation and understanding of these two verses, which are the conclusion and commentary of the verses of inheritance.

The fundamental question of this din, the religion of Islam, and indeed of all the divine heavenly religions sent by Allah through His messengers throughout the whole history of humanity, has always been this: who holds the right of sovereignty over this earth? Who is the Lord of these people? The answer to these two questions is given in these verses, and all the matters of this religion are settled in the light of these answers, and all the affairs of people are settled in the light of these same answers.

Now, what is the answer to this question? Who holds the right of sovereignty and lordship over this earth? Only Allah, alone; no one of His creation shares this right with Him. This is the very essence of faith, this is the very essence of Islam, and this is the religion of Islam. And if this right of sovereignty and lordship is given to any creature, and they are made partners with Allah, or this right is given to anyone independently apart from Allah, then this is clear shirk and manifest kufr.

Either sovereignty and lordship belong to Allah alone, without partner, and in that case people enter only the religion of Allah alone and enter only into the obedience of Allah alone, and its practical form will be that people follow the Islamic system of life. For in this case the right to prescribe a system of life for people belongs to Allah alone; it is Allah alone who lays down for people the ways, laws and regulations; then it is Allah alone who determines for people the standards of good and bad, and who organises the detailed ways and order of their life. And for no individual or society other than Allah will there be any such rights, and their only course will be to obey the Divine Shariah, because this obedience is the logical requirement of Allah's divinity, sovereignty and lordship, and the sole manifestation and particular form of this requirement is the system of Shariah.

And if this is not the case, then the other alternative is that the right of sovereignty and lordship is not held by any of Allah's creation. This right is either held in partnership with Allah, or it is held by these people independently. In this case, those who accept this right will be considered to have entered the religion of these non-Allah powers; thus they will be worshipping others than Allah. Then this will be obedience to others than Allah on the part of man, and its practical form will be that these people become followers of the ways of life, the regulations, the laws and the standards of good and bad prescribed by others than Allah, and all these things have been formulated by some humans. In this legislation and codification they will not be referring to the sovereignty of Allah or to His Book, but all these things will be shaped by some other references, and some other sources will be their sources of authority. Therefore this condition will be devoid of religion, faith will be absent, and there will be no Islam, while this condition is a condition of shirk, kufr, fisq and disobedience.

This is the real truth of the matter. Therefore, in this regard, if anyone breaks just one of the limits of Allah, or entirely rejects the whole Shariah, there is no difference in the actual reality. For one limit is also din, and the whole Shariah is also din. Hence the real target in this is this principle: whether people are affirming Allah as one without partner in sovereignty and lordship, or whether they are associating someone with Him in it, or setting aside the Being of Allah and accepting the sovereignty and lordship of some other people. As for the question of what people verbally claim, that they have entered the religion of Islam and are Muslims, if this claim is not reflected in their conduct, then there is no Islam.

This is that great reality to which the conclusion of these verses of inheritance points. It explains that the assignment of the shares of heirs in the system of inheritance is directly connected with obedience to Allah and to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). Otherwise, in this matter, there will be disobedience to Allah and His Messenger. Or its outcome will be gardens beneath which rivers flow, or its end will be in the form of a humiliating punishment which will be given eternally in the fire of Hell.

And this is the great reality whose expression has been repeated in several verses of this surah, and it has been stated in such a clear and decisive manner that no room has been left in it for any interpretation or hypocrisy.

To those who still introduce themselves in terms of Islam, I would give this invitation: let them clear their minds about this, and see how far they have moved away from the Islamic system of life and the religion of Islam.

After this discussion, it is now necessary to say a few words about the inheritance system of Islam, before which, in connection with (Qur'an 4:7) "For men is a share of what they earn, and for women is a share of what they earn," we stated this general principle, and likewise in connection with (Qur'an 4:11) "For the male is the equivalent of the share of two females," we also discussed it.

The inheritance system of Islam is an extremely just system, and one most harmonious with human nature. It is also most suitable to the practical realities of family life. This becomes clear when we make a comparative study of this system with all the systems that have prevailed in human history or prevail now, whether in ancient ignorance or modern ignorance. In no region of the world and in no nation or community has the system taken into account all the aims of the collective maintenance of the family in such a way. Each person's share and their responsibilities within the family have been determined with regard to one another. For example, the mother and father, who are among the sharers with fixed portions (dhawu al-furud), come first. After them, in this system, importance is given to the agnatic heirs ('asabat). This is because in the absence of parents, the maintenance of an orphan falls upon the agnatic heirs. It is these agnates who bear shares in paying blood money (diyah) and other collective liabilities. Therefore the Islamic system of inheritance is extremely fitting and suitable.

The foundation of this system rests on the principle that this family system has come into being from a single human soul. Therefore, neither children nor women will be deprived, merely because they are women or minors. Thus, if this system makes distinctions of rank in practical responsibilities, it makes no distinction on the basis of the essential nature of humanity. Therefore, in granting rights, no distinction is made in it between the sexes, male and female. Whatever difference there is has been made with regard to collective responsibilities, which arise from the collective maintenance of the family.

This system is in full accord with the nature of all living things and especially with human nature, and with the natural human inclination by which he wishes to maintain a deep connection with his offspring, and that through this progeny his existence is, as it were, given continuity. Therefore, because of this system of inheritance, a person remains content that what he stores up, in the form of wealth, through his effort and struggle, and what is his natural desire, is that the fruit of his labour should reach his children, and that his future generation should not be deprived of it. And the conviction that the fruit of his struggle will reach his children serves as a spur to his striving. He will increase his effort and endeavour further, and this will also be economically beneficial for the whole society. And because of this continuous striving, there will be no decline in the collective system of mutual support of society; rather, in this system it has been fully taken into account.

And the final point is that the inheritance system of Islam shatters the accumulated wealth of an individual when it reaches extremes, and redistributes it afresh. Therefore this system does not allow wealth to gather in one place, nor does it leave it frozen in a few hands. For example, in contrast to a system in which the entire inheritance goes to the eldest son, or is confined within a limited circle of close relatives. In this respect, this system is a means that renews the functioning of economic activity in society and keeps it balanced. And in it there is no visible intervention by any administration or any collective system, which no individual accepts willingly, since love of wealth and greed have been deposited in human nature. As for this continuous breaking of concentrations and repeated redistribution in the Islamic system of inheritance, it continues ongoing, and the human soul also accepts it gladly, because this system is in accordance with human nature and its natural love of property and its greed. And this is the real difference and distinction between this divine system of life and those other systems which man has devised for man. Lesson 13 at a glance:

In the first lesson of this surah, attention was given to the organisation of collective life within the Islamic society, and it was purified of all the impurities of jahiliyyah. In it, the rights of the helpless people of society, of orphans, and the protection of their property were guaranteed, and this protection and safeguarding was provided to them within the natural framework of a family, under collective supervision. After this, the principles of inheritance within a family were stated, and then all these rights and safeguards were linked to the worldview that Allah is the sovereign and Lord of all people. And it is He who, by His command and will, created this creation from a single soul, and that Allah began the collective order of humanity with the unit of a family. Then collective responsibilities of maintenance were imposed within that family. And this regulation of all the circumstances of life was linked to the knowledge and wisdom of Allah and to the limits and bounds He has prescribed, and it was decided that if they obey Allah they will deserve the reward of Paradise, and if they commit disobedience they will deserve the punishment of Hell.

The second lesson now organizes the collective life of the Islamic society from another angle, and cleanses it from the pollutions of jahiliyyah (the pre-Islamic age of ignorance) from another side. That is, it is purified from the licentiousness and immorality of jahiliyyah. For such people, it has been prescribed that they be separated from society and that restrictions be placed on their movement, unless they give up their conduct and sincerely repent, are ready to lead a pure life, and are prepared to return to the Islamic society anew with pure morals and character.

Then, in this second part, woman has been freed from the oppressions under whose millstone she was crushed in the days of jahiliyyah. She used to be buried alive, was treated with contempt, and various kinds of cruelties were inflicted upon her, so that the Islamic society might be built on healthy and firm foundations, with a general atmosphere that is pure and clean, and with a structure resting on a most solid base, with the family as its first brick.

At the end of this part, a further aspect of the family is regulated, namely the circle of prohibited relations (muharramat). Legislation has been made for this under the Shariah, and its method adopted is that the prohibited relations have been mentioned, and all other daughters of Adam have been declared lawful for man.

With these subjects this lesson also concludes, and this juz' of the Qur'an also reaches its end.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 4, verses 15–16 (part 1 of 2):

Review of the previous thirteen parts. Explanation of verses 15 to 16:

In order to curb obscenity, and for its purity and regulation, Islam adopted its own distinctive approach. First, it took measures to confine women guilty of immorality and to keep them away from society, provided that this crime was proven against them. Thereafter, it issued a command concerning men who committed the unnatural act, namely the Lut people (Lutis), that they should be made to suffer, but it did not fix any specific measure for this. And after that, it prescribed one single punishment for these people, namely the punishment of the hadd (prescribed penalty), which was mentioned in Surah al-Nur, that is, one hundred lashes. In addition, it prescribed the punishment of rajm (stoning) which is mentioned in the ahadith. The sole purpose of all these measures was to cleanse society of immorality and to protect the purity, nobility and chastity of society.

However, in all circumstances of punishment, the Shariah has made a complete arrangement for the protection of the accused. Such an arrangement that, with it in place, punishment on the basis of any error, any oppression, or mere conjecture and assumption becomes impossible. Especially in those dangerous crimes whose effects fall upon the flowing and ongoing life of people.

﴿And those who commit lewdness among your women, call against them four witnesses from among you. And if they testify, then confine them to houses until death takes them or Allah ordains for them a way.﴾ (51)

Translation: "And those of your women who commit immorality, call four men from among yourselves to testify against them. And if they testify, keep them confined in houses until death comes to them or Allah makes for them some way out."

In the verse, legislation has been made in a most cautious manner. The women upon whom this crime is imposed have been limited: ﴿min nisa'ikum﴾, that is, Muslim women. Likewise, the testimony that will be established against them has also been limited: ﴿minkum﴾, that is, the witnesses too must be Muslims.

Accordingly, the accused who will be punished are only those whose crime is proven, and the persons who will be presented as witnesses must necessarily be Muslims. If any of the Muslim women commits immorality, the testimony of non-Muslims against them is not accepted; rather, it is necessary that the witnesses, besides being Muslims, be four in number. That is, they must be from the Muslim society, living within that society, subject to Islamic Shariah, obedient to the Islamic leadership, have the sense of Islamic Shariah in their hearts, and be aware of the rights and responsibilities of that society. Therefore, the testimony of non-Muslims is not accepted in this matter. It is possible that a non-Muslim might give testimony merely to entangle a Muslim woman in a case. Moreover, the trustworthiness, integrity, fear of God and sense of propriety of a non-Muslim cannot be relied upon, because a non-Muslim has no interest in the purity of Islamic society, nor does he have an interest in the success of the judicial system in an Islamic society. These limitations and conditions on testimony remained in effect even when the punishment changed, that is, later when the punishment was altered to lashes and stoning.

﴿Then if they testify, confine them to houses﴾: they should not mix in society, should not further pollute it, should not marry, and should not engage in any other activity. ﴿Until death takes them﴾: that they should die in this way, in confinement, confined to houses. ﴿Or Allah ordains for them a way﴾: that is, He changes their condition, or changes the punishment, or brings some other change in their affairs. These words make it clearly evident that this ruling was not final and conclusive. It was for a specific, defined period and for certain particular circumstances, and at that time there were expectations that a final ruling would come for such offenders. And so it happened. This ruling changed into one hundred lashes in Surah al-Nur, and through the ahadith of the Messenger it changed into rajm (stoning). But the guarantees that were given to the accused regarding testimony and proof of the crime remain in force as they were.

Imam Ahmad, may Allah have mercy on him, narrated through Muhammad ibn Ja'far, Sa'id, Qatadah, Hasan, and Hittan ibn Abdullah al-Raqqashi, from Ibn al-Samit (may Allah be pleased with him), this narration: "When revelation descended upon the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, it had an effect upon him; he would become distressed and the colour of his face would change. One day revelation was coming to him, and when the state of the descent of revelation passed, he ﷺ said: 'Take it from me, Allah has made a way for these women. A married person with a married person, and a virgin with a virgin: for the married, one hundred lashes and then stoning with stones; and for the unmarried, one hundred lashes and one year of exile.'" This narration has been related by Imam Muslim from Qatadah, from Hasan, Hittan and Ubadah ibn al-Samit, through them from the Prophet ﷺ. The words are: "Take it from me, take it from me, Allah has made a way. The unmarried with the unmarried: one hundred lashes and one year of exile; and the married with the married: one hundred lashes and stoning with stones." The practical cases of Ma'iz and the Ghamidiyyah, as related in Sahih Muslim, are that the Prophet ﷺ gave them the punishment of rajm but did not strike them with lashes. Similarly, in the cases of the Jewish man and Jewish woman, he decided to stone them and did not lash them. From these practical cases it is known that the final decision was this.

﴿And those of you who commit it, harm them both. Then if they repent and reform, leave them alone. Indeed, Allah is ever Accepting of repentance and Merciful.﴾ (16)

Translation: "And those of you who commit it, cause them both to suffer. Then if they repent and make amends, leave them alone. Indeed, Allah is Oft-Returning, Most Merciful."

The correct view is that this verse refers to the two men who commit sodomy, that is, the act of the people of Lut. This view is that of Mujahid. Ibn Abbas (may Allah be pleased with him), Sa'id ibn Jubayr (may Allah be pleased with him) and others have said that the harm will be inflicted by abusing and reviling them and by striking them with shoes and the like.

﴿Then if they repent and reform, leave them alone﴾: as will come later. Repentance and reform means a complete change in their lives, a complete change in their outlook and the direction of their conduct. This is why, after this complete and all-encompassing reform, their punishment is suspended, and society also does not insist on continuing the punishment of such deviant and misguided individuals. Leaving them alone here means precisely this: that their punishment is to be suspended.

And in this phrase there is a subtle allusion: ﴿Indeed, Allah is Oft-Returning, Most Merciful﴾. He is the One who prescribed this punishment, and He is the One who does not deem it appropriate to continue this punishment after the reform of their condition. In this matter, people have no authority to prescribe punishment, to legislate in this matter, nor do they have the authority to suspend it; their task is only to strive for the implementation of Allah's guidance and law. He is the Accepter of repentance and the Merciful. And He also shows mercy to those who reform.

And there is a second allusion in it: that people too should adopt the character of Allah, and create in themselves divine attributes and morals. Since Allah is the Oft-Returning and the Merciful, it is also their duty that in mutual relations they forgive the one who apologizes, and overlook it, since it was a sin that has occurred and passed. And after that there has been repentance and reform. However, this does not mean that leniency should be shown to criminals or that leniency should be shown to those who spread immorality.
