In such matters the question of leniency simply does not arise. Leniency and kindness will be shown only to those who have repented and become reformed. Concerning such people the ruling is that they should be accepted in society, that their former sins should not be recalled to them, and they should not be taunted, because they have repented and reformed. Therefore, in this process of reforming their condition, they should be supported and encouraged, and their crimes should be forgotten so that they are not harmed by past memories and suffer no hardship in their life in society. For if society does not forget the past of such people, it is possible that they may, in this crime, abandon the path of reform and fall into it again, and persist in it, and be ruined in this world and the Hereafter, and spread corruption in society, further polluting it, and become a further affliction for society.

This punishment too was changed in a later period. Ibn Abbas (may Allah be pleased with him) narrated a marfu' hadith which the compilers of the Sunan have related: the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "If you find someone doing the deed of the people of Lut, kill both the one who does it and the one to whom it is done."

These rulings show how hard the Islamic society strives for its moral purity, especially against immorality. Thus, the Islamic society began paying attention to moral purification very early on. For moral purification, Islam did not wait for the establishment of an Islamic government in Medina, so that once the government was established it would then begin implementing the Shariah laws. Before the implementation of the law, in Surah al-Isra, which is a Meccan surah, adultery was prohibited: ﴿And do not approach unlawful sexual intercourse; indeed, it is an immorality and an evil way.﴾ (23). And in Surah al-Mu'minun: ﴿Certainly the believers have succeeded, those who are humble in their prayer, and those who avoid unlawful sexual intercourse, except with their wives or those their right hands possess, for indeed, they are not to be blamed.﴾

Translation: "Successful are the believers who are humble in their prayer, and who guard their private parts, except from their wives or those whom their right hands possess, for then they are not blameworthy."

And further, in Surah al-Ma'arij, it was mentioned again.

It is no secret that in Mecca there was neither an Islamic government nor an Islamic administration; therefore, despite the prohibition of these crimes, Islam did not prescribe any punishment for them in Mecca. Yes, when an Islamic government and an Islamic administration were established in Medina, then, for the eradication of crimes, mere preaching, exhortation and enjoining good and forbidding evil was not relied upon again. This is because Islam is a realistic religion. It knew that mere guidance, preaching, and enjoining good and forbidding evil are not sufficient to protect society from filth. And it also knew that religion cannot be established without a state and government, and that religion is a complete methodology and a full system of life upon which the entire practical life of people is established. Religion is not merely a name for theoretical consciousness that is confined only to the world of belief, lacks a backing government, lacks a legal system, lacks a defined methodology, and lacks a known and recognized constitution.

As soon as the Islamic worldview settled in the minds of some chosen people in Mecca, this worldview challenged jahiliyyah and jahili concepts within those hearts. This worldview began the intellectual purification of those hearts. And when Islam became a state in Medina, in which the system of the Shariah was enforced and the Islamic way of life came to the fore in a definite form, then the Islamic government began to eliminate immorality from society, and a system of punishment was enforced for it. But the system of preaching and admonition also continued to function in its own place. This is because Islam is not merely a theory that works only in the world of the heart, but is also a system of state which must be enforced in the practical life of people. Therefore, theory and practice are the two feet of Islam; it can never stand on one foot.

This has been the form of every religion that has ever been sent down by Allah upon this earth. Some people have the mistaken notion that there have been religions that had no Shariah. It is absolutely impossible that there be a religion without a Shariah, without a government, because religion is a complete system of life, and it is a practical system. In it people obey Allah alone, take all guidance from Him alone, take their worldview from Him alone, take their moral values from Him alone, and take their law and practical directives from Him alone, and from Him alone they take law and enforce it with the power of government. Those who violate this system and law are punished, and in this way society is purified of the filth of jahiliyyah, so that religion becomes exclusively for Allah, and the whole and complete religion becomes that of Allah, and there is no ilah (deity) other than Allah, in any form. That is, no ilah who is a lawgiver for people, who sets standards of good and evil for them, who organizes their lives, and who holds the position of legislating for human beings. For ilah is precisely that which does all these things. Whoever among humans assigns to himself any of the above aspects, know that he has, in effect, claimed divinity. And it is evident that a system of life that comes from Allah can never permit such a person to make such a claim and act upon it.

Therefore, the logical conclusion is that whatever religion comes from Allah will bring with it a pure worldview and certain intuitive concepts; it will have with it a practical Shariah; and after that it will attain a system of government, in which the Shariah will be enforced.

Such was the situation that Islam created in Madinah Taybah. It laid the foundation of a state, legislation was enacted for it, and crimes were punished. Just as we are seeing the details of these laws and commands one by one in this surah, these commands and laws underwent change from time to time, and they took their final form. Whatever happened, happened as Allah willed.

There is nothing unusual in the Islamic state enacting such strict laws to eradicate indecency from society and uprooting it. Through legislation, its enforcement, punishment, training and discipline, the Islamic society is being purified. This is because in every age the first sign of jahiliyyah (the age of ignorance) is that sexual anarchy is encouraged within it, as we see everywhere in the modern jahiliyyah of our age. Human beings have been reduced to animals in sexual matters. There is no code of conduct for sexual relations, no law remains, and this sexual anarchy and free mixing of the sexes is regarded as personal freedom, and whoever opposes it is called regressive.

The worshippers of jahiliyyah may set aside all their other freedoms, but they are in no way prepared to give up this animal freedom. They can abandon all other freedoms, but whoever seeks to regulate their animal sexual freedom and purify it, they rise up against him.

An important policy of a jahili society is also that all its sectors cooperate with one another in the breaking down of moral codes. All these organizations are engaged in destroying the natural codes present within the human self. They make this animal sexual wantonness appear attractive in the eyes of people, present it under very beautiful and pure titles, stir up excitement in sexual relations by various means, and compel it to be bound by no code. This jahili system removes control from the family over a young person, and indeed it destroys the family system itself, and it transforms healthy sexual consciousness into base, naked sexual wantonness. It declares this to be praiseworthy, and for its sake it promotes obscenity, and this obscenity becomes prevalent simultaneously in the physical, emotional and expressive form, that is, in literature. The body becomes naked, emotions become naked, and literature becomes naked.

When Islam came, all the features of this fallen jahiliyyah were present in society, and one of the goals of Islam was to purify human beings, their concepts and human societies from these filths. These features are present in every jahili system. Those who have read the verses of Imru' al-Qays, the leader of Arab jahiliyyah, will find exactly similar examples in Greek jahiliyyah. Similar examples are also found in Roman jahiliyyah, and this same direction is the orientation of all jahili manners today, including the jahili literature of today's Arabs. Likewise, if the customs of any one jahili society are studied, there will be found in it the vulgarity of women, the tearing of collars of lovers, and unrestrained mixing of men and women, and these are the qualities found in every ancient and modern jahiliyyah. And this is the common ground among them all. These qualities are the product of one and the same thinking and are wholly alike.

History bears witness that it is this sexual wantonness which caused the process of breakdown within civilizations, through which nations fell into the pit of decline. This same situation befell Greek civilization. After that, the same calamity befell the Romans, and the ancient Persian civilization was also destroyed by the same causes. Even today, the European and American societies of Western civilization are falling victim to breakdown because of this sexual wantonness. The civilizational decline of these societies has begun, although their industrial and cultural progress is at its peak. The thinkers and intellectuals of the West are greatly troubled by the beginning of this civilizational decline, but, as is evident from their statements and analyses, they are unable to place any kind of dam against this process of decay. (1) (See Maulana Sayyid Mawdudi, may Allah have mercy on him, Amir of Jamaat-e-Islami Pakistan, in his book "al-Hijab".)

Despite the fact that they know their end well, the standard-bearers of jahiliyyah, in every age and in every place, are pushed toward this decline. Sometimes they renounce all human freedoms, or become ready to do so, but if even a slight obstacle comes before their animal freedom, they are absolutely not prepared for it. They are ready for complete slavery, but they are not ready to abandon this animal sexual freedom.

Is this freedom? Are these rights? I think this is a return from human dignity to animal life, and the worst slavery to animal demands. Rather, these people have fallen even lower than animals. The condition of animals is that their sexual desire is confined within a natural restraint. Allah has fixed a season for animals in which both male and female develop the desire for sexual union. And this sexual union is also not merely for pleasure, but for the purposes of nature, namely the propagation of the species. The female animal accepts the male only at a fixed time, and the male too is inclined only when the female is ready. As for the human being, Allah the Exalted has placed his sexual desire under the control of his intellect, and has made his intellect subordinate to his worldview. Whenever human intellect goes outside the control of his worldview of life, human intellect cannot resist natural desire and pressure; it becomes weak before physical demands. In such circumstances, the restraint of carnal desires becomes difficult and purifying society of this filth becomes impossible. Only a worldview of life can do this, which firmly seizes the reins of the unbridled self. After this, on the strength of this worldview of life, the existence of a political power based upon this creed and worldview becomes necessary, and for this power to come to government is also necessary, so that this government, by means of training, guidance and punishment of deviants, blocks their path, turns the human being away from wrong paths, raises him from the animal station, and brings humanity to the lofty station of the most honoured of creatures.

Whenever a human being enters the age of jahiliyyah, he has no worldview of life. Even the collective government that he has has no worldview. This is why, for a long time, the thinkers of Western jahiliyyah have been crying out, and there is no one who pays attention to them. This is because a human being never pays attention to mere empty talk. Unless these matters are backed by enforcing power, the same applies. Likewise, in the West, the people of the church and religious people have been crying out continuously, but there is no one who listens to them, because people do not pay attention merely to ideas, unless those ideas are backed by government and it supports them, and acts upon the guidance of those ideas, enforcing laws and regulations. This is why humanity is hurrying toward the pit of hell. It is free even from the natural code which Allah Himself has fixed for animals. That is the theory. That theory is also free from the bonds of faith and the Shariah which Allah has revealed for humankind.

The destruction and ruin of this Western civilization is certain, in the light of the previous historical experiences that occurred in the history of all jahili civilizations, however firm and systematized they may appear outwardly, however broad-based they may appear outwardly. This is because the human being is a greater and more important creation than civilization. When the human being is destroyed, human civilization cannot be saved merely on the strength of industry and mass production.

This is the real truth, and once we reach its depths, we will know how great a system of life Islam is, and why it has prescribed such severe punishments for sexual wantonness. Merely so that "the human being" may be saved from destruction, and human life may be founded upon genuinely human foundations. And from this we will also come to realize how great a crime those institutions and governments commit against humanity which are eradicating these human foundations. They commit this crime merely by spreading indecency, by awakening the feelings of animal lust, and by organizing sexual wantonness through obscenity. Sometimes they give it the name of art and craftsmanship, sometimes they call it freedom, and sometimes they call it progressivism. But our duty is that we stand against every form and every title of the destruction of humanity, and check it through admonition, preaching, and reward and punishment. This is the task which in this world only Islam is carrying out, and it does so through the enforcement of Islam's complete system of life, which is extremely firmly founded. (1) (See my book "al-Islam wa al-Salam al-'Alami", the chapter "Gharr ki Salamati" [Security of the Home].)

Yes, despite these legal measures against sexual wantonness, Islam does not close the door of return for wrongdoers. If they repent, take the path of purity and wish to return, the doors of repentance are open. Rather, Islam provides an open path for their return, and it encourages their return. Whenever they repent, Allah accepts their repentance, and Allah has made it binding upon Himself, for the sinners, that He will certainly accept repentance. "Even if you break your repentance a hundred times, return." This is a great favour of Allah which has reached its limit, and no further increase in it is possible now.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 4, verses 15–16 (part 1 of 2):

Review of the previous thirteen parts. Explanation of verses 15 to 16:

In order to curb obscenity, and for its purity and regulation, Islam adopted its own distinctive approach. First, it took measures to confine women guilty of immorality and to keep them away from society, provided that this crime was proven against them. Thereafter, it issued a command concerning men who committed the unnatural act, namely the Lut people (Lutis), that they should be made to suffer, but it did not fix any specific measure for this. And after that, it prescribed one single punishment for these people, namely the punishment of the hadd (prescribed penalty), which was mentioned in Surah al-Nur, that is, one hundred lashes. In addition, it prescribed the punishment of rajm (stoning) which is mentioned in the ahadith. The sole purpose of all these measures was to cleanse society of immorality and to protect the purity, nobility and chastity of society.

However, in all circumstances of punishment, the Shariah has made a complete arrangement for the protection of the accused. Such an arrangement that, with it in place, punishment on the basis of any error, any oppression, or mere conjecture and assumption becomes impossible. Especially in those dangerous crimes whose effects fall upon the flowing and ongoing life of people.

﴿And those who commit lewdness among your women, call against them four witnesses from among you. And if they testify, then confine them to houses until death takes them or Allah ordains for them a way.﴾ (51)

Translation: "And those of your women who commit immorality, call four men from among yourselves to testify against them. And if they testify, keep them confined in houses until death comes to them or Allah makes for them some way out."

In the verse, legislation has been made in a most cautious manner. The women upon whom this crime is imposed have been limited: ﴿min nisa'ikum﴾, that is, Muslim women. Likewise, the testimony that will be established against them has also been limited: ﴿minkum﴾, that is, the witnesses too must be Muslims.

Accordingly, the accused who will be punished are only those whose crime is proven, and the persons who will be presented as witnesses must necessarily be Muslims. If any of the Muslim women commits immorality, the testimony of non-Muslims against them is not accepted; rather, it is necessary that the witnesses, besides being Muslims, be four in number. That is, they must be from the Muslim society, living within that society, subject to Islamic Shariah, obedient to the Islamic leadership, have the sense of Islamic Shariah in their hearts, and be aware of the rights and responsibilities of that society. Therefore, the testimony of non-Muslims is not accepted in this matter. It is possible that a non-Muslim might give testimony merely to entangle a Muslim woman in a case. Moreover, the trustworthiness, integrity, fear of God and sense of propriety of a non-Muslim cannot be relied upon, because a non-Muslim has no interest in the purity of Islamic society, nor does he have an interest in the success of the judicial system in an Islamic society. These limitations and conditions on testimony remained in effect even when the punishment changed, that is, later when the punishment was altered to lashes and stoning.

﴿Then if they testify, confine them to houses﴾: they should not mix in society, should not further pollute it, should not marry, and should not engage in any other activity. ﴿Until death takes them﴾: that they should die in this way, in confinement, confined to houses. ﴿Or Allah ordains for them a way﴾: that is, He changes their condition, or changes the punishment, or brings some other change in their affairs. These words make it clearly evident that this ruling was not final and conclusive. It was for a specific, defined period and for certain particular circumstances, and at that time there were expectations that a final ruling would come for such offenders. And so it happened. This ruling changed into one hundred lashes in Surah al-Nur, and through the ahadith of the Messenger it changed into rajm (stoning). But the guarantees that were given to the accused regarding testimony and proof of the crime remain in force as they were.

Imam Ahmad, may Allah have mercy on him, narrated through Muhammad ibn Ja'far, Sa'id, Qatadah, Hasan, and Hittan ibn Abdullah al-Raqqashi, from Ibn al-Samit (may Allah be pleased with him), this narration: "When revelation descended upon the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, it had an effect upon him; he would become distressed and the colour of his face would change. One day revelation was coming to him, and when the state of the descent of revelation passed, he ﷺ said: 'Take it from me, Allah has made a way for these women. A married person with a married person, and a virgin with a virgin: for the married, one hundred lashes and then stoning with stones; and for the unmarried, one hundred lashes and one year of exile.'" This narration has been related by Imam Muslim from Qatadah, from Hasan, Hittan and Ubadah ibn al-Samit, through them from the Prophet ﷺ. The words are: "Take it from me, take it from me, Allah has made a way. The unmarried with the unmarried: one hundred lashes and one year of exile; and the married with the married: one hundred lashes and stoning with stones." The practical cases of Ma'iz and the Ghamidiyyah, as related in Sahih Muslim, are that the Prophet ﷺ gave them the punishment of rajm but did not strike them with lashes. Similarly, in the cases of the Jewish man and Jewish woman, he decided to stone them and did not lash them. From these practical cases it is known that the final decision was this.

﴿And those of you who commit it, harm them both. Then if they repent and reform, leave them alone. Indeed, Allah is ever Accepting of repentance and Merciful.﴾ (16)

Translation: "And those of you who commit it, cause them both to suffer. Then if they repent and make amends, leave them alone. Indeed, Allah is Oft-Returning, Most Merciful."

The correct view is that this verse refers to the two men who commit sodomy, that is, the act of the people of Lut. This view is that of Mujahid. Ibn Abbas (may Allah be pleased with him), Sa'id ibn Jubayr (may Allah be pleased with him) and others have said that the harm will be inflicted by abusing and reviling them and by striking them with shoes and the like.

﴿Then if they repent and reform, leave them alone﴾: as will come later. Repentance and reform means a complete change in their lives, a complete change in their outlook and the direction of their conduct. This is why, after this complete and all-encompassing reform, their punishment is suspended, and society also does not insist on continuing the punishment of such deviant and misguided individuals. Leaving them alone here means precisely this: that their punishment is to be suspended.

And in this phrase there is a subtle allusion: ﴿Indeed, Allah is Oft-Returning, Most Merciful﴾. He is the One who prescribed this punishment, and He is the One who does not deem it appropriate to continue this punishment after the reform of their condition. In this matter, people have no authority to prescribe punishment, to legislate in this matter, nor do they have the authority to suspend it; their task is only to strive for the implementation of Allah's guidance and law. He is the Accepter of repentance and the Merciful. And He also shows mercy to those who reform.

And there is a second allusion in it: that people too should adopt the character of Allah, and create in themselves divine attributes and morals. Since Allah is the Oft-Returning and the Merciful, it is also their duty that in mutual relations they forgive the one who apologizes, and overlook it, since it was a sin that has occurred and passed. And after that there has been repentance and reform. However, this does not mean that leniency should be shown to criminals or that leniency should be shown to those who spread immorality. In such matters the question of leniency simply does not arise. Leniency and kindness will be shown only to those who have repented and become reformed. Concerning such people the ruling is that they should be accepted in society, that their former sins should not be recalled to them, and they should not be taunted, because they have repented and reformed. Therefore, in this process of reforming their condition, they should be supported and encouraged, and their crimes should be forgotten so that they are not harmed by past memories and suffer no hardship in their life in society. For if society does not forget the past of such people, it is possible that they may, in this crime, abandon the path of reform and fall into it again, and persist in it, and be ruined in this world and the Hereafter, and spread corruption in society, further polluting it, and become a further affliction for society.

This punishment too was changed in a later period. Ibn Abbas (may Allah be pleased with him) narrated a marfu' hadith which the compilers of the Sunan have related: the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "If you find someone doing the deed of the people of Lut, kill both the one who does it and the one to whom it is done."

These rulings show how hard the Islamic society strives for its moral purity, especially against immorality. Thus, the Islamic society began paying attention to moral purification very early on. For moral purification, Islam did not wait for the establishment of an Islamic government in Medina, so that once the government was established it would then begin implementing the Shariah laws. Before the implementation of the law, in Surah al-Isra, which is a Meccan surah, adultery was prohibited: ﴿And do not approach unlawful sexual intercourse; indeed, it is an immorality and an evil way.﴾ (23). And in Surah al-Mu'minun: ﴿Certainly the believers have succeeded, those who are humble in their prayer, and those who avoid unlawful sexual intercourse, except with their wives or those their right hands possess, for indeed, they are not to be blamed.﴾

Translation: "Successful are the believers who are humble in their prayer, and who guard their private parts, except from their wives or those whom their right hands possess, for then they are not blameworthy."

And further, in Surah al-Ma'arij, it was mentioned again.

It is no secret that in Mecca there was neither an Islamic government nor an Islamic administration; therefore, despite the prohibition of these crimes, Islam did not prescribe any punishment for them in Mecca. Yes, when an Islamic government and an Islamic administration were established in Medina, then, for the eradication of crimes, mere preaching, exhortation and enjoining good and forbidding evil was not relied upon again. This is because Islam is a realistic religion. It knew that mere guidance, preaching, and enjoining good and forbidding evil are not sufficient to protect society from filth. And it also knew that religion cannot be established without a state and government, and that religion is a complete methodology and a full system of life upon which the entire practical life of people is established. Religion is not merely a name for theoretical consciousness that is confined only to the world of belief, lacks a backing government, lacks a legal system, lacks a defined methodology, and lacks a known and recognized constitution.

As soon as the Islamic worldview settled in the minds of some chosen people in Mecca, this worldview challenged jahiliyyah and jahili concepts within those hearts. This worldview began the intellectual purification of those hearts. And when Islam became a state in Medina, in which the system of the Shariah was enforced and the Islamic way of life came to the fore in a definite form, then the Islamic government began to eliminate immorality from society, and a system of punishment was enforced for it. But the system of preaching and admonition also continued to function in its own place. This is because Islam is not merely a theory that works only in the world of the heart, but is also a system of state which must be enforced in the practical life of people. Therefore, theory and practice are the two feet of Islam; it can never stand on one foot.

This has been the form of every religion that has ever been sent down by Allah upon this earth. Some people have the mistaken notion that there have been religions that had no Shariah. It is absolutely impossible that there be a religion without a Shariah, without a government, because religion is a complete system of life, and it is a practical system. In it people obey Allah alone, take all guidance from Him alone, take their worldview from Him alone, take their moral values from Him alone, and take their law and practical directives from Him alone, and from Him alone they take law and enforce it with the power of government. Those who violate this system and law are punished, and in this way society is purified of the filth of jahiliyyah, so that religion becomes exclusively for Allah, and the whole and complete religion becomes that of Allah, and there is no ilah (deity) other than Allah, in any form. That is, no ilah who is a lawgiver for people, who sets standards of good and evil for them, who organizes their lives, and who holds the position of legislating for human beings. For ilah is precisely that which does all these things. Whoever among humans assigns to himself any of the above aspects, know that he has, in effect, claimed divinity. And it is evident that a system of life that comes from Allah can never permit such a person to make such a claim and act upon it.

Therefore, the logical conclusion is that whatever religion comes from Allah will bring with it a pure worldview and certain intuitive concepts; it will have with it a practical Shariah; and after that it will attain a system of government, in which the Shariah will be enforced.

Such was the situation that Islam created in Madinah Taybah. It laid the foundation of a state, legislation was enacted for it, and crimes were punished. Just as we are seeing the details of these laws and commands one by one in this surah, these commands and laws underwent change from time to time, and they took their final form. Whatever happened, happened as Allah willed.

There is nothing unusual in the Islamic state enacting such strict laws to eradicate indecency from society and uprooting it. Through legislation, its enforcement, punishment, training and discipline, the Islamic society is being purified. This is because in every age the first sign of jahiliyyah (the age of ignorance) is that sexual anarchy is encouraged within it, as we see everywhere in the modern jahiliyyah of our age. Human beings have been reduced to animals in sexual matters. There is no code of conduct for sexual relations, no law remains, and this sexual anarchy and free mixing of the sexes is regarded as personal freedom, and whoever opposes it is called regressive.

The worshippers of jahiliyyah may set aside all their other freedoms, but they are in no way prepared to give up this animal freedom. They can abandon all other freedoms, but whoever seeks to regulate their animal sexual freedom and purify it, they rise up against him.

An important policy of a jahili society is also that all its sectors cooperate with one another in the breaking down of moral codes. All these organizations are engaged in destroying the natural codes present within the human self. They make this animal sexual wantonness appear attractive in the eyes of people, present it under very beautiful and pure titles, stir up excitement in sexual relations by various means, and compel it to be bound by no code. This jahili system removes control from the family over a young person, and indeed it destroys the family system itself, and it transforms healthy sexual consciousness into base, naked sexual wantonness. It declares this to be praiseworthy, and for its sake it promotes obscenity, and this obscenity becomes prevalent simultaneously in the physical, emotional and expressive form, that is, in literature. The body becomes naked, emotions become naked, and literature becomes naked.

When Islam came, all the features of this fallen jahiliyyah were present in society, and one of the goals of Islam was to purify human beings, their concepts and human societies from these filths. These features are present in every jahili system. Those who have read the verses of Imru' al-Qays, the leader of Arab jahiliyyah, will find exactly similar examples in Greek jahiliyyah. Similar examples are also found in Roman jahiliyyah, and this same direction is the orientation of all jahili manners today, including the jahili literature of today's Arabs. Likewise, if the customs of any one jahili society are studied, there will be found in it the vulgarity of women, the tearing of collars of lovers, and unrestrained mixing of men and women, and these are the qualities found in every ancient and modern jahiliyyah. And this is the common ground among them all. These qualities are the product of one and the same thinking and are wholly alike.

History bears witness that it is this sexual wantonness which caused the process of breakdown within civilizations, through which nations fell into the pit of decline. This same situation befell Greek civilization. After that, the same calamity befell the Romans, and the ancient Persian civilization was also destroyed by the same causes. Even today, the European and American societies of Western civilization are falling victim to breakdown because of this sexual wantonness. The civilizational decline of these societies has begun, although their industrial and cultural progress is at its peak. The thinkers and intellectuals of the West are greatly troubled by the beginning of this civilizational decline, but, as is evident from their statements and analyses, they are unable to place any kind of dam against this process of decay. (1) (See Maulana Sayyid Mawdudi, may Allah have mercy on him, Amir of Jamaat-e-Islami Pakistan, in his book "al-Hijab".)

Despite the fact that they know their end well, the standard-bearers of jahiliyyah, in every age and in every place, are pushed toward this decline. Sometimes they renounce all human freedoms, or become ready to do so, but if even a slight obstacle comes before their animal freedom, they are absolutely not prepared for it. They are ready for complete slavery, but they are not ready to abandon this animal sexual freedom.

Is this freedom? Are these rights? I think this is a return from human dignity to animal life, and the worst slavery to animal demands. Rather, these people have fallen even lower than animals. The condition of animals is that their sexual desire is confined within a natural restraint. Allah has fixed a season for animals in which both male and female develop the desire for sexual union. And this sexual union is also not merely for pleasure, but for the purposes of nature, namely the propagation of the species. The female animal accepts the male only at a fixed time, and the male too is inclined only when the female is ready. As for the human being, Allah the Exalted has placed his sexual desire under the control of his intellect, and has made his intellect subordinate to his worldview. Whenever human intellect goes outside the control of his worldview of life, human intellect cannot resist natural desire and pressure; it becomes weak before physical demands. In such circumstances, the restraint of carnal desires becomes difficult and purifying society of this filth becomes impossible. Only a worldview of life can do this, which firmly seizes the reins of the unbridled self. After this, on the strength of this worldview of life, the existence of a political power based upon this creed and worldview becomes necessary, and for this power to come to government is also necessary, so that this government, by means of training, guidance and punishment of deviants, blocks their path, turns the human being away from wrong paths, raises him from the animal station, and brings humanity to the lofty station of the most honoured of creatures.

Whenever a human being enters the age of jahiliyyah, he has no worldview of life. Even the collective government that he has has no worldview. This is why, for a long time, the thinkers of Western jahiliyyah have been crying out, and there is no one who pays attention to them. This is because a human being never pays attention to mere empty talk. Unless these matters are backed by enforcing power, the same applies. Likewise, in the West, the people of the church and religious people have been crying out continuously, but there is no one who listens to them, because people do not pay attention merely to ideas, unless those ideas are backed by government and it supports them, and acts upon the guidance of those ideas, enforcing laws and regulations. This is why humanity is hurrying toward the pit of hell. It is free even from the natural code which Allah Himself has fixed for animals. That is the theory. That theory is also free from the bonds of faith and the Shariah which Allah has revealed for humankind.

The destruction and ruin of this Western civilization is certain, in the light of the previous historical experiences that occurred in the history of all jahili civilizations, however firm and systematized they may appear outwardly, however broad-based they may appear outwardly. This is because the human being is a greater and more important creation than civilization. When the human being is destroyed, human civilization cannot be saved merely on the strength of industry and mass production.

This is the real truth, and once we reach its depths, we will know how great a system of life Islam is, and why it has prescribed such severe punishments for sexual wantonness. Merely so that "the human being" may be saved from destruction, and human life may be founded upon genuinely human foundations. And from this we will also come to realize how great a crime those institutions and governments commit against humanity which are eradicating these human foundations. They commit this crime merely by spreading indecency, by awakening the feelings of animal lust, and by organizing sexual wantonness through obscenity. Sometimes they give it the name of art and craftsmanship, sometimes they call it freedom, and sometimes they call it progressivism. But our duty is that we stand against every form and every title of the destruction of humanity, and check it through admonition, preaching, and reward and punishment. This is the task which in this world only Islam is carrying out, and it does so through the enforcement of Islam's complete system of life, which is extremely firmly founded. (1) (See my book "al-Islam wa al-Salam al-'Alami", the chapter "Gharr ki Salamati" [Security of the Home].)

Yes, despite these legal measures against sexual wantonness, Islam does not close the door of return for wrongdoers. If they repent, take the path of purity and wish to return, the doors of repentance are open. Rather, Islam provides an open path for their return, and it encourages their return. Whenever they repent, Allah accepts their repentance, and Allah has made it binding upon Himself, for the sinners, that He will certainly accept repentance. "Even if you break your repentance a hundred times, return." This is a great favour of Allah which has reached its limit, and no further increase in it is possible now.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran (Urdu translation)) on surah 4, verse 17:

(Verse) "Indama al-tawbatu 'ala Allahi lilladhina ya'maluna al-su'a bi-jahalatin thumma yatubuna min qaribin fa-ulaika yatubu Allahu 'alayhim, wa kana Allahu 'Aliman Hakiman" (71). "Wa laysat al-tawbatu lilladhina ya'maluna al-sayyi'at, hatta idha hadara ahadahumu al-mawtu qala inni tubtu al-an, wa la alladhina yamutuna wa hum kuffar, ula'ika a'tadna lahum 'adhaban alima" (81).

Regarding this matter, we have discussed repentance in Fi Zilal al-Quran while explaining Surah Al 'Imran, where the verse is: "Wa alladhina idha fa'alu fahishatan aw zalamu anfusahum dhakaru Allaha fa-istaghfaru li-dhunubihim" – "Those who, when they commit an indecency or wrong themselves, remember Allah and immediately seek forgiveness for their sins."

That entire discussion can also be cited in the explanation of this verse. However, the manner of expression adopted here for repentance indicates a different purpose. Here the emphasis is on: what is the reality of repentance?

The repentance that Allah accepts, and whose acceptance Allah has made binding upon Himself, is that which rises from the depths of the self, through which it becomes known that this human self has taken a new birth; remorse has shaken it to its depths and stirred it so much that it has changed its direction, and it has turned towards Allah. In this sense, repentance is a return for the whole of life, a ray of new hope. It carries a renewed resolve to adopt purity, and there is a genuine intention that the one who repents will walk the new paths with sincerity of heart.

(Verse) "Innama al-tawbatu 'ala Allahi lilladhina ya'maluna al-su'a bi-jahalatin thumma yatubuna min qaribin fa-ulaika yatubu Allahu 'alayhim, wa kana Allahu 'Aliman Hakiman" (71)

Translation: "Indeed, the acceptance of repentance by Allah is only for those who commit evil out of ignorance and then repent soon after. Such people Allah turns back to with His mercy. And Allah is All-Knowing and All-Wise."

Those who commit an evil deed out of ignorance, who commit a sin. On this matter there appears to be almost a consensus that ignorance here means doctrinal error, whether it lasts for a long or short period, provided the perpetrator of the sin is not persisting in it, and provided the state of death agony (naza') has not begun. And who are those who repent soon? They are those who return before the sight of death or the onset of the agonies of death (sakarat al-mawt), before the threshold of death has yet appeared to them. Then this repentance is considered repentance of remorse. Coming out of sin, resolving upon righteous deeds, and resolving to make expiation for sins is indeed true repentance, and through it the human self is, as it were, given a new birth, and the conscience awakens afresh.

(Verse) "Fa-ulaika yatubu Allahu 'alayhim" – such people Allah turns back to with His mercy. "Wa kana Allahu 'Aliman Hakiman" – And Allah is All-Knowing and All-Wise. He takes all measures on the basis of knowledge and wisdom, and He provides His weak servants the opportunity to return, so that they may again come and stand in the pure rows. He does not behave in such a way as to drive away sinners while they genuinely intend to refrain. They wish to return to His threshold of mercy and His house of peace.

Allah is Merciful and Generous; He does not reject His weak servants, nor does He pursue them, if they wish to abstain. He is free of need. If they turn back, what benefit is it to Him? It is indeed for their own benefit, it is their own benefit. Their own lives are set in order by it, and the society in which they themselves live is reformed. This is precisely the reason that He provides them with wide opportunities for return, repentance, and adopting a pure conduct.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 4, verse 18:

(Verse) "Repentance is not accepted from those who continue to do evil deeds until, when death approaches one of them, he says, 'Indeed, I repent now.'" Repentance is not for those who keep on doing bad deeds until, when death comes near to one of them, he says, "I have repented now." This is because such repentance is in effect the repentance of one who is desperate, who has sunk into misguidance and is surrounded by wrongdoing. It is the repentance of a person for whom there is no longer any opportunity to commit sin, and who can no longer fall into any wrongdoing. In such a state, Allah does not accept this repentance, because it does not show inner reform or a reform in the practical conduct of life. It does not show that any change has come into this person's heart, or that any better change has occurred in his outlook and direction.

Repentance is accepted because it is a door kept open for those who have fallen into moral decline, so that they may return and enter the peaceful refuge of Islam. They may come back from the darkness of misguidance, from the thick darkness, and humanity may bring them out of the group that works under the banners of Satan and bring them back, so that they may begin a righteous life. It is a separate matter whether, after this return, they are given the opportunity or not. At the very least, there should be the opportunity for them to declare that guidance has triumphed over misguidance, even if after this declaration they are given no further time and their life comes to an end, because no one knows at what moment death will arrive.

(Verse) "And nor is repentance for those who die while they are disbelievers." "And likewise, repentance is not for those who die while still in disbelief." Because these people have severed the connection that lay between them and repentance. They have squandered the respite that was given to them for repentance and for obtaining forgiveness.

(Verse) "For those, We have prepared a painful punishment." "For such people, We have prepared a painful punishment." It is prepared, fully made ready, present, existing, awaiting them. No preparation will be needed.

In short, it is true that the Islamic system has prescribed the severest punishment for immorality, but it has also left the door of repentance fully open. Thus a kind of balance is created within the severity of the punishment, and because of it there have arisen in human life results and effects that no ancient or modern system on this earth has produced.

The second theme of this lesson is woman, the woman's self. In Arab jahiliyyah (the age of ignorance), like all the other jahiliyyahs spread around Arabia, women were treated very badly. They did not have basic human rights. Compared with men, their status was very low; she was regarded as a commodity rather than a human being. And this was her status even while men derived comfort from her, derived animal pleasure from her, considered her a trial for the self, and she was described as a satanic temptation to the qualities of goodness and righteousness. She was merely the object of lustful indulgence and of shameless verses of love poetry. In such circumstances, when the Islamic system of life came, it removed all these oppressions from women. It gave her a genuine place and status within the family and restored her to her true position in human society, a status that fully accorded with the rank and position mentioned at the beginning of this surah: "He who created you from a single soul and created from it its mate, and from the two of them spread forth many men and women." Thereafter, the level of human emotion and human consciousness within married life was raised, and love, respect, compassion, kindness and good treatment toward one another were commanded, so that these relations might rise above the merely animal level to the human station, and be so firm that they do not break apart at a single blow.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 4, verse 19:

(Verse) "Yā ayyuhā alladhīna āmanū lā yahillu lakum an tarithū al-nisā'a karhan wa lā ta'ḍulūhunna litadhhabū biba'ḍi mā ātaytumūhunna illā an ya'tīna bifāḥishatin mubayyinatin, wa 'āshirūhunna bil-ma'rūf, fa-in karihtumūhunna fa'asā an takrahū shay'an wa yaj'alallāhu fīhi khayran kathīran." (19)

Before Islam raised the Arabs from the depths of degradation to the height of honour and nobility, the condition of the Arabs was that when a person died, his heirs became entitled to his wife as well, and she was inherited by them in the same way that other livestock passed to them as part of the estate. Now, if the heir wished, he would marry the woman himself. And if he wished, he would give her in marriage to another person and take her dower. Just as livestock were sold, this woman too was in effect sold. And if these heirs wished, they would keep her at home like a useless limb, without marrying her, leaving her as she was, until she paid off her freedom by giving up her own self (in compensation).

In some places the custom was that when the husband died, his guardian would rush over and throw a cloth over the woman. In this way he would, in effect, keep her away from all other people, and thus take possession of her as one takes possession of spoils of war. If she was beautiful, he would take her into marriage; and if she was ugly, she would remain confined, and after his death this man would become her heir, or she would free her neck by paying him some property. But if, after her husband's death, she immediately went to her parents' house and the heir could not throw a cloth over her, then she would be saved, and she would be considered free.

In some places the custom was that a man would divorce his wife and impose the condition that she could marry only where he permitted. Thus she would buy her freedom with property, returning the dower and giving back other gifts.

If someone had an orphan girl in his custody, he would keep her confined so that his underage son would reach maturity and marry her. Likewise, sometimes a widow would be kept confined for a small child.

These and other such customs were entirely contrary to the standard of nobility and honour, the nobility and honour that Islam grants to humankind. Yet woman is the companion of man, and both were created from a single soul. Through such conduct, just as woman had fallen from the station of honour and dignity, so too the situation was a cause of shame for men; it appeared as though the relationship between man and woman was a commercial relationship or merely an animal relationship.

In short, Islam lifted the relationship between man and woman out of that deep pit of humiliation and brought it to the honourable station of humanity. It gave it a station worthy of human nobility, because according to Islam's conception of humanity, the human being is a creature of honour among the worlds. Therefore it was Islam that granted humankind this exalted station, a lofty station that humans received only from the source and origin of Islam. (1) (The book "Islam's Concept of God, Concept of the Universe, Concept of Life and Concept of Man" is soon to be published.)

Islam declared unlawful the act of acquiring a woman as an item of inheritance, alongside other goods. Likewise, it prohibited confining her and rendering her a useless limb, except where she has committed the crime of immorality. And this too was at a time when the ruling on the punishment for adultery had not yet been revealed. In these circumstances Islam gave the woman the right to marry whomever she wishes, whether it is a first marriage or a second marriage, whether she is a virgin or a widow, divorced or whose husband has died. And it made it binding upon the man to live with her in accordance with what is customary (ma'ruf), even if the man does not like the woman. Yes, it is another matter if living with her has become impossible. For it may be that he dislikes the woman yet there is good for him in her. Therefore it is not appropriate for him that, as soon as aversion arises in his nature, he should divorce her. If he keeps the wife, then in the coming times he may also obtain benefit from her, so he should keep the lamp of hope burning.

(Verse) "Yā ayyuhā alladhīna āmanū lā yahillu lakum an tarithū al-nisā'a karhan wa lā ta'ḍulūhunna litadhhabū biba'ḍi mā ātaytumūhunna illā an ya'tīna bifāḥishatin mubayyinatin, wa 'āshirūhunna bil-ma'rūf, fa-in karihtumūhunna fa'asā an takrahū shay'an wa yaj'alallāhu fīhi khayran kathīran." (19)

"O you who believe, it is not lawful for you to inherit women by force, nor to restrain them in order to take back some of the dower you have given them, unless they commit a manifest immorality (then indeed you have the right to restrain them). Live with them in a good manner. If you dislike them, it may be that you dislike something while Allah has placed in it much good."

This is the final finishing point of this verse. In it, the human self is bound and connected to the Being of Allah. If a state of anger, wrath and agitation arises between husband and wife, it is cooled. If the wife is disliked, the heat of that dislike is somewhat softened so that peace may arise within the human self, and so that the marital bond does not become like a dry leaf which is moved here and there by the slightest breeze. For the marital bond is firmly tied to the bond with Allah. This relationship is joined to the pure and firm bond between the believer and his Lord.

According to the Islamic conception of life, a household, as the basic unit, should be a place of peace, tranquillity, love and compassion for the human being.

Therefore it wishes to establish the relationship between spouses also upon the foundation of affection, love, sympathy and self-sacrifice. And this can happen only if the relationship between husband and wife is founded upon complete consent and freedom, so that feelings of love, affection and sympathy are always present within the family. If ever bitterness arises, Islam's advice is: be patient. "If you dislike your wives, it is possible that you dislike something while Allah gives you good in it." This exhortation is given so that the marital bond is not dissolved at the first gust of emotion, so that the marriage is not broken at the first jolt, and this precious human institution does not fall to pieces and become the prey of man's changing feelings and fluttering inclinations.

Hazrat Umar (radiyallahu anhu) gave an excellent piece of advice to a man who wished to divorce his wife, and the only reason for the divorce was that he did not love her. "May you be ruined! Is there no foundation for establishing a household other than love? What of upbringing and responsibilities?"

As for the so-called intellectuals of today, the nonsense they spout in the name of love refers to changing, agitated and momentary emotions, and because of these transient matters they permit separation between spouses, thereby destroying this important institution. They say that if a wife does not love her husband, then this is a betrayal of her, and if a man does not love a woman, this too is a kind of betrayal on his part.

Those who speak in this way are people of petty spirit. In their minds and hearts there can be no lofty and exalted qualities above transient bodily desires, such as generosity, nobility, good conduct and forbearance; yet these qualities and inclinations and their base thinking are too high for those loud-mouthed people who are their slaves. Their thinking is limited because within it there is no place for Allah, Jalla Shanuhu, and therefore in their consciousness there is no concept of what Allah the Exalted is giving to the believers.

(Verse) "Fa-in karihtumūhunna fa'asā an takrahū shay'an wa yaj'alallāhu fīhi khayran kathīran."

"If you dislike them, it may be that you dislike something while Allah has placed in it much good."

The truth is that it is only through faith that a human being's standing is elevated, a person's priorities become lofty, and the goals of human life become exalted. The standard of human life rises somewhat above mere animal natural inclinations. Man does not remain merely a trader, nor is he an empty and meaningless framework.

If hopes of patience, forbearance, good conduct and reform are all dashed, and a life lived in good harmony becomes impossible, and separation becomes unavoidable in every condition, and the man is compelled to accept that the wife must be replaced, then in such circumstances the dower the woman has received and the property that has come to her shall be hers, and it shall not be lawful to take anything back from her, even if that property is large in quantity and valuable. Taking that property back from her is a manifest sin and a detestable act.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 4, verse 20:

(Ayah) "Wa in aradtumu istibdala zawjin makana zawjin wa ataytum ahadahunna qintaran fa la ta'khudhu minhu shay'an, a-ta'khudhunahu buhtanan wa ithman mubina" (4:20)

"And if you intend to replace one wife with another, and you have given one of them a heap of wealth, then take nothing back from it. Would you take it by slandering her and committing manifest wrong?"

Here too a deep human and intuitive touch is given. A glimpse of family life is shown. The expressions are wondrous and full of allusive signs.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on surah 4, verse 21:

(Verse) "Wa kayfa ta'khudhunahu wa qad afda ba'dukum ila ba'din wa akhadhna minkum mithaqan ghalizan" (12)

"And how could you take it back, when you have already enjoyed one another, and they have taken from you a firm covenant?"

Here the object of the verb afda (to be intimate, to reach/enjoy) has not been specified; the word has been left general. Through this, every kind of meaning can be expressed, and it can apply to all the implications. All the allusions revolve in the mind: physical enjoyment, feelings and inclinations, favours and thoughts, secrets and intimacies, and all the pleasures that can exist between husband and wife. Every form of the day and night of human life falls within the meaning of this word afda. In short, all those matters come before the screen of thought which are linked with the past of time and place of this important institution of husband and wife. Every heartbeat is afda, every longing glance is afda, every touch of the body is afda, sharing in grief and hope is afda. Every shared thought about the present and the future is afda, every past thought is afda, and, most exalted of all, the children born of the two of them are afda.

This is a heap of thoughts and feelings; the freshness of the memories of feelings and inclinations is brought onto the screen in just a few words.

(Verse) "Wa qad afda ba'dukum ila ba'din" – "and you have already enjoyed one another."

In the presence of these memories, a demand by the man for any trivial things now appears extremely petty, and out of shame he refrains from that self-interested demand. This is because he is seeing on the screen the pleasant images of the practical life of the recent past. Now these memories torment him at the time of separation, and he realises that all these events were involuntary.

Along with these memories, another matter, another factor, is also brought to mind. As it were, another image appears on the screen; another colour emerges.

(Verse) "Wa akhadhna minkum mithaqan ghalizan" – "and they have taken from you a firm covenant." The mithaq of marriage is in the name of Allah and with the khutbah in accordance with the sunnah of the Prophet. This marriage contract is a great covenant which cannot be disregarded. For a believer it is a very great matter. This marriage is between believers, and believers regard it as a great contract, indeed a mithaq. Respecting it is obligatory upon them.

At the end, a definitive prohibition is stated concerning a particular practice. This practice was prevalent in the Jahiliyyah: sons would marry their fathers' wives, and at times women were left suspended because of this right of marriage, until the child grew up and married his father's wife; and if he was grown, he would regard the wife of his father as an inheritable property. Islam declared this practice forbidden in the strongest terms.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 4, verse 22:

(Verse) "And do not marry those women whom your fathers have married, except what has already passed. Indeed, it was an immorality and hateful, and an evil way."

"And do not marry the women whom your fathers have married, except for what has already happened. In truth, this is an act of immodesty, disliked, and a bad way of conduct."

Regarding the wisdom behind this prohibition, two or three points come to mind, although it is certainly impossible for a human being to comprehend all the wisdoms and secrets of the Shariah rulings. For us it is enough that Allah has made this law and has explained it for us, and we are certain that there must be some wisdom and benefit in it. Nevertheless, the three things that are understood are these: that a stepmother is also a mother; that for a son to take the place of a father is a breach of respect, because in that case he becomes the equal and partner of the father; and that by nature a person dislikes his spouse's former husband, and thus he would begin to dislike his own father as well. The third point is that the concept of inheritance from the father may become attached to the married woman, whereas in the age of ignorance (jahiliyyah) such customs existed. This is a repugnant concept that is abhorrent to both man and woman at once, because both were created from a single soul, and an insult to one is an insult to the other.

These are the apparent reasons on account of which Allah the Exalted has declared this act to be disliked, disapproved, abominable, and an act of immorality, although there may be many other causes and wisdoms beyond these. Yes, and marriages that took place in the age of ignorance are pardoned, and their matter is left to Allah.

In the third paragraph of this lesson, a list of the women who are forbidden (mahram) is given. This too is one of the important measures in the formation and organization of the family system. After the family comes the regulation of the Islamic society.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran (Urdu translation)) on surah 4, verse 23 (part 1 of 2):

(Verse) "Forbidden to you are your mothers, your daughters, your sisters, your paternal aunts, your maternal aunts, your brothers' daughters, your sisters' daughters, your foster mothers who nursed you, your foster sisters, your wives' mothers, your stepdaughters under your guardianship born of the wives with whom you have consummated marriage, but if you have not consummated marriage with them, there is no blame on you, the wives of your sons who are from your loins, and that you take two sisters in marriage together, except what has already passed. Indeed, Allah is ever Forgiving and Merciful." (32) "And married women, except those whom your right hands possess."

The prohibited persons, that is, the women whom marriage is forbidden with, are well known among all nations and peoples, whether backward peoples or advanced nations. The causes of prohibition and the degrees of prohibition have differed among different nations. Among ancient, backward nations this circle has been very wide, whereas in developed countries it has continued to shrink.

In Islam, in this verse and in the verse preceding it, the prohibited persons have been defined. Some prohibitions are permanent and some are temporary. Some are due to lineage, some due to nursing, and some due to marital relationship.

Apart from these prohibitions and causes, Islam has abolished all other restrictions that were prevalent in other societies, such as those restrictions which were in force on the basis of racial reasons, were in force due to national boundaries, were in force due to color, or those restrictions which were in force due to class distinctions, although in these the spouses were people of one race, one homeland and one region. (1) (For details see the book "Khandan aur Muashra" by Dr. Abdul Wahid Wafi, pp. 62 to 65.)

Because of kinship, four kinds of women are forbidden in Islam.

(1) The ascendants of a person, however far up they go, such as mothers, grandmothers, maternal grandmothers, and all of these are included in the word "ummahat" (mothers).
(Verse) "Forbidden to you are your mothers." (Verse) "Forbidden to you are your mothers."

(2) The second kind is the descendants of a person, however far down they go. For example, marriage with daughters and the daughters' children is forbidden, and these are included in "wa banatukum" (and your daughters).

(3) The descendants of a person's parents, however far down they go: sisters, nieces, and their offspring. These are included in "akhawatukum," "banat al-akh," and "banat al-ukht."

(4) The paternal aunts and maternal aunts of grandfathers and grandmothers will also be forbidden, and so on. All of these are included in "ammatukum wa khalatukum." However, the children of ancestors who are not direct, where an intermediary comes between, are permissible. This is why marriage with a paternal cousin sister, a maternal cousin sister, or a cousin on the father's sister's side is permissible, and also with their children.

Because of affinity (musaharah), five kinds of women are forbidden.

(1) The ascendants of a wife, as far up as they go. Thus the wife's mother, the wife's grandmother, the wife's maternal grandmother, however far up they go, are forbidden. This prohibition is established by the contract of marriage itself, whether consummation has taken place or not. These are included in "wa ummahatu nisa'ikum" (and the mothers of your wives).

(2) The descendants of a wife, however far down they go. For example, the wife's daughter is forbidden, her offspring are forbidden, whether male or female. However, this prohibition is established only when intercourse with the wife has taken place. The Qur'an says:
(Verse) "And your stepdaughters under your guardianship, born of the wives with whom you have consummated marriage; but if you have not consummated marriage with them, there is no blame on you."
"And your stepdaughters who are in your guardianship, born of your wives with whom you have had marital relations. But if you have not had marital relations with them, there is no blame on you."

(3) The wives of fathers, grandfathers and maternal grandfathers, however far up they go. Thus marriage with the wife of one's father, grandfather, or maternal grandfather is forbidden. (Verse) "And do not marry those women whom your fathers have married, except what has already passed." That is, what happened in the period of ignorance has already happened, because in the period of ignorance this was permissible.

(4) The wives of sons and the wives of grandsons, however far down they go. Therefore marriage with the wife of one's own biological son is forbidden. Likewise marriage with the wife of one's biological grandson is forbidden. Similarly, marriage with the wife of a daughter's son is also forbidden, however far down they go. (Verse) "And the wives of your sons who are from your loins." The condition "from your loins" has been imposed because in the period of ignorance the wife of an adopted son was also considered forbidden, so it was restricted to biological sons and grandsons. And it was commanded that adopted sons be attributed to their parents. (Surah al-Ahzab)

(5) The wife's sister is also forbidden, but this prohibition is temporary, existing only while the wife is alive and in marriage. What is forbidden is to keep two sisters in marriage at the same time. (Verse) "And that you take two sisters in marriage together, except what has already passed." There is no accountability for this, because it was permissible in the system of ignorance.

Similarly, through nursing, all those women are forbidden who are forbidden due to lineage and affinity, and this list consists of prohibited persons.

(1) The foster mother who nursed, and her grandmothers, however far up they go. (Verse) "And your mothers who have nursed you."

(2) The foster daughter and her daughters, however far down they go. A foster daughter is one who was nursed by a man's wife, while that wife is married to him.

(3) The foster sister and her daughters, however far down they go. (Verse) "And your foster sisters." 

(4) The foster paternal aunt and foster maternal aunt. The foster maternal aunt is the sister of the one who nursed, and the foster paternal aunt is the sister of the husband of the one who nursed.

(5) The foster mother of one's wife. This is the woman who nursed the wife in childhood. Thus the ascendants of this mother, her grandmothers and great-grandmothers, however far up they go, and this prohibition is established merely by marriage, just as it is in lineage.

(6) The foster daughter of one's wife, that is, the girl whom the wife nursed before she married this man. Likewise all her granddaughters, however far down they go. However, this prohibition takes effect only when intercourse with the wife has taken place.

(7) That is, the foster father and the wife of the foster grandfather are forbidden. The foster father is the one whose wife nursed the child. Therefore not only that woman who nursed becomes a foster mother and is forbidden, but also the co-wife of the foster mother, the wife of her foster father, is forbidden.

(8) The foster son's wife, however far down they go.

(9) Likewise, the wife and the foster sister of the wife are also forbidden; the foster paternal aunt and foster maternal aunt of the wife are also forbidden, or every woman who has become forbidden for him because of nursing.

Among these prohibitions, the first category and the third category have been explicitly stated in this verse. The rest of the list has been arranged in light of the Prophet's (ﷺ) hadith in which it is said: "Whatever is forbidden by lineage is forbidden by nursing." (Muslim, Bukhari)
"Yuharramu min al-rida'ah ma yuharramu min al-nasab."

These are the forbidden women whom the Shariah has made forbidden. In the verse no cause or wisdom is given for this prohibition, neither general nor any specific wisdom or cause. Those who have mentioned various reasons and causes have done so on the basis of their own ijtihad and reflective opinion.

It is possible that all these prohibitions have one single cause and reason, and it is possible that for some prohibitions there are specific causes, and it is also possible that several categories have a common cause. For example, due to marriages among close relatives, children are sometimes weak, and over the passage of time a weak lineage comes into being; that is, hereditary weaknesses continue to accumulate generation after generation. In contrast, if marriages are arranged between distant families and lineages, a healthy generation comes into being, and the capacities of both are combined in one place.

It may also be said that with some prohibited persons, very intimate, tolerant, respectful and dignified relations are desired. Therefore it was necessary to keep these relations away from the delicate relationship of husband and wife, so that no bitterness arises in the event of divorce and separation, and those sentiments which the Shariah wishes to preserve permanently are not injured. For example: mothers, daughters, sisters, maternal aunts, paternal aunts, nieces, and nephews, and the corresponding relations through nursing. All of these fall in this category.

It may also be said that some prohibitions, such as the wife's daughter, the combining of two sisters, and the father's wife, although in them there is no possibility of tension in the feelings of kinship and relations, yet relations may become strained. For example, a mother may fear that her daughter may also become a co-wife. If a sister and her daughter were to become co-wives in one place. Likewise, a father may come to feel that after him his son may become his rival; the same can be said about a daughter-in-law.

It may also be said that among close relatives, family ties already exist from before. The purpose of the Shariah is that marriages and alliances take place among distant families, so that the circle of family relations becomes wider, and permission among close relatives has been given only up to the point where the family tie becomes weak. (Remote)

In short, whatever the cause may be, we nonetheless acknowledge that whatever law Allah has made is certainly not devoid of wisdom. It contains the benefit and welfare of human beings. As for our understanding, sometimes we will know it and sometimes we will not. Our knowledge and understanding does not affect Allah's Shariah, nor does it make any difference to the implementation of the Shariah or obedience to it. We must obey the Shariah with submission and acceptance, because faith does not exist only in the heart. Its requirement is also that the rule of Allah's Shariah be established, and that we fully surrender, and that there be no doubt in our hearts about the rulings of the Shariah.

Now the final point and the remaining explanation of the verses: apart from two, all of these prohibitions were also prohibitions in the customs of the period of ignorance. In the period of ignorance, one could marry a woman who was the wife of a father (stepmother), and secondly, keeping two sisters in marriage at the same time was considered permissible, although the ignorant society considered them disliked. But Islam did not declare these forbidden merely because such things used to happen in the period of ignorance. Allah the Exalted presented this prohibition in reference to His right of sovereignty: (Verse) "Forbidden to you" — they have been made forbidden by Me for you.

This matter is not merely one of words, nor is it merely of outward form; it is a matter of the whole religion. By resolving its knot, the true reality of the entire religion becomes understood, and the principle upon which this religion stands comes into our hands. That is, sovereignty belongs exclusively to Allah alone.

The verdict of this religion is that the authority to determine the limits of what is lawful and unlawful belongs only to Allah. This is because this is an extremely fundamental characteristic of divine sovereignty. Therefore, for the determination of lawful and unlawful, it is necessary that there be a clear authority and proof from Allah. It is that Being who makes some things forbidden for people and some lawful, and He has not granted this authority to anyone other than Himself. Nor can anyone reserve this right for himself, because if anyone claims this right of sovereignty for himself, he is in effect claiming divinity.

This is why every jahili system determines for itself what is lawful and unlawful. And according to the Islamic worldview, these lawful and unlawful determinations made by it are void and null from the very beginning. Therefore, when Islam comes, it nullifies all the regulations of the jahiliyyah, including both the lawful and the unlawful, and does not keep any of them in force. This is because, even if these lawful and unlawful things were correct, they were fixed by people who had no authority to do so. None of them is a god. After this abrogation, Islam itself determines what is lawful and unlawful. If something was declared lawful in the jahiliyyah, it has no standing. That alone is lawful which Islam makes lawful, and that alone is unlawful which Islam makes unlawful, from Allah.

This Islamic theory of lawful and unlawful encompasses all things in this universe and all the actions and activities of human beings. Nothing is outside its scope, because no one other than Allah has the authority to determine what is lawful and unlawful. In marriage and divorce, in eating and drinking, in dress and appearance, in action and movement, in relations and dealings, in customs and traditions, and in laws and regulations, in short in all matters, the source of law is the Being of the Creator.

Whatever source and whatever institution determines lawful and unlawful other than Allah, is by its very reality void; it can neither be enforced nor validated. Has the Islamic Shariah kept some of the rules of the jahiliyyah in force? No, this thinking is not correct. The Shariah has put every matter into force anew from its own side, and its enforcement has come from Allah. It is not correct to think that some rulings are a continuation of jahiliyyah; rather, it issued its own rulings anew, and issued all customs and traditions, under Allah's authority of sovereignty.

The Qur'an has repeatedly emphasized this theory, and in this matter it repeatedly debates with the people of jahiliyyah. It repeatedly challenges them: what authority do you have that you go about making things lawful and unlawful? Who is it that makes things unlawful? (Verse) "Say: Who has forbidden the adornment of Allah which He has brought forth for His servants, and the good things of provision?" (Verse) "Say: Come, let me recite what your Lord has forbidden you." (Verse) "Say: I do not find in what has been revealed to me anything forbidden to one who eats it, unless it be carrion, or flowing blood, or the flesh of swine."

Say: "I find nothing in what has been revealed to me forbidden to any eater who eats it, except that it be blood poured forth, or the flesh of swine."

Through this argument and counter-argument, the Qur'an was leading the people of jahiliyyah (the age of ignorance) back to the principle that the authority to determine the bounds of lawful and unlawful rests with Allah alone. No individual, no class, no nation, and not the entire population of the world has such authority. This prerogative can be exercised only under the sovereign authority of Allah, and only in accordance with His Shari'ah. Indeed, Shari'ah is nothing but the determination of what is permitted and what is forbidden. This is the very essence of the religion of Islam. Therefore, whoever determines what is lawful and unlawful is, in effect, the master of the religion. If it is Allah who makes lawful and unlawful, then those who accept this we will say are upon the religion of Allah, and they will then enter the religion of Islam. If someone else is setting the bounds of lawful and unlawful in a society, then we will say these people are upon the religion of that person, and they will then enter his religion, not the religion of Islam.

This issue, within its own framework, is a matter of the sovereignty and divinity of Allah. It is a matter of religion and its meaning. It is a matter of faith and the limits of faith. I call upon Muslims throughout the entire Islamic world to determine their position from this perspective: where they stand, what their relationship to the religion is, and what their relationship with Islam has been. Despite this, will they continue to claim that they are Muslims?

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 4, verse 24 (part 1 of 3):

**Part 5 at a Glance:**

In the fifth part we again study Surah an-Nisa (the Chapter of Women). This part discusses the main themes and objectives of the surah, which were briefly indicated at the beginning of the fourth part. The same fundamental aims are present in the fifth part. Within these beliefs and aims, several other subjects are discussed again.

The first lesson of this part takes up the remaining matters of organising family affairs. In all these matters, the family has been organised in accordance with the tendencies and demands of the natural order. In family life, temporary difficulties sometimes arise, and measures have been adopted to save the family and conjugal life from them. In this way, along with preserving the family system, arrangements have also been made so that indecency and immorality do not spread in society, and so that the family system and the sanctity of conjugal relations are protected from every harmful influence. Alongside this, in this lesson some collective and economic matters have also been regulated. For example, some financial and commercial matters are discussed, and the regulation of inheritance, in which rights depend on the family, is laid down. Moreover, the property rights of men and women during married life have been safeguarded.
