Now let us look at the statistics of women's sexual relations: only three percent of women have relations with their husbands, twenty-eight percent of women have relations with their fiancés, and sixty-four percent of women have relations only with casual friends. It is further said that eighty percent of women establish sexual relations before marriage, and twenty percent are those who do not even bother with marriage."

"The result of these conditions is that, because of this sexual freedom, marriage is generally delayed very late, and if an engagement takes place, the period before marriage is very long, and along with this the number of illegitimate children keeps increasing."

As a result of all these conditions, the bonds of the family system have broken. The people of Sweden present the following arguments in favour of freedom of love: that Swedish society, after marriage, views infidelity far more severely than all other civilized societies. This is correct, and we do not deny it. But they cannot give any answer to this, and they cannot offer any satisfactory explanation for the racial decline and the enormous increase in divorce statistics resulting from this sexual licentiousness.

At present, Sweden has the highest divorce rate in the whole world. Six or seven out of every marriages end in divorce. These statistics have been taken from the records published by the Ministry of Social Affairs of Sweden. This ratio was initially low, but gradually increased, and in 1996 the situation was that twenty-six out of every thousand marriages ended in divorce. In 1952 this number became one hundred and four. In 1954 it became one hundred and fourteen. The cause of these events is that thirty percent of marriages take place merely out of necessity, under compelled circumstances, and obviously such marriages are not long-lasting like genuine marriages, and the compulsion is that a young woman becomes pregnant. Generally, divorce follows such marriages later, because in Swedish law there is no obstacle in the path of divorce. Whenever the spouses request, declaring that they are both agreed to divorce, the law permits the divorce, and if one of the spouses alone requests divorce, the divorce takes place on some trivial pretext."

"In Sweden, on the one hand there is complete freedom of sexual licentiousness, but along with this people also enjoy another freedom: every person has the freedom to become an apostate. The majority of the people of Sweden deny God. A wide movement is running in Sweden, and people are gaining complete freedom from the church. In Norway and Denmark too, denial of God is common. In schools and universities, the denial of God is encouraged, and among young people, beliefs denying God are spread according to a planned scheme."

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on surah 4, verse 28 (part 2 of 2):

"The people of Sweden and the other Scandinavian countries have become thoroughly morally corrupt. Because of their belief in denying God and their lack of fear of God, they have freed themselves from every kind of moral restraint, and in the end the young people here have become addicted to alcohol and other destructive narcotics. The number of such children whose parents use narcotics is 175,000, and this number constitutes ten percent of family children. The number of adolescent children who take drugs themselves is in addition to this. The number of young people arrested in states of severe intoxication has tripled in the last fifteen years, and the habit of alcohol consumption among young people aged fifteen to seventeen is only getting worse, and its very bad consequences are appearing."

"In Sweden, one in every ten children who reach adulthood suffers from mental and psychological illnesses. The doctors of Sweden say that fifty percent of these psychologically ill people are those whose mental illness is the result of their physical illness. Obviously, the freedom from belief in God and the freedom from moral restraints can have no other result than that the population becomes afflicted with psychological illnesses, the family system's joints become loose, and as a consequence an inferior generation comes into existence."

"This was the condition of Sweden, but the condition of America is also the same. The signs of evil are appearing in dangerous ways, yet the American nation does not pay any attention to this. Signs of destruction have appeared in the very existence of the American nation, although outwardly it appears fresh and vigorous. Despite the manifestations of apparent power and energy, this nation too is moving toward physical and moral decline, and its signs are emerging. In America there are people who sell the sensitive military secrets of their country to their enemies, not because they need money, but merely because they are afflicted with sexual licentiousness, and this licentiousness is the result of the general sexual freedom and promiscuity that prevails in their country. In some states of America, by law, a condition for divorce is that either the husband or the wife must be caught in the act of adultery. For this purpose, some lawyers and doctors formed an organization whose members try to entrap men or women in adultery in such cases. Recently, the American police uncovered such an organization, which had branches in several cities. Although lawyers and doctors are among the most civilized people, several couples who wanted divorce first hired the services of such institutions, entrapped their spouses in adultery, and then filed a case. In America, offices that provide assistance in searching for runaway wives and runaway husbands are common, because no husband is certain that when he comes home in the evening his wife will be present and will not have left with a lover, and likewise a wife is not certain that her husband will return in the evening or that some young woman more attractive than her will have taken him in. In a society where families are in this state, how can anyone's nerves remain strong and sound? And in such circumstances, an American president declares that six out of every seven young people have become unfit for military service because they are all afflicted with sexual licentiousness."

"Maulana Mawdudi (may Allah have mercy on him) writes:"

"An American magazine has described the causes due to which immorality is spreading extraordinarily in that country in this way: There are three satanic forces, a trinity of which has now overshadowed our world, and these three are busy preparing a hell. Obscene literature, which since the World War has been increasing at an astonishing rate in its shamelessness and the abundance of its circulation. Moving pictures, which not only inflame sensual feelings of love but also give practical lessons. The fallen moral standard of women, which appears in their clothing, and at times in their nudity, in the ever-increasing use of cigarettes, and in their mingling with men without any restraint. These three things are increasing among us, and their result is the decline and eventual destruction of Christian civilization and society. If these are not stopped, then our history too will be similar to Rome and those other nations which this same self-worship and sensuality, together with their wine, women and revelry, have already consigned to the jaws of annihilation."

"(Al-Hijab by Sayyid Abul Ala Mawdudi, may Allah have mercy on him, pp. 129–130, Urdu edition pp. 105–106, published 27 June 1985, Islamic Publications, Lahore)"

"But in the world of events, what has happened is that America could not escape the flood of this trinity; rather, it has bowed before it. It has set out on the very path on which Rome walked. Another journalist, writing about the flood of sexual licentiousness among the young people of America, Britain and France, intends by this to show that the licentiousness of young people in our country is not as severe as in those countries:"

"A flood of licentiousness has come upon the young boys and girls of America. The Governor of New York has announced that the remedy for this licentiousness in that state will soon become the foremost of the national reform issues. The Governor has suggested that the establishment of reform nurseries, circles for the refinement of morals, and institutions for physical training is absolutely necessary, but along with this he has also declared that eliminating the spread of narcotics, namely hashish and cocaine, among male and female students of colleges and universities is not included in their program, and that they are handing this matter over to the department of public health."

"According to the report of the last two years, in England there has been an enormous increase in incidents of assault on women and young people, and on small minor girls. Especially on village roads, in most incidents the assailants were adolescents or young men. In some of these incidents, the girl or young woman was strangled and murdered and left as a cold, frozen corpse, so that the secret of the immorality would not be exposed or so that she could not be identified at an identification parade."

"Two months ago, an old man was going to his village. On the road, under a tree, he saw a young man committing intercourse with a girl. This old man approached them. He struck the boy with his staff and rebuked and reproached him, telling him that the act he was committing was not permissible openly. The boy got up and kicked the old man in the stomach. The old man fell. After that, he kept striking him on the head with his boots until he broke his skull. The boy was only fifteen years old, and the girl was only thirteen years old."

"The 'Council of Fourteen' of America, which oversees the moral condition of the country, has reported that ninety percent of the American population is afflicted with deadly secret sexual diseases, and this situation existed at a time when the modern antibiotics penicillin and streptomycin had not yet been invented."

"A judge from Denver writes that one out of every two marriages ends in divorce. And the world-famous doctor Alexis Carrel writes in his well-known book Man, the Unknown:"

"We have come very close to eradicating diseases such as children's diarrhea, tuberculosis, consumption and typhoid, but in place of these diseases, the diseases of moral licentiousness and moral corruption have taken their place, as a result of which nervous and mental diseases are being produced. In some states of America, the number of mental patients has become greater than the number of ordinary patients. Along with madness, there is also an enormous increase in diseases of nervous and physical weakness. As a result of these, every individual has become afflicted with misery, and the family system is near its end. Experts think that intellectual decline is proving more harmful to American civilization than contagious diseases, whereas medical experts have limited their activities to the prevention of these contagious diseases."

"This is a brief glimpse of the calamities and distress that misguided humanity has brought upon itself, because it began to follow those who had become mere followers of lust. They abandoned the way of life designed by God and adopted modern ignorance (jahiliyyah). Yet the Islamic system of life was the method in which legislation was enacted with regard to human weakness and frailty, and in that system man was guided, by protecting him from being a slave to his own desires and sensual inclinations, toward a path that was both peaceful and, by treading upon which, the return from sins became easy for man, and he could adopt the path of purity."

"﴿And Allah desires to turn to you in forgiveness, but those who follow their desires desire that you should deviate into a great deviation. Allah desires to lighten (the burden) for you, for man was created weak.﴾ (4:27–28)"

"The second part of this lesson discusses certain financial matters among the Islamic society so that the methods of mutual dealings may be determined and mutual transactions among the members of the Islamic society may remain pure and clean. Moreover, in it, financial rights are to be given to women in the same way as they have been given to men. Every person should receive his prescribed share. Furthermore, those financial rights which were based on guardianship (wilayah), and which were commonly prevalent in the age of ignorance, and which were also in vogue in the early days after the advent of Islam, are to be abolished, so that the former system may be settled and the path may be cleared for the Islamic system of inheritance, in which inheritance becomes the right only of close relatives, and so that the ancient hereditary system of guardianship may be ended for the future."

The sequence of verses is connected both to the training of the Islamic society and to the field of law within the Islamic system. In the Islamic system of life, training, reform and law work side by side; they are complementary to one another and interlinked. Without one, the other cannot be complete. The purpose of legislation is that the Islamic society be trained and reformed, and that the affairs of people's lives be brought under a discipline. Within legislation, such directives are also given as aim at the training of the human conscience. Then, in this legislation, care is also taken that the law can be implemented well, and that the consciousness of the Islamic society itself be prepared for the implementation of the law, and that society understand that its interest lies not in breaking this law but in its implementation. For this reason, in the Islamic system of life, legislation and reform and guidance walk side by side. Hearts are joined to Allah, and it is instilled in them that this discipline and this law come from the same Lord of Majesty who is guiding us. It is a distinctive feature of the Islamic system of life alone that obedience to the collective system is rendered willingly. And this comprehensiveness of the Islamic system is extremely beneficial for the real and practical life of man. Through it the human conscience continues to be reformed, and the law is also acted upon.

In this part of the verses, we are commanded that the believers should not consume each other's wealth unjustly, and it is also told that the wealth of others can be taken only through trade carried out by mutual consent. The consumption of others' wealth unjustly has been likened to the killing of a human being. It has been stated that this act is destruction and ruin. Along with this, people are warned of the punishment of the Hereafter, and it is said that whoever consumes the wealth of others by oppression will certainly touch the Fire. Along with this threat, a ray of hope also shines. Allah promises gentleness, pardon and forgiveness, and also shows the way to forgive human weakness and his shortcomings. Moreover, in order to reduce the feeling of deprivation in the world, the lesson of self-respect is given, and it is said that if some people in society are prosperous, do not look at them with covetous eyes. Make the Divine Being the object of your gaze, for He is the One who gives to them. Therefore, whatever you have to ask, ask from Him. Here it is also made clear that both men and women may ask from Allah. What men have earned will be theirs, and what women have earned will be theirs. And Allah has full knowledge of the earnings of both men and women. Similarly, if people have made covenants of "wilayat al-irth" (mutual inheritance alliance) with one another, then these covenants should be fully honoured, for along with other witnesses, Allah Himself is also a witness over them. These are the effective intuitive hints and glimpses within which legislation also exists; these are the directives which Allah, the All-Knowing and All-Aware, has sent for the training of man, who is aware of his physical creation and is well acquainted with his psychological inclinations, and who is well acquainted with the mental paths and ups and downs of man.

(Verse) "O you who believe! Do not eat up your property among yourselves unjustly, except it be trading by mutual consent; and do not kill yourselves. Surely Allah is ever Most Merciful to you. And whoever does that by transgression and injustice, We shall cast him into the Fire, and that is easy for Allah." (4:29–30)

"O you who believe! Do not eat up your property among yourselves unjustly." This call is for the believers; they are the ones who have been forbidden to consume each other's wealth by false means.

(Verse) "Yā ayyuhā alladhīna āmanū lā ta'kulū amwālakum baynakum bil-bāṭil" – "O you who believe! Do not eat up your property among yourselves unjustly" (4:29)

From this it is understood that the Islamic society is being purified of the remaining filth of jahiliyyah (the age of ignorance). By addressing them with the words "O you who believe!", the conscience of the Muslims is awakened and they are stirred up to abandon all the practices of jahiliyyah; thus the demands of faith are roused, those demands which are the demands of their title "the believers", so that they do not consume each other's wealth by unlawful means.

Consuming one another's wealth by false means includes all those methods through which wealth passes from one person to another and for whose use there is no permission from Allah, or which Allah has expressly forbidden, such as usurping another's property, taking bribes, consuming wealth through gambling, hoarding the necessities of life in order to sell them at high prices, and all those methods of buying and selling that are prohibited; and riba (usury) is foremost among all of them. We cannot say with certainty whether this verse was revealed before or after the prohibition of riba. If it was revealed earlier, then it serves as a preface to the prohibition of riba, since usury is foremost among false means. And if this verse was revealed after the prohibition of riba, then riba is included in it, as well as all other methods through which others' wealth is acquired unjustly.

Here it was also deemed necessary to state that in a trade carried out by mutual consent, if another's wealth comes as profit, it is lawful.

(Verse) "Illā an takūna tijāratan ʿan tarāḍin minkum" – "except it be trading by mutual consent" (4:29)

This exception is disconnected (istithnā' munqaṭiʿ). The meaning is that if the matter is a transaction based on mutual consent, then that case does not fall within the earlier verse. Trade is brought here in the form of an exception because there is an apparent similarity between trading transactions and the other false transactions. The wealth taken through methods which the law of the Sharia prohibits is consumed by false means. This similarity becomes evident when one studies the verse on riba in Surah al-Baqarah, where the objection of the usurers is quoted: (Verse) "Innamā al-bayʿu mithl al-ribā" – "Verily, trade is only like riba" (2:275). And their objection was refuted thus: (Verse) "Wa aḥalla Allāhu al-bayʿa wa ḥarrama al-ribā" – "Allah has permitted trade and forbidden riba" (2:275). The usurers would create this confusion, and defend their existing usurious business as follows: trade (bayʿ) is also commerce, and in it a person's wealth increases through profit; while in riba, wealth increases through profit too; so there is no special reason apparent why trade should be made lawful and usury forbidden.

The truth is that there is a very great difference between trading transactions and usurious business. The worst consequences which usurious business brings upon commerce, industry and the masses are before us, and so are the pleasant effects which clean trade and industry have upon the common people.

In trade, a trader stands as an intermediary between the one in need, the buyer, and the manufacturer, and this intermediary is beneficial to both. The trader seeks a market for consumer goods and promotes products. He makes them available to those in need, attractively, and provides convenience for them. Thus he is, as it were, beneficial to both parties, and he takes a reward for his services; and that reward is also the return for his struggle and his skill. Then the trader is always ready for both profit and loss, whereas the system of usury is a system entirely different from and contrary to this situation, because in that system, over and above the original costs of the products, usurious charges are added, and this addition is then recovered from the trader and the buyer, the needy. Thus a burden falls upon the entire economic system. And just as these results have practically emerged in the industrial countries of the West, this ominous system, in the end, is neither itself beneficial to industry, nor beneficial to the customers, nor does it keep the interests of both in view; rather its only aim is to obtain the maximum profit on industrial loans and to benefit the capital-holder. Whether the masses have the necessities of life available or not, the production of luxury goods that inflame human passions is increased, even if these are harmful to the human body and health. Moreover, fixing a permanent profit for capital and never letting the capital-holder share in loss, as happens in trade, and consequently not relying on human effort, which is the very soul of the commercial system. These and other such causes which are reckoned to the account of this usurious system are sufficient to show that this system should be ended, as Islam has ended it. (For details see Fi Zilal al-Quran, vol. 3, pages ...; and also for details see the book "al-Riba" by Maulana Abul Ala Maududi (rahimahullah), Amir of Jamaat-e-Islami Pakistan.) (Sayyid Qutb)

Since in some respects the system of riba and the system of trade appeared similar, the Qur'an had to add this note by way of correction: (Verse) "Illā an takūna tijāratan ʿan tarāḍin minkum" – "except that it be trading by mutual consent among you" (4:29). After the prohibition of consuming people's wealth by false means, it is said: "And do not kill one another," although according to the view of the grammarians this is a disconnected exception.

(Verse) "Wa lā taqtulū anfusakum inna Allāha kāna bikum raḥīmā" – "And do not kill yourselves. Surely Allah is ever Most Merciful to you." (4:29)

This sentence comes after the prohibition of unlawfully consuming one another's wealth, and it contains an indication that if you consume one another's wealth by false means, then it is as though you are killing one another, and the effects of the usurious system will be destructive. And Allah, by prohibiting this usurious system, is not oppressing you; rather this is a most merciful command, and in reality it is a great mercy from Allah upon humanity.

In whatever society these matters become common, for example usury, black marketing, gambling, hoarding, deception, theft, snatching, robbery, bribery, the sale of unsaleable things, such as honour and dignity, conscience and morals, responsibility and official duty, and religion and faith, as these things were current in the ancient jahili society and are still practised in the modern jahiliyyah today — in whichever society these matters are found, they will be tantamount to suicide on its part, and that society will be casting itself knowingly into a pit of destruction.

And it is the will of Allah that He save the believers from this destructive suicide and show them mercy. This is in reality also a lightening from Allah upon humanity, a concession for it, and a remedy for human weakness, because on account of this weakness man departs from Allah's guidance and comes under the guidance of those who follow their own carnal desires.

After the threat of punishment in the Hereafter, now those who consume people's wealth by unlawful means are being threatened. Those who transgress the limits and violate the rights of others. For such people there is a threat of the punishment of the Hereafter. That is, not only will a society be destroyed in this world by consuming others' wealth, but in the Hereafter such wrongdoers will also have to face punishment. The ruin in this world will come upon all people: upon the wrongdoer, because he committed injustice, and upon the oppressed, because he did not act against the injustice; for in this world people are collectively responsible for the consequences of evil. Therefore, in whatever society the rights of others are trampled, that society will suffer bad consequences both in this world and in the Hereafter. This is the sunnah of Allah, and this is the decree of Allah.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 4, verse 30:

(Verse) "And whoever does that out of transgression and injustice, We will surely cast him into the Fire, and that is easy for Allah." (4:30)

"Whoever does this out of injustice and transgression, We will surely cast him into the Fire, and this is no difficult matter for Allah."

The Islamic system of life takes the human self to a wide scope, that is, it establishes a code for it and gives it guidance with both worlds, this world and the Hereafter, kept in view. A vigilant and cautious guardian is placed within the human self, which accepts every guidance with open heart and implements every Islamic law with willing consent. Then, in the Islamic society too, every person is made a watcher over the others, because they are collectively responsible. If injustice occurs, all the members of the society are, as it were, killed, and destruction comes upon them; that is, in this world and the Hereafter, there will be an accounting of all those who allowed their society to remain on a path of injustice and did not strive to change its false ways. (Verse) "And that is easy for Allah." (4:30)

"And this is no difficult matter for Allah." No one can prevent Him from bringing about worldly destruction and conducting the final accounting. No one can stand as an obstacle in His way. And when the causes of destruction are made available, the Sunnah of Allah is that it certainly comes to pass.

However, if you avoid the major forbidden things among the prohibitions, one of which is that you stop consuming the wealth of people unjustly and exploiting them, then as a result the mercy of Allah will remain with you. You will be treated gently, for the tranquility of your hearts and to save you from the Fire, and those of your sins that are not major sins will be forgiven, provided you avoid committing injustice and committing indecencies.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran (Urdu translation)) on surah 4, verse 31:

(آیت) ” ان تجتنبوا کبآئر ما تنھون عنہ نکفر عنکم سیاتکم وندخلکم مدخلا کریما “۔ (4 : 31) ”

" If you avoid the major sins which you are forbidden, We will remove from you your minor misdeeds and admit you to an honourable entrance."

Just look! How generous is this religion, and how many facilities have been provided in its system! It openly calls people: O humanity! Come towards heights, towards exalted dignity, towards purity, and towards discipline. Remember that the obligations imposed upon you, the limits prescribed for you, and the commands and prohibitions given to you, all have the sole purpose that pure and clean souls be produced in this world, and then from these good souls a pure and clean society be brought into existence.

But while making this call and imposing these limits and restrictions, human weakness and his natural shortcomings have also been kept in view. These obligations and duties lie within the range of his natural capacity. In them, his nature, the limits of his strength and his inclinations have been taken into consideration. Moreover, the ups and downs of the paths of human life have also been kept in mind.

This is why, in the Islamic system of life, while imposing obligations and duties, a beautiful balance and equilibrium has been maintained between these obligations and human capability. There is also a balance between human needs and human desires. There is balance between inclinations and restraints, balance between commands and prohibitions. There is balance between encouragement (targhib) and warning (tarhib), and similarly, on one side there is a severe warning of the punishment of Allah. If sin is committed, and on the other side, if someone repents and wishes to return, the door of forgiveness has not been closed for him either.

The true aim and objective of the religion of Islam is only this: that it set right the direction of the human self and turn its face towards Allah, and in this orientation one should be sincere. He should, as far as possible, obey his Allah and His Messenger (ﷺ). After this, the boundary of Allah's mercy begins. The mercy of Allah remains encompassing for all, the weak and the frail; it overlooks shortcomings, it accepts repentance, it disregards weaknesses, it forgives sins, and it opens its doors to those who return, and receives those who come back with great affection and love.

In this verse the command given is that you should avoid major sins. Major sins are always clear, open and grave, so no person can make the excuse that he committed those sins which he did not know were sins, or that he did not understand and a sin was committed; because a person who commits these sins cannot say that he tried to protect himself from sin and abstain from it, or that he fully resisted their commission. However, even after committing these sins, if a person repents sincerely and with full devotion, forgiveness is possible with Allah, and Allah has also promised this. Allah the Exalted says:

(آیت) ” والذین اذا فعلوا فاحشۃ او ظلموا انفسم ذکروا اللہ فاستغفروا لذنوبھم ومن یغفر الذنوب الا اللہ ولم یصروا علی ما فعلوا وھم یعلمون “۔ (3 : 135) ”

"And those who, when they commit an immorality or wrong themselves, remember Allah and seek forgiveness for their sins — and who forgives sins except Allah? — and do not persist in what they have done while they know. Those, their reward is forgiveness from their Lord." And such people Allah has counted among the muttaqun (the God-conscious).

Here the discussion is not about repentance from major sins; the point here is that if someone avoids major sins, then his minor sins are directly forgiven by Allah the Exalted. This is what is being promised here, and glad tidings are being given to the Muslims.

Here the question arises: what are these major sins from whose commission the guidance is given to abstain? The Hadith has mentioned them, but no Hadith has mentioned their complete number; rather, according to the occasion and circumstances, those sins from which prohibition was most needed have been mentioned. Therefore it cannot be said that a complete list of major sins has been given in any Hadith. Yes, in various Hadiths different kinds and different numbers have been called major sins, and these crimes may differ in different societies and different communities.

Here we consider it appropriate to narrate the incident of Hazrat Umar ibn al-Khattab (رضي الله عنه). Hazrat Umar (رضي الله عنه) was extremely sensitive and strict in matters of disobedience, and he strictly avoided sins. From this incident it will be known how Islam placed his acute sensitivity onto the right path, and how, despite being sensitive, this scale of his was on such balance, especially when he dealt with collective affairs and the psychological matters of humans.

Ibn Jarir narrated through Ya'qub ibn Ibrahim, Ibn Ali, Ibn Awn and ....., that some people in Egypt asked Abdullah ibn Amr: "We find in the Book of Allah, the Majestic, some commands which we are told to act upon, but they are not acted upon. So we have decided to meet the Amir al-Mu'minin regarding this." So Abdullah ibn Amr came to Madinah, and those people also came with him, and they met Hazrat Umar (رضي الله عنه). He asked: "When did you arrive?" They said: "I arrived on such and such date." Hazrat Umar (رضي الله عنه) asked: "Did you come with permission?" The narrator says that he does not remember what answer Hazrat Abdullah ibn Amr (رضي الله عنه) gave to this question. After this he said: "O Amir al-Mu'minin! I met some people in Egypt, and they asked a question: that we find in the Qur'an some commands which we are told to act upon, but they are not acted upon. So those people expressed the desire that they wish to meet you regarding this." Hazrat Umar (رضي الله عنه) said: "Bring those people to me." He gathered them. Abu Awn said: "I think he said, he gathered them in a sitting place." Then he spoke to the least of them and said: "I ask you, taking Allah as witness and keeping in view the right of Islam upon you: Have you read the whole Qur'an?" He replied: "Yes." Then he said: "Is all of it in your mind?" He replied: "Allah knows, no." If this person had said, "Yes, the whole Qur'an is in my mind," Hazrat Umar would have started a debate with him right there. After this Hazrat Umar (رضي الله عنه) said: "Is the whole Qur'an before your eyes? Do you have the whole Qur'an memorised in words? Do you act upon the whole Qur'an?" In short, he asked such questions to everyone, and he continued asking these questions to each one until the last person; after that Hazrat Umar (رضي الله عنه) said: "May your mother weep for you! Do you hold Abdullah ibn Amr responsible for making people completely conform to the Qur'an? Our Allah knew that there would be sinners among us." After this Hazrat Umar (رضي الله عنه) recited this verse:

(آیت) ” ان تجتنبوا کبآئر ما تنھون عنہ نکفر عنکم سیاتکم “۔ (4 : 31) ”

"If you avoid the major sins which you are forbidden, We will remove from you your misdeeds."

After this Hazrat Umar (رضي الله عنه) said: "Do the people of Madinah know?" or he said: "Does anyone know why you have come here?" They said: "No." He said: "If the people of Madinah knew, I would surely have admonished you." (The meaning of the phrase "lafz ahsiyah fi athrik" is: have you implemented the Qur'an in your whole life? Ibn Kathir has also narrated it and said: "The chain is sahih, the text is hasan. Although it was narrated from Umar by al-Hasan, there is inqita' in it. However, it is well known, and because it is well known we are quoting it.")

Hazrat Umar (رضي الله عنه), a person so sensitive and strict, reforms society with such wisdom. The truth is that the Qur'an had firmly established his consciousness and granted him deep wisdom and understanding. How well he said: "Our Allah had prior knowledge that sins would proceed from us." And obviously we cannot go against Allah's knowledge, so the basis of judgment will be on this: what intention did we make? How much did we intend to correct ourselves, how much effort did we make, how much did we desire, how much did we strive to observe the Shariah, how much struggle and loyalty did we attempt? This is the balance of the Islamic system of life: seriousness, moderation, and endeavour to make things easy in every matter.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 4, verse 32 (part 1 of 2):

"And do not wish for that by which Allah has made some of you excel over others. For men is a share of what they have earned, and for women is a share of what they have earned. And ask Allah for His bounty. Indeed, Allah is ever Knowing of all things." (32) "And for each We have appointed heirs to what is left by parents and close relatives. And for those with whom your oaths have been confirmed, give them their share. Indeed, Allah is ever, over all things, Witness." (33) (4:32–33)

Allah Almighty has forbidden the Muslims to wish for the excellence that Allah has given to others, and this prohibition is general regardless of what form that excellence takes. For example, excellence in rank and position, excellence in ability and capability, excellence in wealth and possessions. In short, whatever distinction or difference exists in this worldly life according to one's portion, one should not harbour wishes against others concerning it. Whatever one seeks should be sought from Allah, and every request should be directed to Allah directly. It should not be that one, without cause, looks with covetous eyes upon the excellences of others and makes one's heart a dwelling-place of longings, and then, along with this wrong wish, the evil emotions of envy, rancour, hatred and vengeance attack people with their whole army, or that feelings and thoughts of deprivation, destruction and ruin arise within them. After these emotions, suspicion arises against everyone, and then complaint arises against both God and creation, that they have been given less. This situation will be so destructive that no trace of peace and tranquillity will remain in society, every person will be a victim of mental anguish and distress, and human energies will be wasted and lost in wrong tendencies and the paths of evil. In contrast, the outlook that Allah is the Giver of everything, that He is the source of grace, generosity and bounty, is excellent. And the belief that giving and bestowing does not diminish His treasures, and that His threshold is so vast that even if all the beggars of the entire universe crowd upon it, there is no shortage, peace and tranquillity are also obtained from His threshold, and hope and support are also available from there. In the search for means and in striving, He shows the positive path, along which no enmity, jealousy, discord or hostility towards one another arises.

While giving a general guidance, this verse is general in its meaning, but within the context of the discourse its meaning becomes specific, and there are also some narrations concerning its occasions of revelation, due to which the generality of the verse's meaning becomes somewhat specific and the excellence of certain matters becomes determined. This verse determines those matters. For example, there is a difference between the shares of men and women. The share of men has been determined as greater in inheritance, which is shown by this verse and also by the context of the discourse, and by the context of the discourse. However, this aspect, namely the special difference in rank between men and women in some matters, does not affect the generality of this verse, because for the correction of relations between men and women, for complete mutual cooperation and solidarity between them, for the formation of one family in the Islamic society, for the mutual consent of the members of society and for the establishment of order among the whole society, this difference has great importance. This is because on account of this difference and gradation of ranks, the duties and responsibilities of both parties become determined. But despite this special difference, the generality of the verse is not affected, and therefore the specific occasions of revelation mentioned in the narrations do not affect the general meaning of the verse.

Imam Ahmad narrated, through the chain of Sufyan, Abu Najih, and Mujahid, from Umm Salamah (may Allah be pleased with her) that Umm Salamah (may Allah be pleased with her) submitted before the Messenger of Allah ﷺ: "O Messenger of Allah! Men engage in jihad, but we women do not take part in jihad, and in inheritance our share is half." Upon this, this verse was revealed: "And do not wish for that by which Allah has made some of you excel over others."

Abu Hatim, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Hakim in al-Mustadrak narrated from Imam al-Thawri's hadith, through Ibn Juraij and Mujahid, from Umm Salamah (may Allah be pleased with her), in this manner: that she said to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ that we women do not take part in war so that we may become martyrs, and in inheritance our full share is not given. Then this verse was revealed: "Indeed I do not waste the work of any worker among you, whether male or female" (Al-Imran 3:195).

Sadi, regarding this verse, says that some people had said: "For us there should be double the reward of women, because by nature we cannot fight in battle; but if Allah had made jihad obligatory upon us, we would have taken part in battle." Allah Almighty refuted these thoughts and commanded that they ask of His bounty, and this bounty is not temporary like the world... A similar narration is also reported from Qatadah. There are other narrations too which show the generality of the meaning of this verse.

Ali ibn Abu Talhah narrated from Ibn Abbas (may Allah be pleased with him), who said: "No one should wish that the wealth of a certain person and his wife would come to him. Allah has forbidden this and has commanded that they seek the bounty of Allah." Similar interpretations are also reported from Hasan, Muhammad ibn Sirin, Ata and Dahhak.

Viewed in terms of the relations between men and women that existed in the Age of Ignorance, the earlier sayings mentioned above reflect traces of the ignorance, whereas on the other hand, the spirit of competition and rivalry between men and women is the result of the fact that the rights and freedoms Islam granted to women, when they were granted, made the emergence of such rivalry a natural matter, because the rights Islam gave to women were based on the principles of human dignity and just treatment of every sex and every group. And this just attitude was taught to every person in such a way that each had to act justly even towards their own self.

The objectives of Islam are that it wishes to implement its interdependent and supportive system of life... Its aim is neither the support of men nor the support of women. Rather, its concern is the human being as human, and the creation of an Islamic society. Islam works absolutely and generally for the reform and welfare of humanity. It desires in this world a general, unrestricted just system, based on comprehensive and all-round just foundations.

The Islamic system of life, in determining duties and obligations, follows the path of human nature. Likewise, in determining the shares of men and women, it keeps in view the natural capacities of both. Nature, from the beginning of creation, made man a man and woman a woman, and placed within each specific capacities, and assigned their duties according to those particular capacities. In determining these duties, no particular purpose has been set aside, nor has one sex been preferred over the other; rather, the whole of human life has been kept in view, whose establishment, organisation, the perfection of its characteristics and the fulfilment of its purposes are possible only if there is a distinction between men and women, and this distinction corresponds to the distinction between their characteristics, capacities and duties, so that they may fulfil the lofty purposes of vicegerency on earth and the worship of Allah. Allah Almighty created diversity between men and women for the organisation and completion of the great institution of human life. He gave them different capacities, assigned them different functional duties, determined different rights for them, and defined separate spheres of action, so that the caravan of life might continue to travel on the right course.

When a person studies the complete Islamic system of life impartially, and especially examines in depth the nature of the relations between men and women within that system, then neither does the conflict found in ancient traditions have any occasion, nor does any reality remain in those modern disputes and conflicts which, in today's age, become fruitless between men and women, and whose clamour sometimes becomes so loud that the voices of serious men and women are drowned out.

It would be a futile effort to depict the situation as though a battle is raging between man and woman, in which each person is presenting their own position, and each is striving to win the war. Some serious writers, too, sometimes adopt a stance in which they find defects in the nature of woman, deny her perfections, and attribute every fault to her. Whether they do this as scholarly debate or from an Islamic viewpoint, both forms are far from the reality as it is. The matter, in fact, is not one of confrontation between the two parties, but rather a matter of the nature and division of functions of both sexes, of mutual solidarity and cooperation, and, according to the Islamic system of life, of the establishment of justice between them.

It is possible that within jahili societies there may be confrontation between men and women, because jahili societies devise their own system of life independently. The system of these jahili societies is based purely on personal and worldly aims, or in these systems the interests of some dominant classes are kept in view, or the protection of the interests of certain families and individuals is desired. For this reason, in these jahili systems, due to the ignorance concerning human reality and the state of jahiliyyah, the rights of women are usurped, or in them the natural duties of men and women are disregarded while their rights and duties are determined, or in them the rights of working women are kept lower than the rights of men doing the same work. And this deficiency arises merely from economic causes, or for example, in the field of the distribution of inheritance and in the sphere of financial dealings, the rights of women are kept lower, just as in modern jahili societies the situation is similar.

As for the Islamic system of life, nowhere in it is such a situation found. In it, first of all, no battle is set up between men and women. In it, there is no enmity among one another based on worldly interests. In it, neither does a man attack the interests of a woman and plunder them, nor does a woman attack the interests of a man and plunder them. Neither of them remains in search of the other's weaknesses in order to expose them. Within the Islamic system, there is no room for such ideas. Despite this clear distinction in natural characteristics between men and women, there is no difference in the duties and obligations between men and women, and these duties and obligations do not affect the rank and status of men and women. Such ideas are based on misunderstanding, and are also outdated in their own place. Regarding the Islamic system, these ideas are based on ignorance, and have come into existence due to deep unawareness of the natural constitution of men and women and their physiological functions.

Consider the matter of jihad! Concerning jihad and martyrdom in the way of Allah, and the participation of women in it and the matter of attaining reward, the righteous women of the earliest era had concern in their hearts. The concern of these righteous women was related solely to the perspective of the Hereafter. It was in no way related to status or superiority in this world. At times this distinction was also related to worldly matters, for example, in inheritance the share of the man was set greater than that of the woman. From ancient times, both men and women had concern in their hearts about this distinction. In the modern age too, these and other similar issues still trouble hearts.

The reality is that Allah Almighty has neither made jihad as an act obligatory upon women, nor has He prohibited women from participating in jihad. Moreover, if the obligation of jihad requires women's involvement and the male population is not sufficient for it, women are not forbidden from it. Furthermore, history of Islam shows that some women did take part in jihad. They took part in jihad as well, besides nursing the sick and carrying loads; but such incidents were few and rare, and occurred at times of extreme necessity; they were not the general principle or the usual practice. In any case, it is a fact that just as Allah Almighty made jihad obligatory upon men, He did not make it obligatory upon women.

Jihad is not made obligatory upon women because they are the producers of mujahidin. The woman has been created precisely so that she gives birth to men. Her physical structure and psychological inclination themselves point towards producing mujahidin and preparing them for jihad fi sabilillah, preparing them to live a good life. In this field a woman can work with greater strength and grace, since her physiological and psychological formation is made precisely for this purpose. This is not said merely on the basis of the woman's physical structure, but especially because within her internal system, through the grafting of cells, that is, whether by Allah's will one is male or female, the woman from the time of birth is solely responsible for this duty. (See the chapter "al-Mara'ah wa 'Alaqat al-Janin", which is part of the book al-Islam wa Mushkilat al-Hadarah.)

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 4, verse 32 (part 2 of 2):

The external organs perform their functions one after another, and after that period great psychological effects are produced upon the pregnant woman. Therefore, her performance of this great duty in the Ummah's jihad against shirk is more beneficial. This is because when the storm of war destroys men in large numbers, the woman fulfils her duty as a means of further population production. She fills the gap by bearing more men. But if the ghoul of war devours both men and women, or if it snatches away only the women and leaves the men, then this arrangement no longer remains. This is because in the Islamic system of life, if there is one man and he makes full use of the concession, he can marry four women at the same time. And those four women at the same time can increase the population, and thus that deficiency can be made up (although after a period of time) which occurs due to jihad and fighting. But if even a thousand men have intercourse with one woman, that woman can still give birth only to the same number of children as she could from the intercourse of one man. In the case of a shortage of women, the decrease in population can never be made up.

And this is only one of the points among the boundless wisdoms of Allah which lie hidden beneath the ruling that Allah exempted women from jihad. This ruling has countless benefits, such as ensuring moral purity in Islamic society, taking into consideration the temperament of the Islamic society, and indicating separate spheres of activity for the two sexes of human beings, and so on, the details of which there is no opportunity to explain here, because this point requires a special and lengthy discussion. (See the chapter "Nizam-e-Aa'ili" in the book "Nahw Mujtama' Islami".)

As for the matter of reward, Allah has given both men and women a full assurance of it, provided that they perform their duties and obligations well, sincerely for the sake of Allah, and reach the level of ihsan in them.

As for the matter of shares of inheritance, at first sight the principle "a male's share is equal to that of two females" seems to show that man has been given preference over woman. But if one casts a glance over the complete duties and obligations of men and women, the superficiality of this opinion quickly becomes apparent. The determination of income and shares has been made in view of responsibilities. It is a permanent principle of the Islamic system of life that benefits are determined in proportion to responsibilities. It has been made obligatory upon the man to pay the mahr to the woman, whereas even if a woman is the richest of the rich, the mahr has not been made obligatory upon her for the man. Then, the expenses of both the woman and her children have been imposed upon the man, whereas this responsibility has not been imposed upon the woman even if she is wealthy. If the man is negligent in performing these duties, he can be given the punishment of imprisonment. Then, various kinds of diyat and compensation (i.e., compensation for wounds) are also imposed upon the man, and he has to pay these compensations collectively, by virtue of being a member of the family, whereas the woman has been exempted from the compensation of diyat and arsh. The man is also obligated to provide maintenance (nafaqah) for the needy and indigent of his family, whether they are men or women, provided they are unable to earn. This obligation begins with the closest relatives, and the woman is exempt from these general family duties. Even with the husband from whom her child is born, if there is no economic partnership or if a divorce has taken place, the arrangements for the child's upbringing are also imposed upon that man, and he is bound to pay them together with the woman's expenses. In short, the Islamic system is a complete and comprehensive system, and in it, at the time of the distribution of inheritance, the financial responsibilities of men and women have also been kept in view. It becomes clearly evident that the heavy burden of responsibilities which the Shari'ah has placed upon men, in proportion to it, the share of men in inheritance is not much more. In all these matters, the greater capacity and skill of men in economic activities has also been kept in view. And the maximum comfort and tranquillity of women has been kept in view, so that they can with full attention look after the precious capital of humanity, that is, the children, which is more valuable than every kind of wealth, every kind of goods and every kind of useful general craftsmanship.

As a result of this reflection, it becomes clear that the Islamic system of life, whose formation was made by a Wise and All-Knowing Being, contains broad balance and profound wisdom, and in this verse Islam has given women the right of individual ownership in these words:

(Verse) "For men is a share of what they have earned, and for women is a share of what they have earned." (4:32) ... And this is the right which Arab jahiliyyah, like all other jahiliyyahs, has always hesitated to grant to women, and this right of women has never been accepted with an open heart. Only rarely has this right been given to women, and even today there are devices to deny women this right, whereas women themselves are still seized as inheritance in the same way and divided like property.

This is the right which modern jahiliyyah is still hesitant to give to women, although its claim is that it has given women rights which were never given to them before. In modern jahiliyyah there are some laws which regard the eldest male heir as entitled to the entire inheritance, and some laws which require that any financial contract a woman makes requires the approval of her guardian according to the law. And these laws allow any disposal by the wife even of her own property only when the husband gives his approval. And these deficient rights modern jahiliyyah gave her only when she ran campaigns to obtain them, brought about great revolutions, and as a result the order of women's lives was ruined, the family system ended, and the general moral condition became unspeakable.

But Islam, from the very beginning, gave women these rights of its own accord, without her preparing any charter of demands for their attainment, before she rose up in rebellion, before she formed women's organizations to obtain them, and before she reached membership of parliament and demanded them. These rights were given by Islam to her purely out of respect for humanity; they were given to her merely because the human soul has two kinds, man and woman, and because Islam has made the family the unit of its collective system. And it has linked this family system, with mutual love and mutual affection, on the principle of equality between man and woman. This is why, from the standpoint of earning and ownership, Islam has given both man and woman, in principle, completely equal rights.

Dr. Abdul Wahid Wani, in his book "Insani Huqooq" (Human Rights), presents a comparative study of the rights of women in Islam and in modern Western countries thus: "Islam gave men and women equal rights from the standpoint of law, and treated men and women as equal in all civil rights, and in this regard no distinction was made between married and unmarried women. There is a very great difference between Islam and the whole Christian world regarding the nature of marriage. According to Islamic law, marriage does not end a woman's name, nor does it end her personality, nor does it affect her capacity to conduct her affairs, nor does it limit her right of ownership. Rather, after marriage a Muslim woman keeps her same name, her legal and civil status also remains in its place, and she retains all legal rights. All the responsibilities that were previously imposed upon her remain imposed upon her. She can make every kind of decision and contract in her affairs, such as buying and selling, mortgage, gift and bequest, etc. The things of which she is the owner, no restriction is imposed upon her right of ownership because of marriage. In short, in Islam even after marriage a woman has a permanent legal status and is the owner of a permanent personality; her property is separate from her husband's property and is her own ownership. The husband has no legal authority to acquire anything of hers without her permission, whether it is small or large. Allah the Exalted says:

(Verse) "And if you desire to exchange one wife for another, and you have given one of them a heap of gold, take not from it anything. Would you take it by slander and manifest sin? (20) And how would you take it when you have gone in unto one another and they have taken from you a solemn covenant?" (4:20-21)

"And if you intend to take a new wife in place of another, and you have given the first a great amount of wealth, do not take back anything from it. Would you take it by slander and manifest wrong? And how could you take it when you have lain with one another and they have taken from you a firm covenant?" If it is not lawful for a husband to take back from his divorced wife the wealth which he himself gave her, then for him to seize the wealth owned by the woman herself is all the more not lawful, unless this is all done with her consent, and she is giving something of her own accord, and Allah's command in this regard is:

(Verse) "And give the women their dowries graciously; but if they give you anything of it willingly, then consume it with enjoyment and satisfaction." (4:4)

And a man cannot exercise any kind of disposal over his wife's wealth, unless she permits him, or she has given her husband permission for some kind of disposal and contract. But even in such circumstances, she is permitted to take back those powers that she has given, and to grant them to any other person she wishes."

"This is the lofty station which a woman, even in today's modern age of democracy, has not reached even in those countries which are the most highly developed on this earth. In France, until the recent past, the condition of women was such that they were, as it were, slave-girls and bondwomen; indeed, this condition still exists. The law has deprived her of her rights in many civil matters. For example, Article 217 of the French Civil Code stipulates that: 'A married woman, even if it has been stipulated in the marriage conditions that the property of the woman and the man will be separate, nevertheless cannot make a gift of her property, nor can she transfer her ownership, nor can she mortgage it, nor can she make any transfer for consideration or without consideration, unless her husband joins her in some contract, or unless she gives written permission for any of these matters.'"

"Although many amendments and changes have been made to this article in later periods, many traces of this law still remain, and it imposes a legal restriction on the French woman: upon marriage a woman loses her own name and her family's name. Thereafter her name is not written as 'daughter of so-and-so,' but she is addressed as 'Madame so-and-so,' or her husband's name is attached to her name. But her father's name and her family's name are not attached to her name. Thus the erasure of the woman's name shows that after marriage the woman's civil and legal status has ended, and she has been lost in the personality of her husband."

"What is even more surprising is that most Muslim women, in solidarity with these Western women, also accept for themselves this lower and secondary status, and instead of using their own name they present themselves as 'Begum so-and-so,' or they attach their husband's and his family's name to their name, and do not like to use their father's and their family's name with their own name, as the desire and temperament of the Islamic system of life demands. This is called a clumsy imitation or blind imitation. But what is surprising is that women who imitate even the slavery of the Western woman, here demand freedom and rights for women, and urge women to imitate men and demand rights, whereas in reality they are renouncing those excellent rights which Islam had given them, although Islam had increased their worth and dignity and had given them an equal status with men in these rights."

(pp. 59–61)

Now we come to the last verse of this lesson. In it, the rulings of those agreements are described which were made before the rulings of inheritance came. Islam's system of inheritance was arranged on the basis of kinship and blood relationship, whereas these agreements of friendship and guardianship also used to exist outside the sphere of kinship, as the details that are coming will show.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 4, verse 33:

(Verse) "Wa likullin ja'alna mawali mimma taraka al-walidani wal-aqraboon, wal-ladhina 'aqadat aymanukum fa-atoohum naseebahum; inna Allaha kana 'ala kulli shay'in shaheedan" (4:33)

"And for every one We have appointed heirs to what parents and close relatives leave. And as for those with whom your oaths have bound you, give them their share. Indeed Allah is ever, over all things, a Witness." (4:33)

After the principle that men shall have a share of what they earn and women a share of what they earn, and after the reference that the shares of men and women have already been fixed by the law of inheritance, now it is said that for every person We have appointed, from among his relatives, heirs who will receive his inheritance, and these heirs will be entitled to that property which he received from his parents and relatives. This wealth will continue to pass from generation to generation according to this system of inheritance. The inheritors will receive it, and then they will add their own earnings to this inherited wealth. This is a picture that shows how the circulation of wealth comes into operation in the Islamic system. This circulation does not stop in any one generation, nor does this wealth get collected and concentrated in one household or in one individual; rather, the system of inheritance always keeps doing its work. It is a continuous distribution that keeps flowing. The owners of property cannot make any alteration in it, nor can the shares of the heirs be increased or decreased. This automatic process of distribution continues at intervals.

After this, the discussion turns to the earlier covenants which the Islamic Shari'ah retained, and according to which, on occasion, non-relatives also became entitled to inheritance. These covenants were called 'uqud al-muwalat. When the Islamic society began, some of them existed in it, such as:

(1) The covenant of muwalat of manumission (mu'tiq): whoever freed a slave would pay the blood money (diyah) on his behalf if it was ever imposed on him, just as blood money used to be paid among his lineage members when he committed a crime. And if such a person died, and he had no 'asabat (agnatic heirs), then this patron would also be entitled to his inheritance.

(2) The second 'aqd al-muwalat: that a person would make a covenant of friendship with a non-Arab, when he had no relatives among the Arabs. By virtue of this covenant, this non-Arab would become a member of some Arab family. The patron would also pay the blood money on his behalf if he committed a crime, and when this person died, the patron would be entitled to his inheritance.

(3) The covenant which the Prophet ﷺ arranged between the Ansar and the Muhajirin in the early days of the Hijrah. In this way the Muhajirin and the Ansar would inherit from each other, provided the Ansar's relatives were Muslims; otherwise there would be no inheritance between them.

(4) Covenants that existed in the Jahiliyyah, in which two persons would make an agreement with each other that "we shall be entitled to each other's inheritance."

Islam annulled all these covenants, especially the third and the fourth, and established that the real and sole basis of inheritance is kinship. However, Islam retained the first two covenants and ordered that such covenants should not be made in future. Allah the Exalted says: "Wal-ladhina 'aqadat aymanukum fa-atoohum naseebahum" (4:33) (Those with whom your oaths have bound you, give them their share). Strict emphasis was also laid on this, and He recorded His own testimony regarding these covenants and their dispositions: "Inna Allaha kana 'ala kulli shay'in shaheedan" (4:33) (Indeed Allah is ever, over all things, a Witness).

The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "La hilfa fi al-Islam, wa ayyuma hilfin kana fi al-jahiliyyah lam yazidhu al-Islam illa shiddatan" (There is no covenant in Islam; but any covenant that existed in the Jahiliyyah, Islam only strengthens). (Ahmad and Muslim)

In the matter of the termination of these covenants, Islam adopted the same policy which it always adopts in all financial laws. Whenever it enforces any law as a financial reform, Islam's policy is the same, namely that Islam does not enforce any financial reform law retrospectively. For example, when the prohibition of riba (usury) law was enforced, its implementation began from the date on which the verse containing the command was revealed. And the interest that had been taken before that was not disturbed, and it was not ordered that those who had taken profits should return them. Although earlier covenants were also annulled, those who had received loans under the covenants were allowed to keep them. Here, in the matter of wilayah, the covenants were not annulled; rather, it was ordered that new covenants should not be made, because under these covenants, apart from financial responsibilities, the foreign contracting persons became members of that family, and complex relationships of various kinds were established among them which it was not appropriate to sever. However, making new covenants was prohibited, and regarding the earlier covenants it was ordered that they be implemented. New covenants were prohibited so that they would not give rise to effects and problems the resolution of which would become necessary.

Because of this decision, on the one hand a facility was given to the people, and on the other hand, within it is found a solution to the problems that were important for that society at that time. This solution was based on greater depth, wisdom and the demands of the whole situation, especially in the circumstances in which Islam was shaping the features of the new Islamic society, and the traces of the former Jahili society were being erased one by one, and in every stage of legislation this work advanced a little further.

(It is related from Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with him) in explanation of this verse that he would give the inheritance according to the law of inheritance, but he would order assistance, support and kindness toward those with whom there were covenants.)

The last topic of this lesson is the organization of the Islamic family system and the regulation of its affairs and dealings. Who holds what status within the family, and what duty each person has within the family. And the arrangements through which the affairs of this important institution have been regulated. And how this institution is to be protected from disputes and the shocks of personal desires. Likewise, how it is to be safeguarded from those elements which become the cause of its collapse and the uprooting of its foundations. Full effort has been made in this regard.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran (Urdu translation)) on surah 4, verse 34 (part 1 of 3):

Before beginning the interpretation and explanation of these Qur'anic texts, and before stating their psychological and social purposes, it is necessary to present an outline of Islam's view of the family: the method on which Islam builds the family, the measures it adopts to protect it, and the aims and objectives Islam has in view through this arrangement. We will present this as briefly as possible, since a detailed discussion of this subject would require many more pages.

The One who created man placed in him the same marital nature that He placed in all the things He created.

(ومن كل شيء خلقنا زوجين لعلكم تذكرون) "And of everything We created pairs, that you may reflect." Within man too, Allah created a pair, but He created this pair from a single soul.

(يا أيها الناس اتقوا ربكم الذي خلقكم من نفس واحدة وخلق منها زوجها) (4:1) "O mankind, fear your Lord, who created you from one soul and created from it its mate." Within the union of this pair, Allah has placed all the secrets of life. In this union He has provided psychological tranquility, nervous calm, spiritual contentment, and physical comfort and rest. Then, within this union, He has placed the means of mutual covering, chastity, and protection from sin. Besides this, the union serves as a field for offspring, through which the continuity of life is established, and the secret of the progress of the ways of life also lies in it. But Islam has shaped this whole system into a training ground, a nursery, in the form of a modest and peaceful family, which begins with the spouses.

(ومن آياته أن خلق لكم من أنفسكم أزواجا لتسكنوا إليها وجعل بينكم مودة ورحمة إن في ذلك لآيات لقوم يتفكرون) (30:21) "And among His signs is that He created for you mates from yourselves that you may find tranquility in them; and He placed between you affection and mercy. Indeed in that are signs for a people who reflect."

(هن لباس لكم وأنتم لباس لهن) "They are clothing for you and you are clothing for them."

(نساؤكم حرث لكم فأتوا حرثكم أنى شئتم وقدموا لأنفسكم واتقوا الله) "Your wives are a tilth for you, so go to your tilth however you wish, and send forth for yourselves, and fear Allah."

(يا أيها الذين آمنوا قوا أنفسكم وأهليكم نارا وقودها الناس والحجارة) "O you who have believed, protect yourselves and your families from a Fire whose fuel is men and stones."

(والذين آمنوا واتبعتهم ذريتهم بإيمان ألحقنا بهم ذريتهم وما ألتناهم من عملهم من شيء) "And those who believed and whose descendants followed them in faith – We will join with them their descendants, and We will not deprive them of anything of their deeds."

What is the position of both sides of the human soul, men and women, before Allah? In humanity, they are equal. Allah made the human soul honoured, which includes women as well as men, and Allah will give both men and women their full reward for their deeds. In Allah's law, just as a man can hold property, so too a woman can hold property.

A man has the right of inheritance, and a woman also has the right of inheritance. A man is a legal person, and a woman is a separate legal person, and we have already discussed all these points earlier in this lesson.

Since the institution of the family could only come into existence through the union of both parts of the human soul, and since obligations and duties arise from this, the Shari'ah gave detailed instructions concerning every aspect of the affairs of this institution. The purpose was that men and women should have opportunities for tranquility, contentment, covering, and protection from evil and immorality. Secondly, that through this family system life should attain continuity and proceed on the path of progress. In the greater part of this surah the family has been consolidated, a part of which we presented at the beginning of this juz', and the complementary rulings were also given in the fourth juz'. Likewise, these rulings were stated in Surah al-Baqarah, whose explanation we presented in the second juz'. Many other surahs of the Qur'an also give detailed instructions regarding the family system, for example, Surah al-Nur and Surah al-Ahzab in the eighteenth juz' (juz' 21–22), Surah al-Talaq and Surah al-Tahrim (juz' 28), and scattered passages of some other surahs. In all these places, the discussions that have been made contain a complete constitution of Islam's family system. From this extensive and wide-ranging discussion and these varied and detailed rulings, it becomes clear that the Islamic system builds human life in accordance with a family system. For this reason, these surahs take up every aspect of family life.

A We hope that readers of this page will keep in mind all the details that we have presented on this subject. For example: the lengthy childhood of human children, the need for prolonged upbringing and care during that period, and then the need for a family for these children so that a child may stand on its own feet and enter the economic struggle of life. Even more important than this economic struggle is the training of the child, which prepares it to discharge its collective responsibilities and makes it capable of becoming a good member of society, so that it may perform its duties in the advancement of humanity. And when it leaves that society, it should leave it in a better condition than the one in which it found it. In short, for a correct understanding of the family system, it is absolutely necessary to reflect on the points mentioned above. Likewise, these matters are extremely important for understanding the purposes of the family, the duties of the family, the protection of the family from every effect of ruin and destruction and keeping it safe and secure, and the position and policy of the Islamic system of life regarding the growth of the family.

From the importance that Islam attaches to the family, about which we have given detailed indications above, it becomes evident that the emphasis Islam has placed on establishing a family system, on its stability, and on creating tranquility and steadiness within it, cannot even be conceived in other systems. Moreover, Islam, for the first time, granted women an honourable position and an honourable personality. The rights that Islam granted to women for the first time in the world are not rights through which she merely obtains love and pleasure, but rights through which a woman discharges her highest duties in relation to human life.

Keeping all these truths in view, we now discuss the last verse of this lesson, which is one of the most important verses in this series, and for this reason we have given the above introductory indications before its explanation.

This verse clarifies the organisation of the institution established between the spouses and the distribution of authority among the members of this institution, and it gives guidance to remove tension in relations among the family members, directing that all Muslims, rather than being subject to base desires and personal impulses and inclinations, should obey the commands of Allah, Glorified is His majesty. The command of Allah is that within the family the qawwam (guardian and head) shall be the man. The reasons for making the man the head are, firstly, that Allah has given men excellence and has endowed them with greater organisational abilities, on which the functioning of the family system depends. The second reason is that Allah has imposed upon the man the duty of being responsible for the economic needs of the family. Since the man has been made the guardian of the family, he has also been given special powers by which he can protect this institution, so that temporary emotions and base desires cannot destroy it. It has also been explained what the means of protection against these momentary desires are. The limits of treatment have also been defined, and if internal remedy is not possible, then external remedy has also been stated, especially in circumstances where this institution faces severe dangers, and there is not merely the danger that its two important sides and parties are separating from each other, but also that, as a result of their separation, the training of innocent children and the young generation is endangered, and even their very existence is threatened. Look closely and see how profound the wisdom behind every measure and step is, and how great is the need for it.

(الرجال قوامون على النساء بما فضل الله بعضهم على بعض وبما أنفقوا من أموالهم) (4:34) "Men are the protectors and maintainers of women, because Allah has given the one more (strength) than the other, and because they spend of their property."

As we have said, the family is the primary institution of human life, in the sense that it is a starting point which affects the whole of human life. It is also a starting point in this sense: that the elements of future life come into being from the family, and from the Islamic perspective, man is the most important element of this universe.

In the world, institutions of lesser importance than the family institution are entrusted for their management and administration to the most capable persons, for example financial institutions such as banks, industrial establishments and factories, and other commercial institutions and companies. The management of these institutions is entrusted to people who have good expertise in their field, who have acquired ample knowledge of that field, and who possess experience and ability.

This is the customary practice regarding the management of institutions whose rank, status and importance are far lower than that of the human institution. Therefore it is appropriate that the same principle be kept in view when entrusting the management and administration of the family, because the family institution is responsible for the nurturing of the most important product of this universe, namely the human race. Clearly, from the standpoint of humanity, man is the most important product.

The Islamic system of life keeps this principle in view. It keeps in view human nature, and it also keeps in view the capacities of both components of the family, men and women. It also keeps in view the duties and obligations which, by the natural constitution, have been placed upon men and women. In imposing duties on both men and women, the Islamic system has kept justice towards both in view, and this justice, that is, the distribution of functions, has been made by considering the nature of men and women. It is undeniable that both men and women are creatures of Allah, and it is also accepted that Allah does not wrong any of His creatures, since He prepares each one for its specific natural duty and grants it the capacity suited to that duty. These matters are most self-evident and accepted.

Allah created people as man and woman and then made them into pairs, just as Allah has made this entire universe in pairs. That is, even among inanimate things there are pairs. Now the natural duty of the woman is that she becomes pregnant, then gives birth, then nurses the child, and she is fully responsible for the fruit that results from the union of man and woman. Viewed from this natural standpoint, a great responsibility is placed upon the woman, which is an extremely important duty.
