It is not an ordinary or easy responsibility, and it cannot be discharged without physical, psychological and deep intellectual preparation and capacity. All these qualities must necessarily be found in the being of the woman. Therefore it was a matter of the utmost justice that a principal duty should also be placed upon the other partner in this partnership, namely that he should be the provider of all the family's needs, and thus he should be responsible for the support and protection of both the mother and the child, so that the woman may be wholly free for her extremely important and precious duty. It should not be an injustice to her that she bears pregnancy, endures the pains of childbirth, nurses and cares for the child, and at the same time works and labours, and remains awake for her child's and her own personal needs. Both duties should not be placed upon her simultaneously. Therefore it was the most equitable division of labour that the field of work for the woman be determined in accordance with her physical and natural capacities, and that the field of work for the man be determined in accordance with his physical, psychological and natural capacities. And Islam has done exactly this in practice, because Islam does not oppress anyone. The Lord, Full of Majesty, does no injustice to anyone.

This is the reason why God has endowed woman with the qualities of gentleness, kindness, being quickly affected, and responding quickly, and all the necessary attributes for the immediate needs of children were placed by nature in the mother. These are qualities that were not created in woman through education and training; rather, she performs these actions without thinking. This is because God did not make the important needs of humanity, even the important needs of a single individual, dependent on someone thinking, reflecting, and then, after time has passed, fulfilling natural needs. Natural needs are also felt involuntarily, and they are fulfilled involuntarily, so that as soon as the demand arises, these needs are met. Indeed, in some circumstances it seems as though the system for fulfilling these natural demands is some compulsory system. Yes, if there is any element of compulsion in it, it is an internal element; there is no compulsion from outside. Sometimes this demand is pleasant and delightful, so that a person is quickly inclined to fulfil this demand of nature, which is a source of joy for him, even though it may involve long hardship and priceless sacrifice. This is the creation of God, who has made everything very good.

The presence of these characteristics in human nature is not a superficial matter. These natural impulses have been placed in the physical, nervous, conscious and psychological structure of woman with great depth. Concerning this, specialists in the field say that these attributes exist within the cell from which a human being is born, because God created these characteristics in the depths of the first cell, and through the division and growth of that cell the child then develops, and all the fundamental traits are present within it.

In contrast, among the qualities given to man, the most important is man's firmness and strength. Man is not quickly affected and is not ready to accept any situation quickly. He does everything after thinking carefully, and before taking any step he also reflects on its consequences. This is because, at the beginning of life, his duty was to hunt and bring food, and to rise up, even to the point of killing and being killed, to protect his children and wife; to manage the economy of his wife and children and to carry out all the duties of life. All his duties require that every step be well considered, that one work through reflection, and that if someone invites him to something, he accept it only after much thought. All these qualities are found in the structure of man's personality, just as the qualities of woman are present in the structure of her personality.

These natural qualities of man make him deserving of being the guardian of the household and, in terms of rank, the senior within the family. Furthermore, since the man is also responsible for the expenses of the whole family, his supervision is necessary, because he is the one who sustains the economic needs of the entire family institution. Since he is the one who spends, it is necessary that he be the manager. These are the two qualities that the Qur'an mentions in this verse, and on their basis man has been made the qawwam (guardian) in Islamic society.

Some of the reasons for man's guardianship are creational reasons, that is, in terms of capacity, and some are related to responsibilities. Moreover, in the distribution of responsibilities, man also becomes the guardian with regard to justice and equity, and when Shari'ah placed responsibilities on man and woman, it also took into account what responsibility is conducive to ease for each, what their nature requires, and what responsibility it supports.

The superiority of man over woman for guardianship has its own reasons, which relate to capacity and experience, and all responsibilities will be carried out taking these reasons of guardianship into account. This is because no institution can run without a manager and guardian, that is, all those institutions which are of much less importance and value compared to the family institution. Furthermore, a portion of humanity has been prepared for certain specific duties. By nature, the performance of those duties is easy for it, and that is why those duties have been imposed upon it. And the other portion of humanity has not been prepared by nature for those duties. Performing those duties is not easy for it, and if those duties were imposed upon it, that would be clear oppression. But even if it were prepared for the performance of those duties, given training for them, and given both academic and practical education, and then it were able to carry them out, its capacity for which it was created and prepared would be badly affected. For example, for woman there are her maternal responsibilities. That is, if other civic responsibilities were imposed on woman, she would no longer be capable of performing the maternal duties that are the requirement of her nature, and whose basic capacity is quickness of being affected and quickness of acceptance. These are centred within woman's nature. Moreover, maternal capacities are placed within the physical and nervous structure of woman, and their effects appear in her conduct and in the yearning feeling she has for the needs of the child, and so on.

These are extremely important issues, so important that a firm decision about them cannot be made merely from the standpoint of human desires, and they are so dangerous that their answers cannot be given merely by shooting arrows in the dark. When ancient and modern jahiliyyahs decided these important issues from the standpoint of man's base desires, they put even the existence of humanity in danger. The retention of human characteristics within man became difficult, those human characteristics upon which human life rests and from which he received his distinctive dignity.

One proof of this is that, despite people denying this reality, abandoning it and considering it entirely strange, these laws of nature have complete control over the existence of man, and human nature clearly points towards them.

Another proof is that whenever humanity has violated this principle, restlessness, corruption and moral decline have arisen as a result within human life, and human life has been afflicted with severe confusion. The order of the family has been destroyed. The marks and distinctions of human life have disappeared, and it has departed from its natural and original station.

Another proof is that woman herself has a psychological desire that there be a man above her as qawwam and ruler, because male authority and superiority within the family is a natural matter. If a woman does not have the protection of a man, she considers herself deprived, deficient and wretched. This situation is observed when she lives with a man who lacks the capacity for guardianship and protection and who entrusts this position to the woman. Even the misguided and wayward women of the modern age acknowledge that it is in woman's nature to have a protector and ruler.

Further, there is the proof that a family institution in which there is no paternal qawwamah does not raise children properly. For example, in a case where the man's personality is weak and the mother's personality dominates the children, or in situations where the father is absent, has died, or in families in which the children have no legal guardian and father at all. In such families, children become ill-mannered and of deficient personality, and it is rare that they escape deviation and wayward behaviour. Moreover, such children are by no means possessed of a complete personality in nervous and psychological terms, nor in moral and practical terms.

These are some important arguments for the legitimacy of man's guardianship and protection, to which human nature itself guides us. Within man's nature this protection exists, and the principles and rules of it operate within human beings with full force, even if people deny it, abandon it and consider it strange.

More than this, the qawwamah of man cannot be discussed here. For the present purpose, this much discussion on man's protection and guardianship, on its legitimacy, its social necessity and its natural demands, is sufficient. But here it is appropriate for us to say this much: that this qawwamah and guardianship of man does not mean that the personality of woman is negated within any family or society, nor does it mean that woman's civic status is being abolished, as we have said earlier. Rather, this guardianship of man is one of his responsibilities within the family system, imposed upon him for the running, protection and preservation of this important institution. It is a reasonable matter that appointing a guardian of an institution means precisely that he will not destroy its existence, will not destroy the personality of any of its members, will not violate the rights of its participants, and will not nullify the duties of those who work within it. In other places Islam has clearly explained the limits and bounds of man's guardianship. It has been made obligatory upon him to fulfil this duty with the utmost gentleness, kindness and mercy. Furthermore, in other places the financial and physical duties of man have also been explained, and it has been stated what the conduct of a man should be towards his wife and children. (For further clarification on this subject, the following references may be consulted: Nahw Mujtama' Islami, the chapter "Society and Family"; the chapter "Woman and the Mutual Relations of Spouses" from the book Islam aur Mushkilat-e-Tehzeeb; the book Purdah by Maulana Mawdudi (rahimahullah); the book "Khandan aur Muashra"; and the book Haq al-Insan by Abd al-Wahid Wafi; Insan, Maddiyat aur Islam by Muhammad Qutb, and others.)

After the explanation of the rights and duties of man, and after the statement of the restrictions placed upon him in view of this general guardianship and of his duties, there now begins the description of the qualities of the righteous and believing woman, and the beginning of the description of her conduct within the sphere of the family, especially her conduct in faith.

(Verse) "Fa-as-salihatu qanitatun hafizatun lil-ghaybi bima hafiza Allah" (4:34) (So the righteous women are obedient, guarding in the unseen what Allah has guarded.)

The natural temperament of the believing and righteous woman, and her necessary characteristic, should be that she is obedient, submissive and compliant. This is the very requirement of her being a believer and righteous. The word qunut means to obey with attention, will, inclination and inner desire, without any compulsion, without any pressure, and without weakness or laxity. For this reason the Qur'an said qanitat and did not say ta'iat. This is because the meaning of the first word is psychological, and upon it there is a colouring of gentleness and freshness. This word is exactly appropriate for the private, peaceful and loving relationship of husband and wife, for a cradle in which children are to be raised, whose atmosphere, whose shade, whose breath and whose every movement affect the child's life.

It is also the temperament of a righteous and believing woman, and also her necessary quality, that she protects her husband's honour and his rights. In the absence of her husband she guards his sacred household, and these qualities too are the result of her faith and her personal reform. When a believing, righteous woman guards the honour of her husband in his absence, then in his presence she will guard it all the more. In this way she does not allow herself to become the target of anyone's gaze, nor does she erase her chastity and honour in anything that is not lawful for anyone other than her husband. This is because man and woman are both one being, and both have been created from one soul.

And what is forbidden for others besides the husband is decided neither by the woman nor by the man; this decision has been made by God. (Verse) "Bima hafiza Allah" (4:34) (By what Allah has guarded) — that is, the matter is not such that a man permits a woman to commit some act concerning her own person, or not, in his presence or behind his back: acts at which the husband does not become angry, or acts to which a society incites that man or that woman, in circumstances where society has fallen into moral decline and has moved far from the Islamic system.

In this field of guarding there is one ruling: it is obligatory upon the woman to protect herself within the limits of Allah's guarding. Here the Qur'an has not used the imperative form for the woman's self-protection, but has adopted an expression that is even more emphatic than the imperative. God says that this guarding is with those means by which God says, and this manner of guarding is the very requirement of the temperament of the righteous women and of their reform and piety.

Here, all the excuses and pretexts of Muslim men and women who have become mentally defeated, and who have submitted themselves to the pressure of the modern misguided society, collapse. And it becomes clear what limits and bounds God has set for the righteous women regarding self-guarding, namely that they are obedient with the utmost submission and inner willingness.

As for those women who are not righteous, they are rebellious. (The meaning of nashizat is that someone stands upon a "nashz", that is, a high place that is visible from every side.) By this word God has given a sensory expression of a psychological condition. The nashiz in reality considers her disobedience permissible, commits sin openly, and adopts rebellion.

The Islamic system of life does not wait for rebellion to occur in practice, for the banners of disobedience and defiance to be raised, for the fear and awe of male supervision to disappear, and for the family to be divided into two camps. This is because once matters reach that point, there is no benefit left in treatment. Therefore, it is necessary that as soon as the threat of rebellion is felt, and before it grows to a dangerous extent, it be addressed, because the consequence of rebellion is the breaking and collapse of this important institution, after which the peace and tranquility of society are destroyed. Then, with the end of this institution, the work of training and preparing the new generation also ends, because the family is the best cradle for the new generation. If a generation is raised outside this institution, that generation will fall victim to psychological diseases, nervous diseases and other physical diseases, and as a result, a morally corrupt generation will be produced.

Therefore, since the protection of the family is a very important matter, measures need to be taken in this regard as quickly as possible, and what is required is that the signs of rebellion be attacked as soon as they appear. For this very reason, in order to protect this institution from evil and corruption, or to save it from complete destruction, the director of this institution has been permitted to take certain disciplinary measures, which very often prove extremely beneficial. These measures are not prescribed merely for revenge, humiliation or physical torment; rather, they are measures of reform, and are for reform at the initial stages and for ending rebellion.

(Verse) "وَاللَّاتِي تَخَافُونَ نُشُوزَهُنَّ فَعِظُوهُنَّ وَاهْجُرُوهُنَّ فِي الْمَضَاجِعِ وَاضْرِبُوهُنَّ فَإِنْ أَطَعْنَكُمْ فَلَا تَبْغُوا عَلَيْهِنَّ سَبِيلًا ۗ إِنَّ اللَّهَ كَانَ عَلِيًّا كَبِيرًا" (4:34)

"And those (women) from whom you fear rebellion, admonish them, forsake them in the beds, and beat them. Then if they obey you, do not seek a means against them. Indeed, Allah is ever Most High, Most Great."

As we mentioned earlier, Allah has made mankind honored, and this includes both men and women. Women have been given those human rights which relate to their human nature, and a Muslim woman has been given all the civil and legal rights that were given to men. Moreover, although men have been made her guardian (qawwam), the guardianship of men does not deprive a woman of the right to choose her husband. In this matter she is completely independent. Furthermore, she may exercise every kind of disposal over her property and wealth. All the other rights which are fundamental elements and basic rights in the Islamic system of life are hers.

If all these matters remain in mind, and if the discussion we made in the earlier pages regarding the importance of the institution of the family also remains in mind, then it is not difficult for us to understand why the Shariah has permitted these measures for the disciplining of a woman and the protection of the family, and why it has prescribed the method by which this discipline is to be carried out, provided our hearts have not been corrupted by following base desires and our minds have not been turned by pride and arrogance.

It is a fact that the Islamic Shariah has taken these measures only as preventive remedies. These measures are taken because the administration of the family institution faces a problem of peace and order, and the administration first corrects souls and sets conditions right, so that this corruption of hearts does not take a dangerous form, and so that hatred and aversion between husband and wife do not increase, and so that the bond between husband and wife does not break and end through inner disintegration.

Within the family, it is not only a contest between man and woman, and the purpose of these measures is not that a man should rise up and crush a woman, beating her severely whenever he feels a threat of disobedience from her and then dragging her back and binding her with a chain like a dog.

Islam certainly does not permit such conduct. Although among human beings some families do exhibit such habits, such treatment and such a relationship between man and woman arise only because all of humanity has abandoned its true station. This was not because one of the man or woman was in the wrong. But when the Islamic society is properly established, the situation will be entirely different, and the aims and purposes of discipline in it will also be different.

(Verse) "وَاللَّاتِي تَخَافُونَ نُشُوزَهُنَّ" (4:34): "And those women from whom you fear rebellion, admonish them." This is the first step in Islam: an attempt will be made to advise such a woman. The first duty of the head and director of a family is to advise. In every situation, it is expected that he will advise his wife in a most courteous manner. Elsewhere Allah the Exalted says:

"يَا أَيُّهَا الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا قُوا أَنفُسَكُمْ وَأَهْلِيكُمْ نَارًا وَقُودُهَا النَّاسُ وَالْحِجَارَةُ" "O you who believe, save yourselves and your families from a Fire whose fuel is people and stones." (66:6)

Protecting one's children and family is always required, but in circumstances where there is a threat of nushuz, what is required is to protect the family from a specific ailment, namely rebellion, before it goes beyond limits.

But sometimes admonition alone is not beneficial. Sometimes the caprice of the self dominates the woman, and she is under the influence of arrogant impressions. Sometimes she takes pride in her beauty; sometimes she is proud of her wealth; sometimes, because of her family status, she pays no heed to her husband; or because of some other qualities and attributes she becomes a victim of self-conceit, and she forgets that in the institution she bears equal responsibility with the man. She has not come to test her strength against him, and there is no occasion here for pride and self-glorification. Therefore, a second measure is prescribed against her: that the man should trample underfoot her attractiveness, her beauty and all the other things in which she takes pride, and psychologically demonstrate that he is superior to this woman, and that he is the manager and director of this institution. The command is: "وَاهْجُرُوهُنَّ فِي الْمَضَاجِعِ" (4:34) (forsake them in the beds). The bedchamber is a place where a woman, through her natural allure, deceives a man, where she imposes her command with the utmost pride. When a man controls his desires and confronts the woman's natural allure, he blunts the most effective weapon she uses against him. When a man stands firm in this position and displays the strength of his personality, very often the woman lays down her arms. However, separating women from the bedchamber has its own specific rules and etiquette: apart from the bedchamber, the other relations with the woman should remain intact. The man should remain separate from her only in the bedchamber. Moreover, this tension between husband and wife should not become apparent to the children, so that they are not adversely affected psychologically. Also, there should be no separation or tension in front of outsiders, which would result in the woman being humiliated or her self-respect being injured, and she would then display even greater rebellion, because the aim is that she give up rebellion. The real purpose is not the humiliation of the woman, nor is it desired to corrupt the children by making them victims of distress. This second measure takes both of these matters into consideration.

But sometimes this second measure too does not succeed. Then should the institution of the family be dissolved? No, there is one further effort. Although this last remedy is somewhat severe, compared with the dissolution and ruin of a family it is very easy and minor.

(Verse) "وَاضْرِبُوهُنَّ" (4:34): "and beat them." From the points we have previously stated and the objectives we have placed before these measures, it becomes clear that the purpose of this beating is not to punish the woman, nor is it desired to take revenge upon her, nor merely to cool anger, nor can it be permitted that this beating be for mere humiliation, degradation or contempt. Nor is the aim to compel the woman to remain alive in a family with which she is in no way content. Rather, this beating is only for the sake of reform, and within this beating there should also be sympathy and love from the man, such as a father shows in beating his child, or as a teacher punishes his students.

It is also evident that if there is complete unity between both parties of the family institution, then what need would there be for this beating? These measures may become necessary only when there is a threat of corruption and disruption within the family, and this happens only when some kind of defect has begun, and it is desired to remove it through these measures.

When admonition does not work and separation in the bedchamber also proves useless, it will be known that this deviation and corruption has taken a dangerous character and has reached a perilous level. It may be that in such circumstances the means of disciplinary beating will succeed.

Some practical incidents and some psychological cases show, and psychologists accept, that sometimes disciplinary beating is the only beneficial thing for a woman's rebellion. Through it she receives psychological treatment, and she quickly comes onto the right path.

It is also said that women suffer from a psychological illness of rebellion, and psychologists give it a name. But the results that the science of psychology has so far presented are not scientific and empirical results that could be called definitively established findings from a scientific standpoint, as Dr. Alexis Carrel says. However, it does often happen that some women do not feel the strength of the man, while their self desires that the man who is their guardian and husband should be stronger, and they acknowledge this only when the man physically keeps such a woman under control. But not every woman has this temperament, nor this psychological desire. Still, some women do indeed seek compulsion and domination from their husbands, and this measure of striking has been prescribed for precisely such cases, so that the important institution of the family may function properly with stability, in peace and tranquility.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 4, verse 35:

(Verse) "Number 35"

Islam does not advise that, as soon as rebelliousness begins on the part of the wife, you should surrender before that rebelliousness and aversion, nor does Islam advise that you immediately dissolve the marriage contract and break the pot of the family upon the heads of those who have no fault in this matter. Therefore Islam, out of regard for its importance, rebuilds it afresh with new bricks so that it may once again grow and flourish.

Now the Islamic system, upon sensing the danger of the marriage institution breaking, begins its final effort. It is commanded that an arbiter (thalith) be appointed from the man's side, of his choosing, and an arbiter be appointed from the woman's side, of her choosing, and that the two of them strive to bring about reconciliation between them. These people should gather in a very calm atmosphere. They should not keep their personal inclinations before them, should step away from the burden of their own feelings and perceptions, and should disregard the economic circumstances and interests which caused tension in the relations between the spouses. This command is to think beyond those circumstances which created bitterness in the atmosphere of life, or which created complications between the parties, and due to which the good elements of shared life between the spouses became ineffective. These arbiters should endeavour to keep in mind the reputation and honour of both families, and if the spouses have young children, they should also keep in mind the future of those children, and they should remove from their hearts the wish that either party succeeds or fails. For in such circumstances each of the spouses considers it a matter of honour for himself or herself to have their own point accepted. Rather, the arbiters should keep in mind the interests of the spouses, the interests of their children, and the interests of the institution which is undergoing breakdown. Along with this, it should also be borne in mind that they will be trustees of the spouses' secrets, because these two arbiters will be representatives of both families and of the spouses. The parties should have no fear that their secrets will be disclosed through them, and nor should they be disclosed, because the publicising of secrets is not in the interest of either party; rather, the interest of both lies in their secrets remaining behind the curtain.

The gathering of these arbiters will be for the sake of reform between the spouses, on condition that there is a genuine desire for the reform of their circumstances on the part of the spouses, and that this desire for reform has not been buried under mere anger. If the hearts of the arbiters contain a genuine desire and they are sincere, then Allah will grant the spouses the ability to reform their circumstances.

(Verse) "If the two of them desire reconciliation, Allah will bring about harmony between them" (4:35) "...": Since they seek reform with sincerity of heart, Allah accepts their efforts and grants them the ability to reform.

This is the connection of people's effort and their hearts with the decree and will of Allah. In reality, it is the decree of Allah alone that is effective in people's lives. But the decree of Allah has given people the choice to strive and endeavour for the reform of circumstances. Whatever results emerge from their effort will be in accordance with the decree of Allah.

Whatever results emerge will be based upon profound knowledge and far-sighted wisdom. (Verse) "Indeed, Allah is ever Knowing, Acquainted" (4:35) "(Allah knows everything and is well-aware)."

In short, in this lesson it is clearly evident that Islam gives great importance to the institution of the family which comes into existence as a result of the relationship between the spouses. We also learn how much Islam emphasises the organisation of this aspect of human life. Then from the hadith it is known how much effort Islam made, in the early period of the Islamic movement, to improve this aspect of life, and how it took the hand of the Islamic movement and drew it out from the filth of jahiliyyah. Placing it on the path of progress, it brought it gradually to the highest station and rank in accordance with Allah's guidance, because no guidance other than Allah's guidance is beneficial to humanity.

Lesson 33 at a glance:

The initial part of this lesson and the subject matter of the whole surah are connected in several ways. Likewise, the subject matter of this lesson and the previous lesson are also connected.

With this lesson began the campaign with which the collective life of the Islamic society was organised, and the undertaking to purify it of all the defilements of jahiliyyah and to clarify and establish within it the modern Islamic features. Part of this campaign was also to keep Muslims alert to the conspiracies of the People of the Book, who, in the form of Jews, were spread around Madinah with all their evil and intrigues, and who were constantly engaged in activities against the Islamic society. Day and night they were striving to create as many obstacles as possible in the path of the formation and completion of that society. Especially, they were greatly apprehensive of the moral values of Muslims and sought that they should not attain moral excellence. Moreover, they were apprehensive of the unity, harmony and mutual cooperation and solidarity of Muslims, since moral values and social unity and solidarity are indeed the real strength of a society.

This new lesson is, in fact, a prohibitive campaign, and its beginning is from the foundational principle upon which the Islamic society is based and from which the Islamic system of life is formed. That principle is pure monotheism (tawhid). The Islamic system of life is founded upon this principle. Every aspect of Islamic life and every dimension of it is a branch sprouting from this principle.

Before this lesson, the organisation of family life had been discussed from several aspects, and likewise collective life matters have also been under discussion. In the lesson preceding it, family life, its organisation and the measures for its protection were discussed, and the ties which make the family stable and strong were examined. Now, going a little further beyond this, this lesson deals with the whole of human relations and connections; that is, those relations which, in an Islamic society, go a little beyond the limited circle of the family and are established on human foundations. Yet they also have a connection with the family system. For example, it begins with instructions concerning parents, which is also connected with the family. Beyond parents, further relations are then described, and these relations come into being as a result of the pure love which exists within the family and whose effects extend to other human relations. A person first experiences the enjoyment of these pleasant relations within his own family; here he learns to maintain good relations. Thus these relations spread from a limited family to a wider human family, whereas previously these pleasant relations were sown within the family.

In the lesson under discussion, some instructions concern the limited nuclear family and some concern a wider human family. From this angle, the standards and measures of values are also indicated; that is, what are the ranks of those who spend and what are the ranks of misers? The lesson begins with the foundational rule upon which all values and measures are based, just as all detailed instructions of life are also based upon this foundational principle, namely the doctrine of tawhid. Every movement and every activity of Muslims, every concept and every impression of theirs, is based upon the doctrine of tawhid, and this is the worship of Allah. Its ultimate aim is the worship of Allah. The ultimate objective of all human activities is obedience to and servitude of Allah, and a Muslim, in belief and action, is a servant of Allah.

Since we are to worship and serve Allah throughout our whole lives, in this connection some rulings have also been stated concerning the specific worship of Allah, namely prayer (salat) and purification (taharah). And since prayer was a stage in which wine was made unlawful, previously it was possible that someone might be under the influence of wine even during prayer. In this regard it was commanded that one should not join the prayer in a state of intoxication. This was one of the comprehensive educational measures of Islam, given in connection with prayer. In short, all the links of this lesson are joined to one another. All its subject matters are related to the preceding lesson, and they are also consistent with the whole central theme of this surah.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 4, verses 36–38 (part 1 of 2):

(Verses) 36 to 43.

This passage begins with the command to worship Allah alone and not associate anything with Him. This command begins with the conjunction "wa" (and), which is a particle of coordination. This conjunction links this command and prohibition with the earlier rulings concerning the organisation and cohesion of the family institution, which were mentioned up to the end of the previous lesson. From the conjunction "wa" it is understood that this religion has a single principle and foundation, and that it is the link among all matters. That is, worship must be directed to Allah alone throughout the whole of life. Islam is not merely a belief and a few ideas that are firmly lodged in a person's conscience; nor is Islam a set of rites of worship performed in the mosque; nor is Islam merely a worldly affair that has no connection with belief and the rites of worship. Rather, it is a system within which all these things exist. Moreover, all its parts are linked with one another, and all these parts are linked with their fundamental principle, namely the doctrine of Tawhid. In all these spheres, to seek guidance from Allah alone and to take guidance from no one else, that is, to regard Allah as the God and Object of worship in the rites of worship, and likewise to regard Him as the Sovereign and Lawgiver in rulership and legislation, are both included in the doctrine of Tawhid. In both of these, Tawhid is a part of Islam, and this is the religion of God.

Together with the command of Tawhid and the negation of shirk, the command is given to do good (ihsan), and this command is given to a family, and it is also given to the entire human family, that is, to society. Greed, pride and arrogance are condemned, and likewise inciting people to greed is condemned. It is also said that concealing the bounty of Allah is also a blameworthy act. The bounty of Allah is general, whether it is material bounty or moral and religious bounty. Then fear of obeying Satan is instilled. Now the address turns toward the Hereafter, and it is explained that that Day will be extremely shameful and humiliating. All these matters are connected with the doctrine of Tawhid, and the source and fountainhead is fixed from which those who worship Allah and do not associate anyone with Him must take guidance. That source is also one; multiplicity in it is not possible. The means of taking guidance is He, and He is also the Lawgiver. In His sovereignty there is no partner, and in His worship and adoration there is no partner either.

﴿Wa-'budu Allaha wa la tushriku bihi shay'an wa bil-walidayni ihsanan wa bi-dhil-qurba wal-yatama wal-masakini wal-jari dhil-qurba wal-jari al-junubi wal-sahibi bil-janbi wa-ibn al-sabili wa ma malakat aymanukum﴾ (4:36)

"And worship Allah and associate nothing with Him, and be good to parents, relatives, orphans, the needy, the neighbour who is a relative, the neighbour who is a stranger, the companion at your side, the wayfarer, and those whom your right hands possess."

In the system of Islamic life, the guidance concerning worship and the guidance concerning legislation are derived from one and the same source, and they revolve around one and the same axis. All these things are derived from faith in Allah, and the focus of faith in Allah is upon the point of Tawhid. Therefore in Islam all guidance and all legislation are interconnected and harmonious. In the Islamic system it is not possible to separate one part of it from another. And if anyone seeks to understand a part of Islam while separating it from its point of focus, namely the doctrine of Tawhid, his understanding will be deficient. Likewise, on the practical plane, by acting upon one part of Islam and abandoning other parts, Islam cannot be fully implemented and established, and such partial Islam cannot yield its fruits in human life.

The basic concepts of this universe, of life, and of human relations spring only from the fountainhead of faith in Allah. These concepts then affect methods of working, the economic system, the political system, the moral system, the legal system and international relations, and these concepts also determine the states of an individual's conscience and the real condition of a society. These concepts also transform worldly affairs into worship. If these affairs are carried out in obedience to God and His Messenger, then, by making acts of worship the foundation of worldly affairs, they produce purity of conscience and cleanliness of action in them, and ultimately these concepts make life a unity that springs from the Islamic system of life. In it guidance is taken only from the One Lord, and the whole of life, in this world and in the Hereafter, returns to Allah.

What indicates this distinctive feature of the Islamic conception of life, the Islamic system of life, and the correct religion of Allah? It is shown by the principle that in this verse, before the commands to do good to parents, to do good to relatives and to do good to all people, it is said: worship Allah alone and associate nothing with Him. After this, the ties of parenthood and relations with other people are strung together in a single thread, and both matters are linked with the Tawhid and worship of Allah, whereas at the close of the previous lesson the doctrine of Tawhid and the worship of Allah had been made the constitution for mutual relations within the family. In this lesson the doctrine of Tawhid and the worship of Allah have been made the foundation for relations among all human beings, as we have explained above, so that in all these matters this doctrine becomes firmly established and a bond, and so that the source of all social relations and legislation becomes one.

﴿Wa'budu Allaha wa la tushriku bihi shay'an﴾ (4:36): "Worship Allah and associate nothing with Him." The first command is to worship Allah, and the second is that in worshipping Allah one should not associate anyone else with Him. This is a definitive and general prohibition, and it applies to all the deities recorded in human history. "Associate nothing with Him": applies to anything at all, whether it is matter and inanimate things, an animal, a human being, an angel, or even Satan. All these things fall within the meaning of "shay'" (thing) when the word is used in this manner.

After this, the command is given to be good to parents. Parents are mentioned specifically, and relatives are mentioned in general. Most of the commands in this matter concern children behaving well towards their parents, although parents too have been instructed to take care of their children. Allah, the Most High, is more merciful to young children in every condition than their parents are. Children are more in need of being directed to do good to their parents, because parents are going to depart from this world. Their connection is with a generation that is passing behind and in the background. Children, generally, in their personality, feelings, inclinations and concerns, turn toward the children who come after them. They do not turn toward the generation that has already passed. In the race of life, these people face forward, and they are negligent in looking back. Therefore, from this Allah, the Most Merciful and Most Compassionate, they receive these instructions, which give instructions both to parents and to children. He neither makes children forget their parents, nor parents forget their children; and He, who gives His servants guidance that they should treat one another with the utmost kindness, whether they are parents or children.

This verse indicates, as several other verses also indicate, that Islam gives guidance regarding goodness in such a way that goodness begins with one's close and extended relatives, and then its circle is gradually widened, and it is extended to all the needy who are connected with the wider human family. This command accords with human nature and runs in the direction of human nature. Feelings of mercy, of sharing in sorrow and pain, begin first in the home, which is a small family. A person who has not learnt or experienced goodness, mercy and love within the home cannot be expected to have such feelings towards a stranger. In terms of disposition and nature, the human self is also inclined to do good and kindness to its close relatives. There is no evil or harm in this feeling, provided that this feeling of goodness also extends beyond the limited circle of the family and a fixed point. After that, this method is in agreement with the collective organisation of Islam: that the system of mutual cooperation and support should begin in the home and then be extended to the circle of the community and society. The reason is that Islam does not wish to place its social security system in the hands of a vast government system, unless the people of the home or village fail, because local arrangements can be more effective. A local association can investigate the condition of the poor with greater ease than a government can, and can deliver timely assistance to those entitled to it with great ease and convenience. Because of this, love and mutual connection also arise among people, which is necessary for a human society.

Here the matter begins by saying: do good to parents. After that it is extended to relatives. After this there is mention of orphans and the needy, even if they live far away, because their need is also more pressing and caring for them is most necessary. After this, the nearby neighbour, then the stranger neighbour, then the companion who sits at one's side, because a neighbour who is a relative is always available, whereas companions at one's side are met only now and then. In the commentary on "the companion at the side" it has been reported that it means the friend and companion who stays with you, both at home and while travelling. Then the wayfarer who is far from his family and dependants, and then the slaves whom circumstances have made slaves, but who are nevertheless, in any case, human beings.

After the command to do good, a second command comes. Pride and arrogance are a bad trait. Greed, inciting others to greed, and concealing the bounty and favour of Allah are bad traits. Likewise, showing off in spending in the way of Allah is also forbidden, and it is explained that those who do such deeds do not in reality have faith in Allah and the Last Day, and that they are obedient to and companions of Satan.

﴿Inna Allaha la yuhibbu man kana mukhtalan fakhura (36). Alladhina yabkhaluna wa ya'murna an-nasi bil-bukhli wa yaktumuna ma atahumu Allahu min fadlihi, wa a'tadna lil-kafirina 'adhaban muhinan (37). Wal-ladhina yunfiquna amwalahum ri'a'a an-nasi wa la yu'minuna billahi wa la bil-yawmi al-akhiri, wa man yakuni ash-shaytanu lahu qarinan fa-saa'a qarinan (38)﴾ (4:36–38)

"Indeed, Allah does not love one who is arrogant and boastful (36). Those who are miserly and enjoin miserliness upon people, and conceal what Allah has given them of His bounty — and We have prepared for the disbelievers a humiliating punishment (37). And those who spend their wealth to be seen by people, and do not believe in Allah or the Last Day. And whoever has Satan as a companion, evil is that companion (38)."

Here, once again, this feature of the Islamic system of life becomes apparent: that in it all matters, all modes of conduct, all tendencies of reason and consciousness, and all relations existing within society are connected with belief and the conception of life. When a person becomes a servant of Allah alone and takes all guidance from Allah, he spontaneously begins to do good to people, seeking Allah's pleasure and hoping for the reward of the Hereafter. He does this work with the utmost humility and gentleness, and he does it acknowledging that what he gives, he gives from what Allah has given; he is not himself the creator of his sustenance, wealth and property. From Allah he receives everything. And as a result of denying Allah and denying the Day of Judgement, pride and arrogance arise, and greed and inciting greed arise. And the bounty of Allah is concealed so that its effects do not appear in the form of giving and generosity; and even if spending does take place, it is for show, and thereafter there is a display of boasting and vanity before people, because for such a person neither the pleasure of God is before him nor the hope of reward in the Hereafter; so before people the display of pride and arrogance is what is desired.

Thus the boundaries between the ethics of faith and the ethics of disbelief are easily determined. For believers, the source of good deeds and good conduct is faith in Allah and the reward of the Hereafter. Their eyes are fixed on attaining the pleasure of Allah, and this is such a lofty motive that the one who spends does not await any return from people, nor does he learn his deeds from the customs and conventions of the people. But if a person has no certainty of one God whose pleasure he seeks and for whose attainment he strives, and likewise no belief in the Day of Judgment and no lure of the reward of the Hereafter, then such people, if they do perform some act of goodness, do it according to custom and for worldly values. For such a person there is no fixed standard in any age or any place, let alone an unchangeable standard for every time and every place. For him, the motive for doing good will then be the very things that have been mentioned, namely pride and vainglory. And this motive will always be unstable and uncertain, and will keep changing along with people's values and their aims. And these blameworthy qualities will always remain attached to his spending: pride, arrogance, miserliness, and the call to miserliness, and showing off to people. Spending in the way of Allah, with sincerity and without self-interest, will never come from such a person.

The Qur'an says: ﴿Allah does not love such people﴾. The Divine Being is free from the states of dislike and love, so the words here refer to the effects of dislike and love. That is, Allah will reject them, will afflict them, and they will be punished for these deeds. ﴿And We have prepared for the disbelievers a humiliating punishment﴾ (4:38). Here, for pride and arrogance, a humiliating punishment is mentioned, which stands in contrast to these evil qualities. The Qur'anic manner of expression is such that it casts its shade beyond the intended meaning, and these allusions of the Qur'an are themselves intended and desired, and because of them aversion and hatred arise against the evil qualities and reprehensible deeds under discussion. As a result, a person regards these things as contemptible and keeps away from them. Especially so, since Allah also stated that people of this kind are companions of Satan, and it is understood that when Satan becomes one's companion, he is a very bad companion: ﴿And whoever has Satan as a companion, then evil is the companion﴾ (4:38).

Some narrations state that these verses were revealed concerning certain Jews of Madinah, because the qualities mentioned apply fully to the Jews, just as they apply to the hypocrites. In the period when these verses were revealed, they concealed the bounty and favour that Allah had bestowed upon them. It may also mean that they concealed the truth that had been given to them, namely the prophecies they possessed concerning the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, his prophethood, and the religion of Islam. However, the wording of the verse is general, and the subject here is goodness through wealth and action, so it is appropriate to let the meaning of the verse remain general, since the general meaning is more consistent with the context of the discourse.

When the inner selves of these people were exposed, when the disgrace of their deeds became manifest, and when their causes, namely denial of God, denial of the Hereafter, and companionship with and following of Satan, were also explained, and after this it was also made clear that the punishment for these evils is a humiliating torment, then Allah, the Exalted, asks in the manner of a rhetorical negation:

He neither makes children forget their parents, nor parents forget their children; and He, who gives His servants guidance that they should treat one another with the utmost kindness, whether they are parents or children.

This verse indicates, as several other verses also indicate, that Islam gives guidance regarding goodness in such a way that goodness begins with one's close and extended relatives, and then its circle is gradually widened, and it is extended to all the needy who are connected with the wider human family. This command accords with human nature and runs in the direction of human nature. Feelings of mercy, of sharing in sorrow and pain, begin first in the home, which is a small family. A person who has not learnt or experienced goodness, mercy and love within the home cannot be expected to have such feelings towards a stranger. In terms of disposition and nature, the human self is also inclined to do good and kindness to its close relatives. There is no evil or harm in this feeling, provided that this feeling of goodness also extends beyond the limited circle of the family and a fixed point. After that, this method is in agreement with the collective organisation of Islam: that the system of mutual cooperation and support should begin in the home and then be extended to the circle of the community and society. The reason is that Islam does not wish to place its social security system in the hands of a vast government system, unless the people of the home or village fail, because local arrangements can be more effective. A local association can investigate the condition of the poor with greater ease than a government can, and can deliver timely assistance to those entitled to it with great ease and convenience. Because of this, love and mutual connection also arise among people, which is necessary for a human society.

Here the matter begins by saying: do good to parents. After that it is extended to relatives. After this there is mention of orphans and the needy, even if they live far away, because their need is also more pressing and caring for them is most necessary. After this, the nearby neighbour, then the stranger neighbour, then the companion who sits at one's side, because a neighbour who is a relative is always available, whereas companions at one's side are met only now and then. In the commentary on "the companion at the side" it has been reported that it means the friend and companion who stays with you, both at home and while travelling. Then the wayfarer who is far from his family and dependants, and then the slaves whom circumstances have made slaves, but who are nevertheless, in any case, human beings.

After the command to do good, a second command comes. Pride and arrogance are a bad trait. Greed, inciting others to greed, and concealing the bounty and favour of Allah are bad traits. Likewise, showing off in spending in the way of Allah is also forbidden, and it is explained that those who do such deeds do not in reality have faith in Allah and the Last Day, and that they are obedient to and companions of Satan.

﴿Inna Allaha la yuhibbu man kana mukhtalan fakhura (36). Alladhina yabkhaluna wa ya'murna an-nasi bil-bukhli wa yaktumuna ma atahumu Allahu min fadlihi, wa a'tadna lil-kafirina 'adhaban muhinan (37). Wal-ladhina yunfiquna amwalahum ri'a'a an-nasi wa la yu'minuna billahi wa la bil-yawmi al-akhiri, wa man yakuni ash-shaytanu lahu qarinan fa-saa'a qarinan (38)﴾ (4:36–38)

"Indeed, Allah does not love one who is arrogant and boastful (36). Those who are miserly and enjoin miserliness upon people, and conceal what Allah has given them of His bounty — and We have prepared for the disbelievers a humiliating punishment (37). And those who spend their wealth to be seen by people, and do not believe in Allah or the Last Day. And whoever has Satan as a companion, evil is that companion (38)."

Here, once again, this feature of the Islamic system of life becomes apparent: that in it all matters, all modes of conduct, all tendencies of reason and consciousness, and all relations existing within society are connected with belief and the conception of life. When a person becomes a servant of Allah alone and takes all guidance from Allah, he spontaneously begins to do good to people, seeking Allah's pleasure and hoping for the reward of the Hereafter. He does this work with the utmost humility and gentleness, and he does it acknowledging that what he gives, he gives from what Allah has given; he is not himself the creator of his sustenance, wealth and property. From Allah he receives everything. And as a result of denying Allah and denying the Day of Judgement, pride and arrogance arise, and greed and inciting greed arise. And the bounty of Allah is concealed so that its effects do not appear in the form of giving and generosity; and even if spending does take place, it is for show, and thereafter there is a display of boasting and vanity before people, because for such a person neither the pleasure of God is before him nor the hope of reward in the Hereafter; so before people the display of pride and arrogance is what is desired.

Thus the boundaries between the ethics of faith and the ethics of disbelief are easily determined. For believers, the source of good deeds and good conduct is faith in Allah and the reward of the Hereafter. Their eyes are fixed on attaining the pleasure of Allah, and this is such a lofty motive that the one who spends does not await any return from people, nor does he learn his deeds from the customs and conventions of the people. But if a person has no certainty of one God whose pleasure he seeks and for whose attainment he strives, and likewise no belief in the Day of Judgment and no lure of the reward of the Hereafter, then such people, if they do perform some act of goodness, do it according to custom and for worldly values. For such a person there is no fixed standard in any age or any place, let alone an unchangeable standard for every time and every place. For him, the motive for doing good will then be the very things that have been mentioned, namely pride and vainglory. And this motive will always be unstable and uncertain, and will keep changing along with people's values and their aims. And these blameworthy qualities will always remain attached to his spending: pride, arrogance, miserliness, and the call to miserliness, and showing off to people. Spending in the way of Allah, with sincerity and without self-interest, will never come from such a person.

The Qur'an says: ﴿Allah does not love such people﴾. The Divine Being is free from the states of dislike and love, so the words here refer to the effects of dislike and love. That is, Allah will reject them, will afflict them, and they will be punished for these deeds. ﴿And We have prepared for the disbelievers a humiliating punishment﴾ (4:38). Here, for pride and arrogance, a humiliating punishment is mentioned, which stands in contrast to these evil qualities. The Qur'anic manner of expression is such that it casts its shade beyond the intended meaning, and these allusions of the Qur'an are themselves intended and desired, and because of them aversion and hatred arise against the evil qualities and reprehensible deeds under discussion. As a result, a person regards these things as contemptible and keeps away from them. Especially so, since Allah also stated that people of this kind are companions of Satan, and it is understood that when Satan becomes one's companion, he is a very bad companion: ﴿And whoever has Satan as a companion, then evil is the companion﴾ (4:38).

Some narrations state that these verses were revealed concerning certain Jews of Madinah, because the qualities mentioned apply fully to the Jews, just as they apply to the hypocrites. In the period when these verses were revealed, they concealed the bounty and favour that Allah had bestowed upon them. It may also mean that they concealed the truth that had been given to them, namely the prophecies they possessed concerning the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, his prophethood, and the religion of Islam. However, the wording of the verse is general, and the subject here is goodness through wealth and action, so it is appropriate to let the meaning of the verse remain general, since the general meaning is more consistent with the context of the discourse.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 4, verses 36–38 (part 1 of 2):

(Verses) 36 to 43.

This passage begins with the command to worship Allah alone and not associate anything with Him. This command begins with the conjunction "wa" (and), which is a particle of coordination. This conjunction links this command and prohibition with the earlier rulings concerning the organisation and cohesion of the family institution, which were mentioned up to the end of the previous lesson. From the conjunction "wa" it is understood that this religion has a single principle and foundation, and that it is the link among all matters. That is, worship must be directed to Allah alone throughout the whole of life. Islam is not merely a belief and a few ideas that are firmly lodged in a person's conscience; nor is Islam a set of rites of worship performed in the mosque; nor is Islam merely a worldly affair that has no connection with belief and the rites of worship. Rather, it is a system within which all these things exist. Moreover, all its parts are linked with one another, and all these parts are linked with their fundamental principle, namely the doctrine of Tawhid. In all these spheres, to seek guidance from Allah alone and to take guidance from no one else, that is, to regard Allah as the God and Object of worship in the rites of worship, and likewise to regard Him as the Sovereign and Lawgiver in rulership and legislation, are both included in the doctrine of Tawhid. In both of these, Tawhid is a part of Islam, and this is the religion of God.

Together with the command of Tawhid and the negation of shirk, the command is given to do good (ihsan), and this command is given to a family, and it is also given to the entire human family, that is, to society. Greed, pride and arrogance are condemned, and likewise inciting people to greed is condemned. It is also said that concealing the bounty of Allah is also a blameworthy act. The bounty of Allah is general, whether it is material bounty or moral and religious bounty. Then fear of obeying Satan is instilled. Now the address turns toward the Hereafter, and it is explained that that Day will be extremely shameful and humiliating. All these matters are connected with the doctrine of Tawhid, and the source and fountainhead is fixed from which those who worship Allah and do not associate anyone with Him must take guidance. That source is also one; multiplicity in it is not possible. The means of taking guidance is He, and He is also the Lawgiver. In His sovereignty there is no partner, and in His worship and adoration there is no partner either.

﴿Wa-'budu Allaha wa la tushriku bihi shay'an wa bil-walidayni ihsanan wa bi-dhil-qurba wal-yatama wal-masakini wal-jari dhil-qurba wal-jari al-junubi wal-sahibi bil-janbi wa-ibn al-sabili wa ma malakat aymanukum﴾ (4:36)

"And worship Allah and associate nothing with Him, and be good to parents, relatives, orphans, the needy, the neighbour who is a relative, the neighbour who is a stranger, the companion at your side, the wayfarer, and those whom your right hands possess."

In the system of Islamic life, the guidance concerning worship and the guidance concerning legislation are derived from one and the same source, and they revolve around one and the same axis. All these things are derived from faith in Allah, and the focus of faith in Allah is upon the point of Tawhid. Therefore in Islam all guidance and all legislation are interconnected and harmonious. In the Islamic system it is not possible to separate one part of it from another. And if anyone seeks to understand a part of Islam while separating it from its point of focus, namely the doctrine of Tawhid, his understanding will be deficient. Likewise, on the practical plane, by acting upon one part of Islam and abandoning other parts, Islam cannot be fully implemented and established, and such partial Islam cannot yield its fruits in human life.

The basic concepts of this universe, of life, and of human relations spring only from the fountainhead of faith in Allah. These concepts then affect methods of working, the economic system, the political system, the moral system, the legal system and international relations, and these concepts also determine the states of an individual's conscience and the real condition of a society. These concepts also transform worldly affairs into worship. If these affairs are carried out in obedience to God and His Messenger, then, by making acts of worship the foundation of worldly affairs, they produce purity of conscience and cleanliness of action in them, and ultimately these concepts make life a unity that springs from the Islamic system of life. In it guidance is taken only from the One Lord, and the whole of life, in this world and in the Hereafter, returns to Allah.

What indicates this distinctive feature of the Islamic conception of life, the Islamic system of life, and the correct religion of Allah? It is shown by the principle that in this verse, before the commands to do good to parents, to do good to relatives and to do good to all people, it is said: worship Allah alone and associate nothing with Him. After this, the ties of parenthood and relations with other people are strung together in a single thread, and both matters are linked with the Tawhid and worship of Allah, whereas at the close of the previous lesson the doctrine of Tawhid and the worship of Allah had been made the constitution for mutual relations within the family. In this lesson the doctrine of Tawhid and the worship of Allah have been made the foundation for relations among all human beings, as we have explained above, so that in all these matters this doctrine becomes firmly established and a bond, and so that the source of all social relations and legislation becomes one.

This is a definitive and general prohibition, and it applies to all the deities recorded in human history. Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran (Urdu translation)) on surah 4, verse 39–40:

"And what would it have harmed them had they believed in Allah and the Last Day and spent from what Allah has provided them? And Allah is ever Knowing of them. Indeed, Allah does not wrong (anyone) an atom's weight; and if there is a good deed, He multiplies it and gives from Himself a great reward." (4:39–40)

What harm would have come upon these people if they had believed in Allah and the Last Day, and spent from what Allah has given them? And if they had done so, the state of their good deeds would not have remained hidden from Allah. Allah does not wrong anyone even to the extent of an atom's weight. If anyone does one good deed, Allah multiplies it, and then bestows a great reward from Himself.

Indeed, what would have happened to them? What is the loss that they fear by believing in Allah and the Last Day? What is it that they fear by spending? That is, spending what Allah has given, in the way of Allah. Allah knows what they spend, and He is also aware of the causes and motives that move them to spend. Allah does not wrong anyone even to the extent of an atom's weight. Therefore there is no reason to fear that Allah will not know of their faith and their spending. Hence the reward Allah will give them will contain no injustice; rather, Allah will add something special from Himself to it. Their good deeds will be increased, and Allah will give from His own side without reckoning.

The path of faith is safe and beneficial in every case. That is, even from the standpoint of material gains and losses. Even if viewed from a purely material standpoint, faith is still a beneficial and safe path. Therefore it is asked what loss they would suffer if they believed in Allah, held firm conviction in the Last Day, and spent from the provision Allah has given them. This is because whatever they spend is not something they produced themselves. Despite this, Allah, by way of His favour and kindness, gives those who spend a multiple reward, and His grace and generosity will be added to it, although what they spend is from what Allah has already given. How magnificent is the grace and generosity of Allah! How excellent a bargain this is! Only an ignorant person could refrain from it.

At the end, the exhortation, command, encouragement and motivation conclude on one of the scenes of the Resurrection witnessed. Here their stance is presented in embodied form, in living characters in motion, just as the Quran always presents the sights of the Resurrection in a living and dynamic form.
