﴿Indeed, Allah commands you to render trusts to their owners, and when you judge between people, to judge with justice. Excellent is that which Allah instructs you. Indeed, Allah is ever Hearing and Seeing.﴾ (4:58)

This is the general outline of this lesson. Now, let us look at a detailed discussion of the texts.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 4, verse 58:

(Verse) No. 58.

These are the duties of the Muslim ummah (community), and this is its code of conduct. It entrusts trusts (amanat) to those who are worthy of them. And if it judges between people, it will judge with justice, and in accordance with the system and law that Allah has taught.

The trusts begin with the greatest trust (amanat kubra). This is the trust to which human nature is bound, and it is the same trust which, when it was offered, the heavens, the earth and the mountains expressed their inability to bear, but man took it up. The burden of trust that man took up was the trust of guidance, recognition (ma'rifah) and faith in Allah. This faith in Allah is faith worthy of purpose, intention and complete attention. This trust is also a demand of human nature. Apart from man, every other creature of God submits to God, is guided, recognises Him, becomes pure and obeys without purpose, intention or attention, and they obey the command of the divine majesty willingly or unwillingly. Man is the only creature for whom Allah has made his nature, his reason, his recognition, his will and his attention, and faith in him, dependent, and has made it obligatory upon him to strive to reach the station of faith. If he strives, then Allah will show him the way.

(Verse) "And those who strive in Our cause, We will surely guide them to Our paths" (29:69) ... This is the first trust which man has to take up along with the other trusts.

Then from this greatest trust, other subordinate trusts and responsibilities follow upon man. Among them the important trust is the trust of bearing witness to the truth, and this witness is to be given by man to the truth of this religion. First of all, the soul of the believer will bear witness that he is a believer; he should be a reflection of faith and Islam. A believer should be an interpreter of Islam and religion in his consciousness, his thoughts, his conduct and his action. People, on seeing him, should say: this is a model of Islam and the religion of Islam. On seeing him people should say that this religion of faith is very good, and its followers are so good, and those who adhere to it possess such morals and virtues. This is the witness to the truth of religion, by which all who see will be affected, and this too is a trust. The second witness is that a believer should invite people to the religion and describe its virtues before people, while the complete virtues themselves are alive within the caller. The personal purity and cleanliness of a believer is not sufficient testimony unless he invites people towards it. If he does not invite, then he has not fulfilled the trust of invitation (da'wah), which is itself a trust. After this, the witness to this religion is the establishment of the religion (qiyam al-din), and the discharge of this trust is obligatory upon the entire earth, in such a way that it becomes the method of the community of believers and also the method of all humanity. For this task, it will be the duty of a believing person to throw all his resources into this path. Whatever resources and means the Muslim community has, it should spend them in this path and bring this system to the stage of establishment in human life. This too is a great trust to be discharged, and it is an expansion of the personal faith of an individual, and this obligation of establishing the religion is not excused for any individual or any group. This is why it was said: "Jihad will continue until the Day of Resurrection" and this jihad is also one of the important trusts.

Among these trusts are also those which arise in people's mutual dealings. It is obligatory that people's trusts be returned to them: the trust of transactions, the financial trust that has been deposited with someone, the trust of advising rulers and subjects, the trust of raising young children, the trust of protecting the honour of the community, the trust of collective wealth, and the trust of guarding borders. In short, all positions, duties and all services are trusts, and they should be entrusted to those who are worthy of them. All these are trusts, and this verse makes a general mention of them.

As for the command that you should act justly among people, this is general and is for all people. It is not a command that you should act justly only among Muslims. Nor is it a command that, leaving other people, you should act justly only with the People of the Book. Justice is the right of every human being and should be given to them as human beings. In the Islamic system of life, justice is connected with this attribute, namely the attribute of "people" (al-nas), and all people are united upon this attribute. If they are believers, they are also "people"; if they are disbelievers, they are also "people". Whether friends or enemies, black or white, Arab or non-Arab, they are all "people", and the Muslim ummah has been entrusted with the charge of establishing justice among "people". Whenever it gets the opportunity to decide the affairs of people. This justice was given to humanity in this form only by Islam, only under Muslim governance, only in the era of Islamic leadership. Before and after that era humanity found it lost; it never even tasted it, in such a noble and honourable form that it is available to all human beings because they are human. It should not be confined to those classes who possess some other attribute alongside the attribute of "people".

This is the foundation of the judicial system in Islam. Just as delivering a trust to its rightful holder is the foundation and the fundamental principle of the Islamic society (for details see the chapter "Mujtama' 'Adil" in the book Nahw Mujtama' Islami), and after these two commands, namely delivering trusts to those entitled to them and acting justly among people, the statement that follows says: remember that this is an admonition from Allah and these are His instructions, and how excellent is this admonition and how excellent are these instructions: (Verse) "Indeed Allah admonishes you with an excellent admonition" (4:58).

Now pause here a little, and see what the style and manner of this phrase is. The essential point is the structure of this sentence. The original would have been: "innahu ni'ma ma ya'izukum Allah bihi". But in this phrase the word Allah has been placed first and made its subject ("inna" with its ism), and "ni'ma ma" (i.e. "ni'ma" together with its related elements) has been placed in the position of the predicate, and the original predicate has been omitted. Through this manner of expression it is established that there is a strong connection between the Being of Allah and this admonition.

This was not merely an admonition but a command; yet the command has been expressed with the word admonition (wa'z) and advice (nasihah), because a person quickly grasps a matter with the words of advice and admonition, and human intuition accepts it quickly, and thus the matter is quickly implemented, since its implementation includes choice, inclination and modesty.

After this, the verse concludes with the final follow-up and result, in which the whole matter is entrusted to Allah's watchfulness, His fear and hope for His mercy. (Verse) "Indeed Allah is ever All-Hearing, All-Seeing" (4:58). Here there is a very subtle and clear correspondence between the thing commanded, namely the discharge of trusts and the establishment of justice among people, and the fact that Allah is All-Hearing and All-Seeing. Allah hears and sees that you discharge trusts correctly and establish justice correctly. The process of justice also needs to listen well, to assess well, and to seek the deep causes behind circumstances and superficial matters, and then decisions should be made after insightful hearing, and the listener should be one of insight and perception.

Now, what is the standard of trustworthiness and justice? What is the method and concept of justice and trustworthiness? What is their definition, and how will they be implemented? That is, in every activity and every matter of life... Should we leave the meaning of trustworthiness and justice, and the methods and means of their implementation and currency, to the customs and terminology current among the common people, and call justice whatever their reason decides, or leave it to their desires?

Undoubtedly human reason and intellect have their own worth, and it is an accepted means for human guidance and for knowledge and recognition. This is entirely correct. But this human reason is in any case the reason of individuals and groups, and these individuals are members of a particular society, and many things influence them. There is no such thing as "human reason" which has an absolute and unrestricted meaning. The real point is that there is my reason, the reason of so-and-so, and then the collection of these reasons is human reason, and the collection of reason is confined within time and place. Therefore these reasons receive impressions from various influences, and sometimes incline in this direction and sometimes in that.

Therefore there is a need for a standard and a balance which does not change and is not affected. All these reasons should be weighed upon that balance and tested by that standard, and it should be determined which reason is right and which is wrong, which rulings are right and which are wrong, which concept is right and which is wrong, and where in these rulings and concepts excess, deficiency, negligence and deviation have occurred. Here the worth of reason is that a tool has been created for man's benefit, so that through it he may keep correcting his rulings and concepts in accordance with that balance. For this balance is one that is not influenced by man's desires, and worldly influences cannot affect it.

As for the scales and measures that humans themselves have devised, they have no standing, because sometimes errors occur within these human measures, and therefore values measured by these measures also suffer error. This error continues to be repeated until people return to that original standard and measure.

Allah the Exalted has set up this balance for mankind so that upon it they may establish trusts and the system of justice, and weigh all other values upon it too, and test all their rulings and all the circumstances of life by it, in every field of life.

(Verse) 59.

In this brief verse Allah states the condition of faith and the definition of Islam, and it also contains the founding constitutional principle of the Muslim community. It also becomes clear from it what the source of sovereignty and authority in Islam is. All these matters begin with Allah and are concluded with reference to the Being of Allah alone. If the Shariah contains no details regarding a ruling, then the people of Islam can turn to this constitutional principle and obtain answers to all their particular issues, and this foundational constitutional principle remains firm and established until the Day of Resurrection. Within it, room for disagreement has also been left for people's opinions and their intellectual endeavours.

The right of sovereignty over human life belongs to Allah alone, whether the matter is apparent or hidden, whether it is a great matter or a small one. In these matters Allah has established the ruling of the Shariah. The Sunnah of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ also exists concerning them, because the Prophet ﷺ did not speak mere whims; all his statements are based on revelation. For this reason, the laws he enacted are also the laws of Allah.

Allah is the One who must be obeyed. The essential characteristic of Allah's divinity is that He makes the Shariah for people. Therefore His Shariah must be implemented, and those who have believed have the obligation to obey Allah. Then they must obey the Messenger of Allah, because what the Messenger says, he also says by the command of Allah. Obedience to the Messenger is obedience to Allah, because it was Allah who sent the Messenger with this Shariah. In His Sunnah He has explained the Shariah for people, so his Sunnah and his judgments become part of the Shariah from this perspective. The faith of people is connected with the implementation of this Shariah, both in existence and in non-existence, because Allah has commanded: ﴿If you believe in Allah and the Last Day﴾ (4:59) (if you truly believe in Allah and the Last Day).

Here, "﴿those in authority from among you﴾" (i.e., those of you who hold authority) is also specified. That is, they must be from among you, meaning those in whom the condition of faith and the definition of Islam are found. That is, those who obey Allah and the Messenger, who grant the right of legislation and the right of obedience to Allah alone, and who in these matters seek guidance from Allah alone. In situations where explicit instructions have come, and also in matters where human understanding differs and on which no text has been revealed, they should likewise turn to Allah and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and apply to these issues the fundamental rulings that have been revealed and are explicit.

In this text, obedience to Allah is made obligatory in principle, and obedience to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ is also declared to be the principal obedience, in the sense that he is Allah's emissary. Obedience to those in authority is obedience subordinate to the obedience of Allah and His Messenger. For this reason, the word ﴿obey﴾ is not repeated a third time with ﴿those in authority from among you﴾, as it is repeated with Allah and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. This is because obedience to those in authority is derived from obedience to Allah and to the Messenger ﷺ. Meanwhile, with the word ﴿from among you﴾ attached to ﴿those in authority﴾, their being from among the believers is necessary. This is a condition for those in authority.

Along with all these emphases, obedience to those in authority belongs to those commands which are explicit and enjoined by Allah, which lie within the bounds set by Allah, and against which no text has been revealed. Moreover, these commands and rulings must not contradict the Shariah in the light of the principles of Shariah. The Sunnah of the Messenger ﷺ has with certainty specified the limits and restrictions according to which obedience to those in authority is rendered.

In the hadith of Hadrat A'mash (may Allah be pleased with him) in the Sahihayn, it is stated: "Obedience is only in what is recognized as good (ma'ruf)" (obedience is only permissible in lawful matters, in what is known to be good).

In the hadith of Yahya al-Qattan in the Sahihayn it is stated: "Hearing and obedience are incumbent upon every Muslim, in matters he likes and in matters he dislikes, so long as he is not commanded to sin. If he is commanded to sin, then there is no hearing and no obedience."

(Hearing and obedience are obligatory upon every Muslim person, both in matters he finds agreeable and in matters he finds disagreeable, as long as he is not commanded to disobedience. If he is commanded to disobedience, then there is neither hearing nor obedience.)

Muslim has narrated the hadith of Umm al-Husayn: "Even if a slave is appointed over you who leads you according to the Book of Allah, listen to him and obey him."

In this way Islam has made every person a trustee and guardian over the Shariah of Allah and the Sunnah of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. It has appointed him as overseer over his faith and his religion, appointed him as overseer over his self and his intellect, and appointed him as overseer over his affairs in both this world and the Hereafter. Islam has not left man in the way a single animal is left in a herd, to be restrained from here and restrained from there, not hearing or obeying, and constantly needing to be driven away with "hish." This is because the Islamic system is clear. The limits of obedience are defined by explicit texts. And if an entirely new matter confronts someone due to difficulties and problems, in later ages, with differences of circumstances, differences of societies, and changing conditions, and in which there is no definitive text or no text at all, where different people hold different opinions and estimations and each person holds a view according to his own intellect, even such issues have not been left completely free; they have not been left without any principle or rule. Nor has it been left such that there is no procedure for ijtihad and istinbat in them. Rather, in this brief text a splendid method has been provided for them, boundaries have been fixed for them as well, and this verse indicates the principle according to which ijtihad can be carried out.

﴿Then if you dispute about anything, refer it to Allah and the Messenger﴾ (4:59). That is, return them to those texts upon which these matters are incidentally applicable. If no texts are found whose application covers these issues, then resolve them in the light of the fundamental principles and general rules that exist in the Islamic Shariah. These issues have not been left unbridled in a state of chaos, nor are these matters like unknown affairs in which human intellects wander about, as some deceivers try to make people think. The Islamic system contains certain foundational and basic principles, and these principles are completely clear and refined. They encompass every aspect of human life. These principles prescribe for life a fence and a boundary such that anyone whose conscience is Muslim can reach the truth with great ease while remaining within them.

﴿If you truly believe in Allah and the Last Day﴾ (4:59). This is the obedience of Allah and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. It is the obedience of those in authority who are believers, who stand upon the Shariah of Allah, and who act in accordance with the Sunnah of the Messenger. Referring disputed matters back to Allah and the Messenger, all these matters are among the conditions of belief in Allah and belief in the Last Day, and all these matters are also requirements of belief in Allah and belief in the Hereafter. If these conditions are absent, then there is no faith at all. Likewise, faith will not be present if the necessary requirements of faith are not fulfilled.

When this verse has presented this matter before us in such a legal manner, then afterward it is brought again in the form of admonition and advice, and people are urged in a manner of affection, just as after the mention of the commands regarding trust and justice the same approach was adopted.

﴿That is better and more excellent in outcome﴾ (4:59) (this is the right course of action and better in its consequence). This method and this operating charter is very good for you. There is good in this world and good in the Hereafter. Its outcome in this world will be good, and its reward in the Hereafter will be good. The matter is not only that by acting upon this charter Allah will be pleased and reward will be given in the Hereafter. Although this too is a great and important matter, beyond it, by adopting this charter there is also betterment in this world. There is betterment in it for an individual, for a society, and for this entire worldly life.

The Islamic system of life is such that those who are given the opportunity to live under its shade lead happy and joyful lives, because it is a system made by Allah. He is the Creator, the Wise, the All-Knowing, the All-Aware, and the All-Seeing. It is a system free from human ignorance, free from human desires, free from human defects. It is a system in which no special treatment is given to any individual, nor is any favour shown to any class, any nation, any race, or any particular tribe, because Allah is the Lord of all people, and Allah is not afflicted with love for anyone; He is not the lover of any class, any colour, race, nation, or tribe.

It is a system whose key characteristic is that its Maker is the Maker of the entire universe, who knows the reality of human nature. He knows the inclinations and tendencies of the human self. He knows human means of address and the method of reforming him. Therefore, a mistake cannot proceed from Allah in any matter. He has no need to experiment with a system and then correct its errors, nor does He permit that people be subjected to difficulties through experiments with systems, leaving them to grope in darkness and remain perplexed. By giving this legal and moral system, Allah has left a vast field of material inventions for them in which they may keep experimenting. This is a domain sufficient for the boundless range of human intellect. For intellect, it is enough that it continues the work of implementing this system and applying it to problems, and that it keeps working through analogy and ijtihad wherever they are needed.

Furthermore, the one who laid down the Islamic system is the very Being who created this universe, so He has given humanity a method that is in harmony with the natural laws of this universe. This system does not wage battle against nature; rather, it is in tune with nature, acknowledges it, and benefits from it. This system both guides it and protects it.

Among the characteristics of this system is that, alongside guiding and supporting humanity, it also honours and respects it. In this system a broad sphere of action has been provided for human reason, and within it there is room for interpretation and ijtihad within the texts and guidance of the Qur'an and Sunnah. Then there is room to resolve matters on which no explicit texts have been revealed according to general principles. Beyond this, it is also the true field of action which this system has kept open for the best use of reason, over which it retains complete control, namely scientific research and discoveries and material inventions in the field of science. ﴿That is better and more excellent in outcome﴾ (4:59) (this is better and a good method of action).

After stating this general rule in this lesson, and after stating the condition of faith and defining Islam, and after expanding the constitutional foundation of the community, and after explaining the method of legislation for the community and its source, the discourse now turns to those who deviate from this constitutional basis and yet claim that they are believers, although they are going against the condition of faith and the definition of Islam. They issue judgments in their courts according to a law which does not conform to the Shariah of Allah. ﴿They seek to take their judgment to the tyrant, though they were commanded to reject him﴾ (4:60) (they have their disputes decided by a tyrannical law, although they were commanded to reject it).

With the turn of the discourse toward this, great astonishment is expressed at such people, and they are severely warned to consider where Satan is leading them. Here the condition of such people is described: when they are invited to implement Islamic law and to decide according to it, they strive to block it in a manner of utmost hypocrisy. Allah describes the hypocritical conduct of these people. It is also stated that the moment a person resolves to have judgments made according to satanic law, he is freed from faith; indeed, such people are not even considered to have entered faith in the first place. It is also made clear here how utterly flimsy and false their excuses are, and that their scheme is extremely deserving of censure and condemnation, and that as a result a calamity is bound to come upon them. Despite this, the Prophet ﷺ is advised to continue calling and admonishing. Then the matter is concluded by stating that messengers were sent precisely so that they might be obeyed. After this, in explicit and definitive words, the condition of faith and the definition of Islam are stated once again.

(Ayat) "Nos. 60 to 65."

The picture drawn of certain people in these verses shows that these verses were revealed in the early days of the Hijrah, in an era when hypocrisy (nifaq) was very strong, and the Jewish hypocrites, in league with them, were a powerful force.

Those who intended that legal judgments should be made according to the taghut (taghut) were hypocrites, as is also explicitly stated in the second verse of this group of verses. By them may also be meant the Jews, because when they were invited to accept that disputes be settled according to the Book of Allah, they refused and wished to have judgments made according to the law that was current in the age of ignorance (jahiliyyah). (The Jews' own mutual judgments were made according to the Torah. Here "Book" would mean the Torah, and sometimes the Prophet ﷺ also decided cases of the Jews, as some judgments show.) But here only the first case is meant, that is, the Book of Allah means the Holy Qur'an, because of the verse: ﴿Have you not seen those who claim that they believe in what has been revealed to you and what was revealed before you?﴾ (4:60). Therefore, here the meaning can only be the hypocrites, because the Jews never expressed the claim that they believed in the speech revealed to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. It was the hypocrites who made the claim that they believed in the Prophet ﷺ and in all the Books revealed before him, that is, a belief such as the Muslims hold: that we believe in the messengers.

And this can only be in the early days of the Hijrah, before the power of the Jews was broken in Banu Qurayzah and Khaybar, and before, by breaking the power of the Jews, the power of the hypocrites themselves was also broken.

In any case, in these verses we find a definitive, complete and comprehensive condition of faith (iman), a sufficient and exclusive condition, and a complete definition of Islam, and we receive from Allah the testimony that those who even intend to make judgments according to the taghut are not believers, because they were commanded to reject the taghut. ﴿And they had been commanded to reject it﴾. Besides this, from Allah in this group of verses we receive a solemn statement, and the Lord Himself swears by His own Self that these people cannot enter into faith and cannot be counted as believers until they make the Messenger of Allah ﷺ the arbiter in their disputes, and then obey his decision, implement his judgment, and this obedience is not without complete submission and acceptance and not without the joy of the heart, that is, submission in a state that has no helplessness or compulsion, but complete contentment and satisfaction.

﴿Have you not seen those who claim that they believe in what has been revealed to you and what was revealed before you? They desire to take their disputes to the taghut, though they were commanded to reject it. Satan wants to lead them far astray.﴾ (4:60)

Have you not seen a strange people who claim to be believers, and then in a moment they declare that claim false? These people (﴿claim that they believe in what has been revealed to you and what was revealed before you﴾ (4:60)) and after this claim of faith they do not have their disputes decided according to the Book that has been revealed to you, nor do they have them decided according to the Book revealed before you, and they wish to have decisions made according to something else, according to another system, according to another command. Rather, they intend to have decisions made according to the taghut, and the taghut is that which is not derived from the Book revealed to you or not derived from the Book revealed before you, and whose principle and standard are not derived from the Book or books revealed to you. This is why the taghut is taghut, and the taghut is taghut because it claims the exclusive sovereignty and legislation of Allah, and that taghut is taghut because it is not based on any independent standard. These people do not act this way merely out of ignorance, nor do they act on the basis of some doubt. They do it knowingly and deliberately, although taking their judgments to that taghut is forbidden. ﴿And they had been commanded to reject it﴾ (4:60).

They were commanded to reject it. These people do not do so out of ignorance or doubt; rather, they do it intentionally. This is why this assumption is not correct, this claim is not correct, that they have believed in this Book and have believed in the books revealed before you. It is Satan who wants to mislead them, so that they cannot refrain from it.

﴿And Satan wants to lead them far astray﴾ (4:60). This is the hidden cause because of which those people intend to have judgments made according to the taghut, and this is the motive which compels them to step outside the limits of faith and the conditions of faith and resolve that they will have judgments made according to the taghut. This is the cause which Allah reveals, so that they may turn back from their intention, and the Muslim community is also told who stands behind these people, and what is the real motive.

Now, in the following matter, the circumstances are described when such people are called to this: come to the law that Allah has revealed to Muhammad ﷺ, or to the law that was revealed before him. These people, who have the claim of faith, say:

﴿When it is said to them, "Come to what Allah has revealed and to the Messenger," you see the hypocrites turning away from you with aversion.﴾ (4:61)

Glory be to Allah, hypocrisy itself reveals itself. It is determined to deny even the clearest matters of natural reasoning. If it were not so, it would not be a situation of hypocrisy.

The natural and clear demand of faith is that a person should make his judgments according to the law in which he believes, and should bring his cases before the court in which he has faith. If someone claims that he believes in Allah and in what Allah has revealed, believes in the Messenger and in what has been revealed to him, and then such a person is called to have his judgments made according to the command and law in which he believes, the self-evident result of this invitation should be that he accepts it, and this is the demand of human nature. But if he refuses and prevents people from following that path, he denies a clear, natural and self-evident matter. This shows that he is a hypocrite and that his claim of faith is false.

This is the natural and self-evident situation to which this verse points. Therefore this verse is about those who claim faith and then do not make judgments according to Allah's law, but even when they are called to it, they shrink from having judgments made in that way.

After this, another hypocritical scheme is revealed through their conduct: that when such people fall into difficulty, or some misfortune occurs because of their wrong policy (and this happens because these people do not come to the sovereignty of Allah, or because they wish to have some judgment made according to the taghut, and as a result their position becomes bad), then these people resort to lame excuses to clear their position.

﴿So how will it be when a disaster strikes them because of what their own hands have sent forth, and then they come to you swearing by Allah, "We intended nothing but good and reconciliation."﴾ (4:62)

These people fell into trouble in this way: their secret would be revealed before a large gathering, and they would be boycotted in the Islamic society, or they would be looked upon with contempt in the Islamic society. Thus these people fell into great difficulty, because the Islamic society could not tolerate people who claim to believe in Allah, His Book, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and the speech revealed upon him, and yet have their judgments made according to some law other than the law of Allah. Such people find acceptance in societies that are neither believers nor Muslims, and who are nominal Muslims like these people, whose Islam and faith are limited only to claim and name.

Sometimes they fall into trouble in this way: they go to a taghut court and are wronged, because there judgments are made according to some law other than the law of Allah. Then they feel shame and return with regret, asking why they went to the court of the taghut and were wronged. If they had brought their case to an Islamic court, justice would have been done.

Sometimes this misfortune comes upon them from Allah as a trial, so that they may reflect and accept guidance. In any case, whatever the form, the Qur'an asks in the form of a rhetorical question what their condition is at that time, that these people return and come back to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ.

﴿They come swearing by Allah, "We intended nothing but good and reconciliation."﴾ (4:62)

This is an extremely shameful situation. They return, and they are aware that they have taken a very wrong path. Their state of shame is such that they cannot face the Prophet ﷺ. But by swearing oaths they conceal their inner false intentions, and they say that in truth they did not want to go to the court of the taghut, but wanted reconciliation between the parties by having judgments made according to custom. This is the claim of all those who want to evade the Islamic system of life. Such people say that they want to avoid difficulties: if the law of the Shariah were implemented, a calamity would come; opposition would arise among the people, although these people want balance among all classes. These excuses belong to those who claim faith but are not believers. Such arguments belong to the hypocrites, and in every age the hypocrites have said this. Allah strips away from them the veil that conceals them, and informs the Prophet ﷺ that Allah knows the inner reality of the hearts of such people and what is within them. Yet despite this, the command of Allah is that harshness should not be shown toward such people, but they should be counseled to refrain from such deceptions.

(Ayat) "Nos. 60 to 65."

(The Jews' own mutual judgments were made according to the Torah. Here "Book" would mean the Torah, and sometimes the Prophet ﷺ also decided cases of the Jews, as some judgments show.) But here only the first case is meant, that is, the Book of Allah means the Holy Qur'an, because of the verse: ﴿Have you not seen those who claim that they believe in what has been revealed to you and what was revealed before you?﴾ (4:60). Therefore, here the meaning can only be the hypocrites, because the Jews never expressed the claim that they believed in the speech revealed to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. It was the hypocrites who made the claim that they believed in the Prophet ﷺ and in all the Books revealed before him, that is, a belief such as the Muslims hold: that we believe in the messengers.

And this can only be in the early days of the Hijrah, before the power of the Jews was broken in Banu Qurayzah and Khaybar, and before, by breaking the power of the Jews, the power of the hypocrites themselves was also broken.

In any case, in these verses we find a definitive, complete and comprehensive condition of faith (iman), a sufficient and exclusive condition, and a complete definition of Islam, and we receive from Allah the testimony that those who even intend to make judgments according to the taghut are not believers, because they were commanded to reject the taghut. ﴿And they had been commanded to reject it﴾. Besides this, from Allah in this group of verses we receive a solemn statement, and the Lord Himself swears by His own Self that these people cannot enter into faith and cannot be counted as believers until they make the Messenger of Allah ﷺ the arbiter in their disputes, and then obey his decision, implement his judgment, and this obedience is not without complete submission and acceptance and not without the joy of the heart, that is, submission in a state that has no helplessness or compulsion, but complete contentment and satisfaction.

﴿Have you not seen those who claim that they believe in what has been revealed to you and what was revealed before you? They desire to take their disputes to the taghut, though they were commanded to reject it. Satan wants to lead them far astray.﴾ (4:60)

Have you not seen a strange people who claim to be believers, and then in a moment they declare that claim false? These people (﴿claim that they believe in what has been revealed to you and what was revealed before you﴾ (4:60)) and after this claim of faith they do not have their disputes decided according to the Book that has been revealed to you, nor do they have them decided according to the Book revealed before you, and they wish to have decisions made according to something else, according to another system, according to another command. Rather, they intend to have decisions made according to the taghut, and the taghut is that which is not derived from the Book revealed to you or not derived from the Book revealed before you, and whose principle and standard are not derived from the Book or books revealed to you. This is why the taghut is taghut, and the taghut is taghut because it claims the exclusive sovereignty and legislation of Allah, and that taghut is taghut because it is not based on any independent standard. These people do not act this way merely out of ignorance, nor do they act on the basis of some doubt. They do it knowingly and deliberately, although taking their judgments to that taghut is forbidden. ﴿And they had been commanded to reject it﴾ (4:60).

They were commanded to reject it. These people do not do so out of ignorance or doubt; rather, they do it intentionally. This is why this assumption is not correct, this claim is not correct, that they have believed in this Book and have believed in the books revealed before you. It is Satan who wants to mislead them, so that they cannot refrain from it.

﴿And Satan wants to lead them far astray﴾ (4:60). This is the hidden cause because of which those people intend to have judgments made according to the taghut, and this is the motive which compels them to step outside the limits of faith and the conditions of faith and resolve that they will have judgments made according to the taghut. This is the cause which Allah reveals, so that they may turn back from their intention, and the Muslim community is also told who stands behind these people, and what is the real motive.

Now, in the following matter, the circumstances are described when such people are called to this: come to the law that Allah has revealed to Muhammad ﷺ, or to the law that was revealed before him. These people, who have the claim of faith, say:

﴿When it is said to them, "Come to what Allah has revealed and to the Messenger," you see the hypocrites turning away from you with aversion.﴾ (4:61)

Glory be to Allah, hypocrisy itself reveals itself. It is determined to deny even the clearest matters of natural reasoning. If it were not so, it would not be a situation of hypocrisy.

The natural and clear demand of faith is that a person should make his judgments according to the law in which he believes, and should bring his cases before the court in which he has faith. If someone claims that he believes in Allah and in what Allah has revealed, believes in the Messenger and in what has been revealed to him, and then such a person is called to have his judgments made according to the command and law in which he believes, the self-evident result of this invitation should be that he accepts it, and this is the demand of human nature. But if he refuses and prevents people from following that path, he denies a clear, natural and self-evident matter. This shows that he is a hypocrite and that his claim of faith is false.

This is the natural and self-evident situation to which this verse points. Therefore this verse is about those who claim faith and then do not make judgments according to Allah's law, but even when they are called to it, they shrink from having judgments made in that way.

After this, another hypocritical scheme is revealed through their conduct: that when such people fall into difficulty, or some misfortune occurs because of their wrong policy (and this happens because these people do not come to the sovereignty of Allah, or because they wish to have some judgment made according to the taghut, and as a result their position becomes bad), then these people resort to lame excuses to clear their position.

﴿So how will it be when a disaster strikes them because of what their own hands have sent forth, and then they come to you swearing by Allah, "We intended nothing but good and reconciliation."﴾ (4:62)

These people fell into trouble in this way: their secret would be revealed before a large gathering, and they would be boycotted in the Islamic society, or they would be looked upon with contempt in the Islamic society. Thus these people fell into great difficulty, because the Islamic society could not tolerate people who claim to believe in Allah, His Book, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and the speech revealed upon him, and yet have their judgments made according to some law other than the law of Allah. Such people find acceptance in societies that are neither believers nor Muslims, and who are nominal Muslims like these people, whose Islam and faith are limited only to claim and name.

Sometimes they fall into trouble in this way: they go to a taghut court and are wronged, because there judgments are made according to some law other than the law of Allah. Then they feel shame and return with regret, asking why they went to the court of the taghut and were wronged. If they had brought their case to an Islamic court, justice would have been done.

Sometimes this misfortune comes upon them from Allah as a trial, so that they may reflect and accept guidance. In any case, whatever the form, the Qur'an asks in the form of a rhetorical question what their condition is at that time, that these people return and come back to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ.

﴿They come swearing by Allah, "We intended nothing but good and reconciliation."﴾ (4:62)

This is an extremely shameful situation. They return, and they are aware that they have taken a very wrong path. Their state of shame is such that they cannot face the Prophet ﷺ. But by swearing oaths they conceal their inner false intentions, and they say that in truth they did not want to go to the court of the taghut, but wanted reconciliation between the parties by having judgments made according to custom. This is the claim of all those who want to evade the Islamic system of life. Such people say that they want to avoid difficulties: if the law of the Shariah were implemented, a calamity would come; opposition would arise among the people, although these people want balance among all classes. These excuses belong to those who claim faith but are not believers. Such arguments belong to the hypocrites, and in every age the hypocrites have said this. Allah strips away from them the veil that conceals them, and informs the Prophet ﷺ that Allah knows the inner reality of the hearts of such people and what is within them. Yet despite this, the command of Allah is that harshness should not be shown toward such people, but they should be counseled to refrain from such deceptions.

(Ayat) "Nos. 60 to 65."

The picture drawn of certain people in these verses shows that these verses were revealed in the early days of the Hijrah, in an era when hypocrisy (nifaq) was very strong, and the Jewish hypocrites, in league with them, were a powerful force.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 4, verse 63:

(Verse) "Ulā'ika alladhīna ya'lamu Allāhu mā fī qulūbihim fa-a'riḍ 'anhum wa'iẓhum wa qul lahum fī anfusihim qawlan balīgha" (4:63). "Those are the ones whom Allah knows what is in their hearts, so turn away from them, admonish them, and speak to them a far-reaching word that reaches into their souls."

These are the people who want to conceal their intentions and their inner purposes, and who put forward false arguments and baseless excuses. But Allah knows the hidden things in their hearts and is also aware of the inner conditions of their consciences. However, the policy that had been fixed at that time was to overlook the hypocrites, to deal with them gently, and to make use of admonition, advice, teaching and training. ... For this purpose a remarkable mode of address has been adopted: "Wa qul lahum fī anfusihim qawlan balīgha" (4:63), "and admonish them in such an eloquent manner that the word enters their hearts." This is a highly figurative expression. It is as though the word is being placed directly in their hearts, and it is settling there.

Allah draws them towards repentance so that they may come onto the straight path and live a life of peace and tranquillity under the protection of Allah and His Messenger. Although they made an effort to have their disputes decided by the court of the tāghūt, and this also became apparent from them, they held back from seeking judgement from the Messenger ﷺ, even though they had been called to it. But despite all these shortcomings, the door of repentance is open, the time of return has not ended, and they can still seek forgiveness from Allah and from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). The Messenger's seeking of forgiveness on their behalf is acceptable, but this seeking of forgiveness will be acceptable only when the fundamental principle is accepted, and that principle is that Messengers are sent only so that people may obey them; otherwise, what would be the meaning of prophethood? Furthermore, a Messenger is not merely a preacher, nor merely a guide.

(Verse 4:64) "We did not send any messenger except to be obeyed by the permission of Allah. And if, when they had wronged themselves, they had come to you, [O Muhammad], and asked forgiveness of Allah, and the Messenger had asked forgiveness for them, they would have found Allah Accepting of repentance and Merciful."

Say (to them): We sent no Messenger except that he should be obeyed by the leave of Allah. Had they, when they wronged themselves, come to you and asked Allah's forgiveness, and had the Messenger asked forgiveness for them, they would surely have found Allah Oft-Returning, Most Merciful. (4:64)

This is a weighty truth. The Messenger is not merely a preacher who gives a speech and departs, such that his speech dissolves into the air. Behind his words and within them there must be an enforcing authority, as some people think, those who seek to deceptively alter the nature of this religion and the nature of prophethood, or as those hold who do not even know the meaning of the word "din" at all.

Indeed, din is the name of a system of life, a real and practical system of life, which has its own administrative, practical and legal form, and which has its own manners and its own values. It has its own ethics and etiquette, and within it are the rites of worship and the religious symbols.

All these things demand that prophethood be accompanied by sovereignty: there must be a system of government that enforces this system and this din, and the common people must be obedient subjects of the government under whose authority this system is enforced. This is the system of Allah, through whose governance Allah intended to give complete life. Because Allah sent every Messenger only so that, by Allah's command, he would be obeyed; therefore obedience to him counts as obedience to Allah. Allah did not send the Messengers so that people would take from them some emotional impressions and hold certain beliefs, or learn from them some rites of worship, and that is all. In understanding religion this is a very great calamity. This understanding of religion does not accord with the wisdom according to which Allah sent the Messengers, and that wisdom and purpose is solely that an Islamic system be implemented in actual and practical life. Otherwise, how easy a "religion" that would be, in which the duties of the Messengers were only to stand on a stage, deliver a speech, and depart, so that those who mock may mock and those who despise may look down with contempt.

This is why Islamic history has been a manifestation of this wisdom. In it there was da'wah and preaching, and there was a system of life and an Islamic state, and after the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) there was the history of the Caliphate. This Caliphate was established on the strength of the Shari'ah and on the basis of the system, and the establishment of that system was the primary aim, and the enforcement of the Shari'ah was the purpose of that Caliphate, so that obedience to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) would continue perpetually and the will of Allah for which He raised up Messengers would be fulfilled. There is no other situation which we can call Islam or call din. If there is to be Islam and din, then in it obedience to the Messenger will take the form of a system of life, even if the forms of that obedience differ somewhat, but the reality must be one. Without this, the reality of Islam and din cannot be found. Obedience to the Islamic system means bringing the system of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) into operation, judging according to the Shari'ah of Allah, obeying what the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) conveyed from Allah, and regarding Allah alone as the one who judges. The meaning of "La ilaha illa Allah" consists in not associating anyone else with Allah in sovereignty, of which the right of legislation is the most important right. Then, one should not take cases to the courts of the taghut, whether the case is minor or major, and in matters where there is no defect, one should turn to Allah and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), especially in circumstances that are newly arising in the modern age and over which there is difference of opinion.

For those who have gone to the taghut to seek judgments in their cases and have strayed from the Islamic path, there is still an opportunity to return, just as there was an opportunity for the hypocrites in the time of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and Allah was inviting them to it.

(Verse) "And if, when they had wronged themselves, they had come to you and asked forgiveness of Allah, and the Messenger had asked forgiveness for them, they would have found Allah Accepting of repentance and Merciful." (4:64)

Whenever anyone repents, Allah is Forgiving; whenever anyone returns at any time, Allah is Merciful and Generous. These attributes Allah mentions for Himself. Those who return to His presence and seek forgiveness from Him, Allah accepts their repentance and bestows mercy upon them. Initially, those to whom this verse applied had the opportunity to seek forgiveness through the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). Although these opportunities no longer exist, the door of repentance and forgiveness from Allah remains open. Allah's promise stands; Allah never breaks His promise. So whoever intends, let him advance; whoever has resolve, let him come forward.

Now comes the final and decisive matter. Allah swears an oath, by His own Self, that no believer can become a believer until he brings his disputes to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) for judgment. Then, when the Messenger decides, he does not accept that decision and become truly content with it in his heart, nor does his state become one in which there is neither bitterness in his heart nor any hesitation in it.

**Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 4, verse 65:**

(آیت) ” فلا وربک لا یومنون حتی یحکموک فیما شجر بینھم ثم لا یجدوا فی انفسھم حرجا مما قضیت ویسلموا تسلیما “۔ (4 : 65)

" No, by your Lord, O Muhammad (ﷺ), they will not truly believe until they make you judge in what they dispute among themselves, and then find within themselves no discomfort at what you decide, and submit with full submission." (4:65)

Once again we stand before the condition of faith; the limits of faith lie before us. Allah Himself decides and swears by His own sacred Being upon this decision. After this, what room is left for anyone to argue? The condition of Islam and the boundaries of faith are indicated, and in the very words in which this is indicated there is no room for any kind of interpretation.

Yes, if someone quarrels needlessly, that is a different matter. His argument will carry no weight, and it might be said that this command was for the time of the Messenger (ﷺ) and was only for the Companions ( رضي الله عنهم أجمعين)... If someone makes this interpretation, it becomes clear that this person knows nothing of Islam and is not acquainted with the style of the Qur'an's speech. In truth, this is a universal principle, brought with an oath and with added emphasis, and it has no limitation of time or place. Nor is there any room for the illusion that the decisions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) mean the judgments of his Shariah. If this meaning were adopted, then after the Messenger (ﷺ) his Sunnah and his Shariah would have no standing. And this statement was in fact about those people who apostatised in the time of Abu Bakr (رضي الله عنه), and Abu Bakr (رضي الله عنه) fought against them in the manner in which apostates are fought. Rather, a harsher attitude was adopted toward them than toward apostates, because they had only refused to pay zakat and had stopped paying it after the Messenger's death.

If it is sufficient for Islam that people have their disputes decided according to Islamic Shariah, then faith has even more conditions than this, such as that they be pleased with these decisions from their hearts, accept them sincerely, and be content with them with joy and tranquillity.

This is Islam, and this is Faith. Everyone should examine themselves to see how far they are from Islam and what the condition of their faith is, and only after that should they claim Islam and faith.

After the determination that people should have their disputes decided by the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and should accept whatever he decides with a willing heart, it is now said that this system to which you are being invited, and this Shariah according to which you are commanded to have your judgments made (and no judgment is permitted according to any other law besides it), and these decisions to which willing acceptance is necessary, this system is in reality extremely easy, straightforward, just and merciful. This system does not command you anything beyond your capacity, nor does it bring upon you any calamity that is unbearable for you, nor does it demand from you any sacrifice that you cannot give. For human weakness is known to Allah, and He shows great mercy to them because of their frailty. Allah, in His knowledge, knew that if heavy obligations were imposed on humans, they would not be able to fulfil them. Therefore Allah did not intend to place on people a burden beyond their strength, nor did Allah intend that people should commit disobedience. So Allah did not make heavy commands obligatory upon them, lest many people should turn to disobedience. If people had acted upon the easy obligations which Allah made incumbent upon them, and had benefited from the admonition which Allah is sending down for them, they would have gathered great good in both this world and the Hereafter. Allah would have helped them to come onto the path of guidance, and it is the sunnah of Allah that whoever strives in the way of Allah, with his action, will and firm resolve, within the limits of his capacity, Allah fully assists him.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 4, verses 66–68:

(Verses) No. 66 to 68.

Islam is a system of life which every person who is upright and sound in nature can act upon. To act upon it, no extraordinary resolve and no great person of firm determination is required. Such people are only a few in the world, and the Islamic system of life was not sent for these few people. It has been sent for all the people of the world, and in the world there are every kind of people, who are of different levels. Some have greater powers and abilities, and some have less. This religion has been sent keeping in view the average number of people, who can act upon the commands and can refrain from sins.

Killing oneself and exile are two commands which are extremely burdensome. If Allah had imposed these things upon people as commands and obligations, it would have become difficult for people to act upon these commands. But Allah did not impose these commands for the reason that Allah did not want to defeat people, nor did He want that people should reject these commands; rather, the purpose was that all people should act upon the commands of Allah. The commands should be such that they are within the reach of all. Within the caravan of faith, all those of average level should also be included, and in the Islamic society people of various classes, people of various aspirations, and people of various capacities and abilities should be included. All these people together should develop the Islamic society, in the form of a large caravan which is long and wide.

Ibn Juraij, Ishaq Abu al-Azhar, Isma'il, through the chain of Abu Ishaq, says Abu al-Haq: When this verse was revealed: "And if We had decreed for them, 'Kill yourselves' or 'Leave your homes,' they would not have done it, except a few of them" (4:66), a man said: "If Allah had commanded us, we would surely have done it. But it is a great mercy of Allah that He has forgiven us." This statement reached the Prophet ﷺ, and he said: "There are people in my ummah whose faith is settled in their hearts more firmly than those mountains which are extremely high."

Another narration Ibn Abi Hatim has narrated from Hazrat Mus'ab (ra). He narrated from his paternal uncle Amir ibn Ubayd ibn Zubayr (ra) that when this verse was revealed:

"And if We had decreed for them, 'Kill yourselves' or 'Leave your homes,' they would not have done it, except a few of them" (4:66)

the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "If this command had been revealed, Ibn Umm Abd would have been among them." He also narrated a report from Shurayh ibn Ubayd, who says: When the Messenger ﷺ recited this verse, "And if We had decreed for them, 'Kill yourselves'" (4:66), the Messenger of Allah ﷺ pointed towards Abdullah ibn Rawahah (ra) and said: "If Allah had imposed these obligations, he would have been among those few people."

The Messenger of Allah ﷺ knew his companions very deeply and very well. Their qualities and abilities were so accurately known to him, that they themselves did not know about themselves to that extent. There are countless incidents in the biography of the Prophet ﷺ from which this ability of the Prophet ﷺ becomes well known, that he had deep knowledge about his companions. Moreover, the Prophet had knowledge of the abilities of the tribes with which he was at war. Like an insightful leader, he was well acquainted with his environment, and sometimes this information was extremely miraculous, because it was based upon knowledge bestowed directly by Allah.

This is not our topic here; what we want to say here is that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ knew that among his companions and in his ummah there would be people who would bear unbearable difficulties, if these difficulties were imposed upon them. But he also knew that he had not been sent as a messenger only to those few outstanding people. This is a truth which awakens every inner feeling in the heart, provided there is some particle of goodness present in a heart, provided there is some seed of righteousness present, provided there is in it some impulse toward an honourable station, entry into the shade of Allah's mercy, and the search for the generosity of Allah's grace. This gathering is for precisely such people as are high-minded and seekers of lofty ranks. This is the grace of Allah, and no one can reach the station of this grace and bounty merely through his obedience and his deeds. Rather, it is only the wide, profound and abundant grace and bounty of Allah, whose general outpouring covers whoever is destined for it.

Here it is fitting that we spend a few moments in the gathering of the Companions of the Prophet ﷺ. These people were eager for the gathering of the Messenger ﷺ, both in this world and in the Hereafter. Some of these gentlemen would become distressed merely at the thought of being separated from him, even though he was then present among them. Therefore these verses were revealed, by which their love was refreshed and their pure sentiment was stirred, and their pure and transparent love became purer still.

Ibn Jarir narrated from Sa'id ibn Jubayr: a man from the Ansar came who was very distressed. The Messenger ﷺ said, "O so-and-so, why are you distressed?" He replied, "O Messenger of Allah, I was thinking about a matter." He asked, "What was it?" He said, "It is that we come to you morning and evening, we look upon your face and sit in your assembly. Tomorrow you will go to the prophets, and we will not be able to meet you." The Messenger of Allah ﷺ gave no answer to this man's question. In the meantime, Jibril (peace be upon him) came with this verse:

﴿And whoever obeys Allah and the Messenger – those are with the ones upon whom Allah has bestowed favour from among the prophets...﴾ (4:69). The Prophet ﷺ sent a message to that man and gave him glad tidings.

Abu Bakr ibn Mardawayh also narrated this report from Aisha (may Allah be pleased with her): a man came to the Prophet ﷺ and said, "O Messenger, you are dearer to me than my own soul, you are dearer to me than my family, and you are dearer to me than my daughters. When I am at home I remember you, and I rise and come and see you, and I cannot be patient. When I think of my death and your death, I realise that you will enter Paradise and join the company of the prophets, and even if I enter Paradise I may not be able to see you." The Prophet ﷺ gave no answer to this man's concerns until this verse was revealed:

﴿And whoever obeys Allah and the Messenger – those are with the ones upon whom Allah has bestowed favour from among the prophets and the truthful and the martyrs and the righteous; and excellent are those as companions.﴾ (4:69)

Sahih Muslim has the hadith of Rabi'ah, who said: I was with the Prophet ﷺ one night. I provided him water for ablution and his other needs. The Messenger ﷺ said, "Ask whatever you wish." I said, "O Messenger of Allah, I seek your companionship in Paradise." He said, "Is there anything else?" He said, "No, just that." The Messenger ﷺ said, "Then help me against your own soul by increasing your prostrations."

In Sahih al-Bukhari this report has come through several chains: a man loves a group but does not meet them, so what will his condition be? The Prophet ﷺ said, "A man will be with those whom he loves." This was the very matter in which their hearts and minds were always occupied: love for the Messenger and companionship with the Messenger in the Hereafter. They had already tasted the company of the Messenger in this world too. Today only that heart can taste this which contains love for the Messenger, and for us, in this last hadith, there appears a ray of light, a means of tranquillity, and a lamp of hope.

Lesson 36 at a glance:

I am inclined to think that the collection of verses in this lesson was revealed in the early period at Madinah, after the Battle of Uhud and before the Battle of the Trench, because the picture it draws of Islamic society shows that it had not yet reached a stage of maturity. Within this society there were various kinds of groups, some of whom were immature, and there were also people who had not truly believed but were merely practising hypocrisy. These verses show that the Islamic society still needed its education and training further, and that in this regard great effort and deep attention were required. It needed to be prepared for that great goal and made capable of bearing the burden which Islam had placed upon its shoulders, and it was also necessary to raise this society to the level of people needed for an Islamic revolution, whether this training and reform was in the field of beliefs and concepts or in the field of confronting opposing camps.

And when we say that some were immature, this does not mean that there was a shortage of people of the very highest standard in that society. Here we are taking the Islamic society of that time as a whole. Various elements existed in this society, but they were not all alike. Therefore there was a need to strive to bring all the elements of this society to a high level so that complete harmony might arise among its members. This is clearly expressed through these verses and guidance.

Through a deep study of these guidances revealed by Allah, we get the opportunity to assess the Muslim society of that time, and the features of the Muslim community emerge in which this society appears as a human society. We often overlook this aspect. In this society we see both high-standard training and strength, and we also see some weaknesses. It is also seen how the Qur'an deals with human weaknesses, the remaining traces of jahiliyyah, and the opposing camp of Islam, and how all this happens at the same time. When we study the Qur'an's method of training, the Qur'an appears to deal with living human beings in the real world, and it is also seen how, through successful effort in the field of training, the Qur'an created a society which was taken from the jahili society, which had people of various ranks and classes and people of various characteristics, and the Qur'an made them so harmonious, so lofty, and so united, the complete image of which is clearly visible in the final period of the Prophet ﷺ, and this was a society so elevated, complete and perfect that it is not possible for human beings to go beyond it.

From the study of any human society we learn what capacities lie within the human soul, and in what form they manifest within the best community and society in the world. That community whose training was itself given by the Messenger ﷺ, and this training was indeed in accordance with the Qur'anic method.

From this we also learn what the Qur'an's method of training was, and how the Qur'an dealt with human souls. How gentle its attitude toward them was, and how it bound together and united people of different levels within the community. We see the Qur'an's method of training, and we see this training system functioning in the real world in accordance with human nature.

One further benefit we gain is that we compare our own circumstances and those of other human societies with that human community which Allah established. Then we study the actual condition of those societies from a human perspective, so that, seeing our own shortcomings, we do not despair of reforming our condition in the modern age and do not abandon the effort to reform ourselves. And lest this first Islamic society become in our imagination merely an imaginary society, and we abandon the endeavour to walk in the footsteps of that community, and in the modern age raise these modern societies from their present decline to a lofty station.

This is a great storehouse of lessons. And when we take this storehouse, living within the shade of Fi Zilal al-Quran, it will be a great means of good for us.

From the verses given in this lesson it is known that the following kinds of people existed in the Islamic ranks at that time:

(A) There were also people who kept themselves back from jihad. Through them, laziness also arose among others, and if they did not go out for jihad and remained safe and sound in their homes, they considered it a success for themselves, while the Muslims who took part in jihad faced difficulties and hardships in it. Similarly, if these people did not go for jihad and the Muslims obtained spoils of war, such people would feel that they had suffered a loss because they did not receive a share of the spoils. In this way these people were trading the world for the Hereafter.

(B) Among these people were some emigrants who, while they were in Makkah and were subjected to persecution, out of a spirit of defence and bravery would say that they wished they were permitted to fight and wage war, but there the permission to fight had been entirely withheld from them. Now, when the command for jihad came in Madinah and it was said that they should begin fighting the disbelievers, these people began to wish that they had been given more time and that the command to fight had not come.

(C) Among them were people who, when some good fortune reached them, would say, "This is from Allah's grace," and when a calamity came, would say, "This calamity is because of the Prophet ﷺ." They did not say this because they had firm faith in and reliance upon Allah, but rather they said these things while criticising the Islamic leadership.

(D) There were also some who, in the presence of the Prophet ﷺ, would show themselves as most obedient, but when they left his presence they would plot against the Muslims and speak something else with their companions.

(E) There were some who lent their ears to rumours and spread them within the Islamic ranks. In this way they created unrest in the Islamic front, whereas they should have taken the matter to proof or referred it themselves to the Islamic leadership.

(F) There were some who doubted whether the source and origin of these guidances was the Divine Being, or not; they thought that the Prophet ﷺ spoke some matters on his own initiative.

(G) There were some who used to defend the hypocrites, as the examples at the beginning of the next lesson show. Their aim was that the community of Muslims should be divided into two groups concerning the hypocrites. From this it was apparent that within their Islamic conception and organisation complete harmony did not yet exist, and these people did not fully understand the duties of leadership and the need for connection with the leadership in such matters.

All these elements that existed in the Islamic ranks were groups of hypocrites. It may be that they all belonged to one group; it is also possible that in Madinah's society these people belonged to several groups of hypocrites, or that among these people there were also weak-faith Muslims whose state of faith had not yet matured. Some of these people may also have been emigrants. In any case, several such groups existed within the Islamic community, and this community at that time was surrounded by the Jews of Madinah, while in Makkah it was in the grip of the polytheists, and throughout the Arabian Peninsula this community was encircled by those waiting to see which way the camel of this movement would sit. This community was continually creating unrest within the ranks of the Muslims. Therefore there was a need for training and purification within the inner ranks, and a need to rouse people to jihad.

From these verses it is known in what manner the Qur'an carried out this inner jihad and training. The Qur'an removed despair from the ranks of the Muslims and reassured every individual of the community. With the utmost depth, precision and patience, and in extremely testing circumstances, the leader of this movement, Muhammad ﷺ, was himself carrying out this training. Let us observe some examples of it.

(A) The command is given to be alert at all times: the mujahidin and believers should not roam alone, and should go together on expeditions and campaigns.

That is, they should go out in detachments and units, or all together as an army, because in the area around them there are various hostilities, and enemies lie in ambush, among whom are hypocrites, or enemies whom the hypocrites are sheltering. Moreover, the Jews are also allied with the enemies of the whole Arabian Peninsula, who are waiting for an opportunity.

(B) Here too there appears a repugnant picture of those who used to fall behind in jihad. Their courage has failed; they are self-interested and extremely fickle, and very quickly change with circumstances. One is astonished at the condition of such people, who were very enthusiastic in Makkah, but now that jihad has become obligatory in Madinah, they lament and wail.

(C) Here too the promise from Allah for those who fight in the way of Allah is clearly visible: that Allah will give them a great reward, and that they will certainly receive one of two good outcomes. That is: "And whoever fights in the way of Allah and is killed, or is victorious, to him We shall give a great reward," in both cases.

(د) The Qur'an also indicates the loftiness of its aims, the purity of its objectives, and the goals of ultimate success, for the sake of which jihad and qital (fighting) have been made obligatory. It is "in the way of Allah, in support of the weak men, women and children, who constantly say: 'Our Lord, bring us out of this town whose people are oppressors; and appoint for us from Yourself a protector, and appoint for us from Yourself a helper.'"

(ھ) Then the Qur'an also records the truth of these aims and establishes that they are backed by a strong authority, and it also shows that the aims for which the disbelievers fight are false and that their authority is weak. The Qur'an was guiding this community with a policy such that it would reach a station of strength and majesty, and then every kind of harmony and unity would come into being within it. These were very far-reaching aims and objectives, because if a community has strong people within it, it still should not be unconcerned if weak people are present in its ranks.
