Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 4, verse 74:

(Let those who) must fight in the way of Allah be those who sell the life of this world for the Hereafter. And whoever fights in the way of Allah, and is killed or becomes victorious, We shall soon give him a great reward. (4:74)

Therefore the believers should fight in the way of Allah. Apart from fighting in the way of Allah, Islam recognises no other war. Hence war should not be waged to secure raw materials for manufactured goods; Islam does not permit war for the sake of booty; it does not permit war for the sake of power; it does not permit war for personal or national superiority; it does not permit war to conquer countries; it does not permit war to enslave people; Islam does not permit a war fought to capture markets; and Islam's war is not for the purpose of investing capital in colonial territories and deriving benefits from them.

Islam does not permit war for personal superiority, nor for the superiority of any family. Islam does not permit war for the superiority of any class or any government, nor does Islam fight for the superiority of any nation or any race. Islam permits war only in the way of Allah, and permits it to raise the word of Allah on earth, so that across this globe, among all human beings, unrestricted justice and equity may prevail, while under this system every person has complete freedom of belief and ideology. Thus, under this divine, human and universal system of life, people may live.

When a Muslim goes forth to fight in the way of Allah, and fights only to make the word of Allah supreme and to struggle for the rule of the Islamic system of life, and then he is killed, he is a martyr. He attains the station of martyrs with Allah. But if he fights for any purpose other than this, he is by no means a martyr, and there is no reward or recompense for him with Allah. Rather, his recompense lies with the leaders of those aims. Those who call such people martyrs fabricate lies against Allah, and they sanctify themselves with something with which Allah does not sanctify anyone. This is nothing but a fabrication against Allah.

Therefore, fighting in the way of Allah is permissible only for this one purpose. And it is those who sell the world and buy the Hereafter who fight this battle, and for them the great bounty of Allah awaits. In both conditions they receive His favour: if they are killed in the way of Allah, there is favour, and if they become victorious in the way of Allah, there is also the favour of Allah.

(4:74) "And whoever fights in the way of Allah, and is killed or becomes victorious, We shall soon give him a great reward."

In this way the Qur'anic system of life elevates these holy souls, and in both conditions they become hopeful of the great favour of Allah. For them, death and the giving of life in the way of Allah become easy. They also rise above the hope of obtaining the spoils of war in this world, because the entire life and the great heaps of booty are nothing in comparison with the great favour of Allah. Likewise, this brief phrase creates in human hearts an aversion to the bargain in which a person exchanges the Hereafter for this world. The word yashtaroon (يشترون) is one of the words that carry opposite meanings: it is used both in the sense of buying and in the sense of selling, but for the most part it is used in the sense of selling. So this transaction will be an utterly losing one, whether or not they obtain booty in this world, for what is this world compared with the Hereafter, and what is the paltry wealth of the spoils compared with the great favour of Allah? The favour of Allah includes wealth, and also includes other honours and bounties besides wealth.

Now the address turns back to the Muslims. Leaving aside the manner of depicting those who shrink from war and shirk it, the Muslims are now addressed directly. Their generosity and manliness are stirred. A sense of duty is awakened in their hearts. Reflect upon the condition of the oppressed in this world and in the Arabian Peninsula: men, women and children who are suffering persecution at the hands of the polytheists in Makkah, and who lack even the strength to migrate to the abode of Islam and flee to save their religion and convictions. They await liberation, and they constantly supplicate, saying: "O Lord, bring us out of this town whose people are oppressors." By directing the Muslims' attention to this situation, it tells them that your war is for lofty purposes, your objectives are high, and the war for which you are being commanded to go forth has most exalted aims. Therefore they should not set out for it with heavy steps. This call is in an extremely emphatic and stirring manner, and sluggishness and holding back are regarded as exceedingly evil.

(Ayat) No. 75.

What excuse do you have for being slack in fighting in the way of Allah, when the freeing of the oppressed and weak men, women and children is among your duties? These are people in a pitiable state, and the Qur'an depicts them in extremely moving words, which stir the honour of the Muslims, awaken their zeal, and rouse the feelings of human compassion and sympathy, because these people are suffering the most severe and harsh of oppressions. And also because these oppressions are inflicted upon them solely on account of their beliefs. They are afflicted for the sake of their religion, and they have no other crime. In short, the hardships that come because of convictions and religion are more severe and harsher than the hardships that come because of life and property, because these hardships come upon a person on account of his human distinctions. The hardship concerning a person's honour, his dignity and his right of ownership comes after that.

The picture of a woman who is broken and shattered, and the sight of children who are frail and weak, is a scene that creates turmoil in the emotions. Especially those weak people and the elderly who cannot even defend themselves, and especially in such circumstances where that defence is connected with religion and faith. This scene is shown at a time when a call to jihad is being made. The truth is that in such circumstances, not rising for jihad would be an extremely detestable act, when the cries and lamentations of the oppressed are being heard. This is a mode of expression which melts hearts and penetrates deep into human consciousness and feeling.

Therefore, let us also cast a glance at this aspect: what is the status of a country and homeland according to the Islamic conception? Here the country and the town are defined thus: (Al-Zalim ahluha), whose people are oppressors, this is, according to Islam, the Dar al-Harb (abode of war). And it is obligatory upon the Muslims to wage war against that country in order to rescue the weak Muslims and their wives and children. And this homeland is Makkah, which was the original homeland of the Muhajirun, and the Muhajirun are given a stirring call to wage war against that master. And the weak Muslims are commanded that whenever they find an opportunity, they should come out of that oppressive land.

Here, the fact that this region and country was the original homeland of the Muhajirun is of no reality, and therefore from the Islamic point of view its status does not change, since the Shari'ah of Allah is not enforced in it. It is not under the Islamic system of life, in which believers are put into trials and tribulations because of their faith, and oppressions are inflicted upon them solely on account of their creed. Rather, from the point of view of those original inhabitants themselves, this country has become Dar al-Harb. They do not defend their original homeland; rather, these people themselves fight against their own original country in order to remove their believing brothers from there. In short, the banner of a Muslim is the banner of his creed, and a Muslim supports only one banner. The homeland for which he fights is the homeland in which the Islamic system of upbringing is enforced, and the land which he will defend is the land that is Dar al-Islam, in which Islamic Shari'ah and the Islamic system are operative. Apart from this, all conceptions of homeland are non-Islamic and Jahili conceptions, and Islam by no means recognises those conceptions.

Another touch is given to this subject: it is another opportunity to renew resolve; a new fervour is created in intentions. In a new path, the lamps of light flash forth. A new definition of aims, interests and values of life comes into view. Every group is seen working for its own values.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 4, verse 76:

Suddenly all of mankind stands at a crossroads. Goals and objectives become fixed, the lines become clear, and people divide into two groups, standing beneath two distinct banners.

(Verse) "Those who believe fight in the cause of Allah." (4:76)

"Those who have chosen the path of faith fight in the way of Allah."

(Verse) "And those who disbelieve fight in the cause of the Taghut." (4:76)

"And those who have chosen the path of disbelief fight in the cause of Taghut (false powers, tyrannical forces)."

The battle lines of the believers are drawn up in the cause of Allah, and they seek to establish the system of life of Allah. They seek the implementation of the Shariah of Allah; in the name of Allah they seek the establishment of justice among people; they do not speak in the name of anyone else or under any other title. They have already acknowledged that there is no deity but Allah, and therefore He alone is the Sovereign.

And those who disbelieve fight in the cause of Taghut; they are devotees of various kinds of tyrannical systems of life. All these tyrannical systems are opposed to the divine system of life. These people seek to establish legal systems that oppose the Shariah. They wish to establish values that are not permitted by Allah. They measure the values of life by standards that carry no weight in the balance of Allah.

Those who believe place their trust in the support, protection and safeguarding of Allah. And those who have chosen the path of disbelief seek help from Taghut. Their helper is Satan, and the banners of Satan are diverse; his methods are diverse; his laws are diverse; his values and standards are diverse. All these people are companions of Satan.

(Verse) "So fight the friends of Satan; indeed, the plots of Satan are truly weak." (4:76)

"So fight against the associates of Satan, and be assured that the schemes of Satan are in reality extremely weak."

Thus the position of the Muslims rests on a firm footing, and their support is solid. They stand on a firm foundation and hold a strong support. Their intuition and consciousness are firm that they are fighting in the cause of Allah. This battle belongs solely to Allah, and no part of their own self has a share in it. No personal interest is hidden in it. Neither the interest of their nation, their lineage, their relatives nor their family is at stake in it. It is for Allah alone, for His system and for His Shariah. Then their awareness also becomes firm that their confrontation is with the people of falsehood, and that they wish to make falsehood prevail over truth, because they are fighting for the jahili societies of humans, and that all human systems are jahili systems. Only the Shariah of Allah is the true system. Whereas they, by subjugating the Shariah, enforce human legal systems and wish to have judgments made according to human law. Every judgment that conforms to human law is injustice. It is an injustice against the law of Allah, because the command of Allah is that judgments be made according to His Shariah.

When these believers enter the battlefield, they enter with the conviction that Allah, the Exalted, will remain their companion and helper. They are conscious that they are going to fight a force whose helper is Satan, and there is no doubt that all the plots of Satan are weak in comparison with the Most Merciful.

Here, in the perception and consciousness of a believer, the outcome of this struggle is decided and its end is fixed. Then, once a believer steps into this struggle, if he is martyred, he is certain that its outcome will be good; and if he is granted victory and dominance in this struggle, he has firm certainty that Allah, the Exalted, will reward him with a great reward.

It was as a result of this true understanding of the matter that two miracles occurred at the hands of the community of the Companions, which form part of Islamic history, and examples of them appear here and there among subsequent generations after the Companions. There is no need here to present some examples of them, for they are very well known. It was this very outlook that resulted in the astonishing spread that Islam attained, and this spread occurred within the shortest span of history. This outlook was one aspect of the superiority that the Muslim community attained because of the Islamic system of life, and this superiority was attained against both the blocs locked in conflict at that time, and we have already alluded to this superiority earlier. The development of this outlook and perception was a part of the mission that the Holy Quran had in view. This mission was being carried out in the psychological world of the believers as well as on the battlefield against those enemies, in which the believers, relative to the armies they faced in number and equipment, were fighting with very great strength. The enemy was defeated despite that great number and equipment, because it was empty-handed in terms of the outlook on life.

Observe how much effort the Holy Quran expended for the development and maturing of this outlook. This was no easy task. It was not merely a matter that was stated verbally. It was continuous struggle. In it, a continuous struggle was waged against human personal narrow-mindedness, the greed to remain alive at any cost, and false notions about gain and loss. In this lesson, some examples of this continuous struggle are also to be observed.

After this, in the context of the discourse, there is an expression of wonder at the conduct of several groups among the Muslims. (It is said that some of them were Muhajirun.) When these people were in Makkah, they had zeal and fervour against the disbelievers, because they were suffering intolerable oppression in Makkah. As a result of this fervour, they wished for permission from Makkah to engage in jihad and fighting, whereas permission had not been given by Allah. But when an Islamic government was established in Madinah, and jihad and fighting became obligatory upon them by the command of Allah, and this was because Allah knew that now there was great good and blessing for them in jihad and fighting, then the Quran portrayed them in these words: "So among them there was a group who feared people as they should fear Allah, or even more intensely, and said: 'Our Lord, why have You prescribed fighting for us? Why did You not grant us a little more respite?'" And these were the people who, if some good befell them, would say, "This is from Allah," and if some misfortune befell them, would say to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), "This is from you." And among them were those who, when in the presence of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), would say "Yes," but when they withdrew from him, they would say other things in their gatherings. And some of them, if they heard some reassuring or frightening news, would immediately spread it.

The Holy Quran expresses wonder at the conduct of such people, and this is the Quran's own particular style of expression, in which a delicate depiction of human psychology is drawn. These inner psychologies are presented in such a way that they appear as moving pictures. In the thinking of such people, the error and crookedness concerning the reality and nature of life and death, victory and defeat, good and evil, benefit and harm, gain and loss, and values and standards, were corrected. And it was stated in the particular, highly effective and allusive style and manner of the Quran. Observe.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 4, verses 77–83 (part 1 of 3):

The four paragraphs of these verses point to people of this very kind, and it is possible that they are the same people who were mentioned in the previous paragraph of this section: "And among you there are those who will surely lag behind" (4:72). These were hypocrites, and it is possible that all these remarks concern the hypocrites from whom such deeds proceeded and who also used to say such things.

We prefer this interpretation, because in the people identified in these verses the features of hypocrisy are more apparent. Hypocrites existed within the ranks of the Muslims, and it is easy to understand that such deeds and such statements proceeded from none but the hypocrites, in keeping with their temperament and their previous conduct. Although the manner of expression of these paragraphs is intermingled, nevertheless the first of these paragraphs, in which it is said:

"It was said to them: Restrain your hands, establish prayer and give zakah. But when fighting was prescribed for them" (4:77),

leaves us in doubt as to whether all these paragraphs concern only the hypocrites. Although these qualities were present among the hypocrites too, and although these verses are similar to other verses and the style also appears to be one, nevertheless my inclination is that this paragraph points to a group of the Emigrants (Muhajirun) who were not hypocrites but were weak in faith, and the final degree of weakness of faith inevitably approaches hypocrisy. As for the other three paragraphs, it is most probable that they refer to the hypocrites. These people had crept into the Islamic ranks, but it is also possible that all these paragraphs concern only the hypocrites who used to do such deeds and say such things.

Why have we adopted the position that by the first paragraph of these verses is meant either the weak-faith Emigrants, or people who were not firm in faith, whose marks of faith within their hearts had not become clearly established and firm, and whose faithful outlook had not become strong?

The reason for this position is that some groups of the Emigrants in Makkah were extremely eager to fight, while at that time fighting was not permitted, and the command was: "Restrain your hands, establish prayer and give zakah" (4:77).

At the Second Pledge of Aqabah, the 27 persons who pledged allegiance at the hand of the Messenger (ﷺ) offered him that, if he wished, they would fall upon the disbelievers present in Mina that very day. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) replied to them that: "I have not yet been permitted to fight." If this event is kept in view, then we cannot say that the people meant by the first paragraph are the same people about whom the following three paragraphs come, namely the hypocrites. Could these people of the Pledge of Aqabah have been weak in faith, as the first paragraph describes? Certainly not, because no weakness is related from these foremost Ansar in Islamic history. There was neither weakness nor hypocrisy in them, for Allah had become pleased with them.

Therefore the closest to the mind is that this first group means only the weak Emigrants. These people had become accustomed to a peaceful life after going to Madinah. Difficulties had been removed from them, and when jihad and fighting became obligatory, they began to show weakness in bearing these difficulties. It is also closest to the mind that the qualities described in the other three paragraphs do not belong to these weak believing Emigrants, but are the qualities of the hypocrites. This is because, although a human being is not free of human weaknesses, it is difficult for us to attribute to any believing Emigrant that, when he encounters hardships, he attributes them to the Messenger (ﷺ) and does not attribute goodness to him, or that any believing Emigrant would claim obedience to the Messenger (ﷺ) to his face and then go home and plot. Yes, it was possible that someone, out of lack of understanding, might spread good and bad news; but this too would show that these people did not understand the system of the community well, and yet even for spreading news one cannot call a person a hypocrite.

In any case, after reflecting on these verses, it appears difficult to say anything definitively, because in the narrations transmitted in the interpretation of these verses no definitive statement has been made, not even about the first paragraph. In some narrations it is said that it refers to a group of the Emigrants, and in others that those meant were also hypocrites.

For this reason we adopt a cautious position regarding them, because we cannot characterise the Emigrants with the qualities of shirking in battle and avoiding the calamities that befall the Muslims, as the previous verses have described, as these paragraphs indicate. Nor can we accuse them of attributing evil to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) while attributing goodness to Allah, or of holding consultations at night against the Messenger (ﷺ). Although, from the context and the general manner of the Qur'an's expression, analysing these paragraphs in this way is no easy task for anyone acquainted with it. Only a person who has pondered over the Qur'an for a long time and is thoroughly familiar with the Qur'an's style of expression can perform this analysis.

"Have you not seen those who were told: Restrain your hands, establish prayer and give zakah? But when fighting was prescribed for them, behold, a party of them fear men as they should fear Allah or with even greater fear, and they say: Our Lord, why have You prescribed fighting for us? If only You had delayed us to a near term. Say: The enjoyment of this world is little, and the Hereafter is better for one who fears Allah, and you will not be wronged a whit. Wherever you may be, death will overtake you, even if you are in towers built up high" (4:77–78).

Allah expresses wonder at the state of these people. When they were in Makkah they were eager to fight; they were about to begin jihad very soon. At that time the polytheists were inflicting oppression upon them, they were surrounded by trials, and at that time Allah did not permit them jihad for their own benefit. But when the suitable time came, which Allah had appointed for them, and conditions became favourable, Allah made jihad obligatory upon them (and that jihad was in the way of Allah). Then a party among them began to lament and be distressed, and this party began to fear those people against whom they had been commanded to fight, although those people were also human beings like themselves, and this fear was as intense as the intense fear of Allah, or even greater than it, although none can punish as severely as Allah.

Nor can anyone's seizure be like the seizure of Allah. Such people say these things in words full of regret and in a state of intense lamentation.

"Our Lord, why have You prescribed fighting for us?" (4:77). For a believer this question seems strange and peculiar. This question shows that in the view of this party the nature of the obligations and duties of this religion was not fully clear, and the wish they express after this question is a very petty and mean wish.

"If only You had delayed us to a near term" (4:77): that is, had we been given a little more time, we would not have been confronted with this terrifying and heavy obligation.

Sometimes it happens that people who enter a matter with bravery, boldness and haste fall very quickly into lamentation, fright and panic. This condition comes upon them when they enter the realities and the matter appears in its true form. Indeed this situation generally occurs as a rule, and this is because such enthusiasm, daring and boldness arise from the fact that such a person has not made a real estimate of the calamities and difficulties. This enthusiasm and fervour does not come from true bravery, from facing difficulties, or from steadfastness. Sometimes it also happens because the likelihood of hardship, distress and suffering is low, and such a person does not see defeat or rout. For this reason the enthusiasm of such people increases, and they advance, move quickly and want to achieve victory at any cost. But they have not properly estimated the difficulties that stand in the way of their action, advance and victory. So when they meet those hardships, they feel that they are harder than their estimates, and more severe than they imagined; and then they are at the front of the ranks of those who turn back on their heels and lament. Those who prepare beforehand for such difficulties, who understand the difficulties of action and advance well, and who know how far their souls can bear these difficulties, are those who make use of patience and steadfastness and who leap into an engagement only after preparation. These fervent, hot-headed and forward-rushing people consider such men weak, and the seriousness and balanced personality of these men does not impress them. But at the time of a real engagement it becomes evident which of them can bear difficulties more, and who has the far-reaching vision.

My view is that the party mentioned in these verses consisted of people of this kind, who in Makkah faced difficulties and harm and could not endure these trials, and who could not bear their own humiliation, since they were noble people. Therefore, in Makkah, in their enthusiasm, they would ask the Messenger (ﷺ) for permission to defend themselves against these harms, so that they might take some action to protect their honour and dignity. And the Messenger (ﷺ), in accordance with the commands of Allah, advised these people to wait a while, that every matter would be at its proper time. Every matter requires training and preparation, every action is taken at its time, and one waits for the appointed hour. People of this kind then came to live in security and peace in Madinah; there they were neither humiliated nor harmed, and this condition came to them after the personal and individual hardships which had been customary in Makkah. Therefore such people had no interest in war, nor did they find any justification for it, or at least they wanted that there be no haste in the matter.

"Then when fighting was prescribed for them, behold, a party of them fear men as they should fear Allah or with even greater fear, and they say: Our Lord, why have You prescribed fighting for us? If only You had delayed us to a near term" (4:77).

This party was probably believers. The evidence for this is that these people are turning to Allah with great humility and in a grieved manner. We should keep in view this humility and sorrowful tone. But the faith of these people does not yet appear firm, and the marks of their outlook on life had not yet become clear. These aims were greater and higher than preserving the person of a few individuals, or saving a people, or saving a homeland. The central point of the aims of the Islamic system of life is that the Islamic system of life be established and dominant over the whole surface of this earth. Its fundamental aim is the establishment of a just order over the whole earth and the establishment of a state which can, with full strength, remove the obstacles standing in the path of the spread of the Islamic call and which prevent people from giving ear to the call of Islam. This government should also have enough power that, if anyone in the world freely and by his own choice adopts a belief, it can protect him from every kind of oppression and pressure, whatever form that oppression may take, such as depriving someone of labour and livelihood, or depriving him of the freedom to strive for his own purposes within society. In short, these are the lofty aims which are far more important than inflicting or not inflicting personal harm upon anyone. That is why the peace and tranquillity obtained in Madinah (if it be assumed that it existed at any time) was not so important that the Muslims should be kept away from this enterprise and movement of jihad for some further period.

This party's faith was not yet so firm that they could remove their own selves from the middle. They would hear Allah's commands and regard those very commands as cause and effect, as the decisive word, even if some deeper wisdom did not become clear to them. But this party's conception of the religion was not yet so firm that they could understand the real mission and purpose of this religion. The believer, as a believer, is the instrument of Allah's power, and Allah, through him, enforces whatever customs and arrangements He wills in the lives of the people of this world. Thus, from the context, the position of such people is depicted, their stance is wondered at, and it is disapproved.

Question: Why did Allah not permit the Muslims in Makkah to take revenge for the persecution they suffered? Why did they bear this aggression, and why did they not treat these stabbing attacks with the use of force, even though most of the Muslims were capable of doing so? For not all of them were weak or cowardly; they could have answered a brick with a stone, and the Muslims in Makkah were not a tiny handful. Why did they restrain themselves from retaliation and content themselves only with establishing the prayer, paying the zakah, and patience and forbearance? Yet some Muslims were subjected to torment that was unbearable. Some, unable to endure it, fell into trial concerning their religion, and some even lost their lives because of these hardships.

What was the wisdom behind this? The truth is that we cannot make any definitive statement in this regard, because whatever wisdom we state, we would thereby be attributing it to Allah, whereas Allah Himself did not state that wisdom. Thus we might also state causes and reasons for the commands and obligations of Allah which in reality are not their causes. It is also possible that the causes we state may be among the actual ones, but that there are other causes and wisdoms besides them, of which Allah has not given us knowledge. In not knowing them lies good and benefit for us. This is the believing stance that anyone may adopt before the commands of Allah and the laws of the Shariah, regarding which Allah has not Himself definitively stated the specific wisdom and cause, whatever cause occurs to our minds and whatever wisdom appears outwardly to us; whatever mode of execution of a command occurs to our minds, or whatever method of performing an obligation comes to our understanding, insofar as reason can grasp it. But the better stance is that a person regards it as only one of several possibilities, and does not assert categorically that this is the wisdom that Allah had in view and that there is no other wisdom. Even if one has full confidence in one's knowledge and understanding, and even if one has pondered the commands of Allah most profoundly, because no one can say that he has encompassed the wisdoms that Allah had in view. This cautious approach which we are proposing is closer to the etiquette of the presence of the Divine court. And caution also demands that a distinction of nature and reality be maintained between the knowledge of Allah and the knowledge of man.

Keeping in mind these etiquettes of the Divine court, I now speak on the subject of why jihad was not made obligatory in Makkah and why it was made obligatory after going to Madinah. On this subject I will set forth what appears to us, that perhaps this may be the cause and wisdom, but both cause and wisdom are being stated only as possibilities, and we leave the real truth to Allah. We do not assume causes and wisdoms for the commands of Allah on our own part. Knowledge of the real truth belongs to Allah alone, and He has not informed us of it through explicit text. ... These causes which we are stating are merely ijtihadi (based on personal reasoning); there is the possibility of their being correct as well as of error. They may be more, and they may be fewer. The purpose of mentioning these causes here is only that we reflect upon the verses of Allah and understand that, after reflection in our age, these causes became clear to us.

(A) This cause may also be that Makkah was a period of training and preparation. This preparation was taking place within a specific family, in a particular people, and under specific circumstances. The goals of this training and preparation were to prepare an Arab personality to be patient in circumstances in which he would never have been patient, for example, when his own person or those dependent upon him were struck, and he endured it. The aim was that this Arab personality should forget his tribal identity and his own self, and that the center of his life should not be his person and those dependent upon him alone, and that he should not direct his life solely for his own person. Furthermore, it was intended to train the Arab temperament to control its nerves, so that he would not be carried away by the first impression, nor go beyond himself at the first agitating action; that moderation would arise in his movement and temperament. It was also intended to give him the training that he be a member of an organized society, and that he have a leadership to which he becomes accustomed to refer in all matters of his life, and that he do nothing except in accordance with the indication of that leadership, even though these commands might be contrary to and opposed to his accustomed life. These were most fundamental matters in the training of an Arab personality. Through this a Islamic society was to be formed, one subject to a leadership, a progressive and civilized society, and not a tribal and uncivilized (barbarian) society.

(B) This reason may also be that in the environment of the Quraysh, peaceful da'wah could be more effective, because this society was a society of nobles, and if the Muslims had begun war within society, these people would have become even more intense in enmity and hostility. In circumstances such as existed in Makkah at that time, bloody fighting would have begun, and an endless chain of killing and slaughter would have started, like the War of Dahis, the War of Basus, and the War of Ghabra. These wars were famous wars of the Arabs and were fought continuously for years. This new war would have been connected with Islam, and all events would have been remembered in reference to Islam. These wars would never have ended, and Islam, instead of being a da'wah, would have become a long saga of war and conflict, and as a result of these sagas the real da'wah of Islam would have receded into the background. The state of this da'wah would have been decided at the very initial stage, and after some time it would have ended altogether.

(C) This was also because, if jihad had been permitted in Makkah, war would have begun in every house. For there was no regular government in Makkah that could control the people. Moreover, there was no government there that inflicted hardships on the Muslims; rather, the torments inflicted on the Muslims were inflicted through each Muslim's own relatives. The relatives themselves would beat those who embraced Islam, torment them, and, according to their own understanding, "train" them. If permission for war had been given in Makkah, it would have meant that war would begin in every house, and people would say: "Look, this is Islam!" Although the charge of causing discord was leveled against Islam even when the Muslims were commanded to keep their hands restrained. But the Quraysh were constantly spreading this very propaganda against Islam among those coming for Hajj and 'Umrah and in the commercial markets. They would say that Muhammad creates enmity between father and son, and between a man and his tribe. If Islam had permitted boys and slaves to kill their parents and their masters and guardians, and war had begun in every house and neighborhood, what would the state of the Quraysh's propaganda have been?

(D) One reason for this may also be that those who were inflicting persecution on their children because of Islam, those who were tormenting their slaves, and those who were oppressing those under their guardianship, were, in Allah's knowledge, people who would later render great services to Islam; they would become soldiers of Islam, sincere ones, and leaders. Do you not see that Hadrat 'Umar (raḍiyallāhu 'anhu) was also among such people?

(E) One reason may also be that the self-respect and nobility of the Arabs required that these people always raise their voices on behalf of the oppressed. An oppressed person who is being unjustly tormented, yet is so firm in his position that he does not desist at any price, especially when people of the highest nobility are being tormented, and several incidents occurred which prove the soundness of this view. Ibn al-Daghinah was not prepared to abandon Hadrat Abu Bakr (raḍiyallāhu 'anhu) and to migrate from Makkah to Madinah. He said that this matter was a great shame for the Arabs. He offered Hadrat Abu Bakr his protection. Another example of this is the siege of the Banu Hashim in the valley of Abu Talib. This siege became so prolonged that people began to die of hunger, and severe calamities befell them. If such an event had occurred in earlier times and in other societies, people would have regarded the oppressed as contemptible, mocked them, and the oppressors would have been looked upon with honor and dignity (but what happened there is a golden example from Arab history).

(F) One cause may also be that the number of Muslims in Makkah was very small, and they could survive only in Makkah itself, because the da'wah had not reached the other areas of the Arabian Peninsula. If it had reached them, only rough and half-baked news about it had spread here and there. People thought there were internal disputes within the Islamic movement and among some of the Quraysh, and that if war had broken out, they would have remained neutral and watched which way the camel would sit. In such circumstances it was possible that this battle would have ended once that small number of Muslims was killed. Even though this small number might have killed twice their number of disbelievers, after their end, shirk would have become even stronger in its place, and this small army of Islam would have been wiped off the face of the earth. The Islamic system of life could not have taken real form in the world, although Islam was a religion whose purpose was that it be established in the world as a system of life and be practically implemented in people's lives.

(G) Along with all these matters, it is also a fact that in the Makkan period there was no real need at all for the Muslims to be permitted to fight, so that by combat they might defend against oppression. For the fundamental work of the Islamic da'wah was being carried on, and the da'wah was continuing unceasingly. The blessed person of Hadrat Muhammad ﷺ was present, and the swords of Banu Hashim were unsheathed at all times for his protection. If anyone raised his hand against him, he faced the danger of his hand being cut off; and the tribal system of that time existed, in which every tribe feared that it might become entangled in fighting with Banu Hashim without cause, and this danger was fully present in every case where a member of any tribe raised his hand against the Messenger ﷺ. Since the person of the caller was protected and was being safeguarded, and since the caller, with the help of Banu Hashim and according to the customs of the existing tribal system of that time, was giving da'wah day and night, the caller was neither keeping the da'wah secret nor concealing his words from anyone. No one in Makkah had the courage to prevent the spread of his da'wah. He was carrying out the work of Islamic da'wah in the gatherings of the Quraysh, at the Ka'bah, on Mount Safa, and in public gatherings, and no one had the courage to put a hand over his mouth. No one could dare to abduct him, imprison him, or kill him, and no one could force him to say what they wished, so that he might say some matters of his religion and remain silent on others. Once, when they offered him that they would not revile their gods and deities and would not speak ill of them, he rejected this offer. Also, when they proposed that they would show some flexibility and the Quraysh would show some flexibility too, he rejected this as well, that is, he refused to adopt a policy of give and take. The proposal was that the Messenger ﷺ accept some of their matters and they would accept some of Islam's, and the Messenger ﷺ rejected this too. In short, the Islamic state existed; the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was present, the Banu Hashim were acting as protectors, and the Messenger ﷺ was free to spread his da'wah in every form and by every means. In such circumstances there was indeed no real need for war and jihad, so that fighting should be begun before its time; and the most important reason was that the family of the Quraysh was receptive to this da'wah, and good results were to emerge from it.

All these aspects, as far as we understand, may be some aspects of the wisdom because of which fighting and jihad did not begin in Makkah, and the Muslims were commanded there to restrain their hands, establish the prayer, and pay the zakah. Through these acts their preparation and training would be completed, and the Makkan plan of Islamic da'wah would also reach its conclusion. The Muslims would await the commands of their leadership, and when the time came they would be able to discharge this obligation; for in the performance of this duty they would now have no personal aim or purpose, and their jihad and fighting would now be solely for Allah, fi sabilillah. Meanwhile the da'wah was, in any case, advancing at its own pace; it was being supported, and there were those who loved it and were its guardians.

Whatever the wisdom behind this plan, at that time there were indeed enthusiastic people present who, apparently, were eagerly awaiting that moment when they would be permitted to fight.

(Verse) "Then when fighting was prescribed for them, behold, a party of them fear men as they should fear Allah, or even more intensely. They say: 'Our Lord, why have You prescribed fighting for us? Why did You not grant us a respite for a little while?'" (4:77)

In the ranks of the Muslims, the presence of a group that shrank from jihad and fighting created a kind of unease. Thus, within the Muslim ranks, on one side was this group that wailed and lamented, and on the other side were the true and complete believers, who were fully steadfast, content with their cause, who accepted the disquiets that come in the path of truth with a cheerful countenance, and who bore the hardships of that path. It is evident that harmony between these two groups could not arise.

The believing party in question also had zeal for the truth; they were people of resolve and determination, and they possessed certainty and steadfastness. But these people would express every feeling in its own place. For when war has not yet begun and its commands have not been given, it will be mere bravado and empty slogan-shouting, and when a real danger is faced, this fever evaporates into the air.

The Qur'an treated such a situation in its own manner:

﴿Say: "The enjoyment of this world is brief, and the Hereafter is better for one who fears Allah, and you will not be wronged even a thread."﴾ [4:77] ﴿Wherever you may be, death will overtake you, even if you should be within towers built high.﴾ [4:78]

These people fear death, desire life, and wish, in a manner of utmost humble longing, that they might be granted some further respite and that their wealth might be increased somewhat.

The excellence of the Qur'an is that it cuts the root of such feelings exactly where they arise, and it clarifies the reality of death and life. ﴿Say: "The enjoyment of this world is brief."﴾ [4:77] (Say: the provision of life is indeed very little.) What is the whole equipment of life, indeed what is the reality of the entire life: a few days, a few weeks, a few months or a few years? Even if some respite is granted, what is its reality? If the whole life is but a brief time, what equipment will they gather in that brief time? For life, after all, is confined within days, months and years, and therefore the length of this brief life is also brief.

﴿And the Hereafter is better for one who fears Allah.﴾ [4:77] (And the Hereafter alone is better for a God-fearing person.) First, because the matter does not end in this world. This world is not the final destination of the human journey; it is one stage, and after this stage comes the Hereafter, and the true wealth is that which is gathered for the Hereafter. Then, the period of the Hereafter is long and without end, and its provision is good and better. Those who are God-fearing consider it better. Here the subject was fear and dread, and in this context Allah mentioned taqwa, which, though it is a kind of fear, is the fear of God. That is, if anyone fears, he should fear Allah; why fear a human being? Yet there is a group among the Muslims that fears people in the way that one should fear Allah. Indeed, one who fears Allah does not fear people; when the fear of God settles in a heart, no room remains in that heart for the fear of anyone else, for if Allah does not will, no one can do him any harm.

﴿And you will not be wronged even a thread.﴾ [4:77] (And you will not be wronged even a thread.) There will be no deficiency in your reward, no loss and no reduction. If something was left out of your share in this world, the Abode of the Hereafter is surely coming, where that shortfall will be made good, where there is no injustice, and where there will be no deficiency in the reckoning, and the final bill of this world and the Hereafter will be received.

Despite these realities, there are some people whose souls harbour the strong desire that they be granted a few more days on this very earth, even though these people believe in the Hereafter and hope for a good recompense there. Nevertheless, they keep such a wish in their hearts, especially those who are at a level of faith like that of the party under discussion.

Here the matter is presented once more in a final glimpse, and with a single sentence the wrong conception and wrong thinking are corrected: the correction is made by reflecting on life and death, destiny and the appointed term. Alongside this, life and death are given a touch from the angle of jihad and fighting. The wailing and lamenting of this party arose precisely because they thought that death comes as a result of fighting, whereas ﴿Wherever you may be, death will overtake you, even if you should be within towers built high.﴾ [4:78] Death comes at an appointed time. It has no connection with fighting or with peace, nor does it depend on the solidity or flimsiness of one's dwelling. Moreover, if someone shirks the duty of war, death cannot be postponed on that account, and neither does death come before its time because of the obligations of war and jihad.

Death has a fixed time, and these matters are entirely separate from it. There is no relation of cause and effect between them. Rather, death has a fixed time, and when that time arrives, some cause is found for it. Apart from the appointed time, there is no other cause of death. Hence, to wish that the obligation of fighting had been delayed is a vain wish. Likewise, in situations of fighting and non-fighting, there is no meaning in fearing anyone other than Allah.

The Qur'an, with a subtle touch, transforms the heart. The very outlook of a person on life and death changes, and the terror and dread that lie in a person's thought and consciousness are suddenly removed.

But this does not mean that a person should not adopt precautionary measures and not use within his power the means of protection and safeguarding. Just now it was stated that Allah commanded the Muslims: ﴿Take your precautions﴾ [4:71], that is, be very cautious. And on the occasion of discussing the rules of the prayer of fear, precautionary measures were also commanded. In another place the command was given ﴿Prepare﴾ [8:60], that is, make thorough preparations. All these commands are right in their place; however, there is no connection between these preparations and life and death. Precautionary measures and the provision of military equipment have their own wisdom, and obedience to these commands is necessary. These are the measures of Allah which He has commanded. But death in any case comes at its appointed time, and this is an entirely different belief and command, and it is obligatory to hold to it as well. Although precautionary measures are obligatory and military preparations also have outward and inward wisdom, both commands must be followed, with complete balance and complete moderation, keeping all aspects in view. These are the guidance of Islam and the correct Islamic policies; this is the Islamic method for the training of individuals and of the community.

It seems that here the discussion of this group of the emigrants ends, and now begins the discussion of another element spread through the Muslim ranks. In that period, this was also an existing constituent element of Islamic society alongside the other elements. Although there is no visible break or start of a new topic within the previous discussion, no section break and no pause that would make clear that the coming matter concerns another element, yet the point of the first party has ended; but regarding this, the points we have already stated earlier and which are before us remain relevant.

If good befalls them, they say, "This is from Allah," but if harm befalls them, they say, "This is because of you, O Prophet." Say, "All of it is from Allah." What is wrong with these people that they can barely understand a word? (ﷺ)

"Whatever good reaches you, it is from Allah, and whatever harm reaches you, it is from yourself." (4:79)

O Muhammad (ﷺ), We have sent you to mankind as a Messenger, and Allah is sufficient as a witness. Whoever obeys the Messenger has indeed obeyed Allah, and whoever turns away, We have not sent you as a guardian over them. (4:80)

Those whose attitude is that they attribute the good that reaches them to Allah, but attribute the evil that befalls them to the Prophet (ﷺ), may have several reasons for this conduct.

The first possibility is this: when there is drought, or when livestock do not breed, or when some misfortune strikes them, they would attribute these things to the Holy Prophet (ﷺ). But when they experienced some good fortune or success, they would say that it came from Allah.

The second possibility is that they deliberately made false accusations against the leadership of the Prophet (ﷺ). They did this so that they could escape the obligations that the Prophet (ﷺ) imposed upon them. It may be that they were trying to free themselves from the duty of fighting in the way of Allah (qital fi sabil Allah). Instead of plainly saying, "Brother, we are weak and cowardly and we fear war," they adopted the method of finding fault with and criticizing the Prophet's leadership. When good came to them, they said it was the grace of Allah, but when evil came to them, they attributed it to the Prophet (ﷺ), or to the Prophet's commands, saying that because of these commands this calamity had fallen upon them. By "good" they meant the good of this worldly life, and by "evil" they meant the loss of this worldly life.

The third possibility is that their view of the events and occurrences that befall people in this world, according to the will of Allah, is very wrong. Likewise, their concept of the relationship between the Messenger of Allah and God Almighty is also very base.

If this is the third possibility, it may refer to those emigrants (muhajirin) whose belief about death and life was not yet firm, and because of this concept of death and life they feared people in the way one ought to fear Allah. And these people used to say:

﴿Our Lord, why have You prescribed fighting for us? If only You had delayed it for us to a near term.﴾ (4:77)

However, my view is that this verse does not refer to those people, but rather to some other people, among whom were some others along with these faces.

The issue taken up in this verse is one aspect of a great and difficult question, and that question is one of the most difficult problems in the history of religions and the history of philosophy. That is the problem of jabr wa qadr (determinism and free will), and the problem of divine decree (taqdir). This issue has come up here incidentally, in the description of the circumstances of certain people. The false notions of these people are refuted here. The Qur'an, while correcting the intellectual error of this group under discussion, has explained this issue with great simplicity and without any complexity. Let us listen to the words of the Qur'an:

﴿If good reaches them, they say, "This is from Allah," but if harm reaches them, they say, "This is because of you, O Prophet." Say, "All of it is from Allah." What is wrong with these people that they can barely understand a word?﴾ (4:78)

Indeed, Allah is the true agent and the first agent. He is the one who acts in this universe, and whatever occurs in it is from Him. Whatever happens to people, or whatever is done by people, all of it is from Allah. Human beings have only the power to pay attention and to strive, but the realization of any act can happen only by the will and decree of Allah.

Because to attribute good, or to attribute the bringing into existence of evil, or to attribute the bringing of evil upon someone, to the Holy Prophet (ﷺ), although he is a human being and a creature, and is like us, is an unreal attribution. And from this it becomes clear that these people do not understand the subject at all.

Sometimes a person turns his attention to a task and strives to gather good for himself. Allah has given him the understanding to use the means of goodness, and he uses them. Yet, despite this, if someone receives good, it happens by the will of Allah, because there is no other decree that can create things, events, and occurrences that take place in this universe except the decree of Allah. So when good reaches someone, it reaches him through the means that Allah has appointed for that good. Therefore, in practice, the understanding will be that this good has come because of Allah, and is the result of His decree.

Sometimes a person turns his attention to committing an evil, or he performs an action which, as a result, brings about evil. But in practice, the occurrence and coming into existence of evil happens solely under the decree and predestination of Allah, because the power to create things and to bring events into being lies in no one's hands except Allah's.

In both cases, whatever occurs of good or evil happens from Allah, and this verse decides this very reality. As for the second verse, namely:

﴿Whatever good reaches you, it is from Allah, and whatever harm reaches you, it is from yourself.﴾ (4:79)

In it another reality is expressed. Its connection to the reality stated in the first verse is not the same, nor does it fall within that earlier reality of decree and predestination. Therefore it is necessary to view it from a different angle.

Allah, according to His sunnah (established way), has laid down a method of action, and He has set a procedure for every matter. Then Allah has warned human beings clearly about evil. When a person follows this method, walks on the path shown by Him, strives for good, and fears evil, then Allah helps him to walk on the path of guidance. Allah says:

﴿And those who strive for Us, We will surely guide them to Our paths.﴾ (Qur'an 29:69)

Then a person succeeds in attaining good. Outwardly, a person appears to be earning and working, but this human earning and effort has no real significance, because the method of earning and working has itself been determined by Allah. Therefore the person's striving itself yields good, and that good is in Allah's scale and comes from Allah, because it is Allah who has laid down the method of good and determined the path of action. It is He who guided to good, and He who granted the ability to do good and warned against evil. When a person does not walk on the method that Allah has determined, and does not adopt the path that Allah has made lawful, and does not strive for good, and does not fear the evil from which he has been warned, then certainly he will be struck by evil. This will be a real evil, both in this world and in the Hereafter, and this evil will be the earning of his own self, because he willingly departed from the method of action pleasing to Allah. (This is the meaning of his earning.) This meaning is different from the first meaning, and their scopes are also separate, and we believe that this point is now clear.

According to this second meaning, there is no effect on the (first) principle. Both good and evil are connected to the will and decree of Allah. Allah alone is the creator of all creatures. He is the creator of every occurrence. He is the originator of every event that happens, whatever the human will and action in that matter may be, and in whatever circumstances it may occur.

What is the real issue that is stated in these texts, or one aspect of which is taken up? It is the issue of compulsion and choice (jabr wa ikhtiyar): to what extent a human being's own will is involved in the actions that proceed from him, or to what extent his own will is involved in the benefits that accrue to him here, and how reward and punishment are attached to his voluntary actions, while we say that the true creator of all actions is Allah. The human wills themselves, human attention, human actions, and all other originated things are created by Allah. These and all similar questions connected with the problem of jabr and qadr are such that the Qur'anic verses make clear that every occurrence comes into being by the will of Allah. The Qur'an is entirely the speech of Allah, and the verses of the Qur'an cannot contradict one another. Therefore there must be a point of connection between these two matters. There is a sphere of human will and action in which a person is responsible and accountable, and for which he must face reward and punishment. If the sphere of this freedom of choice did not also have a relationship with the sphere of divine decree and divine will, how could these spheres be determined? This is a matter whose explanation and clarification is not possible, because a human being cannot grasp how Allah's will and power operate.

Now, after this, Allah clarifies the scope of the Holy Prophet's (ﷺ) role and the limits of his responsibility: what position he will take with regard to people, and how people's relationship with him will be, and that the whole matter will ultimately return to Allah.

﴿Whatever good reaches you, it is from Allah, and whatever harm reaches you, it is from yourself. And We have sent you to mankind as a Messenger, and Allah is sufficient as a witness.﴾ (4:79)

﴿Whoever obeys the Messenger has indeed obeyed Allah; and whoever turns away, We have not sent you as a guardian over them.﴾ (4:80)

The duty of the Messenger is to fulfill the responsibility of conveying the message. His responsibility is not to create good or to create evil; the work of creation belongs to Allah alone. And Allah is the witness that He has sent Muhammad (ﷺ) only to fulfill the duty of prophethood. (Wa kafa billahi shahida: "And Allah is sufficient as a witness.")

As for the relationship of people with Muhammad (ﷺ), whoever obeys him has, in effect, obeyed Allah. Therefore, in the matter of obedience, there is no separation between Allah and His Messenger, and there is no difference or distinction between the word of Allah and the word of the Messenger of Allah. As for the one who turns away and denies the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), his reckoning and the matter of his reward and punishment are left to Allah. Allah did not send the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) so that you would compel people to guidance or compel them to enter the religion. Nor is it the duty of the messengers to protect people in such a way that they do not fall into sins. Nor has it been placed within the power of the messengers to protect people in such a way that they do not fall into sins. Nor has it been given to the messengers to become guardians of people.

Through this explanation, their thoughts and notions are corrected on this matter: that the events which befall them are connected with, and exist by, the will of Allah, and are exactly in accordance with Allah's decree. And whatever good and evil befalls them, whatever meaning good and evil may be taken to have, whether it is apparent good or true good, all of it is from Allah. No one other than Allah can create anything, nor can bring it into existence, nor can sustain it, nor can bring anything into manufacture. The true good that is with Allah is from Allah alone, and the true evil that reaches them is due to their own selves. This evil reaches them because these people turn away from the Islamic system of life and violate Allah's commands.

The duty of the Messenger, both first and last, is that he is a Messenger. He is neither a creator, nor can he bring about any event. These are the attributes of Allah, and in them the Messenger does not share with Allah. He is only one who conveys the commands of Allah; then his obedience is the obedience of Allah. There is no path to the obedience of Allah other than obedience to the Messenger of Allah. The Messenger is not charged with providing guidance for those who turn away, nor can the Messenger prevent them from turning away and disobedience. He can do nothing beyond conveying (al-Balagh) and clarifying. These are decisive and reassuring realities, clear and explicit realities. Through them concepts are built and consciousness is matured. And these realities are a part of the struggle to prepare the Muslim community for its great mission and duty. After this, the flow of the discourse turns to another group. This group has infiltrated the ranks, and perhaps it is a group of the hypocrites (Munafiqun). The Qur'an mentions their conduct under a separate and new heading, but within the manner of expression, abhorrence for this conduct also shines through. Along with this abhorrence, guidance and instruction for the Muslim community is also given.
