If good befalls them, they say, "This is from Allah," but if harm befalls them, they say, "This is because of you, O Prophet." Say, "All of it is from Allah." What is wrong with these people that they can barely understand a word? (ﷺ)

"Whatever good reaches you, it is from Allah, and whatever harm reaches you, it is from yourself." (4:79)

O Muhammad (ﷺ), We have sent you to mankind as a Messenger, and Allah is sufficient as a witness. Whoever obeys the Messenger has indeed obeyed Allah, and whoever turns away, We have not sent you as a guardian over them. (4:80)

Those whose attitude is that they attribute the good that reaches them to Allah, but attribute the evil that befalls them to the Prophet (ﷺ), may have several reasons for this conduct.

The first possibility is this: when there is drought, or when livestock do not breed, or when some misfortune strikes them, they would attribute these things to the Holy Prophet (ﷺ). But when they experienced some good fortune or success, they would say that it came from Allah.

The second possibility is that they deliberately made false accusations against the leadership of the Prophet (ﷺ). They did this so that they could escape the obligations that the Prophet (ﷺ) imposed upon them. It may be that they were trying to free themselves from the duty of fighting in the way of Allah (qital fi sabil Allah). Instead of plainly saying, "Brother, we are weak and cowardly and we fear war," they adopted the method of finding fault with and criticizing the Prophet's leadership. When good came to them, they said it was the grace of Allah, but when evil came to them, they attributed it to the Prophet (ﷺ), or to the Prophet's commands, saying that because of these commands this calamity had fallen upon them. By "good" they meant the good of this worldly life, and by "evil" they meant the loss of this worldly life.

The third possibility is that their view of the events and occurrences that befall people in this world, according to the will of Allah, is very wrong. Likewise, their concept of the relationship between the Messenger of Allah and God Almighty is also very base.

If this is the third possibility, it may refer to those emigrants (muhajirin) whose belief about death and life was not yet firm, and because of this concept of death and life they feared people in the way one ought to fear Allah. And these people used to say:

﴿Our Lord, why have You prescribed fighting for us? If only You had delayed it for us to a near term.﴾ (4:77)

However, my view is that this verse does not refer to those people, but rather to some other people, among whom were some others along with these faces.

The issue taken up in this verse is one aspect of a great and difficult question, and that question is one of the most difficult problems in the history of religions and the history of philosophy. That is the problem of jabr wa qadr (determinism and free will), and the problem of divine decree (taqdir). This issue has come up here incidentally, in the description of the circumstances of certain people. The false notions of these people are refuted here. The Qur'an, while correcting the intellectual error of this group under discussion, has explained this issue with great simplicity and without any complexity. Let us listen to the words of the Qur'an:

﴿If good reaches them, they say, "This is from Allah," but if harm reaches them, they say, "This is because of you, O Prophet." Say, "All of it is from Allah." What is wrong with these people that they can barely understand a word?﴾ (4:78)

Indeed, Allah is the true agent and the first agent. He is the one who acts in this universe, and whatever occurs in it is from Him. Whatever happens to people, or whatever is done by people, all of it is from Allah. Human beings have only the power to pay attention and to strive, but the realization of any act can happen only by the will and decree of Allah.

Because to attribute good, or to attribute the bringing into existence of evil, or to attribute the bringing of evil upon someone, to the Holy Prophet (ﷺ), although he is a human being and a creature, and is like us, is an unreal attribution. And from this it becomes clear that these people do not understand the subject at all.

Sometimes a person turns his attention to a task and strives to gather good for himself. Allah has given him the understanding to use the means of goodness, and he uses them. Yet, despite this, if someone receives good, it happens by the will of Allah, because there is no other decree that can create things, events, and occurrences that take place in this universe except the decree of Allah. So when good reaches someone, it reaches him through the means that Allah has appointed for that good. Therefore, in practice, the understanding will be that this good has come because of Allah, and is the result of His decree.

Sometimes a person turns his attention to committing an evil, or he performs an action which, as a result, brings about evil. But in practice, the occurrence and coming into existence of evil happens solely under the decree and predestination of Allah, because the power to create things and to bring events into being lies in no one's hands except Allah's.

In both cases, whatever occurs of good or evil happens from Allah, and this verse decides this very reality. As for the second verse, namely:

﴿Whatever good reaches you, it is from Allah, and whatever harm reaches you, it is from yourself.﴾ (4:79)

In it another reality is expressed. Its connection to the reality stated in the first verse is not the same, nor does it fall within that earlier reality of decree and predestination. Therefore it is necessary to view it from a different angle.

Allah, according to His sunnah (established way), has laid down a method of action, and He has set a procedure for every matter. Then Allah has warned human beings clearly about evil. When a person follows this method, walks on the path shown by Him, strives for good, and fears evil, then Allah helps him to walk on the path of guidance. Allah says:

﴿And those who strive for Us, We will surely guide them to Our paths.﴾ (Qur'an 29:69)

Then a person succeeds in attaining good. Outwardly, a person appears to be earning and working, but this human earning and effort has no real significance, because the method of earning and working has itself been determined by Allah. Therefore the person's striving itself yields good, and that good is in Allah's scale and comes from Allah, because it is Allah who has laid down the method of good and determined the path of action. It is He who guided to good, and He who granted the ability to do good and warned against evil. When a person does not walk on the method that Allah has determined, and does not adopt the path that Allah has made lawful, and does not strive for good, and does not fear the evil from which he has been warned, then certainly he will be struck by evil. This will be a real evil, both in this world and in the Hereafter, and this evil will be the earning of his own self, because he willingly departed from the method of action pleasing to Allah. (This is the meaning of his earning.) This meaning is different from the first meaning, and their scopes are also separate, and we believe that this point is now clear.

According to this second meaning, there is no effect on the (first) principle. Both good and evil are connected to the will and decree of Allah. Allah alone is the creator of all creatures. He is the creator of every occurrence. He is the originator of every event that happens, whatever the human will and action in that matter may be, and in whatever circumstances it may occur.

What is the real issue that is stated in these texts, or one aspect of which is taken up? It is the issue of compulsion and choice (jabr wa ikhtiyar): to what extent a human being's own will is involved in the actions that proceed from him, or to what extent his own will is involved in the benefits that accrue to him here, and how reward and punishment are attached to his voluntary actions, while we say that the true creator of all actions is Allah. The human wills themselves, human attention, human actions, and all other originated things are created by Allah. These and all similar questions connected with the problem of jabr and qadr are such that the Qur'anic verses make clear that every occurrence comes into being by the will of Allah. The Qur'an is entirely the speech of Allah, and the verses of the Qur'an cannot contradict one another. Therefore there must be a point of connection between these two matters. There is a sphere of human will and action in which a person is responsible and accountable, and for which he must face reward and punishment. If the sphere of this freedom of choice did not also have a relationship with the sphere of divine decree and divine will, how could these spheres be determined? This is a matter whose explanation and clarification is not possible, because a human being cannot grasp how Allah's will and power operate.

Now, after this, Allah clarifies the scope of the Holy Prophet's (ﷺ) role and the limits of his responsibility: what position he will take with regard to people, and how people's relationship with him will be, and that the whole matter will ultimately return to Allah.

﴿Whatever good reaches you, it is from Allah, and whatever harm reaches you, it is from yourself. And We have sent you to mankind as a Messenger, and Allah is sufficient as a witness.﴾ (4:79)

﴿Whoever obeys the Messenger has indeed obeyed Allah; and whoever turns away, We have not sent you as a guardian over them.﴾ (4:80)

The duty of the Messenger is to fulfill the responsibility of conveying the message. His responsibility is not to create good or to create evil; the work of creation belongs to Allah alone. And Allah is the witness that He has sent Muhammad (ﷺ) only to fulfill the duty of prophethood. (Wa kafa billahi shahida: "And Allah is sufficient as a witness.")

As for the relationship of people with Muhammad (ﷺ), whoever obeys him has, in effect, obeyed Allah. Therefore, in the matter of obedience, there is no separation between Allah and His Messenger, and there is no difference or distinction between the word of Allah and the word of the Messenger of Allah. As for the one who turns away and denies the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), his reckoning and the matter of his reward and punishment are left to Allah. Allah did not send the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) so that you would compel people to guidance or compel them to enter the religion. Nor is it the duty of the messengers to protect people in such a way that they do not fall into sins. Nor has it been placed within the power of the messengers to protect people in such a way that they do not fall into sins. Nor has it been given to the messengers to become guardians of people.

Through this explanation, their thoughts and notions are corrected on this matter: that the events which befall them are connected with, and exist by, the will of Allah, and are exactly in accordance with Allah's decree. And whatever good and evil befalls them, whatever meaning good and evil may be taken to have, whether it is apparent good or true good, all of it is from Allah. No one other than Allah can create anything, nor can bring it into existence, nor can sustain it, nor can bring anything into manufacture. The true good that is with Allah is from Allah alone, and the true evil that reaches them is due to their own selves. This evil reaches them because these people turn away from the Islamic system of life and violate Allah's commands.

The duty of the Messenger, both first and last, is that he is a Messenger. He is neither a creator, nor can he bring about any event. These are the attributes of Allah, and in them the Messenger does not share with Allah. He is only one who conveys the commands of Allah; then his obedience is the obedience of Allah. There is no path to the obedience of Allah other than obedience to the Messenger of Allah. The Messenger is not charged with providing guidance for those who turn away, nor can the Messenger prevent them from turning away and disobedience. He can do nothing beyond conveying (al-Balagh) and clarifying. These are decisive and reassuring realities, clear and explicit realities. Through them concepts are built and consciousness is matured. And these realities are a part of the struggle to prepare the Muslim community for its great mission and duty. After this, the flow of the discourse turns to another group. This group has infiltrated the ranks, and perhaps it is a group of the hypocrites (Munafiqun). The Qur'an mentions their conduct under a separate and new heading, but within the manner of expression, abhorrence for this conduct also shines through. Along with this abhorrence, guidance and instruction for the Muslim community is also given.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on surah 4, verse 81:

(Verse) "And they say, 'Obedience,' but when they go out from your presence, a group of them plot by night other than what you say. And Allah records what they plot by night. So turn away from them and rely upon Allah; and sufficient is Allah as Disposer of affairs. (81) Then do they not reflect upon the Qur'an? And if it had been from other than Allah, they would have found within it much contradiction. (82)" (4:81-82)

"They say with their mouths, 'We are obedient,' but when they leave your presence, a group of them gather at night and hold consultations against what you say. Allah is recording their secret conversations. Do not concern yourself with them, place your trust in Allah, for Allah alone is sufficient as a guardian."

Did these people not reflect upon the Qur'an? Had it been from anyone other than Allah, they would have found in it much discrepancy.

This group was such that when they were present with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and heard the Qur'an from him and understood its obligations, they would say that they were obedient. In this way they would declare comprehensive and unqualified obedience, and acknowledge unconditional submission. They would neither raise any objection in it, nor seek any kind of explanation, nor reserve any exception. But as soon as they rose from the gathering of the Messenger, a group of them would gather at night and hold consultations against his words. And they would decide that what the Messenger had said should not be acted upon, and would adopt some plan so that it would not be implemented and they could escape.

The meaning may also be that the community of Muslims, as a collective body, says that they will obey, but a group among them goes out at night and plots a conspiracy contrary to the word of the Muslim community. The aim of this hypocritical group is to create disorder and restlessness within that community. In either case, this hypocritical group is engaged in conspiracy. Their activities create restlessness within the ranks of Islam, while the Muslim community stands firmly against these conspiracies on every front and devotes its full strength to confronting them.

Allah assures the believers and the Noble Prophet ﷺ that this band of conspirators is not hidden from Allah's sight and that Allah is well aware of their cunning. The awareness and feeling that Allah is fully informed of the plots of these conspirators becomes a source of tranquillity and strength in the hearts of the believers. They attain the calm that, while Allah is watching, these plots cannot harm them in any way. From the other side, there is also a severe warning to these conspirators that they will never succeed in their plots.

(Verse) "wallahu yaktubu ma yubayyitun" (And Allah records what they plot by night). The plan that Allah gave His Messenger ﷺ for dealing with the hypocrites was this: that he would deal with them according to their outward condition, and would not treat them according to their intentions. Their secret conspiracies would be overlooked and ignored. This was a plan according to which, in the end, they dispersed, were weakened, and those who remained were scattered and went into hiding. This was one part of that plan.

(Verse) "fa-a'rid 'anhum" (so turn away from them): Along with overlooking them, the Messenger is reassured to rely fully upon Allah's protection and safeguarding.

(Verse) "wa tawakkal 'alallahi wa kafa billahi wakeelan" (And rely upon Allah; and sufficient is Allah as a Disposer of affairs). Indeed, Allah is sufficient for reliance: whoever has Allah as his guardian cannot be harmed by anyone. No conspiracy can harm him, neither can a secret plot prevail against them, nor an open one.

The question is: why would this group make a declaration of obedience before the Messenger ﷺ and then, upon returning, engage in conspiracy at night? The reason is that this group adopted this attitude because they had doubt as to whether the words presented by the Messenger ﷺ were from Allah or not. When such doubt arises even for a moment, the power and majesty of the word are lost. The strength and majesty within the Qur'an and the speech of the Messenger arise from the awareness that this speech is coming from the Lord, as though it is being heard from the very throat of Allah, and that he is not speaking of his own desire. This is why they were given a clear command to rely upon Allah, and this was emphasized again.

Here Allah presents a point before them, and this point is the height of honour and nobility to which the Qur'an wishes to bring man: that he should use his intellect and understand that he is a dignified creation. He is possessed of reason and perception, and this reason and perception has been granted to man by Allah Himself. Allah leaves the judgment about the Qur'an to their consciousness and their intellect and perception. Allah establishes for them a method of insight and vision, and it is shown that if they reflect upon matters according to this method, they will never stumble. This method of understanding the Qur'an has been defined in a very clear manner, and human understanding and perception can itself reach this method. In this way, a person can reach the conclusion that the Qur'an is from Allah, and there is no doubt in it.

﴿Do they not reflect upon the Qur'an? Had it been from other than Allah, they would have found in it much discrepancy.﴾ (4:82)

In this statement and guidance lies a station of the highest honour and dignity for humanity. It places complete trust in human perception and gives great importance to the human person. It also commands that matters be brought before the court of reason, and it does so in a phenomenon whose understanding is not very difficult for the human intellect.

The complete, comprehensive and unconstrained harmony found in the Qur'an is a phenomenon that cannot remain hidden from one who reflects upon this Book. The level and scope of this phenomenon may be broad or narrow according to people's understanding. The conclusions of thought of people of different races and different kinds of intelligence may differ, but every intellect, every race and every age receives from it something according to its capacity, and this difference in degree may correspond to people's understanding, their intellect, and their knowledge and culture. In this regard, the conclusion of thought of different people may be limited or unlimited according to their experience, ability and piety.

This is why every person is addressed by this verse, every generation is addressed by it, and according to the correct method of thought and reflection, one can perceive this phenomenon. That is, the quality that there is no contradiction in the Qur'an, and that complete harmony and coherence is found within it. However, as we have said, this understanding remains within the limits of a person's ability, his scholarly standing, his experience and his piety. This community, which was addressed in the form of the generation present at that time, was being addressed with a speech which it understood well, and through its understanding and perception it put it into practice to the extent of its capacity.

This phenomenon and this attribute, namely the quality of complete unity of thought and harmony, is first manifested in the mode of expression of the Holy Qur'an. In the style of the Qur'an and its artistic method of conveying its purpose, complete harmony is found. Human speech is before us: even in the greatest literary masterpieces there are ups and downs, there is harmony and there are also lapses of expression. If one part is forceful, another part has weakness; if in one there is original thought, in another there is commonplace material; if one part flows smoothly, another is extremely convoluted; if one is very bright, another part is dark. In short, in terms of eloquence, rhetoric and the qualities relating to defect, human speech has its ups and downs. Among the defects of speech, an important one is the lack of flow and harmony in speech, in which the matter quickly drops from one standard or rises above a lowered standard. This phenomenon appears at every step in every human speech. If we take the literary character of a single writer, or his prose, or the works of one and the same writer, or the policies of a single politician, or the war strategies of a single general, or the industrial work of a single person, this disparity of standard will be seen at every step. In the expression of standards, the difference of heaven and earth will be seen.

In the Holy Qur'an this quality is very clear and fully reflected, namely firmness and harmony in speech. This quality has been maintained throughout the entire Qur'an. What we are discussing here is only from the aspect of verbal and expressive harmony. Throughout this entire Book, the speech and style of expression maintain one single standard, and for this reason this Book bears a miraculous character. The topics this Book speaks about may certainly differ in colour according to their subject matter, but in terms of eloquence and rhetoric its standard remains one and the same. Its perfection in style remains intact, and nowhere does the speech fall from its standard level. Nowhere is its condition like that of human speech, where sometimes the standard is one and sometimes another. This Book bears the artistry of Allah. From this it becomes clear that the one who speaks these words does not change, and that He does not shift from one state to another, nor does one condition overtake Him after another. (See: At-Tasvir al-Fanni fi al-Qur'an)

After its artistic style, there is also in this system the quality of non-contradiction and complete harmony and general unity of thought, which is expressed in the verses of the Holy Qur'an and whose meaning is explained within these harmonious passages. That is, the system of thought upon which the human self has been trained, or upon which human society has been trained. Furthermore, all the parts and all the aspects of this system of life possess complete harmony. Likewise, in all the activities of an individual's life, and then in the activities of an individual within a society, and in the changes that occur in the life of an individual and a society generation after generation, there is complete correspondence and balance in all their aspects. Then there is a method and an ordering for the human faculty of perception, which has many aspects, and the human faculties of understanding and the various faculties that serve in the process of perception. Then, within the human being himself and within all his societies, all generations and all levels, a complete harmony has also been placed. There is also complete harmony between the human being and the universe in which he lives. Then, between the worldly life of the human being and his life in the Hereafter, there is also complete correspondence and harmony. Then this Book has maintained full harmony in this human being and in this entire universe, and in the human being's living of his life within it.

When there is a difference between the artistry of a human being and the artistry of Allah in terms of the style of speech and verbal expression, then in the fields of thought, ideology and legislation as well, it is evident that there will be a very clear difference and distinction between human work and divine work. All human ideologies and all human religions and schools of thought bear clearly visible human stamps. And in their viewpoints, partiality and individualism are clearly visible. In all these aspects, the human being appears influenced by temporary circumstances and difficulties. And the human being cannot perceive that within his ideology, his religion and school of thought, and within his plans, there is some contradiction which sets off a conflict within that system of thought and action, and this conflict either begins very soon or begins after some time. Then these human schools of thought and action completely suppress some qualities of the human being, while the human being himself is unaware of them and cannot keep them in view. Then there are qualities within some personalities which a person cannot even imagine. Within human perception itself there are thousands of weaknesses, and its sphere of action is extremely limited. Since the scope of human perception is limited, it cannot see beyond the plan it has made; rather, it is not even fully aware of the pros and cons (مالہ وما علیہ) of its own existing plan. By contrast, since the Qur'anic plan is made by the All-Knowing, the All-Aware, the Qur'anic contents and meanings are free from all these defects. These meanings and plans are permanent, and they are also in harmony with the laws of nature that prevail throughout the universe. These laws of nature, while being permanent and established, are also in constant motion. Likewise, Qur'anic ideas are simultaneously both dynamic and established.

Within these horizons and limits, through reflection upon this attribute of the Holy Qur'an, sometimes human perception cannot grasp its entire horizon, nor can an entire generation sometimes fully comprehend it. Rather, there will certainly be some difference in the perception of all generations, because every generation receives its share from the Holy Qur'an, and for the subsequent, more advanced generations there remain some horizons as well. In any case, in the perception of this attribute, something always remains from even the highest people of various levels, just as in other things there exists some degree of difference. And from that remaining horizon, subsequent generations continue to obtain their share, because there is a difference between what Allah has created and what human beings have created. In what Allah has created there is neither any discrepancy nor any variation or difference. In it there is complete unity and coherence. Yes, there is certainly a difference within the limits of people's understanding and perception, and some people understand this coherence very well, while others understand it a little less. (For details see: At-Tasawwur al-Islami Khasa'isuhu wa Muqawwimatuhu; Nahw Mujtama' Islami; al-Islam wa Mushkilat al-Hadarah; and Hadha al-Din, etc.)

But to the extent that an ordinary person can understand, or a group can understand, or a specific generation can understand, Allah presents the Holy Qur'an before the perception and understanding of people, according to what they possess, and asks them to reflect that this Holy Qur'an is the Word of Allah, and that if it were the word of other than Allah, people would find in it many discrepancies.

Here it seems appropriate that we pause briefly and determine what the limits of human perception are, in this particular matter or in the matter of the whole religion. No person should fall into the delusion that, since Allah has presented this matter before human perception for judgement, human perception is therefore something very great. Human reflection and perception too must remain within its protected limits, lest it become entangled, beyond its restricted and protected sphere, in a labyrinth.

These guidances of the Qur'an have not been properly understood, nor have their limits been properly understood. In both ancient and modern times there have been Islamic thinkers who have given reason and analogy a status equal to the Shariah (the sacred law), and indeed these people make reason and perception the guardian of the Shariah... But the reality is not so. The reality is that this instrument of perception is, in any case, the human faculty of cognition, although in its own place it is extremely important. This is why Allah has presented the question of the Qur'an being the Word of God before the court of reason and reflection; but the task of reason is only to perceive the reality that this Qur'an, and the entire religion established within it, is from Allah. This is because within the Qur'an there are attributes and phenomena which human reason can understand with great ease, and those phenomena and signs are sufficient for the perception that this religion is from Allah. Once this is accepted, the logical consequence of this perception is that human beings should accept the commandments within the religion, whether or not their wisdom becomes clear to human understanding. For once we have accepted that this religion and the Qur'an are from Allah, it automatically follows that wisdom exists within them. Then it no longer matters whether, in present circumstances, the interests of people are served by this religion or not. When the religion is from Allah, then, as it were, the benefit is present and realized within it. Human reason is not equal to the Shariah, let alone that it should come to dominate and rule over the Shariah. For even the wisdoms of the Shariah are grasped by any intellect only to a very limited extent, and it is impossible that reason should be able to encompass all the aspects and all the benefits of the Shariah, neither in one moment nor in the whole of human history, whereas the Shariah of Allah has regard for the benefits of every single moment and for the interests of time and place. Therefore it is not appropriate that any established commandment of the Shariah be left solely to human reason and analogy. In this regard, the task of human reason is only to reflect upon the understanding of the textual sources of the Shariah (nusus shar'iyyah), and upon the derivation of their implications and meanings. Reason cannot be permitted to pass judgement on the benefits of the commandments, because when any verse is revealed by Allah, it necessarily contains some benefit, which is precisely why it has come. The task of reason is in matters where there is no explicit text, which are new issues. With regard to such issues, the method to be adopted, as we have said earlier, is that such matters shall be referred back to Allah and to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). And this is precisely the field left open for genuine ijtihad (independent juristic reasoning), while the understanding and perception of the Qur'anic texts will always, in any case, be through reason. When the meaning of a text has been understood, then at that point it is better to pause, and reason cannot be permitted to pronounce whether there is benefit in that meaning or not. The true domain of human reason is the laws of nature in the universe, and this is an extremely vast domain.

We should give human reason the standing and rank that Allah has given it, which is appropriate for it, and keep it within the sphere that Allah has assigned to reason. Its boundaries should not be exceeded, so that it does not go into a labyrinth and become trapped, and find no perfect guide. And even if it finds a guide, that guide may fall upon paths of which he himself has no knowledge. This situation is more dangerous for a person who is seeking the Straight Path.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 4, verse 83:

Now the flow of the discourse moves forward, and another group present within the Muslim society is taken up.

"And when there comes to them some news of security or of fear, they spread it about. And if they had referred it to the Messenger and to those in authority among them, those who can draw conclusions from it would have known it. And were it not for the grace of Allah upon you and His mercy, you would have followed Satan, except for a few." (4:83)

"Whenever they receive some reassuring or frightening news, they spread it around, whereas if they were to convey it to the Messenger and to the responsible leaders of their community, those among them who are capable of drawing a correct conclusion from it would come to know of it. And were it not for the grace of Allah upon you and His mercy, (your weaknesses were such that) all but a few of you would have followed Satan."

The group referred to here is also a group within the Islamic camp, but it consists of people who are still not well acquainted with the ways and norms of the Islamic system. This group had not yet understood how dangerous and destructive the consequences of spreading unrest within the Islamic camp can be. For rumours are rumours, not facts. Circumstances are sometimes so serious that a casual remark can produce dangerous results. Concerning a single individual, or a group or community, certain outcomes may arise that the person making a careless remark could not even imagine. If such events and consequences come to pass, there is no way at all to remedy or compensate for them. These people speak in this manner because the concept of the brotherhood and fraternity arising among the members of the Islamic camp was not yet clear in their minds. They did not attach importance to what the final outcome of such irresponsible talk would be, or what harm the spread of such matters causes when these reports pass from one mouth to another, whether they concern circumstances of peace or circumstances of anxiety and fear. In both situations, the spreading of certain news is extremely deadly and mischief-making. For example, in an alert, prepared and cautious camp, presenting the activities of the enemy as less than they are can lead to negligence, and the enemy may then become active. In such circumstances, reassuring people about peace can make them heedless and lazy, even though the responsible leaders repeatedly warn them to be cautious. For if danger is over one's head, the vigilance of a person against the enemy is entirely different from taking precautionary measures merely on the basis of the orders of the leaders. This kind of laxity and carelessness sometimes decides the final outcome of a matter. Likewise, if a camp is content with its own strength and remains steadfast because of its confidence, and fear is spread within it, then in such a camp the spreading of frightening news produces agitation and disorder, and people perform actions that are not needed, and because of which fear and panic arise among the people without cause, and sometimes such things produce extremely bad results.

In any case, this is a characteristic of a camp whose organisation is not yet complete, or whose members' loyalty to their leadership is not yet complete, or in which both these weaknesses exist. It appears that both of these matters were present in the Islamic society at that time, because in this early period the Islamic society contained people at different levels of faith. People of varying understanding and perception existed, and in love and loyalty too these people were at different levels and degrees. In short, the Qur'an, in accordance with its purely divine method, was removing this kind of disorder and agitation.

"And if they had referred it to the Messenger and to those in authority among them" (4:83). That is, if these people had brought the news of security and fear to the notice of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, in the period when he was present, or conveyed it to the responsible persons among the believers when he was not present, they would have ascertained the truth of these reports, because they understand the reality of such matters well, and they would have derived the truth from among these conflicting reports, or understood the matter from various kinds of circumstances.

It is the duty of a Muslim soldier that if he hears any such news, he should convey it to his commander, provided that he is the right commander; he should convey it to his Prophet if the Prophet is present, and if the age of the Prophet has ended, he should convey it to those above him. It is not proper conduct for him to spread this news only among his companions, or to spread it among people for whom the Islamic community bears no responsibility, because Islamic leadership is precisely that which is able to understand the reality and also to understand the right occasion for publishing a report. Even if a report is confirmed, it is sometimes not appropriate to publicise it, and not publicising it is the better course.

This was the training of the Qur'an. The Qur'an, while creating firmness of faith in the hearts of Muslims, was also creating loyalty to the Islamic leadership. The Qur'an gathered all the principles of the Islamic military system in just one verse, indeed in just one part of a verse. This verse teaches that a soldier continuously receives news of security and danger and conveys it to his superior officers, and this chain goes on. At the beginning of this one verse, the portrait of a soldier is drawn who receives news, of security as well as of fear, and who keeps publicising it continuously without seriousness, without any investigation, and without presenting it to his leadership to obtain instructions. In the middle part of the verse, a soldier is given this guidance, and in the final part the inner connection of the soldiers is linked to Allah. The grace of Allah is mentioned, and they are moved to render thanks to Allah. They are warned against obeying Satan, who lies in ambush, and who, if the grace and mercy of Allah were absent, would immediately create corruption in their hearts.

"And were it not for the grace of Allah upon you and His mercy, you would have followed Satan, except for a few" (4:83).

This is one verse, and within it has been placed a great abundance of knowledge and insight. All aspects of this matter have been mentioned; this verse has descended into the most hidden recesses of conscience, and guidance and knowledge have been filled into hearts. This is because it is from Allah. And had it not been from Allah,

"they would have found in it much discrepancy" (4:82).

When the discussion reaches this point, the weaknesses in the Islamic ranks are pointed out, weaknesses which can affect the life of the Islamic society and the act of jihad. These errors and their correction have been the work of this section from its very beginning. Now the believers are urged towards jihad and fighting, which has been the subject of this section throughout. Here the Messenger of Allah ﷺ is personally charged with fighting in the way of Allah. After this personal responsibility, no one can remain behind from it, neither because of some defect or flaw found in the Islamic community, nor because of the difficulties of the road. This is because the address is directed solely to the person of the Messenger ﷺ: that he should rise and fight, even if he is alone, since jihad is obligatory upon every individual personally. He too is responsible for his own self; yet along with his own self, he should also urge the believers to fight. Here Allah promises the believers and the Messenger ﷺ victory and success, because this battle is indeed Allah's own battle, and Allah is All-Mighty.

(Verse 84)

From this verse and the one before it, we can clearly see the characteristics of the Muslim community of that time, just as we see the characteristics of human souls in every age.

(a) These verses show that at that time there was serious unease within the ranks of the Muslims and there was no complete unity. Reluctance towards fighting, obstacles in its path, and the weaknesses of holding back from jihad were still present in the Islamic ranks. So much so that, in order to rouse and inspire people to jihad, the Prophet ﷺ himself was commanded here: ﴿So fight in the way of Allah; you are not held responsible except for yourself﴾ (4:84). Even if you are alone, you are responsible only for your own self. Yet, alongside this, you should also encourage the believers. However, the Prophet's ﷺ own participation in jihad does not depend on whether other people rise up for this task or not. Although in practice it was not possible that the believers would all reject the call of the Prophet ﷺ, the purpose of addressing the matter in this manner was that the obligation rests fundamentally upon him. Just as it is a basic principle of the Islamic concept of life that every person is responsible for their own self, and the responsibility of one cannot fall upon another, so too encouraging others to fight remains a separate matter.

(b) This shows how much danger people felt in opening a war against the polytheists in that period, and how many difficulties lay in that path. So much so that Allah Himself assures the Muslims that He will break the might of the disbelievers, and thus the Muslims would be under the protection of Allah's power. At the same time, it is affirmed that Allah is mighty in strength, and when He punishes someone, His punishment is very severe. The words that Allah will break the might of the disbelievers ﴿And Allah is stronger in might and stronger in punishment﴾ (4:84) demonstrate that at that time the people of disbelief were powerful.

Because of their strength, fear was felt within the Islamic ranks, and these circumstances relate to the period between Uhud and the Trench. The period from Uhud to the Trench was the period in which the Muslims in Madinah faced extreme difficulties and dangers. The hypocrites had infiltrated among them, the Jews were spread around them, and they constantly incited the polytheists to mischief. And within the Islamic ranks, the Islamic concept of life was not yet firmly established and clear.

(c) From this we also learn that when a person has to step into difficulties, their support is only the Divine Being, and the shelter of Allah alone is a source of tranquility. At such a time only Allah's help is needed, and reliance upon Allah alone is what proves effective. When dangers reach their extreme limits and all means fail to work, then it is the Divine Being alone who helps, and these are all realities which the Islamic system keeps in view. This is because Allah is the Creator of the human soul, and Allah knows well His own created human soul: how it should be trained, how it should be protected, how it should be stirred up, and how it will be prepared to face difficulties.

At the end of this lesson, the Prophet ﷺ was commanded to urge the believers to fight, and mention was also made of those who held back from fighting and stayed behind. Now a general principle is stated here: that every person should intercede for good and righteous deeds, advise people, give people guidance towards goodness, admonish them, and enjoin cooperation in righteousness.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on surah 4, verse 85:

(Verse) "Number 85."

Now, whoever urges people to fight, encourages them to this purpose and gives the call to jihad, will receive the full reward of that call and of the deed that results from it. And whoever holds back, stays behind, and if bad consequences follow from it, this person too is responsible. From the word "kifl" (portion, share) it is understood that the one who stays behind will be responsible for the evil consequences.

The same principle will apply to every good recommendation, and the same principle will apply to a bad recommendation as well. Although this principle has been mentioned in a particular situation, it is the Qur'an's manner of expression that, in the context of a specific event, it states a general rule, presents even this particular event as a part of that general rule, and then connects all matters to the Divine Being, who is the Guardian and Provider of everything, who has power over everything; and the meanings of the word (muqit) are included in this.

(Verse) "Wa kana Allahu 'ala kulli shay'in muqita" (4:85) (And Allah is ever Watchful over all things).

After the recommendation of good deeds, it is said: if someone greets you, then either return a greeting like it or a better one. In every society, greeting is an act by which the vehicle of life moves with great tranquility and ease, if the etiquette of greeting is well observed; there is a deep connection between greeting and the recommendation of goodness. If two individuals in a society do not greet one another, what further guidance will they give each other?

(Verse 86)

Islam gave the Islamic society a distinctive greeting of its own, by which a Muslim and a Muslim society became distinguished from non-Muslims and non-Muslim societies. This makes the greeting entirely unique and distinct; in their daily life they acquire distinctive qualities, and because of it they are not absorbed or dissolved into other societies, nor do they become like salt in the flour.

Islam has given three forms of greeting: As-salamu alaikum; As-salamu alaikum wa rahmatullah; and As-salamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh. The reply to a greeting is either the same or better, except in the case of the third phrase. For example, the reply to "As-salamu alaikum" is either "Wa alaikum as-salam" or the better "Wa alaikum as-salam wa rahmatullah." The reply to the second is "Wa alaikum as-salam wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh." And the reply to the third is the same as it: because in it all the words have already been used, so the reply to the third is the same. This is the narration from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ.

In this there is, firstly, that distinctiveness which is the special colour of the Islamic society. Islam desires that its followers have distinct features and particular habits, just as Islam has given a specific legal and organisational system. On this subject we have already discussed, at the occasion of the change of the qiblah, that just as Islam gave this ummah a way of life, it also gave it a specific qiblah. (See Surah al-Baqarah, Part Two.)

Secondly, Islam sought to create in the individuals of the Muslim ummah a very firm love and brotherhood: for example, the spread of greeting, that the reply to a greeting should be better than the greeting itself, and other relations through which very firm bonds of brotherhood and affection arose within the Islamic society. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ was asked which deed is good, and he replied: "That you feed people, and that you greet whoever you know and whoever you do not know." This is a command that the community of Muslims should greet one another, and it is a sunnah; as for replying to the greeting, it is obligatory by the ruling of this verse. The effects of the habit of greeting in an Islamic society are practically felt when, through greeting, strangers become acquainted with one another and turn towards each other, and those who continually exchange greetings establish mutual ties. This is a quality that becomes manifest to everyone who studies the effects of this habit and reflects on its results.

Thirdly, in the midst of the verses on fighting, this verse is a gentle breeze of friendly relations, and it points to the fundamental principle of Islam: that the foremost principle of Islam is that peace and security be established in the land, because Islam is a religion of peace. The war of Islam is in reality for peace, that is, to establish peace on the earth, and this peace is desired in its broad sense: a peace that is based upon the Islamic system of life.

Lesson 37 at a glance:

This lesson mentions one of the basic principles of the Islamic conception of life, namely the belief in the oneness of Allah and regarding Him as one and without partner in His sovereignty. Then, in accordance with this principle, the relations of the Islamic society and the Islamic community with other camps are determined. But even before determining the nature of the relationship of the Islamic society with other societies, this lesson subjects the Muslims themselves to severe criticism, because they divided into two groups regarding the hypocrites. It appears that this group was separate from the hypocrites living in Madinah. These commands are founded upon the fundamental principle of Islam, and this criticism too is in accordance with the principle upon which the Islamic conception of life and the Islamic system rest. This principle is mentioned constantly whenever the Islamic system gives any guidance or any legislation is enacted.

These commands concern various camps, and these commands are part of those principles and laws which Islam first introduced into human history. The laws relate to international law. Islam was the first to make certain rules, departing from the decision of the sword in international affairs; in the international rules consisting of the proof of strength and the law of the jungle, Islam was the first to present civilised codes.

In Europe, the beginning of international law occurred only in the seventeenth century CE (corresponding to the eleventh century AH), but this law had no standing beyond paper and ink, and the international bodies that were established were merely instruments for giving legal cover to the secret aims of international colonial powers. Moreover, these bodies were a battlefield for the cold war. Their purpose was by no means that rights reach those entitled to them, nor did these bodies truly dispense justice. These bodies were brought into existence merely because some disputes had arisen among certain large countries that were equal to one another in power, and as soon as the balance of power between those countries was lost, neither those international laws retained any value, nor did those international bodies retain any worth.

When Islam came, which is the system of life of the Lord of Majesty for mankind, it legislated in international affairs in the seventh century CE, that is, in the first century AH. This law was formulated by Islam of its own accord, and there was no pressure from any equal government in making this law. Islam made this law of its own accord and acted upon it of its own accord, so that the Islamic society, on its basis, might establish its relations with other camps, raise the banners of justice for humanity, and lay down signposts for it. Although the jahili enemy camps of that age did not deal with the Muslims in light of these Islamic international laws, this was because these principles and laws had been introduced by Islam for the first time. These international principles are scattered across various surahs of the Holy Qur'an, and if they are gathered together, a complete code of international law emerges. Within it lies the solution to all the situations that could have confronted an Islamic state and other countries at any time: whether these countries are at war and in opposition, at peace, hostile, neutral, allies of the belligerent, allies of the peaceful treaty-partner, or allies of the neutral.

There is no need here to mention the details of these principles and rulings; such detailed discussion is the task of specialists in international law. However, we present a summary of the principles that have come in these verses. In this lesson, dealing has been made with the following people:

(a) Hypocrites who did not reside in Madinah.

(b) Those people who belong to a people with whom there is a covenant between them and the Muslims.

(c) Neutral people who neither like to fight alongside the Muslims nor like to fight alongside their own people, but who remain upon their former religion.

(d) Those people who toy with the Islamic conception of life: when they come to Madinah they declare their Islam, and when they go to Makkah they announce disbelief.

(e) The rule concerning accidental killing among Muslims and intentional killing among people of different standing, i.e., people holding different citizenship. In all these situations we find clear rulings, which are explicit on their subject, and they apply to all situations. These principles form part of the codification of international relations, and their ruling is the same as the other rulings of international law on this subject.

Lesson No. 37: Explanation of the Verses

87 to 94

This lesson begins with the principle on which the edifice of the Islamic system is built, and all its aspects derive from this principle.

(Verse) 87

The first step of the Islamic system of life is the creed of Tawhid (Oneness of God), and the summary of the creed of Tawhid is that Allah alone is the Sovereign. Whether one legislates an Islamic law or establishes an Islamic administration, whether the law of the system relates to the internal affairs of the Islamic society or to the international law by which the Islamic society deals with other societies, the verse under discussion is the opening of some internal and international laws.

The journey of the training of the human soul begins with the belief that one day Allah will stand all the servants before Him in the place of gathering, and will call them to account for the proper use of the freedoms He gave them in this world. There will also be a questioning there as to how far you acted upon Allah's guidance and His laws, and how far you observed the Islamic regulations in the small and great matters of your life in this world, since you were sent there precisely for this trial and test. In the Hereafter, every matter, small or great, will be reckoned and accounted for. It is this very otherworldly conception of accountability and answerability that guarantees adherence to the administrative and legal regulations of the Shariah, because within every person's conscience there sits a living watchman, who keeps watch even when the watchmen of the government are asleep.

And Allah the Exalted says:

﴿And who is more truthful in statement than Allah?﴾ (4:87), and this is His promise, which cannot be contrary to.

After giving this awareness to the hearts of the Muslims, the main point now begins. Creating this awareness is a general method of the Islamic approach to training, and its purpose is to show that the entire ideological and practical edifice of the Islamic system of life rests upon this belief. Thus, after this awareness, expression of surprise is now being made that the Muslims are not unified regarding the hypocrites and the hypocrisy, and in dealing with them they do not adopt a decisive approach, although the circumstances demand that a decisive and clear-cut position be taken towards them. Unity of view is one thing; the Muslims have clearly split into two groups regarding them, and each has its own opinion. This difference of opinion arose concerning some hypocrites living outside Madinah, the details of which are coming later. The interrogative negative form is used to point out why there is no intellectual harmony among the Muslims regarding these matters. This also shows that Islam's policy is to adopt a decisive and clear-cut stance in matters, and to maintain unity of attitude in dealing with and regarding the hypocrites, and to deal with them according to their outward conduct, provided that a plan has been settled and there is a need for leniency toward them.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran (Urdu translation)) on surah 4, verse 88–89 (part 1 of 2):

(Verse) No. 88 to 89.
Several narrations are reported about who these people were, of which two are important.
Imam Ahmad (rahimahullah) has narrated this report from Zayd ibn Thabit (radiyallahu anhu) through the chain of Bahz, Shu'bah, Adi ibn Thabit, Abdullah ibn Zayd (radiyallahu anhu): that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) set out toward Uhud, and some people who had set out with him turned back. Concerning them, the companions of the Prophet (ﷺ) divided into two groups. One group said that these people should be killed, and another group said that killing them is not permissible, since they are believers. Upon this, this verse was revealed:
﴿So what is the matter with you that you have become two groups concerning the hypocrites?﴾ (4:88) The Prophet (ﷺ) then said: "It (Medina) is pure, and it will expel the impure people just as the furnace expels the dross of iron." (The Sahihayn have narrated it from Shu'bah.)
Awfi has narrated from Ibn Abbas (radiyallahu anhu) that this was revealed concerning those who outwardly had become Muslims but who used to assist the polytheists in Makkah. These people went out of Makkah for some need of theirs. They were saying in their hearts that if they met the companions of Muhammad (ﷺ), they would have no fear of them. When the Muslims were informed that these people were travelling, a group of Muslims said: "Go out and kill these cowards, since they assist our enemies, the polytheists." But another group of Muslims said: "Subhan Allah" (or however they said it): "Will you kill a group who have uttered the same words that you have uttered, merely because they have not made hijrah and have not left their homeland? Should we make their lives and property lawful?" Thus the Muslims became two parties on this matter. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was present, and he did not refute the opinion of either of them. Upon this, this verse was revealed: ﴿So what is the matter with you that you have become two groups concerning the hypocrites?﴾ (4:88) (Narrated by Ibn Abi Hatim). Similar narrations are also reported from Salamah, Ikrimah, Mujahid and Dahhak (may Allah be pleased with them all) and others.
Although in terms of chain and transmission the first narration is stronger, we prefer the content of the second narration, because it is a historical fact that no command to fight the hypocrites of Medina was ever issued. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) neither fought against them nor killed them. There was a different plan for dealing with them: that their activities be overlooked, and that the Islamic society of Medina itself be given the opportunity to spit them out. What the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was doing was cutting off the connections the hypocrites had around Medina. For example, the Jews who incited these hypocrites and were their supporters were expelled from Medina and then from the entire Arabian Peninsula. As for the verse under discussion, it commands that the hypocrites in question be seized and killed wherever they are found; therefore, this group must be some other group than the hypocrites residing within Medina. It may be said that their apprehension is conditional upon hijrah, since the verse says:
﴿So do not take from among them allies until they emigrate in the way of Allah. But if they turn away, then seize them and kill them wherever you find them.﴾ (4:89)
"Therefore do not take any of them as friends until they emigrate, and if they turn away, seize them and kill them wherever you find them."
This warning was revealed concerning those people so that they might come out of that situation, and it is possible that they came out of such circumstances; therefore the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) did not enforce this ruling against them. But by the word (yuhajiru) it is definitively established that the hypocrites in question were not from the people of Medina. The purpose was that these people should migrate and come to Medina. This event must have been before the conquest of Makkah, and hijrah existed before the conquest of Makkah, because the definition of hijrah is migrating from the abode of disbelief to the abode of Islam. People kept coming from the Islamic movement and kept coming under the Islamic system; otherwise their lives would pass either in disbelief or in hypocrisy. In the next lesson of this same surah there is severe criticism of those who were still residing in the abode of disbelief, Makkah, without any excuse or weakness, and who were Muslims. At that time Makkah was for them the abode of disbelief and the abode of war, although it was their original homeland and they were residing in it. These are the reasons on the basis of which we prefer the second narration, and that the group of hypocrites under discussion was residing in Makkah, or in some settlement around Makkah. They used to affirm Islam with their mouths and by their actions support the disbelievers. In short, let us read the verse under discussion once more:
﴿So what is the matter with you that you have become two groups concerning the hypocrites, while Allah has overturned them for what they have earned? Do you wish to guide those whom Allah has sent astray? And whoever Allah sends astray, you will never find for him a way. They wish that you would disbelieve as they have disbelieved, so that you would be equal. So do not take from among them allies until they emigrate in the way of Allah. But if they turn away, then seize them and kill them wherever you find them, and do not take from among them any ally or helper.﴾ (4:88–89)
"In these verses there is severe reproach for the fact that disagreement arose concerning the hypocrites, and why each party adopted this astonishing position about them. Because in that position, one party showed great leniency, and it was being displayed that the Muslims' awareness of Islam was not yet firm. Some of them said: 'Will you kill people who have uttered the same words that you have uttered, and merely because they did not abandon their homeland and make hijrah?' Is this alone sufficient to make their lives and property permissible? Their concept of Islam was not firm, because they were keeping in view only that these hypocrites had also recited the same shahadah that we recited, although there was evidence against that group of hypocrites. First, their own statement that the companions of Muhammad (ﷺ) would not say anything to them; second, that a group of believers had also disclosed about them that they assist the enemies of the Muslims. Despite this evidence, the position of these people concerning those hypocrites was a weak position, although they should have adopted a decisive and plain position, because orally reciting the testimony of faith while practically assisting the disbelievers was a clear proof of hypocrisy. Such people did not need any leniency or overlooking. This was not a minor mistake, but rather it was showing weakness in the concept of Islam. That is why in this verse strong astonishment was expressed and severe warning was given.
As for the hypocrites of Medina, the Muslims were intellectually completely clear about them, that they are hypocrites. But overlooking them was adopted because it was being done under a specific plan, namely that they be dealt with on the basis of their outward circumstances, and that they be given respite for a time.
But this was a different situation: a group among the Muslims was defending them on the ground that they too had recited the same kalimah that we recited, and they too had testified with their tongues that Allah is One and Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), although these people were definitively assisting the enemies of Islam. Because of this intellectual weakness among the Muslims and their difference of opinion (while the hypocrisy of the hypocrites was completely clear), this verse issued a severe warning. And then after the warning, it was also clarified: (Wallahu arkasahum bima kasabu) (Allah has overturned them because of what they earned). You dispute about them, and Allah, because of their evil deeds and their evil intentions, has placed them in circumstances in which they appear overturned. This is Allah's testimony against them: that because of their thinking and their actions, they are in a state that is not worthy of envy.
After this warning, another warning was given: (Atureedoon an tahdoo man adalla Allah) (Do you wish to guide those whom Allah has sent astray?). That is, the group among the Muslims which was adopting a lenient attitude toward them had the intention that they be given an opportunity to come onto the right path, so that they would give up this hypocritical attitude. Allah the Exalted considered the position of these people inappropriate, and has placed the hypocrites in such circumstances because of their deeds and evil intentions; therefore the hope of their being guided is futile.
(Wa man yudlili Allahu falan tajida lahu sabeelan) (And whoever Allah sends astray, you will never find for him a way).
And Allah sends people astray because they adopt the path of misguidance by their own intention and will. Then they strive for misguidance and go very far along that path, so far that the way of guidance is closed to them, because they have adopted the opposite direction, and they are no longer seekers of Allah's help for guidance, and they have lost the signposts of the way.
Now let us take one step further! The real stance of these hypocrites is expressed thus: not only have they themselves become misguided and, because of their intention and action, become deserving of the state in which they are, but they themselves wish that the people of Islam would also adopt the path of disbelief, and that it would be good.
(Wadda lau takfuroona kama kafaroo fatakoonoona sawa'an) (They wish that you would disbelieve as they have disbelieved, so that you would be equal). Certainly they have adopted the path of disbelief, although they too have recited the same kalimah that Muslims recite, and they have borne witness to both matters; but their deeds refute that testimony, by which these people assist the enemies of Islam. But they do not stop even at this limit, because whoever adopts disbelief does not stop at any limit. He does not sit at ease until Islam and Muslims are erased from the entire surface of the earth. He remains engaged in continuous effort for this wicked purpose. He strives for this aim, and conspires, so that the present people of Islam too may return to disbelief, and thus all people become equal.
This is the first clarification of the stance of the hypocrites under discussion, and this clarification has been made in such a way that every kind of doubt is removed from the thinking of the people of Islam about them. This thinking is now founded on the clear testimony of their words and deeds, and now this thinking is free from contradiction. The reality of outward profession of Islam becomes nothing when all the indicators show that the stance of these people is hypocritical.
The Qur'an gives a pinch to the consciousness of the Muslims, from which a frightening feeling arises in their consciousness, and this feeling arises from the words of the Qur'an:
(Wadda lau takfuroona kama kafaroo fatakoonoona sawa'an) (They wish that you would disbelieve as they have disbelieved, so that you would be equal). This fear arises because the people of Islam had recently abandoned disbelief and tasted Islam, and they still had awareness of how great a change had come into their lives: how high their consciousness had risen, how high their general standard had become, and how much exaltation their society had attained in Islam in comparison to Jahiliyyah. This distinction existed both in their consciousness and in the reality of the situation, and this indication alone was sufficient for them to become enemies of the one who was plotting to bring them back to those former lowliness, that is, to the lowliness of that Jahiliyyah from which Islam had raised them by the hand. Then it had not left them at a common level, but had raised them through general progress to the highest peak.
That is why the Qur'anic system of training, by taking support from this reality, in dangerous circumstances and in circumstances of advancing, warns the Muslims about the enemy in this manner and gives strict emphatic commands:
(Fala tattakhidhoo minhum awliya'a hatta yuhajiroo fi sabeelillah, fa-in tawaw fakhudhoohum waqtulohum haythu wajadtumoohum wa la tattakhidhoo minhum waliyyan wa la naseera) (So do not take from among them allies until they emigrate in the way of Allah. But if they turn away, then seize them and kill them wherever you find them, and do not take from among them any ally or helper). (89) (4:89)
"Therefore do not take any of them as friends until they emigrate in the way of Allah. Then if they refuse this condition, seize them, kill them wherever you find them, and do not take any of them as friend or helper."
When Allah the Exalted said here: "do not take any of them as friend or helper," it indicates that until then there were still family and tribal ties and relations between Muslims and non-Muslims, and these ties still had value in the hearts of Muslims, and it is possible that these ties were still for the sake of some economic interests. This method of training of Islam was uprooting completely every remaining trace and tie of Jahiliyyah. And just as the Qur'an was purifying thoughts, in the same way it was also establishing for the Muslim community the principles of international relations.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran (Urdu translation)) on surah 4, verse 88–89 (part 2 of 2):

The Qur'an was telling the ummah that no ummah can ever come into being on the basis of family and tribal ties alone. An ummah can arise on the basis of ties of blood and kinship, of residence in the same country and region, and of commercial and other economic interests. An ummah always comes into being on the basis of a specific way of life (nazariyah-e-hayat), and of a society and collective system that rises upon that way of life.

For this reason, the bonds of friendship and wilayah (guardianship/allegiance) cannot remain in place between the people of Dar al-Islam (the abode of Islam) and the people of Dar al-Harb (the abode of war). At that time, Dar al-Harb was Makkah, which was the original homeland of the muhajirin. Therefore, friendship between the people of Makkah, even those who had professed Islam verbally, and the Muslims of Madinah could not be established until they made hijrah, a hijrah that is purely for Allah and in the path of Allah, and is for no other purpose. That is, it must be solely for the establishment of a society that lives in accordance with the Islamic system of life, and there must be no other aim. With a most pure, most decisive and most defined purpose, one free of any adulteration and any confusion, with no goal other than the Islamic system of life, and with no other interest.

If they fulfil this condition, though they have professed the kalimah of Islam verbally, by leaving their families, forsaking their homeland and interests, and migrating to Dar al-Islam so that they may live here under the Islamic system, which is based on the Islamic way of life and within which the Islamic Shari'ah is in force, then they will become members of the Islamic society. They will be the fellow citizens of the Muslim ummah. But if they do not accept this condition and refuse hijrah, then the kalimah they have recited verbally has no value.
