Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran (Urdu translation)) on surah 4, verse 88–89 (part 1 of 2):

(Verse) No. 88 to 89.
Several narrations are reported about who these people were, of which two are important.
Imam Ahmad (rahimahullah) has narrated this report from Zayd ibn Thabit (radiyallahu anhu) through the chain of Bahz, Shu'bah, Adi ibn Thabit, Abdullah ibn Zayd (radiyallahu anhu): that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) set out toward Uhud, and some people who had set out with him turned back. Concerning them, the companions of the Prophet (ﷺ) divided into two groups. One group said that these people should be killed, and another group said that killing them is not permissible, since they are believers. Upon this, this verse was revealed:
﴿So what is the matter with you that you have become two groups concerning the hypocrites?﴾ (4:88) The Prophet (ﷺ) then said: "It (Medina) is pure, and it will expel the impure people just as the furnace expels the dross of iron." (The Sahihayn have narrated it from Shu'bah.)
Awfi has narrated from Ibn Abbas (radiyallahu anhu) that this was revealed concerning those who outwardly had become Muslims but who used to assist the polytheists in Makkah. These people went out of Makkah for some need of theirs. They were saying in their hearts that if they met the companions of Muhammad (ﷺ), they would have no fear of them. When the Muslims were informed that these people were travelling, a group of Muslims said: "Go out and kill these cowards, since they assist our enemies, the polytheists." But another group of Muslims said: "Subhan Allah" (or however they said it): "Will you kill a group who have uttered the same words that you have uttered, merely because they have not made hijrah and have not left their homeland? Should we make their lives and property lawful?" Thus the Muslims became two parties on this matter. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was present, and he did not refute the opinion of either of them. Upon this, this verse was revealed: ﴿So what is the matter with you that you have become two groups concerning the hypocrites?﴾ (4:88) (Narrated by Ibn Abi Hatim). Similar narrations are also reported from Salamah, Ikrimah, Mujahid and Dahhak (may Allah be pleased with them all) and others.
Although in terms of chain and transmission the first narration is stronger, we prefer the content of the second narration, because it is a historical fact that no command to fight the hypocrites of Medina was ever issued. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) neither fought against them nor killed them. There was a different plan for dealing with them: that their activities be overlooked, and that the Islamic society of Medina itself be given the opportunity to spit them out. What the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was doing was cutting off the connections the hypocrites had around Medina. For example, the Jews who incited these hypocrites and were their supporters were expelled from Medina and then from the entire Arabian Peninsula. As for the verse under discussion, it commands that the hypocrites in question be seized and killed wherever they are found; therefore, this group must be some other group than the hypocrites residing within Medina. It may be said that their apprehension is conditional upon hijrah, since the verse says:
﴿So do not take from among them allies until they emigrate in the way of Allah. But if they turn away, then seize them and kill them wherever you find them.﴾ (4:89)
"Therefore do not take any of them as friends until they emigrate, and if they turn away, seize them and kill them wherever you find them."
This warning was revealed concerning those people so that they might come out of that situation, and it is possible that they came out of such circumstances; therefore the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) did not enforce this ruling against them. But by the word (yuhajiru) it is definitively established that the hypocrites in question were not from the people of Medina. The purpose was that these people should migrate and come to Medina. This event must have been before the conquest of Makkah, and hijrah existed before the conquest of Makkah, because the definition of hijrah is migrating from the abode of disbelief to the abode of Islam. People kept coming from the Islamic movement and kept coming under the Islamic system; otherwise their lives would pass either in disbelief or in hypocrisy. In the next lesson of this same surah there is severe criticism of those who were still residing in the abode of disbelief, Makkah, without any excuse or weakness, and who were Muslims. At that time Makkah was for them the abode of disbelief and the abode of war, although it was their original homeland and they were residing in it. These are the reasons on the basis of which we prefer the second narration, and that the group of hypocrites under discussion was residing in Makkah, or in some settlement around Makkah. They used to affirm Islam with their mouths and by their actions support the disbelievers. In short, let us read the verse under discussion once more:
﴿So what is the matter with you that you have become two groups concerning the hypocrites, while Allah has overturned them for what they have earned? Do you wish to guide those whom Allah has sent astray? And whoever Allah sends astray, you will never find for him a way. They wish that you would disbelieve as they have disbelieved, so that you would be equal. So do not take from among them allies until they emigrate in the way of Allah. But if they turn away, then seize them and kill them wherever you find them, and do not take from among them any ally or helper.﴾ (4:88–89)
"In these verses there is severe reproach for the fact that disagreement arose concerning the hypocrites, and why each party adopted this astonishing position about them. Because in that position, one party showed great leniency, and it was being displayed that the Muslims' awareness of Islam was not yet firm. Some of them said: 'Will you kill people who have uttered the same words that you have uttered, and merely because they did not abandon their homeland and make hijrah?' Is this alone sufficient to make their lives and property permissible? Their concept of Islam was not firm, because they were keeping in view only that these hypocrites had also recited the same shahadah that we recited, although there was evidence against that group of hypocrites. First, their own statement that the companions of Muhammad (ﷺ) would not say anything to them; second, that a group of believers had also disclosed about them that they assist the enemies of the Muslims. Despite this evidence, the position of these people concerning those hypocrites was a weak position, although they should have adopted a decisive and plain position, because orally reciting the testimony of faith while practically assisting the disbelievers was a clear proof of hypocrisy. Such people did not need any leniency or overlooking. This was not a minor mistake, but rather it was showing weakness in the concept of Islam. That is why in this verse strong astonishment was expressed and severe warning was given.
As for the hypocrites of Medina, the Muslims were intellectually completely clear about them, that they are hypocrites. But overlooking them was adopted because it was being done under a specific plan, namely that they be dealt with on the basis of their outward circumstances, and that they be given respite for a time.
But this was a different situation: a group among the Muslims was defending them on the ground that they too had recited the same kalimah that we recited, and they too had testified with their tongues that Allah is One and Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), although these people were definitively assisting the enemies of Islam. Because of this intellectual weakness among the Muslims and their difference of opinion (while the hypocrisy of the hypocrites was completely clear), this verse issued a severe warning. And then after the warning, it was also clarified: (Wallahu arkasahum bima kasabu) (Allah has overturned them because of what they earned). You dispute about them, and Allah, because of their evil deeds and their evil intentions, has placed them in circumstances in which they appear overturned. This is Allah's testimony against them: that because of their thinking and their actions, they are in a state that is not worthy of envy.
After this warning, another warning was given: (Atureedoon an tahdoo man adalla Allah) (Do you wish to guide those whom Allah has sent astray?). That is, the group among the Muslims which was adopting a lenient attitude toward them had the intention that they be given an opportunity to come onto the right path, so that they would give up this hypocritical attitude. Allah the Exalted considered the position of these people inappropriate, and has placed the hypocrites in such circumstances because of their deeds and evil intentions; therefore the hope of their being guided is futile.
(Wa man yudlili Allahu falan tajida lahu sabeelan) (And whoever Allah sends astray, you will never find for him a way).
And Allah sends people astray because they adopt the path of misguidance by their own intention and will. Then they strive for misguidance and go very far along that path, so far that the way of guidance is closed to them, because they have adopted the opposite direction, and they are no longer seekers of Allah's help for guidance, and they have lost the signposts of the way.
Now let us take one step further! The real stance of these hypocrites is expressed thus: not only have they themselves become misguided and, because of their intention and action, become deserving of the state in which they are, but they themselves wish that the people of Islam would also adopt the path of disbelief, and that it would be good.
(Wadda lau takfuroona kama kafaroo fatakoonoona sawa'an) (They wish that you would disbelieve as they have disbelieved, so that you would be equal). Certainly they have adopted the path of disbelief, although they too have recited the same kalimah that Muslims recite, and they have borne witness to both matters; but their deeds refute that testimony, by which these people assist the enemies of Islam. But they do not stop even at this limit, because whoever adopts disbelief does not stop at any limit. He does not sit at ease until Islam and Muslims are erased from the entire surface of the earth. He remains engaged in continuous effort for this wicked purpose. He strives for this aim, and conspires, so that the present people of Islam too may return to disbelief, and thus all people become equal.
This is the first clarification of the stance of the hypocrites under discussion, and this clarification has been made in such a way that every kind of doubt is removed from the thinking of the people of Islam about them. This thinking is now founded on the clear testimony of their words and deeds, and now this thinking is free from contradiction. The reality of outward profession of Islam becomes nothing when all the indicators show that the stance of these people is hypocritical.
The Qur'an gives a pinch to the consciousness of the Muslims, from which a frightening feeling arises in their consciousness, and this feeling arises from the words of the Qur'an:
(Wadda lau takfuroona kama kafaroo fatakoonoona sawa'an) (They wish that you would disbelieve as they have disbelieved, so that you would be equal). This fear arises because the people of Islam had recently abandoned disbelief and tasted Islam, and they still had awareness of how great a change had come into their lives: how high their consciousness had risen, how high their general standard had become, and how much exaltation their society had attained in Islam in comparison to Jahiliyyah. This distinction existed both in their consciousness and in the reality of the situation, and this indication alone was sufficient for them to become enemies of the one who was plotting to bring them back to those former lowliness, that is, to the lowliness of that Jahiliyyah from which Islam had raised them by the hand. Then it had not left them at a common level, but had raised them through general progress to the highest peak.
That is why the Qur'anic system of training, by taking support from this reality, in dangerous circumstances and in circumstances of advancing, warns the Muslims about the enemy in this manner and gives strict emphatic commands:
(Fala tattakhidhoo minhum awliya'a hatta yuhajiroo fi sabeelillah, fa-in tawaw fakhudhoohum waqtulohum haythu wajadtumoohum wa la tattakhidhoo minhum waliyyan wa la naseera) (So do not take from among them allies until they emigrate in the way of Allah. But if they turn away, then seize them and kill them wherever you find them, and do not take from among them any ally or helper). (89) (4:89)
"Therefore do not take any of them as friends until they emigrate in the way of Allah. Then if they refuse this condition, seize them, kill them wherever you find them, and do not take any of them as friend or helper."
When Allah the Exalted said here: "do not take any of them as friend or helper," it indicates that until then there were still family and tribal ties and relations between Muslims and non-Muslims, and these ties still had value in the hearts of Muslims, and it is possible that these ties were still for the sake of some economic interests. This method of training of Islam was uprooting completely every remaining trace and tie of Jahiliyyah. And just as the Qur'an was purifying thoughts, in the same way it was also establishing for the Muslim community the principles of international relations.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 4, verse 90:

(Verse) "No. 90."

There is also an exceptional case within the ruling on taking such people captive and killing them. If these hypocrites, who support the enemies of Islam, reside within a state or a territory that has already concluded a covenant with the Islamic movement or the Islamic government, whether that covenant is a treaty of peace or a treaty of alliance, then in that case they shall be treated in the same way as those with whom a covenant has been concluded.

﴿Except those who join a people between whom and you there is a covenant﴾ (meaning: those hypocrites are excepted who join a people with whom you have a covenant). This ruling shows that where there are opportunities for peace, and where no peace agreement conflicts with the fundamental principles of Islam, where freedom to accept Islam and freedom to propagate Islam are not being curtailed because of it, where obstacles are not being placed by force in the path of the Islamic call, and where Muslims are granted peace and are protected from trials and hardships, and the Islamic call is not at risk of stagnation, then in such circumstances Islam may enter into a treaty of peace.

For this reason, any enemy who joins a people with whom there is a treaty of peace or a treaty of friendship, in such a case those treaties also apply to that individual; he is treated in the same way and those people remain in peace in the same manner. Such rulings show that the spirit of peace, safety and reconciliation is very clearly present within them.

Likewise, the ruling on taking captives and killing them excludes those hypocrites who are connected with such people, such tribes and such groups, who are neutral towards the Islamic state. They neither side with the Muslims, nor, when war breaks out with the Muslims, do they assist their own peoples; that is, these people do not consider it appropriate to fight against the Muslims alongside their own people. Nor do they join either side. Neither with them, nor with those.

﴿Or those who come to you with hearts constrained from fighting you or fighting their own people﴾ (meaning: likewise, those hypocrites are excepted who come to you, their hearts averse to fighting, neither wishing to fight you nor their own people).

This ruling also shows that Islam, in every case, desires to avoid bloodshed and fighting, provided that others do not wish to fight, do not place obstacles in the way of the Islamic call, and remain neutral between the Islamic movement and its opponents. Such people, who neither wished to fight alongside the Muslims nor wished to fight alongside their own people, existed at that time in the Arabian Peninsula, and indeed within the Quraysh themselves. Islam did not impose on such people the obligation to fight alongside the Islamic camp or alongside the opposing camp. For Islam, it was sufficient that they did not wage war against Islam. (After the conquest of Makkah, when Surah al-Tawbah was revealed, practical experience established that the presence of any other religion alongside Islam in the central land of Islam, the Arabian Peninsula, is not permissible. Therefore a slight change was made to these rulings.) Moreover, it was expected that if difficulties were removed, these people would join the Islamic camp, as indeed happened in practice later.

Allah instructs the Muslims that dealing with these neutral people in this manner is very beneficial for them. If this matter is not understood by them, let them consider what other option could be better. Clearly, the only other option would be that these people, cooperating with the enemies who are at war with the Muslims, begin actual warfare against the Muslims, which in no way would be better for the Muslims. So since Allah has made such people neutral, this is in your interest, and therefore it is best to leave them in the condition in which they are.

﴿Except those who join a people between whom and you there is a covenant, or those who come to you with hearts constrained from fighting you or fighting their own people. Had Allah willed, He would have given them power over you, and they would have fought you. So if they keep away from you and do not fight you and offer you peace, then Allah has not made for you any way against them﴾ (90).

Thus the wise method of the Qur'an's education, with great wisdom, inclines zealous Muslims towards adopting neutrality regarding such hypocrites, although they could not readily accept this position. But Allah instructs the Muslims that there is good for them in this. This is Allah's favour upon you that some people have become neutral regarding you. Had they not been neutral, the military burdens imposed upon the Muslims would have increased further. Allah tells the Muslims that if good comes to you from any quarter, do not reject it, and if some evil passes you by without touching you, do not needlessly provoke it. The neutrality of these people has had no effect on your religion; no weakness has arisen in your way of life through it, nor do you obtain peace by paying a heavy price.

Indeed, Allah has forbidden the Muslims from obtaining peace by paying a heavy price, because abandoning any of the objectives of Islam in order to purchase peace is in no way permitted. The peace that Islam desires is a peace in which no right of the Islamic call is lost, nor is any right of the Muslims lost (not their personal and individual rights), but rather those rights of the Muslims which relate to their way of life and by which they are called Muslims.

The right of Islam is that all obstacles on its path be removed, which stand in the way of the call and propagation, because Islam does not tolerate any obstruction to the call and propagation anywhere on this earth. Islam also holds that there should exist behind it in the world a political power which causes fear to all those forces that place obstacles in the way of the Islamic call, whatever form they may adopt, or that harm in some way those who accept Islam. If such matters were absent, then peace and safety would be a lost treasure of Islam. But let this saying of the Prophet (ﷺ) also remain before us: that jihad will continue until the Day of Resurrection.

Now another group comes forward, with whom Islam does not adopt the same kind of forbearance it adopts towards those who are wholly neutral, because this is the group of the true hypocrites, and in addition to hypocrisy they are also mischievous. This group is connected neither with any people with whom the Muslims have a covenant, nor is it allied with any friendly tribe. Regarding this group the Islamic state has no restriction. They shall be treated in the same way as the true hypocrites are treated.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 4, verse 91:

(Verse) No. 91.

Ibn Jarir reported from Mujahid that this verse was revealed concerning a group from among the people of Makkah. These people would come to the Prophet (ﷺ) and embrace Islam hypocritically, and then, when they returned to the Quraysh, they would turn back on their heels and resume worshipping the idols. Their aim in adopting this policy was to remain safe on both sides. So Allah ordered concerning such people that, if they did not abandon this policy and reform themselves, they should be killed. Thus Allah's command, that if they do not withdraw from confronting you, do not offer you complete peace and security, and do not restrain their hands from fighting you, then you have the right to seize them and imprison them, and to kill them wherever you find them, because the proof has been established against them.

This is a realistic and decisive aspect of Islam, whereas in the previous injunction, tolerance and overlooking had been enjoined. Every policy was appropriate and necessary in its own place. Different stances and policies were adopted according to the demands of events and circumstances.

By studying these two pages of Islam's international policy in this manner, a Muslim's consciousness gains a very good balance. Moreover, this balance is created within the Islamic system of life as well, and this balance and harmony is the fundamental and distinguishing characteristic of the Islamic system of life. However, we see that among Muslims, on one side, there are extremely severe and zealous people who are always ready to kill and be killed, although this is not the policy of Islam. On the other side, there are people of extremely weak character who melt away and who do not believe in jihad in Islam at all. These people speak about Islam in a manner as though Islam is an accused standing in the dock of criminals, and these people are conducting the defence of this dangerous accused. These people find in Islam only tolerance, peace, overlooking and forgiveness. If any war has taken place in Islam, these people try to prove that this war was a defensive war for the Islamic government and the Islamic movement, and they try to prove that this war was defensive for the Islamic government and the Islamic movement, and that it was not for the purpose of removing the obstacles from the path of the Islamic call and enabling its propagation to proceed unhindered to every corner of the world.

In the view of these people, it was also not the aim that all those people who have accepted the Islamic ideology of life should live a peaceful life in every corner of this earth. Moreover, in the view of these people, this policy is also of no importance: that there should be in the world a system of government and a legal and constitutional system under which people can live with complete ideological freedom, and be able to adopt whatever belief they wish. Yet the thinking of such people is by no means Islamic thinking, nor is it the true policy of Islam. From the international principles that Islam has given, as mentioned above, it is clearly apparent what the true policy of Islam is.

These were the relations of Muslims with other international countries and blocs. As for the mutual relations of Muslims within the Ummah, even though they may be citizens of entirely different countries, and even though at that time the situation was such that Muslims lived in different countries just as they live in different countries today, killing among them is absolutely forbidden. A Muslim may be killed only in the case of hadd or qisas. Therefore, there is in the world no thing or cause more important than the belief and ideology of the Muslims. For this reason, a Muslim is in no circumstance permitted to unjustly kill another Muslim, because between them there exists a powerful bond of unity of ideology of life and belief. Yes, it may happen that a Muslim kills another Muslim by mistake. For this reason, legislation concerning killing by mistake was considered necessary here. As for intentional killing, there is no expiation for it, because Islam cannot even conceive of a Muslim unjustly killing a Muslim at the hands of a Muslim. This act lies outside the bounds of Islam.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 4, verses 92–93:

(Verses) No. 92 to 93.

These rulings relate to four kinds of situations. Three of them relate to the crime of unintentional killing (qatl-i-khata, killing by mistake). Such a killing may occur within Dar al-Islam (the abode of Islam), and it may also occur internationally, between persons who are citizens of different countries. The fourth situation relates to deliberate killing among Muslims (qatl-i-amd bain al-Muslimin), which Islam regards as almost impossible to occur. Islam expects that this crime should never take place among Muslims. For if the interests of the whole world were placed on one side of a scale, and the blood of one innocent Muslim on the other, the side of the Muslim's blood would be heavier. Islam does not conceive of any situation in this world in which the killing of one Muslim by another Muslim would be justified. Islam creates between one Muslim and another such serious, deep, great, precious relations of honour and respect that it does not even assume that relations between them could become so bad that matters would reach the point of killing and fighting. This is why the Holy Qur'an begins with unintentional killing.

(Verse) "And it is not for a believer to kill a believer except by mistake" (4:92). In the Islamic consciousness, only the possibility that this crime might occur through inadvertence can be imagined. This is the real possibility, because a Muslim living in the neighbourhood of another Muslim is a great thing. It is a great blessing, very great indeed. Therefore the Islamic consciousness cannot even conceive that a Muslim should separate another Muslim from his neighbourhood, and it would be a very evil thing if he were to raise his hand deliberately and intentionally against a Muslim, because this is for a Muslim on this earth an extremely precious treasure. Only from a Muslim can it be expected that he should know its value and worth. Therefore, in Islamic ethics it is extremely difficult that one Muslim should kill another Muslim. This is a matter that only the people of Islam and the friends of Islam can understand. They carry this feeling within their own selves and their own consciousness. Allah, Exalted is He, has taught the people of Islam this brotherhood through the Islamic way of life and the Islamic bond of brotherhood. This is the fraternity because of which they all gather around the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). After the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), this doctrine keeps them united and gathered in the name of Allah. Among them there arises Islamic brotherhood and love, and all of this is because of the verbal guidance.

If unintentional killing occurs, then it has three states, and the rulings for all three have been stated here.

The first state is that another believer is killed by mistake at the hand of a believer within Dar al-Islam, and the heirs of the victim are also Muslims. In this case, the killer must free one believing slave, and the full blood-money (diyah) must be paid to the family of that Muslim. The ransom of freeing a believing slave is, as it were, paid by the killer to the Islamic society as compensation for its loss. Thus, by freeing the slave, he has restored to life a dead person by granting freedom; in this way, it is as though he has freed many slaves. As for the blood-money, it will cool the feelings of the heirs of the slain. But along with imposing this compensation, Islam also indicates to the family of the slain that if they forgive the blood-money, this is good for them, provided their hearts willingly agree to it. Forgiveness and pardon are a most beneficial act for the Islamic society and Islamic brotherhood, so the command is given:

(Verse) "And whoever kills a believer by mistake, the freeing of a believing slave is required, and blood-money paid to his family, unless they remit it" (4:92).

The second case is that the crime of unintentional killing falls upon a believer, and his heirs are at war with Dar al-Islam. In this condition, the compensation owed to Dar al-Islam for its loss is that the killer must free one believing slave, but the blood-money is not paid to the warring family, because in that case they would use that money against the Muslims. Nor in this case is the consoling of the victim's dependants sought, nor the restoring of bonds of love with them, because they are enemies of the Muslims and are at war with them.

The third state is that the heirs of the slain are a covenanted people, with whom there is a treaty of peace or a treaty of friendship. In such circumstances, the Holy Qur'an did not impose the condition that the victim be a believer. Therefore some jurists and exegetes have kept the ruling of the verse in this state general, and have commanded that in such circumstances too the killer must free a believing slave and pay blood-money to the heirs of the victim, even though the victim is not a believer, because by reason of the covenant with the believers, their life and property also have the same status as the life and property of the believers.

However, it appears that from the beginning of the discourse the matter concerns the killing of a believer. The verse says: "It is not for a believer to kill a believer, except by mistake." After that, the circumstances are described in which the victim is a believer; and in the second case, when the victim is mentioned, it is then said: (Verse) "If he is from a people who are your enemy but he is a believer" (4:92). Here "and he is a believer" is stated because before it the words "from a people who are an enemy" had come. This is further confirmed by the fact that in the third case, the blood-money also carries the condition of "a believing slave" (raqabah mu'minah). If the victim had not been required to be a believer, then the slave would not have been required to be a believer either, and only the words "freeing a slave" would have been stated, which shows that the victim here too is a believer; otherwise the expiation would not have required faith either.

Traditions relate that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) paid the blood-money for some persons of the covenanted people, but he did not command that believing slaves be freed (no such tradition exists). From this it is known that if the covenanted victim is not a believer, then only blood-money is obligatory, and this blood-money is established not by the ruling of this verse but by the practice of the Messenger (ﷺ). And the three situations mentioned in this verse all relate to the killing of a believer, whether that believer is a resident of Dar al-Islam or a citizen of a warring nation and is in Dar al-Harb, or there is a treaty between them, whether it is a treaty of peace or a treaty of alliance. This interpretation is more suited to the context of the discourse.

This was the ruling for unintentional killing. As for deliberate killing, it is such a great sin that its commission together with faith cannot even be imagined. Its expiation is neither by blood-money nor by freeing a slave, and this sin cannot be forgiven by these means. The punishment of such a person is that he will be delivered to the punishment of Allah.

(Verse) "And whoever kills a believer intentionally, his recompense is Hell, abiding therein forever, and Allah will be angry with him and curse him and prepare for him a great punishment" (4:93).

This is a crime of killing, but it is not only against a single life; it is also the killing of a great, honoured, beloved, and most precious brotherhood of Islam, which Allah, by His grace and bounty, created between one believer and another. It is not only an injustice but also a denial of the way of life and of faith. This is why Allah has mentioned it alongside shirk (associating partners with Allah) in several places in the Holy Qur'an. Some of the early generations adopted the view that it will not be forgiven even through repentance; this is the opinion of Ibn Abbas. However, some other scholars hold that forgiveness is possible, and they have argued from this verse:

(Verse) "Indeed, Allah does not forgive that partners be associated with Him, but He forgives what is less than that to whom He wills" (4:116). Therefore, if the killer repents, hope of his forgiveness may be entertained. Such people have explained "abiding" (khulud) to mean a long period of time.

Those who had earlier been trained in the Islamic school were seeing with their own eyes the killers of their fathers, sons and brothers, who had committed those killings before Islam and had now entered Islam. Among some of them, the bitterness would be freshly renewed in their hearts, but they did not even think of taking revenge against those people. They never thought of revenge, and even in the most severe conditions and at the most painful moments, the thought of killing did not come into their hearts; rather, they did not try to nullify any of the rights that Islam had granted to such people.

For the sake of protecting a believer from being killed, even if by mistake, and for the sake of purifying the hearts of Muslims from all desires, and for the sake of clearly highlighting before them the purpose of fighting solely in the way of Allah, Muslims are now commanded that if they go out for jihad and fighting, they should, before beginning the battle, ascertain whether the people are Muslims or not; and if anyone outwardly declares Islam and says "As-salamu alaykum," they should not attack. For in the circumstances of war they cannot investigate whether this profession of Islam is based on reality or not.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 4, verse 94:

(Verse) "94."

Several narrations have been reported about the occasion of revelation of this verse. The summary is this: a patrol of the Muslims came upon a man who had his goats with him. This man greeted the military unit with "As-salamu alaykum," meaning that he was a Muslim. Some of them thought that he had said "As-salamu alaykum" merely to save himself, so they killed him. Upon this, this verse was revealed, and the Muslims were commanded not to act in this way. Thus, the notion of worldly gains was removed from their hearts. They were given the impression that they should not be hasty in any decision. Islam does not approve of either of these two things.

Allah, may He be exalted, reminds the believers that the time and the era are not so distant that you too were in that darkness of ignorance, in which your decisions were based on extreme haste and rebelliousness; you were only seekers of wealth. Allah makes them realize that it was His favour that He purified your hearts and your aims became elevated. And now they do not fight for worldly interests as in the times of ignorance, and it is Allah who has set for you legal limits and boundaries, and now it is not the case that the first provocation should issue final judgments as used to happen in the time of ignorance.

This verse also contains the indication: behold, there was a time when you yourselves concealed your faith from your own people, because you were weak and fearful. Only the Muslims knew who was a Muslim and who was not. This man who was killed was concealing Islam from his own people, and when he met the Muslims, he revealed his Islam and said "As-salamu alaykum."

"(Kadhalika kuntum min qablu famannallahu 'alaykum fatabayyanu inna Allaha kana bima ta'malu khabira)" (4:94) (In this very state you yourselves were before, then Allah bestowed His favour upon you; therefore, exercise verification. Surely Allah is aware of what you do.)

Thus Islam shakes the world of the heart so that hearts may be alive, cautious, and may perceive the great blessing of Allah. And under the shade of this awareness and God-fearing, they should implement Allah's commands and laws and make decisions after thoroughly examining circumstances. You have seen how, in this lesson, certain local and international matters have been treated with such breadth and detail, and legislation has been made in a completely new field, with such pure feelings and pure objectives. And keep in mind that this happened fourteen hundred years ago, when the very existence of international law did not exist in the world.

Lesson No. 38: At a Glance

This lesson is closely connected with the previous lesson and with the one before that; it is, in a sense, the completion of those two lessons. If the aspect of international affairs and international law (in which Islam legislated for the first time) were not in view, we would count these three lessons as one lesson, since their subject and theme are the same. The basic theme of this lesson is that all Muslims should migrate and gather in the Abode of Islam (Dar al-Islam). Those who still remain in the Abode of War (Dar al-Harb) and the Abode of Disbelief (Dar al-Kufr) should migrate immediately, reach the Abode of Islam, and strive with their wealth and their lives in jihad, leaving behind the relative comfort they enjoy in Makkah with their families and the facilities available to them there. This very purpose is found in the opening words of this lesson, where it is said:

(Verse) "Those believers who sit at home, other than those who have a disability, are not equal to those who strive in the way of Allah with their wealth and their lives. Allah has raised those who strive with their wealth and their lives above those who sit at home by a degree; and to each Allah has promised good, but Allah has preferred those who strive over those who sit at home with a great reward." (4:95)

There were no sitters-at-home in Madinah. Those who held back from jihad in Madinah were either hypocrites or those who obstructed the work, and Allah has spoken about both in the previous lesson.

Yet immediately after this verse, the next verse gives a severe warning to those who are still sitting in the Abode of Disbelief, who have the full ability to migrate to Madinah, and who die in exactly those circumstances. Of them it is said that they are wronging themselves, and that their abode is Hell, which is a most evil destination.

In the next verse, Allah gives a guarantee to those who migrate in the way of Allah, and this guarantee begins from the moment they leave their homes, provided they undertake this migration sincerely for Allah alone. In it, Allah has removed all the apprehensions that trouble them before taking this step, and likewise the dangers that confronted them at that time and the frightening conditions, under which resolving to act was difficult and a cause of anxiety.

The discussion of migration and jihad advances further. It is explained how Muslims are to conduct their mutual affairs in the Abode of Migration, and what their relationship will be with other people outside the Abode of Migration. In particular, it is explained what the end will be of those Muslims who do not migrate.

This lesson also mentions the conditions of prayer in a state of fear, such as prayer during the journey of migration and prayer on the battlefield. This shows how great the importance of prayer is in Islam, such that even in such dangerous conditions no exemption from it is granted. Moreover, a state of constant readiness for war is created among Muslims, because the conditions are such that a slight negligence or carelessness may be exploited severely by the enemy.

At the end, this lesson gives a very effective touch and rouses Muslims to jihad in the way of Allah: it is true that you face extremely painful hardships, but the condition of the enemies is also not good, and there is a difference between their aims and your aims, and between their hopes and your hopes.

(Verse) "And do not slacken in pursuing the enemy. If you are suffering pain, they too are suffering pain as you suffer, but you hope from Allah for what they do not hope for." (4:104)

With this portrayal, the paths of the two groups become separate; their methods become separate. Every grief and every pain becomes easier for the Muslims. The very feeling of lethargy and weariness disappears from the hearts of the Muslims, because after all the opposing camp too faces difficulties, while they do not have the hope from Allah that the Muslims have. In the topics discussed in this lesson and the method of training adopted in it, it is shown how the Islamic movement dealt with the changes taking place in the formation of the Muslim community, the practical difficulties that arose in its organization, and the ideological and practical obstacles that existed. It shows how the Islamic movement coped with the apprehensions arising in people's minds and the way they became a cause of weakness, or the remnants of jahiliyyah (ignorance) that remained within society and the souls of the community's members, and the way they became a cause of difficulties; as well as the new hardships and calamities that arose on the path of the Islamic movement and the problems created by the natural effect of these trials on human nature; and those who, despite these difficulties, kept themselves steadfast in loyalty upon condition of firmness. All such scenes and observations are depicted in this lesson. The wise method of the Qur'an has taken up all these problems, moved the human conscience, and stirred it to overcome these difficulties.

All these matters are conveyed by drawing a correct picture of the actual situation, and they are expressed both through an effective style of encouragement and stirring, and through the remedy prescribed as a solution to natural apprehensions and practical difficulties. Likewise, this is well understood through the act of remaining steadfast in prayer in the very midst of the battlefield, while it is also indicated that even at the very time of prayer they should keep watch on the enemy. Then a guarantee of a great reward is given to the migrants, and through the announcement of a reward for those who go out in the way of Allah and a painful torment for the disbelievers, the whole picture of these pains and difficulties comes before us.

This lesson shows how Allah deals with the human soul in its state of weakness and in its state of strength. Moreover, in a single passage several lines appear regarding how a human community is formed and trained, and how it is treated at this stage. In a few words, a sense and awareness of its strength and superiority is instilled in the hearts of the community, so that its enemy appears insignificant to it; and at the same time it is commanded to be cautious, watchful and always prepared in the face of danger, while in the same passage the points of weakness are also identified, and strict and very severe instructions are given regarding those points of weakness.

This is a remarkable method, extremely complete and fully suited to human psychology. New lines are drawn upon the tablet of the human soul, new strings are established between various points, and all these strings sing, and every string moves immediately at the strike of the divine plectrum.

It is clearly evident that the Islamic society of Madinah, in terms of its method of training and its collective organization, held a very great superiority over all existing societies, and the whole of humanity of that time was witnessing this superiority with its own eyes, and seeing that this young society, in those difficult circumstances, on one hand was treating its own shortcomings and weaknesses, and on the other hand was consuming the surrounding jahili societies. Gradually it was gaining dominance over them, and this dominance was not merely military dominance but a civilizational dominance, in the manner in which a young civilization consumes old and worn-out civilizations. A new system was prevailing over old systems. A new model of life was being displayed before the world like goods in a showroom; a modern age and a modern human being were coming into being. Having made these observations, now let us turn to the verses and texts.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran (Urdu translation)) on surah 4, verse 96 (part 1 of 2):

Verses 95 to 104.

This passage deals with a particular situation in the Islamic society of its time. At that moment, some people among the ranks of the Muslims were showing slackness. They were not sacrificing their lives and wealth on the path of the Islamic revolution. These were people who, in Mecca, were delaying their migration (hijrah) in order to protect their wealth, because the people of Mecca did not allow any emigrant to take anything with him. This slackness was also arising because the path of hijrah was full of severe difficulties, hardships and dangers, since the polytheists did not even permit weak people to migrate at all. They would seize them and imprison them, or torture them; and if someone was already being tortured and they suspected that he intended to flee, they would subject him to even harsher torture. It is possible that the meaning of these verses is those people who had not migrated to the abode of Islam (Dar al-Islam) (I prefer this opinion). Or it may refer to some people inside Dar al-Islam itself who were not very enthusiastic about jihad with wealth and life. These people were separate from those who were slow and evasive in matters of jihad, and who have been mentioned in the previous lesson. It is possible that the meaning of these verses includes all those who were within Dar al-Islam and were avoiding jihad, and were hypocrites, or were Muslims but lazy, or those who had not migrated at all so that they might perform jihad. In any case, there were some circles that were being slack, and this verse is addressing such a situation. However, the Qur'an, without specifying particular people in this verse, speaks in the manner of a general principle, which is not confined to time and place or to any single family, and it explains that this is a principle which Allah will apply to the Muslims in every age: that those who, without excuse of illness or helplessness, do not take part in jihad in the way of Allah, whether jihad with wealth or with life, and who do not migrate when migration is needed for it, cannot be of the same rank with Allah as those who migrate and sacrifice their lives and wealth. This is a general rule and a general principle, and it will apply in every time and place.

(Verse) "Those believers who sit at home, other than those with a disability, and those who strive in the way of Allah with their wealth and their lives, are not equal." (4:95)

(Meaning: Among the Muslims, those who remain sitting at home without any excuse and those who strive in the way of Allah with their lives and wealth are not equal in status.)

Allah does not leave the matter vague or ambiguous here, but explains it fully and decides that those who strive with their lives and wealth have a very great rank.

(Verse) "Allah has preferred those who strive with their wealth and their lives over those who sit at home by a degree." (4:95)

(Meaning: Allah has given a higher rank to those who strive with their lives and wealth over those who sit.)

The rank of the mujahidin mentioned in this verse has been clarified by the Messenger of Allah ﷺ by describing the details of their station in Paradise. In the hadith of Abu Sa'id al-Khudri (may Allah be pleased with him) in the Sahihayn, the Prophet ﷺ said that there are one hundred degrees in Paradise which Allah has prepared for the mujahidin, and the distance between each degree is like the distance between the earth and the heavens.

Al-A'mash narrated from Amr ibn Murrah, who narrated from Abu Ubaidah, from Abdullah ibn Mas'ud (may Allah be pleased with him) that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: whoever shoots one arrow will receive the reward of one degree. A man asked, "O Messenger of Allah, how great is one degree?" He ﷺ said: "It will not be equal even to the threshold or the step of your mother's house. The distance between two degrees will be a journey of one hundred years."

The distance mentioned by the Messenger of Allah ﷺ can be easily imagined by us in the modern age, because our knowledge of this universe has reached very great distances. Even travelling from one planet to another at the speed of light takes many light years. Those who heard the words of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ at that time would say (we believe and we affirm), but we people of the modern age have measured these distances and have brought the vast distances of this universe close, and strange information has come before us.

However, while mentioning the elevated ranks of the mujahidin in the way of Allah, the Almighty also tells us that, although those who strive with wealth and life have higher ranks than those who sit without any excuse or compulsion, (Verse) "and to each Allah has promised good" (4:95) (Meaning: Allah has promised goodness to each), no one is deprived. Nevertheless, faith has in itself a fundamental rank. Those who fulfil the requirements of faith have degrees according to their struggle and jihad, and especially those who perform jihad with wealth and jihad with life have the highest degrees. From these words it is understood that by those who sit, mentioned in the above verses, are not meant the hypocrites who evaded jihad, i.e., those who lagged behind; rather, they were some other people who were extremely righteous and sincere but weak in the aspect of jihad with wealth and jihad with life. The address in these verses of the Holy Qur'an is directed towards these very people. They are being urged to make up for their shortcomings. Since goodness is present in these people, one may hope that they will respond.

This note now ends, and the earlier principle is now repeated again. It is explained once more with great emphasis and in more detail so that people may rush to obtain the great reward in exchange for it.

(Verse) "And Allah has preferred those who strive over those who sit by a great reward" (4:95), "degrees from Him, and forgiveness and mercy. And Allah is ever Forgiving and Merciful." (4:96)

(Meaning: "But with Him the mujahidin's service is recompensed far above those who sit; for them are great degrees from Allah, and forgiveness and mercy, and Allah is most forgiving and most merciful.")

This great emphasis, these beautiful promises, this great appreciation of the mujahidin, and the mention of the supreme degrees and great reward over those who sit, for which the hearts of the believers long, then this general announcement of forgiveness of faults and sins from Allah — through all these things two matters are made manifest.

The first point is that these verses were revealed in circumstances that actually existed in the Islamic society at that time, and these verses were providing a remedy for them. From this we receive a fine lesson: that we comprehend human nature properly and come to know what the temperament of human communities is. Whatever height of faith, action, piety and excellence a human community may have reached, and whatever weaknesses, decline, avarice, miserliness and shortcomings may overtake it, and wherever a shortfall occurs in duties, especially the duty of jihad, whether it is a shortfall in jihad with wealth, jihad with life, or a lack of sincerity in jihad in the way of Allah, at the time these shortcomings appear it needs training and reform. It needs continuous struggle to purify it from weakness, avarice, miserliness and shortcomings. It is not a suitable policy that we should despair and abandon the work of reform, and society should keep falling further into the decline of its present condition, and we should say that this is the real state of society and we should accept it, and leave the weakness, greed, avarice and shortcomings within society as they are, and proclaim that this is the situation existing within society. Society is fallen and one should deal with it while keeping it in that state. The real matter is that we should keep the call to reform within society going, and strive to raise society higher and higher according to the Qur'anic method.

The second matter that comes before us is what value Allah places on jihad with wealth and jihad with life. In the temperament of the Islamic ideology of life and the Islamic system of life, jihad in the way of Allah has very great importance. In the methods of establishing the religion, jihad holds fundamental importance. In every age, the opponents of the religion can be confronted only through jihad. There is no other successful method apart from this.

Jihad in the way of Allah is not confined to the era of the Noble Messenger ﷺ. In every age in which the work of Islamic call begins, jihad will be necessary. It is extremely wrong for some people to say that at the dawn of Islam there were two great empires in the world, and therefore the Muslims at that time, being influenced by their environment, thought that for their survival they needed coercive force so that a balance of power might be established.

Those who hold these views appear not to have understood Islam properly, and their views are based merely on conjecture and speculation. But if the obligation of jihad in Islam were of this temporary kind, arising from temporary circumstances, then it would not have been mentioned so repeatedly in this manner in the Book of Allah, and it would not have been so repeatedly emphasised in the Sunnah of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ.

If jihad were merely a temporary matter, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ would not have said: "Whoever dies without having fought in battle and without even having the desire to fight in the way of Allah, dies in one of the states of hypocrisy." This saying of the Prophet ﷺ is extremely general, complete, comprehensive and all-inclusive.

Yes, it is correct that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ in certain individual cases did not permit some people to take part in jihad, and that too only because of their particular family circumstances. In the Sahihayn there is this hadith: a man came seeking to take part in jihad, and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ asked him, "Are your parents alive?" He said, "Yes." The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said, "Then strive in (service of) the two of them."

This was a decision for one person according to his individual circumstances; it does not make the general rule specific. Furthermore, when there are countless mujahidin, the need for one particular person is sometimes not felt; a shortage is not created by the absence of a single individual. Moreover, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was aware of the circumstances of each individual. It is possible that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ learned that this man's parents were in great need of support, and therefore he ﷺ gave him this instruction.

Therefore, no one can say, on the basis of this one man, that jihad was a temporary action, necessary according to the conditions of the time of the Messenger ﷺ, and that now circumstances have changed so jihad is no longer needed. Jihad was not made obligatory because Islam's policy is simply to set out with drawn sword, so that whenever the unbelievers appear, their heads are cut off like carrots and radishes. Rather, the nature of the practical life of the people and of this call and movement is this: the sword should be in our hand, and we should remain always ready and vigilant for jihad.

Allah knows full well that an Islamic government is an ideal which kings do not like. Allah also knew that those in power would always obstruct the path of Islam, because Islam is opposed to their way of life and their system of life. This matter is not confined to yesterday. Tomorrow too, those who hold power would not like the Islamic system, and they will not like it tomorrow either. In every age and every place this has been so, and so it is happening now.

Allah knew that evil is always insolent and shameless. Evil is never just. The temperament of evil is that it does not let goodness and righteousness flourish, even if righteousness adopts the most peaceful and friendly method, because the spread of goodness is always dangerous for falsehood. The very existence of truth is a threat to falsehood, and evil cannot exist without aggression.

Therefore, falsehood always tries to strangle the truth and to eliminate it by the force of arms. This is the nature of evil, and this condition does not arise in evil only temporarily. It is the real nature and disposition of evil.

This is why jihad has been made obligatory. Jihad is obligatory in every condition. It is necessary that a person begin jihad first against his own self. After that, its battlefield should expand, and jihad should be carried on and seen in practice within the events and circumstances of this outward world. Remember that armed good is needed against armed evil, and if falsehood has defensive power, then truth too must be fully prepared. If there is no preparation against falsehood, truth will commit suicide; and if it does not commit suicide, it will be mere idle talk, which is not befitting of believers.

The sacrifice of life and wealth in the way of Islam is necessary. This is Allah's demand, and Allah has purchased from the believers their lives and their wealth in exchange for Paradise. Either they will prevail, or they will attain the rank of martyrdom. This is the command of Allah, and wisdom lies hidden in it. As for the believers, for them there are two good outcomes with their Lord. People all die when their term is complete, but it is those who are martyred who bear witness to the truth.

In this worldview there is a central point, and upon this point its practical system stands, and this practical system advances along its determined lines. This line and the believer have one temperament, and their nature is clear-cut, and within them there is no change in accordance with circumstances, time or place.

These are the points that must remain illuminated in the conception of a true believer, whatever the circumstances may be. It is from these fundamental points that the process of jihad begins, concerning which Allah the Exalted has stated that this jihad is solely in the way of Allah, solely under the banner of Allah. Those who are killed in this struggle are martyrs, and in the higher realm their funeral is raised with great pomp.

Now a second group is brought onto the screen, set against the scene of jihad: those who sit back. These people are still sitting in Makkah, the abode of disbelief, and have not migrated. They have some material interests, some considerations of expediency, or their natural weakness keeps them seated. They do not find within themselves the courage to face the hardships of migration and the troubles of the road. If they resolve to bear sacrifice and difficulties, they can migrate. On the screen, they are seen wandering around in the places of Makkah, the abode of war, in such a way that Azrael (ʿAzrāʾīl) comes and snatches away from them that which is most dear to them. The condition of such people, on the screen of the Qur'an, is extremely wretched and extremely detestable; every person who sits far from jihad will wish to flee from their religion, their way of life, and this state of evil end before Allah, and will not want to be seen standing in that extremely repugnant scene.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran (Urdu translation)) on surah 4, verse 97–99:

(Verse) "Number 97–99."

This verse deals with a situation that actually existed in the Arabian Peninsula. This situation was practically present in Makkah and elsewhere after the Hijrah of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), when the Islamic state had been established in Madinah. Until then, there were Muslims in Makkah who had not performed the Hijrah. They had stayed there because of certain considerations and their property. The circumstances were such that the Mushriks of Makkah would not allow anyone who was migrating to take anything with him, or these people were sitting idle because of the hardships of Hijrah, since whoever migrated, the people of Makkah would obstruct his path and forbid him. Some people were in fact unable to migrate at all. Some were elderly, some were women, and some were children. For these people there was simply no way to migrate or escape.

The Muslims who had remained in Makkah were now subjected to great severity by the people of Makkah, because they had failed to capture the Prophet (ﷺ) and Abu Bakr (رضي الله عنه). The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), having established a government in Madinah, had begun to harass the caravans of Quraysh, and then, at the Battle of Badr, they were inflicting severe persecution upon the Muslims, subjecting them to various kinds of torment, and oppressing them in a state of great panic.

Some people had been turned away from the religion of Islam through physical torture. Some were outwardly expressing disbelief through taqiyyah (dissimulation) and outwardly participating with the Mushriks in their idolatrous worship. This taqiyyah was permissible for them at the time when there was no Islamic government and no opportunities for Hijrah. But when the Islamic state was established in the blessed city of Madinah, then their remaining amidst such trials, or compelling themselves to taqiyyah, was neither permissible nor reasonable, since they could both migrate and live a life of peace in the Dar al-Islam.

It was in these circumstances that these verses were revealed. These people were not refraining from Hijrah merely out of wealth and expediency, or sitting in Makkah because of the difficulties and hardships of Hijrah. In such circumstances, if they died, Allah Ta'ala calls such people zalim (wrongdoers), because they were wronging themselves, since they had deprived themselves of the free life of the Dar al-Islam, where they could live a pure, dignified and life of their own choice, whereas in the Dar al-Kufr they were living in humiliation, weakness and oppression, and oppression was being inflicted upon them. Allah Ta'ala says that these people will remain in Jahannam, which is a very evil abode. It appears that this is a warning for those who had in truth adopted disbelief out of fear.

But the Quran portrays the condition of such people in a very vivid and dynamic manner. A dialogue is taking place between them and the angels, and this dialogue is, as it were, taking place on a stage between living persons.

(Verse) "Indeed, those whom the angels take in death while they are wronging themselves, they will say, 'In what state were you?' They will say, 'We were oppressed in the earth.' They will say, 'Was not the earth of Allah spacious that you could have emigrated therein?'" (4:97)

(The angels asked those who were wronging themselves, when they took their souls, "In what condition were you?" They replied, "We were weak and helpless in the land." The angels said, "Was not the earth of Allah wide, so that you could have migrated in it?")

The Quran was training human beings, so its aim before it was to stir up their feelings of goodness, honour and nobility, and to strive to eliminate the qualities of weakness, miserliness, greed and laziness found within them. Therefore, in depicting this scene, the Quran has presented a truly realistic situation. But the Quran uses this depiction for the reform of people, and through it the souls of human beings are reformed.

The time of death is frightening for every human being. What happens in the state of agony (naza') becomes deeply imprinted upon the mind of a person with great rapidity, and then the appearance of the angels upon this scene creates an even more frightening situation, and a person's senses work with great swiftness.

These people are sitting in Makkah, and it is evident that they are wronging themselves; and in exactly such circumstances the angels arrive and begin to take their souls. Since these people are wronging themselves, every living person is affected by this situation: that these people are sitting in such oppressed circumstances while the angels are taking their souls. Now there is no opportunity left for them to be just to themselves by migrating, because the opportunity of life comes only once.

And these angels do not take their souls in silence, but they also bring their past before them and ask in a most disapproving manner: how did you spend the precious days of your life? What was your occupation in the world? What lofty aims were those for which you were running about? (Verse) "They say, 'In what state were you?'" (4:97) (In what conditions did you remain?)

Because the circumstances in which these people remained were nothing but loss. That is, they had no other occupation except wasting time, and these people, upon whom the state of agony had descended, answer in the state of agony, and in a most disapproving condition, with the utmost humiliation, they think that perhaps this will serve as an excuse for them, whereas it is humiliation. (Verse) "They say, 'We were weak in the land.'" (4:97) (We were indeed weak people in the land.)

"We were weak; powerful people had suppressed us. We were humiliated and degraded. We had nothing in our hands." Every person will dislike that this dialogue should take place with him in the state of agony, because it expresses the utmost helplessness of these people, and that they spent their whole lives in this helplessness, and yet the angels did not leave them even when they fell into the state of agony. When they were in the state of agony, they were told that they had not made use of the opportunity.

(Verse) "Was not the earth of Allah spacious, so that you could have migrated in it?" (4:97) The truth is that they were not placing themselves in this humiliation, poverty, trial and weakness because they were in fact in such circumstances and were helpless. Rather, there were other causes due to which they had accepted this humiliation. They were greedy, and because of worldly considerations they were not migrating, and for this reason they remained settled in the Dar al-Kufr while the Dar al-Islam existed. These people were keeping themselves in constriction, although the earth of Allah was spacious. They could have migrated, and they could have endured the difficulties.

(Verse) "Those, their abode is Jahannam, and it is an evil destination." (4:97) (Those are the people whose abode is Jahannam, and it is a truly evil abode.)

After this, those who are truly compelled and have no means to escape from this situation and reach the Dar al-Islam are excepted from the aforementioned outcome. These people consist of children, weak elderly men and women. Regarding such people it is said that their cases may be considered, and perhaps they will be pardoned, since their excuse is apparently reasonable and they cannot relocate from Makkah to Madinah.

(Verse) "Except the men, women and children who are truly helpless and find no means or way out, for perhaps Allah will pardon them. And Allah is ever Pardoning and Forgiving." (4:98–99)

This ruling will remain until the end of time. These rulings are not confined to the circumstances that existed at that time in the particular society of Makkah al-Mukarramah, but they are general rulings. In any country where a Muslim is facing difficulties regarding his religion, and remains there merely because of his wealth and property, or because of relatives and friends, and remains there merely out of fear that if he emigrates from that country he will face difficulties, provided that a Dar al-Islam has been established somewhere in the world, in which people live in peace, and in which such a person can openly express his creed, can fulfil the commands of Allah well there, can live a pure life according to the Islamic Shari'ah, and can live a dignified and honourable life; otherwise he will be considered to be compelled.

The context, while training human souls, moves further forward. Those who fear the hardships of Hijrah and therefore do not dare to migrate: regarding such people, in the preceding verses a very effective and frightening scene was presented, and Muslims were made to abhor this condition. In the following verses a ray of hope is shown. Whoever migrates, whether he reaches the Dar al-Islam or dies on the way, and his death occurs in the state of Hijrah, then it is said that upon leaving his home, his reward becomes his right, and Allah Ta'ala says that he will attain great expansiveness; he will live freely, and he will be delivered from constriction and hardship.
