Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 4, verses 123–125:

(Verses) 123 to 125.

The Jews and the Christians used to say: (Nahnu abna'u Allahi wa ahibba'uhu) "We are the sons of God and His beloved." They also used to say: (Lan tamassana al-naru illa ayyaman ma'dudah) "The Fire will not touch us except for a few counted days..." And the Jews, even to this day, call themselves the chosen people of God.

It is possible that some Muslims too have such a thought in their hearts, that they are a community brought forth for all people, and that God will forgive all their mistakes simply because they are Muslims.

Thus this verse was revealed to refute such notions, which are not correct on either side. Everyone will be saved by their deeds. There is one standard for all people: that people, all of them, turn towards God and submit themselves, worship God with utmost humility, and follow the principles of the Millah of Ibrahim (Millat Ibrahim, the religion of Abraham), which is the very essence of Islam. For this reason God made Ibrahim (peace be upon him) His friend.

The best religion is the religion of the Millah of Ibrahim, and the best deed is the deed of ihsan (excellence, perfection of conduct). And ihsan is that you worship God as if you see Him, and if you do not see Him, then indeed He sees you. Islam has taken ihsan into consideration in every matter. Even for slaughter it has prescribed ihsan, that the blade should be sharp so that the animal does not suffer much pain at the time of slaughter. In this verse, complete equality is also expressed between the two sexes of human beings regarding deeds and their rewards.

(Verse) "And whoever does righteous deeds, whether male or female, while being a believer, those will enter Paradise and they will not be wronged even to the extent of a speck (naqir)" (4:124). (And whoever does good deeds, whether male or female, provided they are believers, such people will enter Paradise, and not the slightest injustice will be done to them.)

This is a clear text that there is no distinction or preference between men and women regarding deeds and their rewards. This text is also clear that without faith no deed is accepted, and that in God's sight no deed has any value that is not based on faith or not accompanied by faith. This is most logical and natural, because only faith determines the ideology and intention with which a doer performs an action, and only faith can make a deed lasting and natural; otherwise a deed would be merely a personal and individual impulse.

These clear words are entirely contrary to the opinion expressed by the respected Mufti Muhammad Abduh in his tafsir of Juz' 'Amma, under the verse (Man ya'mal mithqala dharratin khayran yarah). He said that in this verse both Muslims and non-Muslims are included. This and all other verses are against that. Likewise, the opinion of Ustadh al-Maraghi is also not correct, on which we expressed our views in the thirtieth part.

The saying of God Most High was very heavy upon the Muslims: (Man ya'mal su'an yujza bihi wa la yajid lahu min dunillahi waliyyan wa la nasira) "Whoever does evil will be recompensed for it, and will not find for himself any protector or helper besides God" (4:123). They knew human nature well, and they were certain that human beings would commit wrongdoing, however righteous one might become and however many good deeds one might do.

The people of the first era knew the human self well. They knew themselves well. They did not deceive themselves and did not conceal anything from themselves. Nor did they overlook the fact that at times mistakes occurred from them; therefore they neither denied their shortcomings nor concealed them. That is why, on hearing this verse, they trembled. When they saw that every evil deed would be punished, they trembled as though they were standing in the place of gathering on the Day of Resurrection, seeing it with their own eyes. This was the distinctive quality of the Companions of the Messenger: they perceived the Hereafter in the manner in which we perceive ordinary things. They lived in the thought and concern of the Hereafter in the way we live in this world, not merely because it is coming, but as though it has already been established. That is why they began to tremble the moment they heard this verse.

Imam Ahmad says: Abu Bakr (may Allah be pleased with him) said: "O Messenger of Allah, after this verse how will there be salvation? God says (Laysa bi-amaniyyikum wa la amani ahli al-kitab, man ya'mal su'an yujza bihi)" (4:123) (It is not by your wishful thinking nor by the wishful thinking of the People of the Book; whoever does evil will be recompensed for it). The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Abu Bakr, may Allah forgive you. Do you not fall ill? Do you not become weary? Do you not become distressed? Do you not sigh?" He said: "Yes." He said: "Then with these you will also be rewarded." (Narrated by al-Hakim through Sufyan al-Thawri.)

In the narration of Abu Bakr ibn Mardawayh, it is stated that Abu Bakr said: When this verse was revealed, I was with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). (Man ya'mal su'an yujza bihi wa la yajid lahu min dunillahi waliyyan wa la nasira) (4:123) (Whoever does evil will receive its recompense, and will not find for himself any protector or helper against God.)

So the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Abu Bakr, shall I tell you what verse has just been revealed?" Abu Bakr says: I said: "Tell me, O Messenger of Allah." He recited the verse to me, and I know not how, but I felt as if something in my back had broken and I straightened up. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) asked: "Abu Bakr, what has happened to you?" I said: "May my parents be sacrificed for you! Which of us has not done wrong, and the meaning of the verse is that we will be punished for all evil deeds?" The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Abu Bakr, you and the believers will be recompensed in this world, until you meet Allah having no sin at all; as for the others, their evil deeds will accumulate and on the Day of Resurrection they will be recompensed for them." (Narrated by al-Tirmidhi.)

Aisha (may Allah be pleased with her) said to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "O Messenger of Allah, I know the hardest verse of the Qur'an." He said: "Which?" I said: (Man ya'mal su'an yujza bihi) (4:123). He said: "A believing servant is afflicted with hardships." (Narrated by Ibn Jarir.)

It is narrated from Abu Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him) that when this verse was revealed (Man ya'mal su'an yujza bihi) (4:123) (whoever does evil will be recompensed for it), it weighed heavily upon the Muslims. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Close the gaps and draw near to one another, for every calamity that befalls a Muslim expiates his sins, even a thorn that pricks him." (Muslim, Tirmidhi, Nasa'i.)

In any case, this verse was an important link for the correction of Islamic concepts and the believing outlook. Through it, on the one hand, the thinking of the people of religion was corrected, and on the other hand their conduct was set right. This verse shook them powerfully and their hearts trembled, because they took every command with the utmost seriousness. They knew very well the truth of God's promise and the implementation of it. They lived their lives within those promises, and they dwelt in the Hereafter while they were still in this world.

And at the end comes the concluding statement, that after faith, polytheism, deeds and their recompense: whatever is in the heavens and the earth belongs to Allah, and Allah encompasses all things in this world and in the Hereafter.

They lived their lives within those promises, and they dwelt in the Hereafter while they were still in this world.

And at the end comes the concluding statement, that after faith, polytheism, deeds and their recompense: whatever is in the heavens and the earth belongs to Allah, and Allah encompasses all things in this world and in the Hereafter.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 4, verses 123–125:

(Verses) 123 to 125.

The Jews and the Christians used to say: (Nahnu abna'u Allahi wa ahibba'uhu) "We are the sons of God and His beloved." They also used to say: (Lan tamassana al-naru illa ayyaman ma'dudah) "The Fire will not touch us except for a few counted days..." And the Jews, even to this day, call themselves the chosen people of God.

It is possible that some Muslims too have such a thought in their hearts, that they are a community brought forth for all people, and that God will forgive all their mistakes simply because they are Muslims.

Thus this verse was revealed to refute such notions, which are not correct on either side. Everyone will be saved by their deeds. There is one standard for all people: that people, all of them, turn towards God and submit themselves, worship God with utmost humility, and follow the principles of the Millah of Ibrahim (Millat Ibrahim, the religion of Abraham), which is the very essence of Islam. For this reason God made Ibrahim (peace be upon him) His friend.

The best religion is the religion of the Millah of Ibrahim, and the best deed is the deed of ihsan (excellence, perfection of conduct). And ihsan is that you worship God as if you see Him, and if you do not see Him, then indeed He sees you. Islam has taken ihsan into consideration in every matter. Even for slaughter it has prescribed ihsan, that the blade should be sharp so that the animal does not suffer much pain at the time of slaughter. In this verse, complete equality is also expressed between the two sexes of human beings regarding deeds and their rewards.

(Verse) "And whoever does righteous deeds, whether male or female, while being a believer, those will enter Paradise and they will not be wronged even to the extent of a speck (naqir)" (4:124). (And whoever does good deeds, whether male or female, provided they are believers, such people will enter Paradise, and not the slightest injustice will be done to them.)

This is a clear text that there is no distinction or preference between men and women regarding deeds and their rewards. This text is also clear that without faith no deed is accepted, and that in God's sight no deed has any value that is not based on faith or not accompanied by faith. This is most logical and natural, because only faith determines the ideology and intention with which a doer performs an action, and only faith can make a deed lasting and natural; otherwise a deed would be merely a personal and individual impulse.

These clear words are entirely contrary to the opinion expressed by the respected Mufti Muhammad Abduh in his tafsir of Juz' 'Amma, under the verse (Man ya'mal mithqala dharratin khayran yarah). He said that in this verse both Muslims and non-Muslims are included. This and all other verses are against that. Likewise, the opinion of Ustadh al-Maraghi is also not correct, on which we expressed our views in the thirtieth part.

The saying of God Most High was very heavy upon the Muslims: (Man ya'mal su'an yujza bihi wa la yajid lahu min dunillahi waliyyan wa la nasira) "Whoever does evil will be recompensed for it, and will not find for himself any protector or helper besides God" (4:123). They knew human nature well, and they were certain that human beings would commit wrongdoing, however righteous one might become and however many good deeds one might do.

The people of the first era knew the human self well. They knew themselves well. They did not deceive themselves and did not conceal anything from themselves. Nor did they overlook the fact that at times mistakes occurred from them; therefore they neither denied their shortcomings nor concealed them. That is why, on hearing this verse, they trembled. When they saw that every evil deed would be punished, they trembled as though they were standing in the place of gathering on the Day of Resurrection, seeing it with their own eyes. This was the distinctive quality of the Companions of the Messenger: they perceived the Hereafter in the manner in which we perceive ordinary things. They lived in the thought and concern of the Hereafter in the way we live in this world, not merely because it is coming, but as though it has already been established. That is why they began to tremble the moment they heard this verse.

Imam Ahmad says: Abu Bakr (may Allah be pleased with him) said: "O Messenger of Allah, after this verse how will there be salvation? God says (Laysa bi-amaniyyikum wa la amani ahli al-kitab, man ya'mal su'an yujza bihi)" (4:123) (It is not by your wishful thinking nor by the wishful thinking of the People of the Book; whoever does evil will be recompensed for it). The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Abu Bakr, may Allah forgive you. Do you not fall ill? Do you not become weary? Do you not become distressed? Do you not sigh?" He said: "Yes." He said: "Then with these you will also be rewarded." (Narrated by al-Hakim through Sufyan al-Thawri.)

In the narration of Abu Bakr ibn Mardawayh, it is stated that Abu Bakr said: When this verse was revealed, I was with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). (Man ya'mal su'an yujza bihi wa la yajid lahu min dunillahi waliyyan wa la nasira) (4:123) (Whoever does evil will receive its recompense, and will not find for himself any protector or helper against God.)

So the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Abu Bakr, shall I tell you what verse has just been revealed?" Abu Bakr says: I said: "Tell me, O Messenger of Allah." He recited the verse to me, and I know not how, but I felt as if something in my back had broken and I straightened up. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) asked: "Abu Bakr, what has happened to you?" I said: "May my parents be sacrificed for you! Which of us has not done wrong, and the meaning of the verse is that we will be punished for all evil deeds?" The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Abu Bakr, you and the believers will be recompensed in this world, until you meet Allah having no sin at all; as for the others, their evil deeds will accumulate and on the Day of Resurrection they will be recompensed for them." (Narrated by al-Tirmidhi.)

Aisha (may Allah be pleased with her) said to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "O Messenger of Allah, I know the hardest verse of the Qur'an." He said: "Which?" I said: (Man ya'mal su'an yujza bihi) (4:123). He said: "A believing servant is afflicted with hardships." (Narrated by Ibn Jarir.)

It is narrated from Abu Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him) that when this verse was revealed (Man ya'mal su'an yujza bihi) (4:123) (whoever does evil will be recompensed for it), it weighed heavily upon the Muslims. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Close the gaps and draw near to one another, for every calamity that befalls a Muslim expiates his sins, even a thorn that pricks him." (Muslim, Tirmidhi, Nasa'i.)

In any case, this verse was an important link for the correction of Islamic concepts and the believing outlook. Through it, on the one hand, the thinking of the people of religion was corrected, and on the other hand their conduct was set right. This verse shook them powerfully and their hearts trembled, because they took every command with the utmost seriousness. They knew very well the truth of God's promise and the implementation of it. They lived their lives within those promises, and they dwelt in the Hereafter while they were still in this world.

And at the end comes the concluding statement, that after faith, polytheism, deeds and their recompense: whatever is in the heavens and the earth belongs to Allah, and Allah encompasses all things in this world and in the Hereafter.

(Verse) No. 126.

Wherever the Qur'an states that Allah is One and that He alone is the Deity (al-Ilah), it also states that He is the Owner and the Guardian (al-Malik, al-Muhaymin), that is, He is the King and the One who controls. Thus the Islamic doctrine of tawhid is not merely that Allah is One and has no partner in His Being; it is a positive tawhid, and He alone is the Doer and the Effective Agent in this universe, and sovereignty and guardianship also belong to Him alone.

When the consciousness takes firm root in the human soul that whatever is in the heavens and the earth belongs to Allah, and that He encompasses everything, and that nothing lies outside His knowledge and His dominion, then a person readily becomes prepared to accept Allah as the one Deity and Ruler, to worship Him alone, then to strive to please Allah, and to submit to His commands. This is because everything belongs to Him, is in His possession, and He encompasses everything.

There are some philosophies which accept Allah as One, but after this belief in tawhid they fall into the error that Allah does not possess will, some say that Allah has no knowledge, some do not accept Allah's sovereignty, and some do not accept Allah's ownership (for details, see "The Fallacies of the Philosophers"). Consequently, in the view of the philosophers, the concept of God is a negative concept. In this concept, Allah has no connection with people's lives; He has no influence over their conduct or their morals. The tawhid of the philosophers is nothing but mere talk. But in Islam, Allah is the Being who is the Owner of the heavens and the earth; therefore He is the Owner of everything, He encompasses everything, and He is the Guardian. Therefore, under the shade of this concept, the reformation of the conscience, the reformation of conduct, and the reformation of the whole of life can be achieved.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran (Urdu translation)) on surah 4, verse 127 (part 1 of 2):

Lesson No. 41: At a Glance

At the beginning of this surah, Islam began the work of reforming jahili (pre-Islamic ignorance) society, and this lesson is a part of that work. This reform is connected with the rights of women and the family system. Among the children born of a family, some are left orphaned. Their problems are addressed here. The Islamic society is warned that the inequities left over from the age of jahiliyyah (the age of ignorance) within these problems should be removed, and that a household should be raised on the foundation that both man and woman are respected within it, and that the interests of both are taken into account. The measures for reforming the differences that arise within a family are the subject of this lesson. That is, if differences arise, they should be reformed before affairs deteriorate, so that households do not break apart; especially so that the children who are already born into these households, and for whom the family is a nursery, may be properly raised. Likewise, within general society the weak should be looked after, so that it does not happen that the law of the dominant and powerful prevails, and the rule of "might is right" flourishes.

This lesson reforms certain matters by linking them to the order of the universe. Through this it is intended to give the reader the understanding that the problems of women, households, families and the weak within society are not minor problems. They have very great importance, the details of which we have already given in this part (juz'). In the introduction to the fourth part (juz'), we have explained in detail how great importance Islam gives to the family system, and how enormous a struggle the Islamic system has undertaken to purify the family institution from the evil customs of jahiliyyah, and how much effort it has made to raise the moral, psychological and collective level of people within society, so that the Islamic society would surpass all the societies that were spread around it at that time, which did not accept the religion of Islam, whose upbringing was not according to the Islamic methodology, and which were not under the rule of the Islamic system.

Now, let us take up the verses under discussion with some detail.

Lesson No. 41: Explanation of the Verses

Verses 127 to 134

(Verse) 127.

The verses that were revealed at the beginning of Surah al-Nisa had given rise to many questions, and people used to ask questions. In the early period of the formation of the Islamic society, it was a common practice among Muslims to ask questions about various matters, and underlying this was the impulse that they wanted to learn the rulings relating to the Islamic system of life, because the transition from jahiliyyah to Islam was in fact a profound revolution in their lives. As a result, doubt arose in their consciousness about all the actions performed in the age of jahiliyyah and about the Messenger. They always felt that in some matter that arose, Islam might not have abrogated the previous practice. This alertness and the impulse to mould their lives according to Islamic rulings was a general characteristic of these noble people. Despite this, some traces of jahiliyyah remained in their lives. The real point is that there existed within them a national spirit, according to which they shaped all the circumstances of their lives according to Islam, and with this spirit they made inquiries about certain rulings. They did not do this merely for the sake of knowledge and culture, or merely for the sake of asking, as today most questions put to muftis are merely for the acquisition of knowledge and culture; nobody asks in order to act upon them.

At that time, Muslims had a genuine need to ask about religious matters, because this religion was for them a system of life, and they were very keen in asking about its rulings, with the aim that their practical lives should conform to the commands of the religion. They were passing through the process of emerging from jahiliyyah, and were fearful of all the customs, traditions and practices of jahiliyyah, lest any matter should be contrary to the system of Islam. They were very sensitive about the transformation and revolution that Islam had brought about in them. In other words, Islam reached them through their sincere resolve and their zeal for Islam. In a form in which the special favour and attention of Allah was directed towards them, the Essence of the Lord Himself directly answered them in response to their inquiry.

(Verse) "They ask you concerning women. Say: Allah gives you a verdict concerning them" (4:127).

They used to ask the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and Allah used to say to the Prophet ﷺ: "Say: Allah gives you a verdict regarding your questions and the remaining matters mentioned in this verse." This is a favour of Allah whose worth only the Companions truly knew. Allah, with great kindness and great honour, Himself gives a verdict to the community of Muslims, and this is by way of deputising, or as cherishing His servants and mercy, and the answer to the questions necessary for the new life of the servants is being given by Himself. This question concerned the practical circumstances that were the daily routine in jahiliyyah, the jahiliyyah from which Allah and His system had brought out those who asked. Secondly, these questions concerned those matters through which the new Islamic society was intended to be developed further.

(Verse) "Say: Allah gives you a verdict concerning them, and what is recited to you in the Book concerning the orphan women whom you do not give what is prescribed for them, and whom you desire to marry, and concerning the weak among the children, and that you should stand up for orphans with justice" (4:127).

(Say: Allah gives you a verdict regarding them, and He reminds you of the rulings that have already been recited to you in this Book. That is, the rulings concerning those orphan girls to whom you do not give their rights, and whom you refrain from marrying (or, out of greed, you yourselves wish to marry them), and the rulings concerning those children who have no power at all. Allah guides you to uphold justice towards orphans.)

Ali ibn Abi Talhah narrated from Ibn Abbas (may Allah be pleased with him) concerning this verse that in the age of jahiliyyah, whoever had an orphan girl would throw his cloak over her, and when he had done this, no one could ever marry that girl. If she was beautiful and he liked her, he would marry her himself and continue to consume her property. And if she was ugly, he would not permit her to be married to others either, until she died and he became her heir. Allah declared this act forbidden and prohibited it for the future. And Allah said: "and the weak among the children" (4:127). Who were they? In jahiliyyah, in fact, weak children were not given a share of the inheritance, and girls were not given one either. Allah says: "you do not give them what has been prescribed for them" (4:127), meaning, you do not give them the right which Allah has made obligatory. Allah forbade this too, and fixed the share of every rightful heir in the Qur'an, and said that the share of a male is equal to two females, whether the females are young or old.

Sa'id ibn Jubayr (may Allah be pleased with him) says that the interpretation of "and that you should stand up for orphans with justice" (4:127) is that if the orphan girl was wealthy and beautiful, the guardian would say, "I choose her for myself," and would marry her; and if she was not wealthy and beautiful, he would give her in marriage to others.

(Verse) "They ask you concerning women. Say: Allah gives you a verdict concerning them" up to "and whom you desire to marry" (4:127): concerning this, A'ishah (may Allah be pleased with her) said: This concerns a man who had an orphan girl. He was her guardian and heir. She would share with him in his property, even in a bunch of dates that he picked for eating. He would not even like to marry her, nor would he give her in marriage to another person, lest she share with him in his property. Thus that woman would remain suspended. (Bukhari, Muslim)

Ibn Abi Hatim (may Allah have mercy on him) narrated from Urwah ibn al-Zubayr another narration from A'ishah (may Allah be pleased with her), who said: After this verse, people asked the Messenger of Allah ﷺ again about these women, and this verse was revealed:

(Verse) "They ask you concerning women. Say: Allah gives you a verdict concerning them. Say: Allah gives you a verdict concerning them, and what is recited to you in the Book" (4:127).

A'ishah (may Allah be pleased with her) says that the statement in this verse, "what is recited to you in the Book" (that is, the earlier rulings), refers to the earlier verse: "And if you fear that you will not deal justly with the orphan girls, then marry what seems good to you of women" (4:3). That is, if they are not wealthy and beautiful and you do not wish to marry them; and if they are wealthy and beautiful and you wish to marry them only for the sake of their wealth, then do not marry them unless you intend to marry them with justice.

From these narrations and Qur'anic verses it becomes known what was happening in the age of jahiliyyah, especially with orphan young women. Dishonesty would be practised by the guardian with regard to the wealth of the orphan girl, and injustice would also be done to her in her dower. Her property would be squandered, and if she was ugly, her property would also be seized and she would not be married at all. Nor would she be given in marriage to anyone else, lest she become a sharer with the guardian in property, since the property was under the guardian's control.

The same was the situation of young children and girls. They were deprived of inheritance, because they were weak and could not defend that property, or could not fight. Therefore they had no right or share, and this was in accordance with the tribal concept of life, according to which all the property of the tribe belonged to those who fought, and the weak had nothing.

These were the Bedouin and ugly customs which Islam began to change, and in their place it laid the foundations of advanced Qur'anic customs. This change was not such that, as if by a long jump, a revolutionary change was made very rapidly and the Arab society was turned into an advanced society; rather, it was a new birth for the Arabs. Their reality was changed and a new reality was given to them.

The important point that we wish to place on record here is that this renaissance was not a renaissance under any plan, nor was any special plan made for it, nor was any preliminary preparation made for a plan, nor did this progress occur due to some material change, and it occurred only in the lives of the Arabs.

This is because abolishing the jahili cause of ownership, which was war, and in its place establishing the right of ownership on a human basis, and granting human rights to children, orphans and women, was not merely because a change had come about in society, and because possessing military strength or defence was no longer the decisive factor in that society; for this reason the removal of the distinctive status of the family members who possessed military strength. Now the family had no need at all for members possessing military strength, nor any need for their distinctive status.

This is by no means the case. For in the Islamic period too, the importance of the men of war remained in its place. They were needed too. But the difference that arose was that the Islamic system had come, and this was a new birth for humanity. This birth was received through a book. They received this birth through a system, and the new society was established by this new system, and on the very same soil on which jahiliyyah had stood, and in the very same circumstances in which the means of production had not been changed. Neither matter nor its properties had been altered; rather, a revolution had occurred in the concept of life and the ideology of life. And this revolution occurred solely because of this new ideology.

It was also a reality that the Islamic system made the most prolonged struggle to erase the traces of jahiliyyah from people's minds and conduct, and laboured hard to install in their place Islamic concepts and Islamic customs. It was also a reality that some practices of jahiliyyah were still striving to preserve themselves, and in certain individual circumstances they would reappear. These customs wished to keep themselves alive in various forms.

It is also a fact that the system which descended from the heavens, and the concepts which this system bestowed, were precisely what was engaged in striking jahiliyyah out from its roots; and it was not the case that material circumstances, or the contradictions within them, were effective in this change, or that a change had occurred in the means of production, or that there was some Marxist factor which was bringing about change in society through a change in matter or the means of production.

What was new in the life of the Arab nation was the religion which descended upon them from the higher world. Some souls responded to it, because it spoke to human nature, and this nature exists within every human being. This is why this great revolution took place; indeed, humanity received this new birth, which transformed all the features of life, transformed them from every aspect, and erased all the traces of jahiliyyah.

The commentary on surah 4, verse 127 (part 2 of 2):

Whatever degree of tension may be seen between the modern and ancient features of society, and whatever pain, suffering and sacrifices may have been endured on the path of this purification and renewal, all of this came about because of heavenly messengership. It was an ideological and doctrinal conception that was the first and last factor for this revolution. Rather, it was the sole first and last agent for that new birth. Then what happened? The storm of this revolution was not confined merely to Islamic society; it enveloped all human values and all human societies in its grip.

This is why the followers of Islam had asked the Messenger only about women, and Allah answered about the rights of orphan girls, young children and the weak, in addition to those women. Thus Allah Ta'ala tied this question and answer to the source through which this revolution had come.

﴿And whatever good you do, indeed Allah is ever Knowing of it﴾ (4:127)

Whatever you do will not remain unknown or be lost. It is recorded with Allah, and what is recorded with Allah will certainly never be lost.

This is the final reference to which a believer sends his deeds, and it is this qibla toward which the orientation of the believer's thought and action turns. The strength and grip of this reference is the strength and grip of those guidances and of this system, and its influence extends over the human self, its habits and conduct, and indeed over the entire life.

It is not important that someone gives or writes many guidances, or proposes a system of life, or establishes a new order. The real significance lies in the grip and strength that stands behind any guidance, any system and any organisation. It is that grip from which all these concepts and all these institutions derive executive force. Between the systems of life and values that a human being receives from Allah, and those that a human being receives from fellow humans, there is a difference like that between heaven and earth. To suppose, in this case, an equivalence between human systems and divine systems, as though in other attributes, and to assume that both systems are extremely lofty and advanced, is clearly both impossible and madness. Unless a person considers who it was that uttered this statement, what our thinking about it is, and what our opinion of it is. On one side is the word of Allah, the Exalted, the Mighty, and on the other is the word of a son of man. A single step of collective regulation... This too was within the sphere of the family and within the society which Islam was giving a new birth, and this birth was taking place from the Higher Assembly through the Islamic system of life, and within it there was no intrusion of any earthly factor or agent, whether material or relating to production. Observe.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 4, verses 128-130:

(Verses) No. 128 to 130.

The Islamic system had earlier enacted legislation concerning ill-treatment and disobedience on the part of the wife, and had made all the arrangements for measures to be taken against any harm arising in this regard. (See the opening verses of this part.) Here, mention is made of indifference and disobedience, which come from the husband, and by which the dignity and self-respect of the woman are endangered, and as a result of which there is a fear that the family will be destroyed, because hearts can change and there can be alteration in inclinations and tendencies. Islam is a system that encompasses all aspects of life within social affairs, and it resolves the difficulties and dangers that may arise. Islam resolves all these matters according to its own inclinations and principles, and takes all measures in accordance with its own scheme.

If tension arises in the mutual relations between a man and a woman, and there is a threat of divorce, or the threat that the husband will leave the wife suspended and hanging, neither a wife nor a divorced woman, then in such a situation there is no prohibition for both of them to adopt a policy of "give and take" regarding financial and other rights against one another. For example, the woman may forgo some or all of her financial maintenance. Or, if there are several wives, a wife may renounce her turn and the like. For example, if some other wife is more beloved to the man, then a wife may renounce her right in her favour, or, for example, in the case where the wife who forgoes has lost interest in certain rights. This applies on the condition that the woman, having examined all the circumstances and matters, and having thought it over, decides with complete freedom that this state is better for her than divorce.

(Verse) "And if a woman fears ill-treatment or indifference from her husband, there is no blame upon them if the husband and wife make a settlement between themselves (regarding a mutual adjustment of some rights) by way of reconciliation." (4:127)

(Translation of the verse is as above.)

This is the same reconciliation to which we alluded above.

After this it is said that reconciliation is always better than litigation. Reconciliation is good in comparison with every situation: indifference, dry relations and divorce. (Verse) "And reconciliation is best" (4:127). Through reconciliation, cool breezes begin to blow over hearts that have become dry and cruel; the relationship is refreshed by the dew of affection and love, and the impulse to preserve marital ties arises; and if they have already ended, marital ties can be re-established again.

Islam deals with the human soul realistically. By employing all means and resources, it raises the human soul to a level for which it has prepared its temperament and nature. But while employing all these means, Islam also keeps in view that human nature has its own limits and bounds. Islam does not compel human nature and temperament to perform acts that lie beyond its capacity and scope. Islam does not command people to dash their heads against walls, saying, "This is My command, so do it," whether or not one has the ability.

The Islamic system does not permit the human soul to remain in a state of weakness or to be content with shortcomings. Nor does it allow a person who is sunk up to his ears in the swamp of human filth to praise and glorify it, seeking justification by saying that this is simply how man is in reality. Nor does it bind him by a rope to the higher realm and leave him dangling, swaying wherever he wishes, for in that case his feet would not be on the ground, and we would call that condition elevation and exaltation.

Islam is the middle way between these extremes. It is a system in which realistic actuality, or serious realism, is found. This system deals with man and treats him as a human being. By his nature, man is a strange creature: a creature whose feet are on the earth while his spirit is in the heavens. His spirit is in his body and also in the heavens. In short, the body is on the earth and the spirit is in the heavens.

In giving this command, the Islamic system deals with a human being and, in this matter, mentions a general characteristic of man. (Verse) "And souls are swiftly inclined to stinginess" (4:128). The meaning is that stinginess is always present in souls; it persists within the self. There are many kinds of stinginess: stinginess with wealth, stinginess in emotions. In the life of spouses, at times there come together such causes that miserliness and tightness of heart arise. Circumstances come into being such that the husband becomes very tight-hearted toward the woman. Now, if the woman forgoes her outstanding dower, or waives her maintenance, or pays a financial compensation and keeps the marriage intact, the matter can be averted from ruin. For sometimes it also happens that a woman forgoes her rights of conjugal intimacy but does not want divorce. If the situation is that the husband has another wife who is more beloved, and the first wife no longer has attraction or freshness, and the woman, respecting the husband's feelings, pleases him, and in this way the marriage remains, then in all these circumstances the matter has been left in the hands of the wife. She is free to adopt whatever course her interest lies in. The Islamic system does not impose anything on her; rather, she has the option to reflect on her affair and make for herself a better decision.

But Islam does not leave the matter entirely to stinginess; it also calls to another mode of conduct, because stinginess is not the only permanent characteristic of human nature; benevolence and God-fearing are also present in human nature.

(Verse) "But if you do good and fear God, indeed God is ever, of what you do, Aware" (4:128).

The final reliance is upon benevolence and piety, and no act of benevolence and piety will be lost. It will not be lost because God's knowledge encompasses all things. He is aware of every person's deed and also aware of the intention lying beneath that deed. Calling the human soul to adopt benevolence and piety as its way, and [reminding it] that God is aware of all actions, is a call that has a profound effect upon the human soul. Every person responds to this call. Indeed, it is the one invitation and exhortation for which every soul becomes ready very quickly.

Once again we observe that the Islamic system of life deals with the circumstances of human life and its actual state. This treatment is ideally realistic, or it is realistic idealism. Islam acknowledges those matters which are an inseparable part of human nature and are also hidden, and this acknowledgment is in an extraordinarily remarkable manner.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran (Urdu translation)) on surah 4, verse 129:

(Verse) "And you will never be able to be just between wives, even if you should strive [to do so]. So do not incline completely [toward one] and leave her [as if] suspended. And if you amend [your conduct] and fear Allah, then indeed Allah is ever Forgiving and Merciful." (129) "And if they separate, Allah will enrich each of them from His abundance, and Allah is ever Vast and Wise." (130)

Full and perfect justice between wives is not within your power. Even if you wish for it, you cannot achieve it. Therefore (to fulfil the purpose of the Divine law, it is sufficient that) you do not incline toward one wife in such a way that you leave the other hanging. If you keep your conduct upright and fear Allah, then Allah is Forgiving and Merciful. But if the spouses separate from one another, Allah will, by His vast power, make each of them free from need of the other. The refuge of Allah is very broad, and He is All-Knowing and All-Wise.

Allah is the Being who created man, and He fully knew, concerning His creation, that after this there are inclinations over which it is not possible for man to gain control. Therefore Allah gave man the reins in his hands, so that he would keep these inclinations under control and keep their movement within bounds, but would not attempt to eliminate them entirely.

One of these inclinations is that a person may incline more toward one of his several wives than toward the others. This inclination is of a kind that lies beyond human capacity. A person cannot eliminate it, so what is the solution? Islam does not call a person to account for something beyond his capacity. It does not consider it a sin, nor does it impose a punishment for it. Islam places this matter in the account of what is beyond one's power. Thus it is declared that you will never be able to achieve complete justice between your wives, even if you try, because this is beyond your power. What falls within your intention is that you act justly in dealings, justly in distribution, justly in providing maintenance, justly in the rights of marital companionship, even justly in smiling, and justly in the words you speak. This is what is demanded of you. This is the rein that will keep these inclinations under control. Restraint is required; the killing of inclinations is not required.

(Verse) "fa-la tamilu kulla al-mayli fa-tadharuha kal-mu'allaqah" (4:129) (do not incline completely [toward one] and leave her [as if] suspended)

This is what is meant: inclining entirely toward one side in outward matters, in such a way that the rights of the other are lost, so that she is neither a wife nor a divorced woman. Along with this, the believers are addressed with a highly effective call.

(Verse) "wa in tuslihu wa tattaqu fa-inna Allaha kana Ghafuran Rahima" (4:129) (And if you amend [your conduct] and fear Allah, then indeed Allah is ever Forgiving and Merciful)

Islam deals with the human self in such a way that it is a being created from a handful of clay and the breathing of the spirit into it, fully in accordance with the powers and capacities within it. Moreover, it deals with the human being in accordance with a realistic idealism, or real idealism, so that he is a human being with his feet on the ground, yet possessing a spiritual elevation in which there is neither contradiction nor breakdown.

This is Islam. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ was at the pinnacle of perfection from the human standpoint. All his faculties were balanced and harmonious, and remained within the limits and nature of man.

The Messenger of Allah ﷺ was capable of distributing and dividing justly among his wives; he did not give preference to one wife over another. But control over inner feelings is not within anyone's power. (Allahumma hadha qasmi fima amliku fa-la talumni fima la amliku) (O Allah, this is my division in matters over which I have control, so do not blame me for matters over which I have no control), meaning the heart (Abu Dawud).

Yes, when hearts become dry, relations become strained, and living together between the spouses becomes difficult, then separation is better. Islam does not consider it appropriate to keep spouses together by binding them with ropes and chains. Nor can spouses be kept together through imprisonment and confinement. Only the two parties can be bound by feelings of love and mutual compassion, or they can be kept united through the fulfilment of obligations and duties and through good treatment, especially hearts in which hatred has already arisen, because hearts cannot be confined within the fortresses of hatred. Moreover, a relationship that outwardly appears connected while inwardly being completely severed.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 4, verse 130:

﴿وَإِن يَتَفَرَّقَا يُغْنِ اللَّهُ كُلًّا مِّن سَعَتِهِ ۚ وَكَانَ اللَّهُ وَاسِعًا حَكِيمًا﴾ (4:130)
(If the two separate, Allah will enrich each of them from His abundance. Allah is ever All-Encompassing, All-Wise.)

Allah promises both of them that, by His grace and mercy, He will make each of them independent. Allah is extremely expansive toward His servants, and within His limits and wisdom, and with regard to the welfare of His servants, He determines the measure of their provision according to the circumstances of each person.

The wonder with which Islam deals with human consciousness and the hidden inclinations of the self, and the realism with which it views the ways of life, is so astonishing that even if people were to thank Allah day and night, they would still be unable to fulfil the right of that thanks. This is a system in which great care has been taken for human ease, and it is evident that this system has been prescribed for humankind. It takes human beings by the hand and raises them from the most debased condition and brings them to the highest exaltation, and this process corresponds exactly to human nature. It does not prescribe for them any target of elevation and loftiness unless there is a motivation within their nature to attain it and some root of it exists in their temperament. In this way, Islam takes them to that lofty station to which no other system can take them. It does this with an idealistic realism, or with a realism for which there is no precedent, and in a manner that accords with the true nature and temperament of this wondrous creature, humankind.

These rules of family order, which relate specifically to the marital life of the spouses, are a part of the Islamic system of life, and the Islamic system of life is a part of the great law (nāmūs akbar) of this universe, which Allah has set in motion throughout the whole cosmos. Therefore the Islamic system is in harmony with the nature of this universe, and at the same time it is in harmony with human nature, because humankind is also a part of this universe. This is a very profound secret of the Islamic system of life. For this reason, immediately after the issues of family and domestic order, Allah mentions the cosmos, by which these family laws become connected with the natural order of the entire universe. It is as if, just as there is the sovereignty of Allah in human life, so too He alone is the Sovereign in this universe. He is the One who owns the heavens and the earth, and He is the very Being who has given you these commands. He is the One who gave these commands to the earlier nations as well, and all these commandments and admonitions are one and come from one source. The Islamic system rests upon the principle that from it results the good of both this world and the Hereafter, and these are principles founded upon truth, justice and God-consciousness.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran (Urdu translation)) on surah 4, verse 131–134:

(Verse) 131 to 134.

After the statement of commands and prohibitions in the Qur'an, there repeatedly follows the reminder that Allah is the Owner of everything in the heavens and the earth, or the phrase occurs that whatever is in the heavens and whatever is in the earth belongs to Allah. These two matters are inseparably linked, because the one who is king and owner also has the command and the prohibition in his kingdom. Those who dwell in his kingdom will be his subjects, and since in this universe Allah alone is the Owner, in this world only His command will prevail, and He alone will have the right to make law for people. The two matters are joined to one another.

Regarding those upon whom the Book was revealed, Allah here has enjoined upon them the charge that they should fear God, and this charge comes after the indication that whatever is in the heavens and the earth belongs to Allah; therefore the right to enjoin also belongs to Allah, and the right to legislate belongs to Allah, so fear Him.

(Verse) "Wa lillahi ma fi as-samawati wa ma fi al-ard, wa laqad wassayna alladhina utu al-kitaba min qablikum wa iyyakum an ittaqu Allah." (4: 131)

(Whatever is in the heavens and the earth is all Allah's. We enjoined those given the Book before you, and you as well, to fear Allah while acting.)

The fact is that people fear the one who possesses true authority, and God-fearing is the only path through which "hearts" can be reformed. Further, God-fearing is the only path through which a "system" can be reformed and its details can be put into practice. Those who do not recognize their station in this ownership of Allah, Allah warns them that He can remove them from this world and bring another population in their place and settle them in His possession.

(Verse) "Wa in takfuru fa-inna lillahi ma fi as-samawati wa ma fi al-ard, wa kana Allahu ghaniyyan hamida (131). Wa lillahi ma fi as-samawati wa ma fi al-ard, wa kafa billahi wakila (132). In yasha yudhhibkum ayyuha an-nas wa ya'ti bi-akharin, wa kana Allahu ala dhalika qadira (133)." (4: 131–133)

(If you disbelieve, then disbelieve; to Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth, and He is Self-sufficient, worthy of all praise. To Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is in the earth, and Allah suffices as Guardian. If He wills, He can remove you, O people, and bring others; and Allah is capable of that.)

Allah enjoins those who charge others to fear Allah; if they do not fear Allah, it causes no harm to the Being of Allah. And if they all adopt the attitude of disbelief, still there is no loss to Allah in it, because because of people's disbelief, nothing diminishes from Allah's ownership. (Verse) "Fa-inna lillahi ma fi as-samawati wa ma fi al-ard" (4: 131) (Indeed, to Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth). He is also capable of removing you from here and settling another in your place. What He enjoins upon them, He enjoins for their good, and to set their circumstances right.

Just as Islam regards the human being as the crown of this entire universe, declares human dignity, and declares him superior to all the creatures of the earth, so too, if a human being disbelieves in Allah, Allah regards him as the worst creature of this universe, because he turns away from the command of Allah; rather, by arrogance he partakes in the attribute of sovereignty belonging to Allah and makes himself the ruler here. And he does so without any entitlement. In the Islamic conception of life these two matters are equal, and this is indeed the reality.

These verses conclude with the reminder that those who are caught only in the greed for worldly aims should know that the grace of Allah is very vast. With Allah there is the good of both this world and the Hereafter, and those who sit with their gaze fixed only on this world should raise their gaze a little and see that with Allah there is the good of this world and the Hereafter.

(Verse) "Man kana yuridu thawab ad-dunya fa-inda Allahi thawab ad-dunya wal-akhira, wa kana Allahu sami'an basira." (4: 134)

(Whoever desires the reward of this world, let him know that with Allah is the reward of this world and the reward of the Hereafter, and Allah is All-Hearing, All-Seeing.)

It would be a clear folly and a clear lack of resolve for a person who could attain success in both this world and the Hereafter, and who could receive the reward of both, and for whom the Islamic system of life provides the guarantee of this success—a realistic, practical and exemplary system—yet who, despite this guarantee, seeks only the world. He would devote his entire effort to the pursuit of the world and live exactly as animals, cattle and insects live. Whereas this person could live comfortably as a human being, in such a way that his feet walk upon the earth while his soul roams and flutters in the heavens; and in such a way that, as a living being moving upon this globe in accordance with natural laws, he also keeps his life connected with the higher world.

In short, these partial and subsidiary commands are fully linked with the principles of the Islamic system of life, and from them it is apparent that the family system holds a very great importance in Islam—so great that these commands have been linked with the great matters of this universe, and upon all these matters this warning and comment has been made: that if you do not accept these commands of Allah, Allah has the power to destroy you and settle another creation in your place. This is an extremely dangerous comment, and from it one learns that, in Allah's view, the commands that arise regarding the organization of a family are of the same importance as the great guidance given to the religions.
