Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 4, verses 163–165 (part 1 of 3):

(Verses) No. 163 to 165.

In short, this is a caravan that can be seen moving along the highway of history, and the links of this chain are joined to one another. It is one message and it has one single aim: that mankind be warned in advance, and that good people be given the glad tidings of a good end in advance. In this caravan, chosen individuals from among the servants of the Divine Court and from among mankind come one after another. Here is Prophet Noah (peace be upon him). Here is Prophet Abraham (peace be upon him). Here is the mount of Ismail. After them come Prophet Isaac (peace be upon him), and immediately after him comes Prophet Jacob. Now various groups emerge: Prophet Job (peace be upon him), Jonah (peace be upon him), Aaron (peace be upon him), Solomon (peace be upon him), David (peace be upon him), Moses (peace be upon him) and Prophet Jesus (peace be upon him) have come, each in his own turn; and there are also some people who have come whose names we do not know. Finally, Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ), the Seal of the Prophets, is coming, and the final end of this caravan now reaches its conclusion. In this caravan there are some people whose mention the Holy Qur'an has presented. In this caravan there are prophets of various colours and various races, and this caravan is visible in different regions of the globe. And in different eras and different times, among different societies and different families, these messengers continued their work. All of them brought the message from one single source and fountain. All of them were bearers of one single light that shows the way. All of them, without exception, warned and gave warning and gave glad tidings. All of them took the reins of the caravan of humanity into their hands and kept bringing it into the light of guidance. Whether someone came for a single family, whether someone came for a single nation, whether someone came for a single city or a single region, or whether someone came for all of mankind and earned the title of Seal of the Prophets.

All of them received revelation from the One (Wahdahu). None of them presented any matter from himself. If Allah spoke directly with Prophet Moses (peace be upon him), that too was a form of revelation. We are not aware of this condition, nor can it be comprehended, because the Holy Qur'an is the record of the final revelation, and it is such an accurate record that it is above every kind of doubt and suspicion; and the Qur'an has not described the details or the manner of that conversation. What was its nature? With which special qualities and which faculty of perception was Moses (peace be upon him) receiving it? All these matters pertain to the unseen (ghayb). The Qur'an has not stated anything about them. And whoever speaks on this subject from his own mouth, apart from the Holy Qur'an, will be speech without authority, philosophy, or a tale and story.

Why were these messengers, some of whose names were mentioned and some of whose names were not mentioned, sent? The compassion, mercy and justice of Allah demanded exactly this: that He send messengers, so that they might give the glad tidings to the believers and the obedient among the servants of Allah that Allah has prepared for them what blessings; countless blessings and the good pleasure of Allah await them. And that they might warn the disbelievers and the disobedient that the wrath of Allah and a painful punishment await them. And why was all this done? ﴿So that mankind should have no argument against Allah after the messengers.﴾ (4:165) (so that after their dispatch, people would have no proof against Allah). And that these messengers should tell people what proofs lie within their own selves and within the universe spread around them. Let them be told that Allah Most High has endowed the human species with the treasure of reason, and it is their duty to seek proofs through it within their own selves and within the universe spread around them. Messengers were sent even though reason existed; this was a special compassion and mercy from Allah towards His servants, that He sent messengers, because He knew that human personal desires and inclinations would overpower his reason and as a result this great faculty would be crushed. Therefore, out of His special mercy, Allah sent to them messengers who were bearers of good news and warners. They kept reminding them. They gave them sight and insight. They kept freeing their nature and their rational faculty from beneath the heaps of carnal desires, under which it had become difficult for their reason and nature to attain the proofs of guidance and the requirements of faith, whether these proofs lie within the human self or within this universe spread around him.

﴿And Allah is ever Mighty, Wise.﴾ (4:165) (And Allah is in every case Mighty and Wise). He is Mighty in that when His servants commit crimes, He can seize them. He is Wise in that He manages all the affairs of this universe according to His wisdom. He settles every matter in its proper place, and the decrees and measures that Allah has determined for this universe are all made according to wisdom and His will.

Now, look at the scene before you! ﴿So that mankind should have no argument against Allah after the messengers﴾ (4:165). In this scene lies a treasury of guidance and indications: deep hints and clear directives. We mention two or three of them, and that too very briefly, in keeping with the nature of Zilal al-Quran.

The first point that appears from this verse is: what is the place of human reason in the system of religion? What are its purposes? And what is the importance of reason in the most important matters of man, such as the matter of faith? Because the life of people was to be organised on the foundations of faith, and all the elements of life, all its tendencies, its complete practical form and all its dealings in the universe were to be built upon the ideology of faith, just as its entire outcome in the Hereafter depended on that faith.

If by its own powers (and Allah is most knowing about man and his powers, and these powers were deposited in man by Allah Himself), this man could be guided by his reason alone, and could seek the path of benefit for his own self and his life, and could seek good for himself both in this world and in the Hereafter, then Allah Most High would never have continued this long succession of messengers throughout the whole of human history, nor would He have established proof against people through messengers; and man, on the strength of his reason, would have found for himself the proofs of guidance and the indications of faith and certainty. He would have discovered these proofs from within his own self, and from the horizons of the universe spread around him he would have brought them forth. He would have fashioned for himself a system of life that would resolve all the problems of his life. He would have walked straight upon the path of truth and the straight way. There would be no need at all for the succession of messengers, no need for their missionary activities, and Allah would not say that if there were no messengers, people would have had an argument. As it has been said:

﴿So that mankind should have no argument against Allah after the messengers﴾ (4:165).

But Allah knew well that the means of perception and understanding that He had given to reason was in itself incapable of grasping these matters, and that reason alone, without the guidance of the prophets and without the organisation and assistance of the messengers, could not reach guidance. Moreover, without the guidance of the messengers it is not possible for it to devise another way of life for the whole of human existence in which lies their complete benefit and which guarantees a good outcome for them in both this world and the Hereafter. Since Allah knew well the shortcomings of human reason, the wisdom of Allah and His compassion required that He send messengers to people, and that He should not call anyone to account without the dispatch of messengers and the conveying of guidance. Allah Most High says: ﴿And We would never punish until We have sent a messenger﴾ (17:15). And this matter is so self-evident that it is definitively established by the verse, and even if it is not definitively established, the necessary implication of this verse certainly demands it.

Now the question arises: in the field of faith and guidance, and in the matter of establishing a detailed system of life on the foundation of faith and guidance, what role then remains for reason?

The answer to this question is that the role of human reason is to discharge its duties in receiving guidance from the messengers. It is the duty of reason to reflect upon the call of the messengers. The duty of the messengers extends only so far as to convey and explain, and to clear away the heaped layers of false notions that lie upon human nature, and to remove nature from beneath them, and to draw man's attention to the fact that within his own self and within the universe spread around him there are clear proofs of knowledge of the Creator. For this purpose, these messengers establish a correct system of training and a correct method of studying the universe, and they lay down a system of life for human beings on which the caravan of their life may move forward and flourish, and in which lies their good in this world and the Hereafter.

It is not the role of reason to become a mufti and a judge in matters of religion and theology, passing judgment on the validity and invalidity of these subjects. It is not for it to have the authority to accept whatever it wishes and reject whatever it wishes, when that matter has been definitively established from the Qur'an and Sunnah, after the meaning has been clearly understood; that is, in the light of the lexical and technical meanings of the textual evidences of the Qur'an. If human reason had the authority of acceptance and rejection, that is, after correct comprehension of the meaning and implication, in such a way that our reason does not accept that meaning or does not wish to accept it, then after the statement of God and the Messenger, a person would not deserve punishment. Therefore reason is bound to accept the essentials of religion, once these beliefs have reached it correctly, and once reason has also correctly understood the meaning and intent of these texts.

The Messenger's mission (ﷺ) addresses reason. It awakens reason, establishes for it a correct method of thought and vision, and places it on the right path. But this address does not mean that reason has the authority to issue a verdict on whether this mission is correct or false, or that it is able to do so, or that it has the power to accept or reject matters of the mission. Rather, this address means that when a matter is established by a text, that itself is the command of Allah, and it is the duty of human reason to accept it, obey it, and implement it on this earth, whether this meaning of the text is familiar and acceptable to its mind or strange and bizarre to it.

The role of human reason in this matter is only this: that it make a correct effort to understand the texts, and seek to determine what meaning the text bears according to the Arabic language and the technical terminology of the Shariah. Here the work of reason ends, and the correct meaning derived from the textual evidence of the Shariah cannot be rejected by any rational proof or analogy, because as far as the text is concerned, it is from Allah. A mere rational interpretation cannot be superior to the text, because reason does not have the status of God, nor does it have the status of accepting or rejecting the texts of Allah.

On this important point a great confusion arises in ideas. Some people grant human reason the status of God; they treat it as the judge even in their own affairs. And some do not permit reason the slightest intrusion into the fields of faith and guidance. The correct method is what we have explained above: that the Message has addressed reason so that it may strive to understand the decisions of the Message. The Message also lays down, for reason as well, a method regarding its practical and theoretical decisions, so that it too may function within its own sphere, and comprehend the decisions of the Message throughout the whole of life. When reason has understood the decisions of the Message, that is, what the texts of the Shariah and the Message mean, then for reason there remains no path other than attestation, obedience and implementation. The Shariah does not require that a person act upon the texts without understanding their meanings; rather, the aim of the Shariah is that the texts be acted upon with understanding. But when reason comprehends them, it becomes obligatory upon it to act accordingly and not to raise any hesitation or quibble. It must accept the matter according to the meanings of the texts. And to confront the texts with objection and hesitation would mean accepting some of them and rejecting others, declaring some correct and others wrong, despite knowing that these texts and this guidance have come from Allah. Allah speaks only what is true, and whatever command He gives, there is good in it.

In the Islamic system of life, the correct way to receive guidance from Allah is this: once the correct meaning of the texts of the Qur'an and Sunnah has been grasped, intellectual horses should not be galloped within them; this understanding should accord with the principles of understanding. A person should not study the Qur'an and Sunnah having already settled certain decisions in his mind, such as deriving certain logical conclusions in his religion, or settling certain matters on the basis of his limited observation, or accepting certain things as facts in accordance with his deficient experiences, and then strive to mould the Qur'an and Sunnah to match them. The correct methodology of study is to take the texts as they are, and the decisions the texts have made are, in any case, decisions, and they are better than his personal thinking, and their system and their methodology are stronger than his personal methodology. Therefore, reason cannot pass judgement upon the decisions of religion. When it becomes established to reason that this decision is of the religion, the decisions told by people cannot gain superiority over the principles of religion. Reason will in any case be subservient to these religious principles, on condition that the principles and standards of religion are clearly established and come forward.

Reason does not have the status of a god such that it may declare that the results it has derived are the decisions of Allah. Yes, human reason certainly has the right to present a meaning of a text according to human reason, in comparison with another meaning, which is itself also a rational meaning. This is the domain of human reason, and there is no restriction upon reason in it, nor is there any harm in it, on condition that this meaning and understanding of the texts is correct and within the bounds of the principles, the aim is the interpretation of texts and mutual understanding, and there is room for interpretation within the texts. This interpretation and explanation should also be within those rules and standards which religion itself has laid down for this purpose. These rules are such that they fulfil all the requirements of human freedom of thought and provide a vast field for human understanding and comprehension. In the Islamic system there is no such institution, no such collective restriction and no such official who has the authority to lock minds, so that people cannot reflect upon the Shari'ah texts, cannot give a good opinion regarding their application, or cannot present reasonable justifications, on condition that a Shari'ah text is capable of bearing these opinions, these interpretations and justifications, and these interpretations are also within the limits of the Islamic system and are based upon the principles of religion. This is the meaning of the statement that the Muhammadan message addresses reason.

Indeed, Islam is a rational religion. It presents its issues, beliefs and decisions before reason. Islam does not impose these decisions and beliefs upon people in a supernatural manner such that there remains no alternative but to accept them; rather, that rational religion, in the sense that it addresses reason and invites it to reflection, presents before it the proofs of guidance and the straight path, so that it may reflect upon those signposts found within its own self and in the horizons, and extract the original nature of man from beneath the thick layers of customs and traditions. Likewise, that reason should free itself from misleading desires and from influences that overwhelm reason and nature. The Qur'an addresses reason so that, after reflecting upon the matters which the Qur'an has settled in its texts, it may accept them, and it is not the Qur'an's manner to compel people to accept a matter without explaining it. Yes, when a person, by employing reason, grasps the meaning and implication of a text and comprehends the realities, then there is no alternative for him but to bow in submission. After understanding, if they accept, they are believers, and if they do not accept, they are disbelievers. As for the Qur'anic and Islamic decisions, they were made before being presented to reason. Reason does not have the authority to decide whether they are right or wrong, nor does reason have the authority to reject Islamic decisions after understanding and comprehension. Today some people grant reason the authority to reject Islamic decisions. For such people, their reason becomes their god. Now this god of theirs accepts whichever decisions of the Shari'ah it wishes and rejects whichever it wishes. It chooses whichever matters it wishes and leaves whichever it wishes. Regarding such people, Allah the Exalted has said:
(verse) "Afatu'minoona ba'da al-kitabi wa takfuroona ba'd" — Do you believe in some of the Book and disbelieve in some? This conduct is disbelief, and such people will be given a severe punishment in the Hereafter.

Now, whether Allah has made a decision concerning this universe, or concerning man, or concerning any other creature, or Allah has made a decision concerning the law of inheritance, or concerning obligations and prohibitions, all these decisions of Allah are worthy of acceptance, and for those to whom these decisions reach and who comprehend the implications of these decisions, it is obligatory for them to accept these decisions. For example, the saying of Allah:
(verse) "Allahu alladhee khalaqa sab'a samawatin wa min al-ardi mithlahunna" (65:12) — Allah is He who created seven heavens and of the earth the like of them.
(verse) "Wallahu khalaqa kulla dabbatin min ma'" (24:45) — and Allah created every moving creature from water.
(verse) "Khalaqa al-insana min salsalin ka al-fakhkhar" (14), "wa khalaqa al-janna min maarijin min nar" (15) (55:14–15) — He created man from clay like pottery, and He created the jinn from a smokeless flame of fire.

These and countless other verses of this kind relate to the nature of this universe and the reality of living and non-living things. Thus, whatever Allah has said is the truth. Now reason has no capacity to say that these matters are not within my decisions in this way, or that this matter does not fit within my understanding, or that this matter has not yet come within my experience. This is because the decisions reason has made in such matters may be correct and may also be wrong. But whatever Allah has said can only be correct, and there is no possibility of error in it. However, our understanding may err in comprehending the correct meaning of the texts, and this is the case when we do comprehend the correct meaning of the texts. Similarly, in other verses Allah says:
(verse) "Wa man lam yahkum bima anzala Allahu fa-ulaika humu al-kafiroon" (5:44) — Those who do not judge by what Allah has revealed are the disbelievers.
(verse) "Ya ayyuha alladhina amanu ittaqu Allaha wa dharu ma baqiya mina al-riba in kuntum mu'minin (278). Fa-in lam taf'alu fa-adhanu bi-harbin mina Allahi wa rasulihi, wa in tubtum fa-lakum ru'usu amwalikum, la tazlimuna wa la tuzlamun" (2:278–279) — O you who believe, fear Allah and leave what remains of interest owed to you by people, if you are truly believers. But if you do not do so, then be informed of a declaration of war from Allah and His Messenger. Yet if you repent, you are entitled to your principal; you shall not wrong and you shall not be wronged.
(verse) "Wa qarna fi buyutikunna wa la tabarrajna tabarruja al-jahiliyyati al-ula" (33:33) — Stay in your houses and do not display yourselves as in the former time of ignorance.
(verse) "Wa liyadribna bi-khumurihinna 'ala juyubihinna" (24:31) — and let them draw their head-coverings over their chests and not reveal their adornment.

These and other verses and guidance concerning human life are such that what Allah has said in them is the truth, and reason may not be permitted to say that according to reason such-and-such matters have greater benefit, which contradict Allah's decisions, or are matters which Allah has not permitted and has not made law for people. In a matter where reason sees benefit, there is possibility of both error and correctness, and the intrusion of momentary emotions and carnal desires is quite possible in it. Therefore, whatever decision Allah makes can only be correct, and there is no possibility of error in it.

Whatever the position of reason regarding the beliefs and concepts which Allah has enjoined, or the methodology and mode of conduct of life which He has prescribed, as long as the text is authentic, definitive in meaning, and not limited by any time, we cannot permit reason to say that as far as beliefs and ideologies are concerned we take them according to the texts, but as for the detailed system of life, the matter is that the age has changed greatly and become highly advanced. Therefore, if Allah had wished that the Shari'ah texts be effective only up to a particular time, Allah could have done so. As long as a text is absolute, it will be as effective in the final age as it was at the time of its revelation; otherwise it would necessarily follow that we would presume to hold Allah, who is free of every defect, responsible.

The question will arise: has the gate of ijtihad been closed? No. Ijtihad will consist in applying a text to a particular situation. It is not ijtihad that we make a change in a general principle or ruling, or reject it, or say something in one age or generation under any principle of reason.

Nothing in the above remarks that we have presented is such that it diminishes the importance of reason and intellect in human life, because there is a vast field of activity open to reason for applying Islamic texts and principles to the most modern and newest circumstances, provided reason comprehends well the Islamic viewpoint and Islamic standards, which are derived from the understanding of religion along correct lines. An even wider field is that of the natural principles of this universe, its forces and the treasures hidden within it. The nature of this universe, knowledge of the creatures living in it, the means of benefiting from these forces, and the means and causes of making life easier for living creatures in it are vast fields for reason, in which reason alone can work. Here man can be advanced, and the days and nights of his life can be changed while remaining within the limits of Allah. However, reason may not be permitted to place humanity's reins in the hands of whims, lusts, and pleasure and passion, where reason stumbles and nature is buried beneath the thick sediment of desires.

Pause here again and look once more at this verse: "Li-alla yakuna lil-nasi 'ala Allahi hujjatun ba'da al-rusul" (4:165) — so that after the messengers were sent, people would have no argument against Allah. From this verse we learn how great the responsibilities placed upon the shoulders of the prophets are, and how great the responsibilities placed upon those who believe in the prophethood of the prophets, in relation to all humanity. Indeed, these are great and heavy responsibilities.

All the people who inhabit this world, their destinies, in this world and the Hereafter, are linked to the messengers and the followers of the messengers. For instance, the messengers and their followers are responsible for conveying Allah's message to them, and it is through this conveyance that the good fortune and misfortune of people will be decided, and through this conveyance and invitation they will become deserving of reward and punishment, both in this world and in the Hereafter.

Indeed, this is a terrifying, frightening and great responsibility, but there is no other path. For this reason all the messengers (peace be upon them) had a keen sense of this great responsibility. Allah also informed them clearly of the burden that had been placed upon them. This is what Allah tells His Prophet:
(verse) "Inna sanulqi 'alayka qawlan thaqeelan" (73:5) — Indeed, We are going to send down upon you a weighty word.
And the preparation for it would be thus:
(verse) "Ya ayyuha al-muzzammil (1). Qumi al-layla illa qalilan (2). Nisfahu awi-nqus minhu qalilan (3). Aw zid 'alayhi wa rattili al-qur'ana tartilan (4). Inna sanulqi 'alayka qawlan thaqeelan (5)" (73:1–5) — O you who wrap yourself up, stand [in prayer] at night, but a little, half of it, or reduce it a little, or add to it, and recite the Qur'an with measured recitation. Indeed, We are going to send down upon you a weighty word.
(verse) "Inna nahnu nazzalna 'alayka al-qur'ana tanzeelan (23). Fa-isbir li-hukmi rabbika wa la tuti' minhum atheeman aw kafooran (24). Wa udhkuri isma rabbika bukratan wa asila (25). Wa min al-layli fa-usjud lahu wa sabbihhu layla tawila (26)" (76:23–26) — Indeed, We have sent down to you the Qur'an in stages. So be patient for the decision of your Lord, and do not obey from among them any sinner or disbeliever. And mention the name of your Lord morning and evening. And during the night prostrate to Him and exalt Him through the long night.

This is the matter which Allah makes the Prophet aware of, and orders him to say it, and to understand well what its reality and significance is.
(verse) "Qul inni lan yujirani min Allahi ahadun wa lan ajida min dunihi multahada (22)" (72:22) — Say: No one can protect me from Allah, nor shall I find any refuge other than Him. My duty is only to convey the messages of Allah and His communications.
(verse) "'Alimu al-ghaybi fa-la yuzhiru 'ala ghaybihi ahada (26). Illa man irtada min rasulin fa-innahu yaslukuhu min bayni yadayhi wa min khalfihi rasada (27). Li-ya'lama an qad ablaghu risalati rabbihim wa ahata bi-ma ladayhim wa ahsa kulla shay'in 'adada (28)" (72:26–28).

"He is the Knower of the unseen, and He does not disclose His unseen to anyone, except to a Messenger whom He has chosen. Then He sets guards before him and behind him, so that He may know that they have conveyed the messages of their Lord; and He encompasses all that is with them, and He has counted everything in number."

Indeed this is a fearful and great duty. It is a matter of the life and death of people, of their happiness and misery, of their reward and punishment. It is the matter of the final destiny of all humanity. The summary of this duty is that this message will either be conveyed to people so that they accept it and follow it, as a result of which they will attain success in this world and the Hereafter; or the message will reach them and they will cast it far away, and will be struck by misery in both this world and the Hereafter; or the message will not reach them, and the result will be that people will have a proof against their Lord in hand, and the responsibility for this worldly misery of these people and for their misguidance will rest upon those who are responsible for conveying God's message to them in this world and who do not fulfil this responsibility.

As for the Messengers of God, they fully discharged their responsibility. They conveyed God's message and trust to people. They went to their Lord in the state of having fully fulfilled their responsibilities. They did not fulfil these responsibilities merely to the extent of verbal preaching, but they gave practical form to God's message in their own lives, showing it to people, and day and night they strove in the way of God, removing the difficulties and obstacles that stood in the path of this message. Whether these difficulties took the form of doubts that troubled people's minds, or of misguidance that was imposed upon people, or of satanic forces that prevented people from giving ear to this call and that were a trial for their religion, they removed them. The Seal of the Prophets ﷺ demonstrated the complete implementation of Islam in his practical life, because he was the final preacher. His Messengership was the conclusion of all messengerships, so he did not suffice with mere verbal preaching. He removed these difficulties and obstacles also by the force of the sword and power: "So that there is no more fitnah and religion is entirely for Allah" (2:193). Now this heavy responsibility falls, after him, upon those who believe in his Messengership. Ages have passed, generations upon generations have passed and will continue to pass. After the Messenger ﷺ, the work of preaching has come into the responsibility of his followers, and for them there is no way to be absolved of this difficult and heavy responsibility. They must establish the proof against people. They must save people from the misery of the world and the failure of the Hereafter. This duty and this responsibility can only be discharged through preaching, and it can only be discharged on the same method upon which the Messenger of God ﷺ discharged it, because the Messengership is the same, and the believers are the same. The misguidances, the desires of the soul, the doubts and objections are also the same; those satanic forces too exist in the same way, obstructing the arrival of the Islamic call to people. These forces are casting Muslims into trial regarding their religion and misguiding them by force. The position is the same as it was, the difficulties are the same as they were, and the people are the same as they were.

The Islamic call is a duty from which we cannot turn away or deny. Therefore it is necessary that we preach; it is very necessary that we discharge this duty. Preach through writing and speech; preach through your conduct, so that preachers, through their action and character, become a walking preaching; and strive to remove the obstacles that stand in the way of preaching and the call, for this too is a form of preaching. Free those who are caught in trial. If this work is not done, there will be no preaching, the duty will not be discharged, and God's proof will not be completed upon people.

There is no alternative to undertaking these responsibilities, otherwise its heavy consequences will appear. The whole world will be afflicted with misguidance; it will be struck by misery in this world, and in the Hereafter there will be no proof against it before God, and the proof will be in their hands. If the ummah does not discharge this responsibility, people will not be saved because of it.

Who will consider this burden light? It is a back-breaking burden; every joint and every limb of the body trembles under it. Whoever claims to be a "Muslim" will either discharge this duty and carry out the work of calling to the religion, or else for him success is not possible in this world or the Hereafter. When he claims that he is a Muslim, and then does not carry out the work of calling to religion and does not fulfil his duty, according to all the methods that call to it and that are prescribed for the discharge of duty, then he is in effect bearing witness against the Islam he has claimed. His testimony is not in favour of Islam but against it, although he has been raised up so that he may bear witness for Islam.

"And thus We have made you a middle nation, that you may be witnesses over mankind, and the Messenger may be a witness over you" (2:143). (For details, see the book Shahadat-e-Haq by Maulana Sayyid Abul A'la Maududi.)

The beginning of the witness of truth and of testimony for Islam will be this: a Muslim himself, then his home and family, then his people and relatives, should be a practical model of the religion to which he is inviting the world. After this, let his witness advance one more step, so that a community is produced that can be called the community of the call (ummat-e-da'wah). After presenting Islam and the Islamic call in practical form within the bounds of his home, family and kinship, he should also take up responsibility for establishing this call in personal affairs and in the political affairs of the country. After that, he should bear such witness that he removes the obstacles that stand in the way of Islam, that misguide people and cast them into trial regarding this call, whatever kind of obstacles they may be. If any Muslim has given testimony in this sense, then he will truly be a witness and also a martyr (shahid). Having borne witness, he will reach his Lord. This is the true martyr.

Last of all, we stand with folded hands before God, in His court of majesty and grandeur. This court is a court of justice and is based upon profound knowledge. In this court, the grace and mercy of God cast their shade, and in it everyone is dealt with kindness and favour, and all this happens to that human being who sometimes comes in the form of one who denies the truth and sometimes commits gross disobedience.

We see that God Almighty has adorned the human being with the ornament of knowledge and has placed within his being immense powers. In his being He has created the capacity for both guidance and misguidance. What results come about if this knowledge is not made subservient to reason? Furthermore, God has given man a great weapon of knowledge, and that in man's self and in his horizons there are countless proofs for guidance and the acceptance of faith. God knew that against the great weapon of knowledge that man possesses, there also exists in man the force of lust and animality, and it is quite possible that the numerous proofs and signs found within the self and the horizons may be overpowered by man's base desires, and his shortcomings and ignorance may hide them from his sight. It will be possible for man to reflect upon these proofs only when Messengers are sent to him and he is repeatedly reminded. Likewise, even after the explanation of guidance, God did not place upon man the burden of devising for himself a system of life, but made a system of life and made it his duty to establish that system in the world. Then He left him free in this world again. Even after these limits and bounds, a wide sphere of action remained for him in this great kingdom. He was permitted to make whatever new inventions he wishes in it, to bring about whatever changes he wishes, to make whatever combinations he wishes, and to benefit fully from the way God has subjected this whole universe for man. In this, man will sometimes make right decisions and sometimes wrong ones; sometimes he will slip and sometimes he will walk firmly upon the straight path.

It is also worth reflecting here upon the importance of justice with God, which is expressed in this verse. If Messengers had not been sent, people would have had a proof against God. But God sent Messengers who gave glad tidings to people and warned them of the evil end, although in this universe there were cosmic proofs for faith in the existence of God, and this universe lay open before all like a book unfolded. Moreover, the human soul too was present before man as an open book, within which there were countless proofs for the existence of the Creator.

Through these, the unity of God could be well known; through these, one could well learn about God's decree, God's governance, God's power and His knowledge. Furthermore, within human nature there exists a strong and true inclination, through which man receives a very firm longing to reach the Creator of this universe, and he becomes certain that there must be a Creator. Then there exists a kind of harmony between this nature and the cosmic proofs. These proofs show that there exists a Creator and Manager of this universe. Then God gave man intellect, which has the capacity to draw conclusions through observation. But God well knew that all these powers of man come under weakness. Sometimes these powers become inoperative; sometimes influences corrupt these powers. Sometimes these intellectual faculties are obliterated; sometimes an error occurs in the judgements of reason and reason becomes confused. Therefore God excused people from this duty, that they should seek the path of guidance only from the proofs and signs of this universe, or attain the path of truth merely through natural proofs by the strength of their intellect, until a Messenger comes to them, so that this Messengership may purify all these excellences and powers of man from all these impurities, and bring these intellectual faculties within those regulations which God's Messengers have brought. When all these natural powers of man are regulated within the Islamic method of thought, then the only task left for these powers is to decide that they should acknowledge this Messengership, serve God, and follow the Messenger. Or if they reject it, then the proof is completed against them and they become liable to punishment on the Day of Judgement.

Then we learn how merciful God is toward His servants, how much He takes care of them, how He bestows upon them from His grace and generosity, and how much He honours and empowers them. Despite knowing that man is a figure of error and deficiency, God nonetheless entrusts this world to him. He makes him a khalifah on the earth. Yet this universe is very vast in comparison to him, and God is so self-sufficient that if even an atom exists in His great universe, it cannot be lost.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 4, verses 163–165 (part 1 of 3):

(Verses) No. 163 to 165.

In short, this is a caravan that can be seen moving along the highway of history, and the links of this chain are joined to one another. It is one message and it has one single aim: that mankind be warned in advance, and that good people be given the glad tidings of a good end in advance. In this caravan, chosen individuals from among the servants of the Divine Court and from among mankind come one after another. Here is Prophet Noah (peace be upon him). Here is Prophet Abraham (peace be upon him). Here is the mount of Ismail. After them come Prophet Isaac (peace be upon him), and immediately after him comes Prophet Jacob. Now various groups emerge: Prophet Job (peace be upon him), Jonah (peace be upon him), Aaron (peace be upon him), Solomon (peace be upon him), David (peace be upon him), Moses (peace be upon him) and Prophet Jesus (peace be upon him) have come, each in his own turn; and there are also some people who have come whose names we do not know. Finally, Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ), the Seal of the Prophets, is coming, and the final end of this caravan now reaches its conclusion. In this caravan there are some people whose mention the Holy Qur'an has presented. In this caravan there are prophets of various colours and various races, and this caravan is visible in different regions of the globe. And in different eras and different times, among different societies and different families, these messengers continued their work. All of them brought the message from one single source and fountain. All of them were bearers of one single light that shows the way. All of them, without exception, warned and gave warning and gave glad tidings. All of them took the reins of the caravan of humanity into their hands and kept bringing it into the light of guidance. Whether someone came for a single family, whether someone came for a single nation, whether someone came for a single city or a single region, or whether someone came for all of mankind and earned the title of Seal of the Prophets.

All of them received revelation from the One (Wahdahu). None of them presented any matter from himself. If Allah spoke directly with Prophet Moses (peace be upon him), that too was a form of revelation. We are not aware of this condition, nor can it be comprehended, because the Holy Qur'an is the record of the final revelation, and it is such an accurate record that it is above every kind of doubt and suspicion; and the Qur'an has not described the details or the manner of that conversation. What was its nature? With which special qualities and which faculty of perception was Moses (peace be upon him) receiving it? All these matters pertain to the unseen (ghayb). The Qur'an has not stated anything about them. And whoever speaks on this subject from his own mouth, apart from the Holy Qur'an, will be speech without authority, philosophy, or a tale and story.

Why were these messengers, some of whose names were mentioned and some of whose names were not mentioned, sent? The compassion, mercy and justice of Allah demanded exactly this: that He send messengers, so that they might give the glad tidings to the believers and the obedient among the servants of Allah that Allah has prepared for them what blessings; countless blessings and the good pleasure of Allah await them. And that they might warn the disbelievers and the disobedient that the wrath of Allah and a painful punishment await them. And why was all this done? ﴿So that mankind should have no argument against Allah after the messengers.﴾ (4:165) (so that after their dispatch, people would have no proof against Allah). And that these messengers should tell people what proofs lie within their own selves and within the universe spread around them. Let them be told that Allah Most High has endowed the human species with the treasure of reason, and it is their duty to seek proofs through it within their own selves and within the universe spread around them. Messengers were sent even though reason existed; this was a special compassion and mercy from Allah towards His servants, that He sent messengers, because He knew that human personal desires and inclinations would overpower his reason and as a result this great faculty would be crushed. Therefore, out of His special mercy, Allah sent to them messengers who were bearers of good news and warners. They kept reminding them. They gave them sight and insight. They kept freeing their nature and their rational faculty from beneath the heaps of carnal desires, under which it had become difficult for their reason and nature to attain the proofs of guidance and the requirements of faith, whether these proofs lie within the human self or within this universe spread around him.

﴿And Allah is ever Mighty, Wise.﴾ (4:165) (And Allah is in every case Mighty and Wise). He is Mighty in that when His servants commit crimes, He can seize them. He is Wise in that He manages all the affairs of this universe according to His wisdom. He settles every matter in its proper place, and the decrees and measures that Allah has determined for this universe are all made according to wisdom and His will.

Now, look at the scene before you! ﴿So that mankind should have no argument against Allah after the messengers﴾ (4:165). In this scene lies a treasury of guidance and indications: deep hints and clear directives. We mention two or three of them, and that too very briefly, in keeping with the nature of Zilal al-Quran.

The first point that appears from this verse is: what is the place of human reason in the system of religion? What are its purposes? And what is the importance of reason in the most important matters of man, such as the matter of faith? Because the life of people was to be organised on the foundations of faith, and all the elements of life, all its tendencies, its complete practical form and all its dealings in the universe were to be built upon the ideology of faith, just as its entire outcome in the Hereafter depended on that faith.

If by its own powers (and Allah is most knowing about man and his powers, and these powers were deposited in man by Allah Himself), this man could be guided by his reason alone, and could seek the path of benefit for his own self and his life, and could seek good for himself both in this world and in the Hereafter, then Allah Most High would never have continued this long succession of messengers throughout the whole of human history, nor would He have established proof against people through messengers; and man, on the strength of his reason, would have found for himself the proofs of guidance and the indications of faith and certainty. He would have discovered these proofs from within his own self, and from the horizons of the universe spread around him he would have brought them forth. He would have fashioned for himself a system of life that would resolve all the problems of his life. He would have walked straight upon the path of truth and the straight way. There would be no need at all for the succession of messengers, no need for their missionary activities, and Allah would not say that if there were no messengers, people would have had an argument. As it has been said:

﴿So that mankind should have no argument against Allah after the messengers﴾ (4:165).

But Allah knew well that the means of perception and understanding that He had given to reason was in itself incapable of grasping these matters, and that reason alone, without the guidance of the prophets and without the organisation and assistance of the messengers, could not reach guidance. Moreover, without the guidance of the messengers it is not possible for it to devise another way of life for the whole of human existence in which lies their complete benefit and which guarantees a good outcome for them in both this world and the Hereafter. Since Allah knew well the shortcomings of human reason, the wisdom of Allah and His compassion required that He send messengers to people, and that He should not call anyone to account without the dispatch of messengers and the conveying of guidance. Allah Most High says: ﴿And We would never punish until We have sent a messenger﴾ (17:15). And this matter is so self-evident that it is definitively established by the verse, and even if it is not definitively established, the necessary implication of this verse certainly demands it.

Now the question arises: in the field of faith and guidance, and in the matter of establishing a detailed system of life on the foundation of faith and guidance, what role then remains for reason?

The answer to this question is that the role of human reason is to discharge its duties in receiving guidance from the messengers. It is the duty of reason to reflect upon the call of the messengers. The duty of the messengers extends only so far as to convey and explain, and to clear away the heaped layers of false notions that lie upon human nature, and to remove nature from beneath them, and to draw man's attention to the fact that within his own self and within the universe spread around him there are clear proofs of knowledge of the Creator. For this purpose, these messengers establish a correct system of training and a correct method of studying the universe, and they lay down a system of life for human beings on which the caravan of their life may move forward and flourish, and in which lies their good in this world and the Hereafter.

It is not the role of reason to become a mufti and a judge in matters of religion and theology, passing judgment on the validity and invalidity of these subjects. It is not for it to have the authority to accept whatever it wishes and reject whatever it wishes, when that matter has been definitively established from the Qur'an and Sunnah, after the meaning has been clearly understood; that is, in the light of the lexical and technical meanings of the textual evidences of the Qur'an. If human reason had the authority of acceptance and rejection, that is, after correct comprehension of the meaning and implication, in such a way that our reason does not accept that meaning or does not wish to accept it, then after the statement of God and the Messenger, a person would not deserve punishment. Therefore reason is bound to accept the essentials of religion, once these beliefs have reached it correctly, and once reason has also correctly understood the meaning and intent of these texts.

The Messenger's mission (ﷺ) addresses reason. It awakens reason, establishes for it a correct method of thought and vision, and places it on the right path. But this address does not mean that reason has the authority to issue a verdict on whether this mission is correct or false, or that it is able to do so, or that it has the power to accept or reject matters of the mission. Rather, this address means that when a matter is established by a text, that itself is the command of Allah, and it is the duty of human reason to accept it, obey it, and implement it on this earth, whether this meaning of the text is familiar and acceptable to its mind or strange and bizarre to it.

The role of human reason in this matter is only this: that it make a correct effort to understand the texts, and seek to determine what meaning the text bears according to the Arabic language and the technical terminology of the Shariah. Here the work of reason ends, and the correct meaning derived from the textual evidence of the Shariah cannot be rejected by any rational proof or analogy, because as far as the text is concerned, it is from Allah. A mere rational interpretation cannot be superior to the text, because reason does not have the status of God, nor does it have the status of accepting or rejecting the texts of Allah.

On this important point a great confusion arises in ideas. Some people grant human reason the status of God; they treat it as the judge even in their own affairs. And some do not permit reason the slightest intrusion into the fields of faith and guidance. The correct method is what we have explained above: that the Message has addressed reason so that it may strive to understand the decisions of the Message. The Message also lays down, for reason as well, a method regarding its practical and theoretical decisions, so that it too may function within its own sphere, and comprehend the decisions of the Message throughout the whole of life. When reason has understood the decisions of the Message, that is, what the texts of the Shariah and the Message mean, then for reason there remains no path other than attestation, obedience and implementation. The Shariah does not require that a person act upon the texts without understanding their meanings; rather, the aim of the Shariah is that the texts be acted upon with understanding. But when reason comprehends them, it becomes obligatory upon it to act accordingly and not to raise any hesitation or quibble. It must accept the matter according to the meanings of the texts. And to confront the texts with objection and hesitation would mean accepting some of them and rejecting others, declaring some correct and others wrong, despite knowing that these texts and this guidance have come from Allah. Allah speaks only what is true, and whatever command He gives, there is good in it.

In the Islamic system of life, the correct way to receive guidance from Allah is this: once the correct meaning of the texts of the Qur'an and Sunnah has been grasped, intellectual horses should not be galloped within them; this understanding should accord with the principles of understanding. A person should not study the Qur'an and Sunnah having already settled certain decisions in his mind, such as deriving certain logical conclusions in his religion, or settling certain matters on the basis of his limited observation, or accepting certain things as facts in accordance with his deficient experiences, and then strive to mould the Qur'an and Sunnah to match them. The correct methodology of study is to take the texts as they are, and the decisions the texts have made are, in any case, decisions, and they are better than his personal thinking, and their system and their methodology are stronger than his personal methodology. Therefore, reason cannot pass judgement upon the decisions of religion. When it becomes established to reason that this decision is of the religion, the decisions told by people cannot gain superiority over the principles of religion. Reason will in any case be subservient to these religious principles, on condition that the principles and standards of religion are clearly established and come forward.

Reason does not have the status of a god such that it may declare that the results it has derived are the decisions of Allah. Yes, human reason certainly has the right to present a meaning of a text according to human reason, in comparison with another meaning, which is itself also a rational meaning. This is the domain of human reason, and there is no restriction upon reason in it, nor is there any harm in it, on condition that this meaning and understanding of the texts is correct and within the bounds of the principles, the aim is the interpretation of texts and mutual understanding, and there is room for interpretation within the texts. This interpretation and explanation should also be within those rules and standards which religion itself has laid down for this purpose. These rules are such that they fulfil all the requirements of human freedom of thought and provide a vast field for human understanding and comprehension. In the Islamic system there is no such institution, no such collective restriction and no such official who has the authority to lock minds, so that people cannot reflect upon the Shari'ah texts, cannot give a good opinion regarding their application, or cannot present reasonable justifications, on condition that a Shari'ah text is capable of bearing these opinions, these interpretations and justifications, and these interpretations are also within the limits of the Islamic system and are based upon the principles of religion. This is the meaning of the statement that the Muhammadan message addresses reason.

Indeed, Islam is a rational religion. It presents its issues, beliefs and decisions before reason. Islam does not impose these decisions and beliefs upon people in a supernatural manner such that there remains no alternative but to accept them; rather, that rational religion, in the sense that it addresses reason and invites it to reflection, presents before it the proofs of guidance and the straight path, so that it may reflect upon those signposts found within its own self and in the horizons, and extract the original nature of man from beneath the thick layers of customs and traditions. Likewise, that reason should free itself from misleading desires and from influences that overwhelm reason and nature. The Qur'an addresses reason so that, after reflecting upon the matters which the Qur'an has settled in its texts, it may accept them, and it is not the Qur'an's manner to compel people to accept a matter without explaining it. Yes, when a person, by employing reason, grasps the meaning and implication of a text and comprehends the realities, then there is no alternative for him but to bow in submission. After understanding, if they accept, they are believers, and if they do not accept, they are disbelievers. As for the Qur'anic and Islamic decisions, they were made before being presented to reason. Reason does not have the authority to decide whether they are right or wrong, nor does reason have the authority to reject Islamic decisions after understanding and comprehension. Today some people grant reason the authority to reject Islamic decisions. For such people, their reason becomes their god. Now this god of theirs accepts whichever decisions of the Shari'ah it wishes and rejects whichever it wishes. It chooses whichever matters it wishes and leaves whichever it wishes. Regarding such people, Allah the Exalted has said:
(verse) "Afatu'minoona ba'da al-kitabi wa takfuroona ba'd" — Do you believe in some of the Book and disbelieve in some? This conduct is disbelief, and such people will be given a severe punishment in the Hereafter.

Now, whether Allah has made a decision concerning this universe, or concerning man, or concerning any other creature, or Allah has made a decision concerning the law of inheritance, or concerning obligations and prohibitions, all these decisions of Allah are worthy of acceptance, and for those to whom these decisions reach and who comprehend the implications of these decisions, it is obligatory for them to accept these decisions. For example, the saying of Allah:
(verse) "Allahu alladhee khalaqa sab'a samawatin wa min al-ardi mithlahunna" (65:12) — Allah is He who created seven heavens and of the earth the like of them.
(verse) "Wallahu khalaqa kulla dabbatin min ma'" (24:45) — and Allah created every moving creature from water.
(verse) "Khalaqa al-insana min salsalin ka al-fakhkhar" (14), "wa khalaqa al-janna min maarijin min nar" (15) (55:14–15) — He created man from clay like pottery, and He created the jinn from a smokeless flame of fire.

These and countless other verses of this kind relate to the nature of this universe and the reality of living and non-living things. Thus, whatever Allah has said is the truth. Now reason has no capacity to say that these matters are not within my decisions in this way, or that this matter does not fit within my understanding, or that this matter has not yet come within my experience. This is because the decisions reason has made in such matters may be correct and may also be wrong. But whatever Allah has said can only be correct, and there is no possibility of error in it. However, our understanding may err in comprehending the correct meaning of the texts, and this is the case when we do comprehend the correct meaning of the texts. Similarly, in other verses Allah says:
(verse) "Wa man lam yahkum bima anzala Allahu fa-ulaika humu al-kafiroon" (5:44) — Those who do not judge by what Allah has revealed are the disbelievers.
(verse) "Ya ayyuha alladhina amanu ittaqu Allaha wa dharu ma baqiya mina al-riba in kuntum mu'minin (278). Fa-in lam taf'alu fa-adhanu bi-harbin mina Allahi wa rasulihi, wa in tubtum fa-lakum ru'usu amwalikum, la tazlimuna wa la tuzlamun" (2:278–279) — O you who believe, fear Allah and leave what remains of interest owed to you by people, if you are truly believers. But if you do not do so, then be informed of a declaration of war from Allah and His Messenger. Yet if you repent, you are entitled to your principal; you shall not wrong and you shall not be wronged.
(verse) "Wa qarna fi buyutikunna wa la tabarrajna tabarruja al-jahiliyyati al-ula" (33:33) — Stay in your houses and do not display yourselves as in the former time of ignorance.
(verse) "Wa liyadribna bi-khumurihinna 'ala juyubihinna" (24:31) — and let them draw their head-coverings over their chests and not reveal their adornment.

These and other verses and guidance concerning human life are such that what Allah has said in them is the truth, and reason may not be permitted to say that according to reason such-and-such matters have greater benefit, which contradict Allah's decisions, or are matters which Allah has not permitted and has not made law for people. In a matter where reason sees benefit, there is possibility of both error and correctness, and the intrusion of momentary emotions and carnal desires is quite possible in it. Therefore, whatever decision Allah makes can only be correct, and there is no possibility of error in it.

Whatever the position of reason regarding the beliefs and concepts which Allah has enjoined, or the methodology and mode of conduct of life which He has prescribed, as long as the text is authentic, definitive in meaning, and not limited by any time, we cannot permit reason to say that as far as beliefs and ideologies are concerned we take them according to the texts, but as for the detailed system of life, the matter is that the age has changed greatly and become highly advanced. Therefore, if Allah had wished that the Shari'ah texts be effective only up to a particular time, Allah could have done so. As long as a text is absolute, it will be as effective in the final age as it was at the time of its revelation; otherwise it would necessarily follow that we would presume to hold Allah, who is free of every defect, responsible.

The question will arise: has the gate of ijtihad been closed? No. Ijtihad will consist in applying a text to a particular situation. It is not ijtihad that we make a change in a general principle or ruling, or reject it, or say something in one age or generation under any principle of reason.

Nothing in the above remarks that we have presented is such that it diminishes the importance of reason and intellect in human life, because there is a vast field of activity open to reason for applying Islamic texts and principles to the most modern and newest circumstances, provided reason comprehends well the Islamic viewpoint and Islamic standards, which are derived from the understanding of religion along correct lines. An even wider field is that of the natural principles of this universe, its forces and the treasures hidden within it. The nature of this universe, knowledge of the creatures living in it, the means of benefiting from these forces, and the means and causes of making life easier for living creatures in it are vast fields for reason, in which reason alone can work. Here man can be advanced, and the days and nights of his life can be changed while remaining within the limits of Allah. However, reason may not be permitted to place humanity's reins in the hands of whims, lusts, and pleasure and passion, where reason stumbles and nature is buried beneath the thick sediment of desires.

Pause here again and look once more at this verse: "Li-alla yakuna lil-nasi 'ala Allahi hujjatun ba'da al-rusul" (4:165) — so that after the messengers were sent, people would have no argument against Allah. From this verse we learn how great the responsibilities placed upon the shoulders of the prophets are, and how great the responsibilities placed upon those who believe in the prophethood of the prophets, in relation to all humanity. Indeed, these are great and heavy responsibilities.

All the people who inhabit this world, their destinies, in this world and the Hereafter, are linked to the messengers and the followers of the messengers. For instance, the messengers and their followers are responsible for conveying Allah's message to them, and it is through this conveyance that the good fortune and misfortune of people will be decided, and through this conveyance and invitation they will become deserving of reward and punishment, both in this world and in the Hereafter.

Indeed, this is a terrifying, frightening and great responsibility, but there is no other path. For this reason all the messengers (peace be upon them) had a keen sense of this great responsibility. Allah also informed them clearly of the burden that had been placed upon them. This is what Allah tells His Prophet:
(verse) "Inna sanulqi 'alayka qawlan thaqeelan" (73:5) — Indeed, We are going to send down upon you a weighty word.
And the preparation for it would be thus:
(verse) "Ya ayyuha al-muzzammil (1). Qumi al-layla illa qalilan (2). Nisfahu awi-nqus minhu qalilan (3). Aw zid 'alayhi wa rattili al-qur'ana tartilan (4). Inna sanulqi 'alayka qawlan thaqeelan (5)" (73:1–5) — O you who wrap yourself up, stand [in prayer] at night, but a little, half of it, or reduce it a little, or add to it, and recite the Qur'an with measured recitation. Indeed, We are going to send down upon you a weighty word.
(verse) "Inna nahnu nazzalna 'alayka al-qur'ana tanzeelan (23). Fa-isbir li-hukmi rabbika wa la tuti' minhum atheeman aw kafooran (24). Wa udhkuri isma rabbika bukratan wa asila (25). Wa min al-layli fa-usjud lahu wa sabbihhu layla tawila (26)" (76:23–26) — Indeed, We have sent down to you the Qur'an in stages. So be patient for the decision of your Lord, and do not obey from among them any sinner or disbeliever. And mention the name of your Lord morning and evening. And during the night prostrate to Him and exalt Him through the long night.

This is the matter which Allah makes the Prophet aware of, and orders him to say it, and to understand well what its reality and significance is.
(verse) "Qul inni lan yujirani min Allahi ahadun wa lan ajida min dunihi multahada (22)" (72:22) — Say: No one can protect me from Allah, nor shall I find any refuge other than Him. My duty is only to convey the messages of Allah and His communications.
(verse) "'Alimu al-ghaybi fa-la yuzhiru 'ala ghaybihi ahada (26). Illa man irtada min rasulin fa-innahu yaslukuhu min bayni yadayhi wa min khalfihi rasada (27). Li-ya'lama an qad ablaghu risalati rabbihim wa ahata bi-ma ladayhim wa ahsa kulla shay'in 'adada (28)" (72:26–28).

"He is the Knower of the unseen, and He does not disclose His unseen to anyone, except to a Messenger whom He has chosen. Then He sets guards before him and behind him, so that He may know that they have conveyed the messages of their Lord; and He encompasses all that is with them, and He has counted everything in number."

Indeed this is a fearful and great duty. It is a matter of the life and death of people, of their happiness and misery, of their reward and punishment. It is the matter of the final destiny of all humanity. The summary of this duty is that this message will either be conveyed to people so that they accept it and follow it, as a result of which they will attain success in this world and the Hereafter; or the message will reach them and they will cast it far away, and will be struck by misery in both this world and the Hereafter; or the message will not reach them, and the result will be that people will have a proof against their Lord in hand, and the responsibility for this worldly misery of these people and for their misguidance will rest upon those who are responsible for conveying God's message to them in this world and who do not fulfil this responsibility.

As for the Messengers of God, they fully discharged their responsibility. They conveyed God's message and trust to people. They went to their Lord in the state of having fully fulfilled their responsibilities. They did not fulfil these responsibilities merely to the extent of verbal preaching, but they gave practical form to God's message in their own lives, showing it to people, and day and night they strove in the way of God, removing the difficulties and obstacles that stood in the path of this message. Whether these difficulties took the form of doubts that troubled people's minds, or of misguidance that was imposed upon people, or of satanic forces that prevented people from giving ear to this call and that were a trial for their religion, they removed them. The Seal of the Prophets ﷺ demonstrated the complete implementation of Islam in his practical life, because he was the final preacher. His Messengership was the conclusion of all messengerships, so he did not suffice with mere verbal preaching. He removed these difficulties and obstacles also by the force of the sword and power: "So that there is no more fitnah and religion is entirely for Allah" (2:193). Now this heavy responsibility falls, after him, upon those who believe in his Messengership. Ages have passed, generations upon generations have passed and will continue to pass. After the Messenger ﷺ, the work of preaching has come into the responsibility of his followers, and for them there is no way to be absolved of this difficult and heavy responsibility. They must establish the proof against people. They must save people from the misery of the world and the failure of the Hereafter. This duty and this responsibility can only be discharged through preaching, and it can only be discharged on the same method upon which the Messenger of God ﷺ discharged it, because the Messengership is the same, and the believers are the same. The misguidances, the desires of the soul, the doubts and objections are also the same; those satanic forces too exist in the same way, obstructing the arrival of the Islamic call to people. These forces are casting Muslims into trial regarding their religion and misguiding them by force. The position is the same as it was, the difficulties are the same as they were, and the people are the same as they were.

The Islamic call is a duty from which we cannot turn away or deny. Therefore it is necessary that we preach; it is very necessary that we discharge this duty. Preach through writing and speech; preach through your conduct, so that preachers, through their action and character, become a walking preaching; and strive to remove the obstacles that stand in the way of preaching and the call, for this too is a form of preaching. Free those who are caught in trial. If this work is not done, there will be no preaching, the duty will not be discharged, and God's proof will not be completed upon people.

There is no alternative to undertaking these responsibilities, otherwise its heavy consequences will appear. The whole world will be afflicted with misguidance; it will be struck by misery in this world, and in the Hereafter there will be no proof against it before God, and the proof will be in their hands. If the ummah does not discharge this responsibility, people will not be saved because of it.

Who will consider this burden light? It is a back-breaking burden; every joint and every limb of the body trembles under it. Whoever claims to be a "Muslim" will either discharge this duty and carry out the work of calling to the religion, or else for him success is not possible in this world or the Hereafter. When he claims that he is a Muslim, and then does not carry out the work of calling to religion and does not fulfil his duty, according to all the methods that call to it and that are prescribed for the discharge of duty, then he is in effect bearing witness against the Islam he has claimed. His testimony is not in favour of Islam but against it, although he has been raised up so that he may bear witness for Islam.

"And thus We have made you a middle nation, that you may be witnesses over mankind, and the Messenger may be a witness over you" (2:143). (For details, see the book Shahadat-e-Haq by Maulana Sayyid Abul A'la Maududi.)

The beginning of the witness of truth and of testimony for Islam will be this: a Muslim himself, then his home and family, then his people and relatives, should be a practical model of the religion to which he is inviting the world. After this, let his witness advance one more step, so that a community is produced that can be called the community of the call (ummat-e-da'wah). After presenting Islam and the Islamic call in practical form within the bounds of his home, family and kinship, he should also take up responsibility for establishing this call in personal affairs and in the political affairs of the country. After that, he should bear such witness that he removes the obstacles that stand in the way of Islam, that misguide people and cast them into trial regarding this call, whatever kind of obstacles they may be. If any Muslim has given testimony in this sense, then he will truly be a witness and also a martyr (shahid). Having borne witness, he will reach his Lord. This is the true martyr.

Last of all, we stand with folded hands before God, in His court of majesty and grandeur. This court is a court of justice and is based upon profound knowledge. In this court, the grace and mercy of God cast their shade, and in it everyone is dealt with kindness and favour, and all this happens to that human being who sometimes comes in the form of one who denies the truth and sometimes commits gross disobedience.

We see that God Almighty has adorned the human being with the ornament of knowledge and has placed within his being immense powers. In his being He has created the capacity for both guidance and misguidance. What results come about if this knowledge is not made subservient to reason? Furthermore, God has given man a great weapon of knowledge, and that in man's self and in his horizons there are countless proofs for guidance and the acceptance of faith. God knew that against the great weapon of knowledge that man possesses, there also exists in man the force of lust and animality, and it is quite possible that the numerous proofs and signs found within the self and the horizons may be overpowered by man's base desires, and his shortcomings and ignorance may hide them from his sight. It will be possible for man to reflect upon these proofs only when Messengers are sent to him and he is repeatedly reminded. Likewise, even after the explanation of guidance, God did not place upon man the burden of devising for himself a system of life, but made a system of life and made it his duty to establish that system in the world. Then He left him free in this world again. Even after these limits and bounds, a wide sphere of action remained for him in this great kingdom. He was permitted to make whatever new inventions he wishes in it, to bring about whatever changes he wishes, to make whatever combinations he wishes, and to benefit fully from the way God has subjected this whole universe for man. In this, man will sometimes make right decisions and sometimes wrong ones; sometimes he will slip and sometimes he will walk firmly upon the straight path.

It is also worth reflecting here upon the importance of justice with God, which is expressed in this verse. If Messengers had not been sent, people would have had a proof against God. But God sent Messengers who gave glad tidings to people and warned them of the evil end, although in this universe there were cosmic proofs for faith in the existence of God, and this universe lay open before all like a book unfolded. Moreover, the human soul too was present before man as an open book, within which there were countless proofs for the existence of the Creator.

Through these, the unity of God could be well known; through these, one could well learn about God's decree, God's governance, God's power and His knowledge. Furthermore, within human nature there exists a strong and true inclination, through which man receives a very firm longing to reach the Creator of this universe, and he becomes certain that there must be a Creator. Then there exists a kind of harmony between this nature and the cosmic proofs. These proofs show that there exists a Creator and Manager of this universe. Then God gave man intellect, which has the capacity to draw conclusions through observation. But God well knew that all these powers of man come under weakness. Sometimes these powers become inoperative; sometimes influences corrupt these powers. Sometimes these intellectual faculties are obliterated; sometimes an error occurs in the judgements of reason and reason becomes confused. Therefore God excused people from this duty, that they should seek the path of guidance only from the proofs and signs of this universe, or attain the path of truth merely through natural proofs by the strength of their intellect, until a Messenger comes to them, so that this Messengership may purify all these excellences and powers of man from all these impurities, and bring these intellectual faculties within those regulations which God's Messengers have brought. When all these natural powers of man are regulated within the Islamic method of thought, then the only task left for these powers is to decide that they should acknowledge this Messengership, serve God, and follow the Messenger. Or if they reject it, then the proof is completed against them and they become liable to punishment on the Day of Judgement.

Then we learn how merciful God is toward His servants, how much He takes care of them, how He bestows upon them from His grace and generosity, and how much He honours and empowers them. Despite knowing that man is a figure of error and deficiency, God nonetheless entrusts this world to him. He makes him a khalifah on the earth. Yet this universe is very vast in comparison to him, and God is so self-sufficient that if even an atom exists in His great universe, it cannot be lost.
